parties.name: Freedom Party of Austria
parties.description:
Right-wing populist party, formed in 1955-1956 as successor of [[atVdU|Federation of Independents]], representing pan-Germanists and national liberals opposed to socialism and Catholic clericalism, represented by the [[atSPO|Social Democratic Party of Austria]] (SPÖ) and the [[atOVP|Austrian People's Party]] (ÖVP), respectively. Its first leader, Anton Reinthaller, was a former Nazi functionary and SS officer, but the FPÖ did not advocate far-right policies and presented itself as a centrist party. The FPÖ was long the third largest in Austria and had modest support. Under the leadership of Norbert Steger in the early 1980s, it sought to style itself on Germany's [[deFDP|Free Democratic Party]] (FDP) The FPÖ gave external support to SPÖ chancellor Bruno Kreisky (SPÖ) after the 1970 election and joined Fred Sinowatz's government, as the SPÖ's junior partner, after the 1983 election.
 
 Jörg Haider became leader of the party in 1986, after which it began an ideological turn towards right-wing populism. This resulted in a strong surge in electoral support, but also led the SPÖ to break ties, and a splinter in the form of the [[atLiF|Liberal Forum]] in 1993. In the 1999 election, the FPÖ won 26.9% of the vote, becoming the second-most popular party, ahead of the ÖVP by around 500 votes. The two parties eventually reached a coalition agreement in which the ÖVP retained the office of chancellor. The FPÖ soon lost most of its popularity, falling to 10% in the 2002 election, but remained in government as junior partner. Internal tensions led Haider and much of the party leadership to leave in 2005, forming the [[atBZO|Alliance for the Future of Austria]] (BZÖ), which replaced the FPÖ as governing partner. Heinz-Christian Strache then became leader, and the party gradually regained its popularity, peaking at 26.0% in the 2017 election. The FPÖ once again became junior partner in government with the ÖVP. In May 2019, the Ibiza affair led to the collapse of the government and the resignation of Strache from both the offices of vice-chancellor and party leader. The resulting snap election saw the FPÖ fall to 16.2% and return to opposition. On 30 June 2024, ANO 2011, the Freedom Party of Austria, and [[huFidesz|Fidesz]] created a new alliance named [[euPfE|Patriots for Europe]].

parties.name: People's Union
parties.description:
Big tent flemish nationalist party, preceded by the electoral alliance [[beCVV|Christian Flemish People's Union]] (CVV).

On 13 October 2001 the party openly split into three factions: the progressive wing around Bert Anciaux, the conservative nationalist wing around Geert Bourgeois, and a centrist group opposing the imminent split. An internal referendum was held on the future of the party.

The right wing won a large plurality at a party referendum, with 47 percent. However, while it inherited VU's structure, it did not take the VU name due to falling short of a majority and not being allowed to use the party name under Belgian electoral law. Instead, it reconstituted itself as a new party, and re-registered itself as the [[beNVA|New Flemish Alliance]] (N-VA). 

The left wing under Anciaux broke off and became [[beSLP|Spirit]], while the liberal members joined the [[beAnders|Flemish Liberals and Democrats]] (VLD). The two parties proceeded to form new electoral alliances, known in Belgium as cartels, with the N-VA allying with [[be        CD&V|Christian Democratic and Flemish]] and Spirit with the [[beVooruit|Socialist Party – Different]] (sp.a). These cartels broke up in 2008 as the parties continued their decline, until the N-VA experienced a sudden resurgence in 2009, eventually becoming the largest party in Flanders and going on to participate as a coalition partner in the Belgian government, while Spirit ceased to exist, merging with [[beGroen|Groen]].

parties.name: Vlaams Blok
parties.description:
The party originated from split within the [[beVU|Volksunie]] (VU) party after the right-wing separatist and national conservative wing became disgruntled with the compromise of accepting Belgian federalism over Flemish interests, and what they saw as the VU's move to the left. 

The former VU members created the [[beVNP|Flemish National Party]] (VNP) and the [[beVVP|Flemish People's Party]] (VVP) which formed an electoral alliance called Vlaams Blok in 1978, before merging to create Vlaams Blok as a political party in 1979. 

Vlaams Blok was the most notable militant right wing of the Flemish movement and its track record in the Flemish and Belgian parliament elections was strong, making it one of the most successful nationalist parties in Western Europe and it ultimately surpassed the People's Union in support. 

The party initially focused solely on the issues of Flemish autonomy and political freedom, which remained its core philosophy, but subsequently gained wider public support through broadening its campaigns to include immigration and law-and-order themes.

Following a 1989 agreement, known as the cordon sanitaire, the party was effectively blocked from entering any level of government. 

The court of appeal in Ghent in April 2004 ruled that some of the party's organizations had breached the 1981 anti-racism law and that the party sanctioned discrimination. The ruling was made definite on 9 November 2004, and the party shortly after reorganised itself as the [[beVB|Vlaams Belang]]. By 2004, the party had arguably become the single most popular Flemish party in Belgium, supported by about one in four of the Flemish electorate, as well as being one of the most successful radical right-wing populist parties in Europe as a whole.

parties.name: Agrarian Union "Aleksandar Stamboliyski"
parties.nativeName:
Земеделски съюз „Александър Стамболийски“
Zemedelski sŭyuz „Aleksandŭr Stamboliĭski“
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[bgBZNSe|Bulgarian Agrarian National Union-United]] (BZNS-E)
parties.description:
The Bulgarian Agrarian National Union "Alexander Stamboliyski" was formed in 1993 after separating from the Bulgarian Agrarian National Union. Its leader until 2005 was Svetoslav Shivarov.

At the congress on 12 February 2005, Spas Panchev was elected chairman of the Union. The Bulgarian Agrarian National Union "Alexander Stamboliyski" participated in the 2005 parliamentary election as part of the [[bgBSPOL|Coalition for Bulgaria]]. Its chairman Spas Panchev is the Deputy Minister of Defense, and the head of the cabinet of the Minister of Transport is the deputy chairman and member of the Permanent Presence of the "Al. Stamboliyski" Union.

According to the latest requirements of the Law on Political Parties of the Congress of the Union in December 2005, the BZNS "Alexander Stamboliyski" was renamed, and since February 2006 it has been officially registered in court as the Agrarian Union "Aleksandar Stamboliyski".

In 2009, the "Alexander Stamboliyski" Union participated in the elections for the XLI National Assembly, with chairman Spas Panchev being second on the list of the [[bgBSPOL|Coalition for Bulgaria]], for the 27th MIR-Stara Zagora. He was elected as a member of the people's representative in the XLI National Assembly, a member of the standing committees on agriculture and forestry and foreign policy and defense.

In 2023-2024 was part of [[bgLevitsata|The Left!]] coalition.

The party was created in the winter of 2020–2021 by several progressive deputies of the National Assembly of Bulgaria who split from the [[bgBSP|Bulgarian Socialist Party]]. 

The BPL participated in the April 2021 Bulgarian parliamentary election but did not meet the electoral threshold. The party had 3,751 votes (0.15%).

In July 2021, the party entered the [[bgLSChSR|Left Union for a Clean and Holy Republic]] coalition with the [[bgPBK|Party of the Bulgarian Communists]], the [[bgLA|Left Alternative]], the [[bgSPBP|Socialist Party "Bulgarian Way"]], and the [[bgVO|Revival of the Fatherland]].

Prior to the 2023 Bulgarian parliamentary election, the party was registered as part of the [[bgLevitsata|Levitsata!]] coalition.[6]

In the June 2024 Bulgarian parliamentary election, the parties nominal leader, Krasimir Yankov, ran as part of [[bgBV|Bulgarian Rise]].

parties.relations:
Preceded by the [[bgBKP|Bulgarian Communist Party]] (BKP);
Since 1991, it leads the [[bgBSPOL|BSP – United Left]] coalition.
parties.ideology:
Founded as the legal successor to the [[bgBKP|Bulgarian Communist Party]], the BSP describes itself as a democratic socialist party, espousing socialist policies and values, while supporting a social market economy. It has also been described as a populist and social-democratic party. The party's policies have oscillated during its existence from a customary understanding of socialism during the Videnov era, to a more social-liberal worldview under Stanishev, to a socially conservative strain of socialism under Ninova.

Like most [[euPES|Party of European Socialists]] (PES) member parties, the BSP has a pro-European stance, although it has taken some Eurosceptic positions and called for an end to sanctions against Russia. Some news outlets, such as Novinite, The Wall Street Journal, and The Washington Post, have described its orientation as soft Russophilia.

In recent times under the leadership of Korneliya Ninova and unlike the majority of PES parties, the BSP has been described as more conservative on social issues, and like European Union politics it is more divided, with some leaders, such as Ninova, opposing same-sex marriage in Bulgaria. Many party leaders opposed the Istanbul Convention because they were against educating children about sexuality if it also meant same-sex relationships, and after a long debate decided to vote against it, despite internal division about it. Former BSP leader and then-PES head Sergey Stanishev strongly supported the Istanbul Convention. Under Ninova's leadership, BSP additionally shifted to a more nationalist position.

parties.name: George's Day Movement
parties.description:
The party was founded in December 1996 by members of the political satire television programme Canaletto. Members of the show, which succeeded Ku-Ku in the mid-1990s, participated in the 1997 Bulgarian protests, and had previously tried to create a party named the [[bgKuKu|Ku-Ku People’s Movement]] in 1994, but the registration was denied by the Supreme Court of Cassation of Bulgaria, with tacit support from the two major political parties at the time, the [[bgSDS|Union of Democratic Forces]] and the [[bgBSP|Bulgarian Socialist Party]].  The founder of the party, Lyuben Dilov Jr. estimated that had it run in the 1997 parliamentary election, the party could have earned roughly 10% of the vote and over 30 seats in the parliament. Ultimately, it opted to instead focus on the local elections held in 1999, until which time it de facto operated as a union of clubs alongside the Civil Society Against Corruption Association. Future [[bgITN|There is Such a People]] founder Slavi Trifonov was a supporter of the party during this time and a member of the television program Ku-Ku and its successor.

It joined the [[bgSDS|United Democratic Forces]] before the 2005 elections. 

Since 2013, Assoc. Prof. Dragomir Stefanov has held the position of chairman. Lyuben Dilov Jr. was elected honorary chairman for life. The George's Day Movement also established a Youth George's Day Movement (MDG) in 2015. Dr. Daniel Parushev was elected as the leader of the youth, and he headed the MDG until 2017.

The party participated in an [[bgGERBSDS|electoral coalition]] with [[bgGERB]] and the Union of Democratic Forces since elections in 2021.

Lyuben Dilov Jr. died on 2 June 2026.

parties.relations: Split from the [[bgZP|Green Party]] (ZP).
parties.description:
The logo was drawn based on the party statute and may differ from the actual one, which is not published anywhere.

ZS emerged from the confused aftermath of the 2009 split in [[bgZP|Green Party–Bulgarian Greens]]. Rival congresses led by Alexander Karakachanov and Trifon Grudev each claimed legitimacy over the older party. Karakachanov then founded the legally separate Left Greens in June 2010. The new organisation was subsequently renamed "Green Party", functioning as a parallel vehicle during the dispute over the older ZP's leadership and name. It finally became "Green Union" in 2013.

In the October 2024 parliamentary elections, the party participated in the [[bgSI|Free Voters]] coalition together with the [[bgRzB|Republicans for Bulgaria]] (RB) and [[bgSSD|Union of Free Democrats]] (SSD).

parties.description:
In May, 2021, former Bulgarian Prime Minister, Zhan Videnov, announced his intention to form a new party called "Left Alternative", justifying his decision by the poor electoral results of the [[bgBSP|Bulgarian Socialist Party]]. The party announced its intention to participate in a broad left-wing coalition during the upcoming parliamentary elections.


On the 23d of May, Videnov presented the alliance, composed of the following parties: [[bgBPL|Bulgarian Progressive Line]], the Left Alternative, the [[bgPBK|Party of the Bulgarian Communists]], the [[bgSPBP|Socialist Party "Bulgarian Way"]], and the more conservative [[bgRVO|Revival of the Fatherland]]. Former BSP MP and Videnov ally, Ivan Atanasov, was selected as the alliance's leader, while Videnov assumed the role of organisational secretary.

parties.nativeName:

Dvizhenie za prava i svobodi – Novo nachalo
parties.relations:
One of two factions during the 2024-2025 crisis in the [[bgDPS|Movement for Rights and Freedoms]] (DPS).

Coalition members (Oct 2024 election):
- [[bgDPS]]-Peevski faction (legally recognized),
- [[bgBG|Bulgarian Voice]],
- [[bgNL|New Leaders]].
parties.description:
The coalition was set up in response to the removal of Peevski as co-leader of the [[bgDPS]], ahead of the October 2024 Bulgarian parliamentary election. Its registration was submitted electronically early in the morning on 2 September, in order to be approved before the [[bgAPS|Alliance for Rights and Freedoms]], the competing DPS faction. This move was unprecedented, and the electoral commission decided to allow both electoral coalitions to run with the same abbreviation. 

On 11 September, the SAC ruled that DPS was part of DPS-NN, because their registration had been submitted first. Peevski's removal from party leadership was later overturned by the Sofia City Court.

Despite the original DPS being listed as part of both electoral coalitions, the Commission decided on 4 September that both had to prove the original party was not part of either group, something neither wing agreed to do by the 7 September deadline. Because it was technically registered first online, the Supreme Administrative Court of Bulgaria accepted the application filed by DPS–Peevski and as such the official DPS was part of DPS–Peevski

Following the split in the DPS, its elected mayors split roughly evenly between Peevski and Dogan's factions. In April 2025, Peevski launched a campaign to attract elected mayors to join his faction, targeting municipalities which had remained loyal to Dogan. According to research by Deutsche Welle, by 1 May 2025, DPS-NN had 34 mayors. By 17 June, all mayors in the Kardzhali Province were aligned with DPS–NN.

In early 2026, DPS under the leadership of Peevski registered on their own ahead of the upcoming election.

parties.description:
The statute of the political party was adopted at a constituent assembly on 22 March 2003, and was supplemented a month later. The party's governing bodies are: congress, central council, executive committee, central control and audit commission.

In the 2005 parliamentary elections, the party participated in the composition of the Attack Coalition, which won 8.14% of the votes (296,848 votes) and 21 deputies.

On June 7, 2009, the new chairman of the party, Todor Rashev, submitted an application for participation in the parliamentary elections, which was supported by the signatures of 17,130 voters. In the elections held on July 5 of the same year, the party won 0.04% of the votes (1,784 votes)

In August 2014, it joined the [[bgPF2014|Patriotic Front]] coalition.

In June 2024 parliamentary election, NDSO participated inside [[bgLevitsata|The Left!]] coalition.

parties.name: New Dawn
parties.description:
The party has a newspaper, the weekly Nova Zora. 

In May 2009, the party was inspected by the State Agency for National Security (DANS) following a complaint by the GERB party regarding the financing of the incriminating videos directed against Boyko Borisov, with suspicion that their campaign was financed by the [[bgBSP|BSP]]. In 2009, it joined the Coalition for Bulgaria and had one representative in the XLII National Assembly (2013–2014), who supported the ruling coalition of the BSP and the [[bgDPS]]. It has no representative in subsequent national assemblies. Currently, the party is practically inactive, and its website is closed.

In the 2005 elections, it was part of the [[bgNOAtaka|National Alliance "Attack"]], but was expelled from it due to attempts to get it to support the coalition between the BSP and the [[bgDPS]]. It participated in the elections in 2009, 2013, 2014 and 2017 as part of the [[bgBSPOL|Coalition for Bulgaria]] and [[bgBSPOL|BSP-Left Bulgaria]], dominated by the BSP. It does not have a single independently elected mayor or municipal councilor.

parties.relations: Split from the [[bgDPS|Movement for Rights and Freedoms]] (DPS).
parties.description:
The party was founded on 1 December 2012 at the National Palace of Culture, where over 1,000 people gathered. Among the founders were Kasim Dal and Korman Ismailov, who left the ranks of the [[bgDPS]] in early 2011. Among the guests at the founding meeting were delegations from Turkey, the Republic of North Macedonia, Kosovo and Montenegro. The founding meeting was also attended by the Minister of Culture Vezhdi Rashidov, who stated that he was invited as a personal friend of Kasim Dahl. Upon its establishment, the party received congratulations from the chairman of the [[bgSDS]] Emil Kabaivanov, the leader of the [[bgNDSV]] Hristina Hristova and Petya Stavreva from the [[bgOZ|United Agrarians]].

In the 2013 parliamentary election, NPSD and the [[bgNDSV|National Movement for Stability and Progress]] (NDSV) participated in a coalition under the name "Center – Freedom and Dignity". Coalition received 57,611 votes, or 1.62%.

In the 2014 parliamentary elections, the NPSD was part of the [[bgRB|Reformist Bloc]] (RB). The coalition received 291,806 votes, or 8.89%. Korman Ismailov became a member of the National Assembly from the NPSD.

At the first regular congress of the party, held on 27 November 2016, Orkhan Ismailov was elected chairman.

parties.relations:
Preceded by the [[bgSiK|Blue Coalition]] (SK);

Coalition members: 
- [[bgSDS|Union of Democratic Forces]] (SDS),

- [[bgBDF|Bulgarian Democratic Forum]] (BDF),
- [[bgZNS|Agrarian People's Union]] (ZNS),
- [[bgGN|People's Voice]] (GN) - 2017-2018,
- [[bgDSB|Democrats for a Strong Bulgaria]] (DSB) - left in the end of 2016, 
- [[bgNPSD|People's Party "Freedom and Dignity"]] (NPSD) - left in February 2017,
- [[bgBZNS2008|Bulgarian Agrarian National Union]] (BZNS) - left until 2017,
- [[bgDBG|Bulgaria for Citizens Movement]] (DBG) - left,
- [[bgKhDP|Christian Democratic Party of Bulgaria]] (KhDP) - left.

Partially succeeded by the [[bgDB|Democratic Bulgaria (DB).
parties.description:
The coalition agreement to form the alliance was signed on 20 December 2013. The five parties that signed the agreement were: [[bgDSB|Democrats for a Strong Bulgaria]], [[bgDBG|Bulgaria for Citizens Movement]], [[bgSDS|Union of Democratic Forces]], [[bgNPSD|People's Party "Freedom and Dignity"]], and the [[bgBZNS2008|Bulgarian Agrarian National Union]]. At the time of signing the coalition the parties had one seat in the European Parliament but none in the National Assembly.

In early August 2014 spokesperson Radan Kanev resigned because of what he said was a lack of unity within the alliance: "The image of a united multi-party coalition was replaced by an image of a traditional coalition with many and often conflicting interests."

RB initially supported the government, led by Prime Minister Boyko Borisov. Politicians from the Reformist Bloc received ministerial posts as coalition partners.

In December 2015,[[bgDSB|Democrats for a Strong Bulgaria]] turned into opposition because of the discontent with the speed and depth of the judicial reform by the second government of Boyko Borisov. Minister Petar Moskov retained his post but was excluded from his DSB leadership. This event marked a new flaw in the Reformist Bloc. The other coalition partners remained in the government. The Parliamentary Group of the Reformist Bloc does not split up. At the end of 2016 DSB left the block. In February 2017, the [[bgNPSD|People's Party "Freedom and Dignity"]] left to join Lutvi Mestan's [[bgDOST|DOST]].
parties.ideology: Christian democratic and conservative parties were represented in the Bloc.

parties.name: Resistance
parties.description:
On 1 December 2013, the Association of Bulgarian Pensioners, Bulgarian Criminal Detachment, Association of Argoecological Producers and others met to establish the Bulgarian National Unification (BNO) party with Georgi Georgiev as chairman.

On 20 March 2014, BNO was officially registered by the court.

BNO participated in several elections, but received more media attention in 2016, when it nominated Mityo Pishtova for presidential candidate. In 2019, Evgenia Baneva was nominated as an MEP, but soon after they withdrew their support for her.

In February 2021, BNO became a mandate holder and submitted its lists for the parliamentary elections in April to the [[bgGPBL|Civil Platform "Bulgarian Summer"]], which was established by businessman Vasil Bozhkov.

Prior to the October 2024 parliamentary elections, the party renamed itself to the name "Bulgars". 

The party was once again renamed to "Resistance" prior to the 2026 Bulgarian parliamentary election.
parties.ideology: The party describes itself as center-left and patriotic. BNO states that it will fight for a complete revision of the status quo, raising the standard of living by stimulating the economy and offering better conditions for small and medium-sized businesses.

parties.description:
In March 2025, 12-year-old Siyana Popova died in a car crash in a collision with a truck in the Pleven region of Bulgaria. Her father, Nikolay Popov, said that many reports had been submitted about the poor condition of the road prior to the death of his daughter. The incident led to protests across the country on the condition of the roads.

Following the incident, Popov campaigned on corruption in the country and particularly the court system. As a part of this movement, he garnered 22,000 signatures on a petition calling for the Supreme Court of Cassation president Galina Kakharova to resign due to corruption.[2] He formed a movement named after his daughter in February 2026.

In March 2026, Popov announced that his movement would be taking part in the 2026 Bulgarian parliamentary election, forming a civic electoral list. To run in the election, they allied with two smaller parties: [[bgVolt|Volt Bulgaria]] and [[bgONB|Society for a New Bulgaria]].

parties.name: Union of Communists in Bulgaria
parties.nativeName:
Съюз на комунистите в България
Sŭyuz na komunistite v Bŭlgariya
parties.description:
A communist party in Bulgaria, registered in 1995. It has participated in all elections since then, alone or in coalition.

In 2011, the party tried to claim ownership over the Buzludzha monument.

On 23 June 2013, the Central Committee of the SKB accepted the resignation of its then presiding chairman Kostadin Chakarov (2010–2013), a former adviser to Todor Zhivkov, and elected by an overwhelming majority Pavel Ivanov as the new chairman of the party.

In the 2013 parliamentary election the party received 6,168 votes (0.17% of the popular vote), remaining outside parliament.
parties.ideology: The Union of Communists takes its name from Union of German and European Communists, established in the 19th century by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. It unites citizens and adopts Marxism as its political creed. The Union of Communists in Bulgaria considers itself the conceptual and political heir of [[bgBKP|Bulgarian Communist Party]].

parties.name: African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde
parties.nativeName: Partido Africano da Independência de Cabo Verde
parties.relations: Split from the [[gwPAIGC|African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde]].
parties.description:
In 1956, its forerunner, the [[gwPAIGC|African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde]] (PAIGC), was founded by the Cape Verdean nationalist leader Amílcar Cabral (born in Guinea-Bissau). PAIGC fought to overthrow the Portuguese Empire, unify Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau, and use its vanguardism to advance socialist revolution.

From 1961 on, the PAIGC fought a guerrilla warfare campaign in cooperation with its fraternal party umbrella group, the [[intCONCP|CONCP]], during the Portuguese Colonial War. By 1973 the PAIGC controlled Guinea-Bissau, while Portugal's own Carnation Revolution in 1974 effectively dissolved the empire, relinquishing Cape Verde within the next year.

After the wars of national liberation, the PAIGC established a socialist state within both territories under Amilcar Cabral's brother, Luís Cabral.

Following a military coup in Guinea-Bissau that ousted Cabral in November 1980, the Cape Verde portion of the party became the PAICV in January 1981; it was headed by the President of Cape Verde, Aristides Pereira. The PAICV was Cape Verde's sole legal party from 1981 until the abolition of the one-party state in 1990.

At an extraordinary party congress in February 1990, the PAICV approved the introduction of multiparty democracy. Pereira stepped down as General Secretary of PAICV in July 1990, and Prime Minister Pedro Pires replaced him in August 1990. The PAICV won 23 of the 79 National Assembly seats in the January 1991 multiparty parliamentary election, losing to the [[cvMpD|Movement for Democracy]] (MpD). Pereira was subsequently defeated in the February 1991 presidential election, and PAICV again fared poorly in the December 1991 local elections. At a party congress in August 1993, Pires was replaced as General Secretary by Aristides Lima and was instead elected as President of PAICV.

The PAICV won 21 out of 72 National Assembly seats in the December 1995 parliamentary election. At a PAICV congress in September 1997, Pires faced José Maria Neves in a leadership contest, and Pires was elected with 68% of the vote. Pires stepped down as PAICV President in 2000 in preparation for a presidential bid in the next year's election and he was succeeded by Neves.

In the presidential election held on 11 and 25 February 2001, PAICV candidate Pedro Pires, who won 46.52% of the vote in the first round, narrowly defeated the MpD's Carlos Veiga by a margin of only 12 votes in the run-off.

In the parliamentary election held on 22 January 2006, PAICV won 52.28% of the popular vote and 41 out of 72 seats in the National Assembly.

In the presidential election held on 12 February 2006, Pedro Pires again narrowly defeated Carlos Veiga, winning 50.98% of the vote.

In the parliamentary election held on 7 February 2011, the PAICV led by Jose Maria Neves won 52.68% of the popular vote and 38 out of 72 seats in the National Assembly.

In the presidential election held on 7 and 21 August 2011, Manuel Inocêncio Sousa lost to Jorge Carlos Fonseca (MpD) with 32.66% of the votes in the first round and 45.74% in the second round.

PAICV lost 2016 presidential elections and president Jorge Carlos Fonseca was re-elected with very clear majority of the votes. PAICV even failed to forward a candidate. Before that PAICV had lost the 2016 parliamentary election. The main opposition party [[cvMpD|Movement for Democracy]] (MpD) won the parliamentary elections, taking back power after 15 years.

As a result of the 2026 Cape Verdean parliamentary election, PAICV returned to power after 10 years of being the opposition.
parties.ideology:
The PAICV describes itself as democratic socialist, but began to trend towards social democracy in the 2010s. The party has been placed as left-wing on the political spectrum.

The party is a full member of the Socialist International.

parties.description:
A center-right political coalition established in Cape Verde in the early 2000s and led by Eurico Monteiro, António Delgado Monteiro, and Onésimo Silveira.

The ADM was established in late 2000 for the January 2001 parliamentary elections. It was an alliance between the [[cvPCD|Democratic Convergence Party]], the [[cvUCID|Democratic and Independent Cape Verdean Union]], and the [[cvPTS|Labour and Solidarity Party]]. The Alliance received 6% of the vote, winning only two seats in the National Assembly. 

Its presidential candidate in the 2001 elections was Jorge Carlos Fonseca. In the 2001 presidential elections, its candidate, Jorge Carlos Fonseca, received almost 4% of the vote, finishing third behind Pedro Pires and Carlos Veiga.

The Alliance split before the 2006 parliamentary elections, and the Democratic Convergence Party did not participate in them.

parties.name: Democratic and Independent Cape Verdean Union
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[cvUDCV|Democratic Union of Cape Verde]] (UDCV).
parties.description:
The party had its roots in the [[cvUDCV|Democratic Union of Cape Verde]] (UDCV), a group that emerged from the Juridicial Congress of Cape Verde on 23 February 1975.[4] However, the UDCV was excluded from negotiations on independence with the Portuguese government.

The Democratic and Independent Cape Verdean Union was formally established in Lisbon, Portugal in 1981 by a group of centre-right Cape Verdean exiles. When multi-party politics was introduced at the start of the 1990s, the party did not contest the 1991 parliamentary elections after failing to file its application papers in time. In internal elections in 1993, Celso Celestino was elected as the party's new leader.

In the 1995 parliamentary elections, the party received just 2,369 votes (1.5%), failing to win a seat. It supported incumbent President António Mascarenhas Monteiro of the [[cvMpD|Movement for Democracy]] in the 1996 presidential elections, with Monteiro winning unopposed.

In the buildup to the January 2001 parliamentary elections, the party joined the [[cvADM|Democratic Alliance for Change]] (ADM), a coalition including the [[cvPCD|Democratic Convergence Party]] and the [[cvPTS|Labour and Solidarity Party]]. The alliance received 6% of the vote, winning two seats in the National Assembly. In the presidential elections a month later, ADM candidate Jorge Carlos Fonseca finished third of the four candidates with 3% of the vote.

The UCID contested the 2006 parliamentary elections alone, winning two seats with 2.6% of the vote. It did not nominate a candidate for the presidential elections later in the year. It retained both seats in the 2011 parliamentary elections, increasing its vote share to 4.4%. It did not nominate a candidate for the 2011 presidential elections. After the 2016 parliamentary election, UCID has three seats, one additional.

parties.name: Democratic Union of Cape Verde
parties.relations: Succeeded by the [[cvUCID|Democratic and Independent Cape Verdean Union]] (UCID).
parties.description:
A short-lived conservative political party that existed in Cape Verde during the final stage of the Portuguese colonial regime. It was founded in May 1974, immediately after the fall of the Estado Novo dictatorship through the Carnation Revolution, forcibly neutralized in December of that same year with the seizure of its main headquarters, and legally dissolved in July 1975 with Cape Verde's independence as a one-party state. It was led throughout its existence by the lawyer João Baptista Monteiro.

During its brief existence, the UDC represented the main anti-communist opposition force to the [[gwPAIGC|African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde]] (PAIGC), which advocated the immediate independence of the archipelago and its unification with Guinea-Bissau. The UDC, closely aligned with the Portuguese provisional regime of António de Spínola, rejected immediate independence, promoting island autonomy under a federal model or "adjacency" to eventually hold a referendum on independence. The party operated primarily on the island of São Vicente (its main stronghold being Mindelo, the country's second most populous city) and to a lesser extent on Santo Antão, disseminating its ideas through Rádio Barlavento, the main dissenting voice of the PAIGC during the brief period of political pluralism.

Along with the [[cvUPICV|Union of the People of the Cape Verde Islands]] (UPICV), the UDCV was consistently excluded from independence talks by the PAIGC, which was recognized by international organizations as the "sole legitimate representative" of the Cape Verdean people. On 28 September 1974, the fall of Da Spínola in Portugal left the UDC without political support and ended any hope of preserving the colonial status. Two months later, on 9 December 1974, PAIGC militants seized control of the headquarters of Rádio Barlavento. Simultaneously, numerous party leaders and members were arrested by the interim government authorities. In July 1975, following one-party elections, Cape Verde became independent under a socialist regime, with the PAIGC as the only legal party.

In 1977, during a wave of arrests in São Vicente, former UDCV leaders were detained or forced into exile. On 13 May 1978, UDCV militants exiled in Portugal, along with late-stage PAIGC dissidents, founded the [[cvUCID|Democratic and Independent Cape Verdean Union]] (UCID), considered the direct successor to the UDC, which would become the main political organization of the Cape Verdean exile community. With the establishment of multiparty democracy in 1990, the UCID was legalized and continues to be the third largest political party in the country.

parties.name: Movement for Democracy
parties.description:
The MpD was established on 14 March 1990 by Carlos Veiga after Prime Minister Pedro Pires of the [[cvPAICV|African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde]] (PAICV, formerly the sole legal party) allowed its creation. The party was publicly launched in May 1990 and its first convention was held in November 1990.

In the January 1991 parliamentary elections, the first multi-party elections in the country's history, the MpD won 56 of the 79 seats in the National Assembly. In the presidential elections the following month, MpD candidate António Mascarenhas Monteiro defeated the incumbent PAICV President Aristides Pereira.

Following the MpD's second convention in January 1993, splits developed within the party, with two groups, List A and List B, emerging. A split in 1994 led to the creation of the Democratic Convergence Party. Despite losing six seats, the party retained its parliamentary majority in the 1995 elections, whilst Monteiro was re-elected unopposed in the presidential elections the following year.

The January 2001 parliamentary elections saw the party lose another 20 seats, as it was defeated by the PAICV. In the February 2001 presidential elections the MpD nominated Veiga, but he was defeated by the PAICV's Pires by just 12 votes in the second round of voting.

In the 2006 parliamentary elections party lost another seat and was reduced to 29 MPs. Veiga was again defeated by Pires in the presidential elections later in the year.

Despite gaining three seats in the 2011 parliamentary elections, the MpD remained in opposition. However, in the presidential elections in the same year, MpD candidate Jorge Carlos Fonseca defeated the PAICV's Manuel Inocêncio Sousa by 54–46%.

In July 2013, Ulisses Correia e Silva, the mayor of the capital, Praia, became party's new chairman, following Carlos Veiga, who stepped down after five years.

Fonseca was re-elected as president in the 2016 presidential election. The MpD also won a majority in the National Assembly during the 2016 parliamentary elections, ending fifteen years of PAICV majorities in that body and electing its leader Ulisses Correia e Silva as Prime Minister of Cape Verde.

The party is serving in the opposition since the 2026 election.
parties.ideology:
Although typically classified as center-right on the political spectrum, the MpD has been a diverse and ideologically diffuse party since its formation. Founded on a Christian Democratic platform, it also has economically liberal and social-liberal sectors. It considers itself a "centrist, civic, and humanist" party, centering its values ​​on the defense of a modern liberal democracy, and periodically holding internal party elections. Internationally, it is a member of the Centrist Democratic International and advocates a pro-EU position, in contrast to the Africanist stance of the PAICV.

MpD members are nicknamed "the fans," because of the party emblem resembling a fan, and primarily identify with the color green, although since the 2006 presidential campaign, the use of red has increased in party publications.

parties.name: People Work and Solidarity
parties.description:
The Labour and Solidarity Party was registered with the Constitutional Court of Cape Verde on 10 November 2000. In the same year, PTS joined the [[cvADM|Democratic Alliance for Change]] (ADM) coalition, formed by the [[cvUCID|Independent and Democratic Cape Verdean Union]] (UCID), the [[cvPCD|Democratic Convergence Party]] (PCD) and the PTS, registered on 26 November 2000.

The creation of the party was associated with Onésimo Silveira, one of the most relevant political figures in São Vicente in the period following the democratic opening. In addition to his party involvement, Silveira distinguished himself as a writer, diplomat, former Cape Verdean ambassador to Portugal and the first elected president of the São Vicente Municipal Council in the multi-party context.

The party participated in several legislative elections without achieving representation in the National Assembly of Cape Verde. In 2016, it ran under the leadership of José Augusto Fernandes, presenting itself as a political force dedicated to defending the most disadvantaged social sectors.

In the 2011 legislative elections, the PTS obtained 1,040 votes, without electing any deputies to the National Assembly. In 2016, it ran only in the Santiago Sul electoral district, obtaining 94 votes. In 2021, it expanded its electoral presence to six districts and obtained 2,088 votes, remaining without any elected deputies.

The reorganization of the PTS in 2021 occurred in a context of rapprochement between the party and figures from independent candidacies that had participated in the 2020 municipal elections. In Praia, the independent group Liderança União Trabalho e Amor (LUTA), led by Carlos Lopes, known as Romeu di Lurdes, obtained 866 votes, corresponding to 2.3%, finishing third in the municipality, without electing municipal representatives. In Tarrafal de Santiago, Cláudio Sousa was a candidate for the Municipal Council for the Movimento Independente Tarrafal (MIT), a citizens' group that obtained 1,157 votes in the 2020 municipal elections.

In the 2021 legislative elections, Cláudio Sousa assumed the interim leadership of the PTS and was the party's head of list for the Santiago Norte electoral district.

In August 2021, the PTS held a national congress in Praia to elect new bodies, review the statutes, and update the organization's political identity. Carlos Lopes was elected president of the party, succeeding José Augusto Fernandes.

The reorganization marked the change from the name Partido do Trabalho e da Solidariedade (Party of Labour and Solidarity) to Pessoas Trabalho e Solidariedade (People, Work and Solidarity), while maintaining the acronym PTS. The change sought to associate the party's identity with the centrality of people, work, and solidarity, preserving the historical continuity of the acronym. Carlos Lopes' leadership was recognized by the outgoing president José Augusto Fernandes, who validated the legality of the national congress.

José Augusto Fernandes died in October 2021, and the party publicly expressed its condolences for the death of the former leader.

Following the death of Carlos Lopes, the PTS entered a new process of internal reorganization. In March 2026, the party leadership announced its political reactivation with a view to the legislative elections of May 17 of that year.

The new leadership was headed by Jónica Brito Tavares, with Jailson de Aguiar as vice-president and Jailson Gonçalves da Silva as secretary-general.
parties.ideology:
PTS presented itself as an alternative to the political dominance of the [[cvMpD|Movement for Democracy]] (MpD) and the [[cvPAICV|African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde]] (PAICV).

The PTS has centered its political discourse on valuing people, work, and solidarity, emphasizing themes such as social justice, youth inclusion, housing, health, inter-island transport, domestic production, and the participation of the diaspora in national development.

During the 2026 legislative campaign, the party leadership presented the fight against bipartisanship as one of the central axes of its political intervention. The PTS also advocated the need to bring parliamentary representation closer to peripheral communities, young people, and social groups with less access to political decisions.

In June 2026, following the fire in Ponta Belém, in the city of Praia, the party advocated for a national debate on security, protection of traders, and conditions of markets and informal trading spaces in Cape Verde.

parties.name: People's Party of Cape Verde
parties.description:
A Cape Verdean political party with a left-wing ideology founded in April 2015 by Amândio Barbosa Vicente, which makes it the most recently founded party in the country.

The party contested the 2016 parliamentary elections and obtained only 777 votes, achieving no representation in the National Assembly. In the municipal elections, PP obtained 342 votes. In the 2020 municipal elections, PP achieved an agreement with the [[cvPAICV|PAICV]] in the municipality of Boavista, disputing only the category of councilors and obtaining 20.6% of the votes and 3 votes in the Municipal Assembly. In the 2021 parliamentary elections PP got 2.93% of the votes in Boavista, but it didn't manage to get any votes and obtained fewer total votes than in previous elections.

The PP was the only Cape Verdean political party that openly repudiated the arrest of the Colombian businessman Alex Saab in June 2020 and demanded his release, considering that it was a «subordination to the interests of the United States» on the part of the government of Ulisses Correia e Silva.
parties.ideology: The PP focuses its speech on the fight for social justice and economic diversification, while criticizing the prevailing bipartisan system between the [[cvPAICV|African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde]] and the [[cvMpD|Movement for Democracy]]. PP was described as a leftist party.

parties.relations: Split from the [[cvUCID|Democratic and Independent Cape Verdean Union]] (UCID).
parties.description:
A centrist Cape Verdean political party founded in 1992 as a splinter group from the [[cvUCID|Democratic and Independent Cape Verdean Union]] (UCID). It obtained its legal registration on 7 July 1995, and contested the parliamentary elections that same year, participating in all subsequent elections until 2021. However, it has never surpassed one percentage point, generally placing last, nor has it ever won a seat in the National Assembly. It is one of seven legally recognized political parties in the country.

The party has consistently denounced the lack of media coverage for minority parties and the dominance of the two-party system as the main cause of its weak electoral performance. Following the 2021 parliamentary elections, it filed numerous complaints against media outlets with the National Electoral Commission, without success.

parties.name: Union of the People of the Cape Verde Islands
parties.nativeName: União do Povo das Ilhas de Cabo Verde
parties.description:
A Cape Verdean political party with Maoist ideology, established in the first half of 1974 as an independence movement in Portuguese Cape Verde, immediately following the Carnation Revolution, which ended the authoritarian Estado Novo regime and precipitated the independence of the Portuguese colonies. It was led throughout its existence by José Leitão da Graça.

During the final months of the colonial administration, UPICV acted as the main opposition force to the [[gwPAIGC|African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde]] (PAIGC), which had waged the war of independence against the Portuguese government in Guinea-Bissau with a platform that included the unification of Guinea and Cape Verde into a single state. The UPICV, which adhered to Mao Zedong Thought and defined itself as pro-People's Republic of China, opposed both the continuation of the Portuguese colony and a merger with Guinea-Bissau, criticizing the PAIGC as an instrument of "Soviet imperialism." Despite its Maoist leanings and its rejection of a potential merger, the UPICV was also influenced by the Pan-Africanist thought of Kwame Nkrumah. It advocated for the implementation of broad and radical socio-political transformations, as well as the nationalization of the means of production and industry.

From its inception as a party, the UPICV was involved in the power struggle against the right-wing [[cvUDCV|Democratic Union of Cape Verde]] (UDCV), which favored a federation with Portugal, and primarily against the PAIGC, which established a Transitional Government for independence and worked towards transforming Cape Verde into a one-party socialist state. The party was not allowed to field candidates in the first parliamentary elections before independence, and Leitão da Graça was forced into exile. Party leaders captured in the country were sent to Chão Bom prison.

Leitão da Graça returned to Cape Verde in 1986. With the advent of multiparty politics in 1990 following the fall of communism, he attempted to revive the UPICV, but was unsuccessful.

parties.name: Defenders of the Homeland
parties.description:
During the first half of 2025, groups supporting Abelardo de la Espriella's presidential candidacy organized on social media and at regional events as part of the campaign. On 16 July 2025, De la Espriella registered the "Defenders of the Homeland" campaign committee with the National Registry, with the goal of collecting signatures for an independent presidential candidacy. The chosen slogan was "Firm for the Homeland."

On 31 May 2026, the movement came in first place in the presidential elections with a total of 10,361,499 votes, representing 43.74% of the total valid votes, which allowed them to advance to the second round and compete against Iván Cepeda. In that instance, Abelardo de la Espriella was the candidate with the most votes, becoming the president of Colombia, a position he assumed on 7 August 2026.

On 3 August 2026, with 6 votes in favor, 1 against, and 2 abstentions, the plenary session of the National Electoral Council approved the organization's legal status. Thus, it officially became a political party.

parties.description:
The movement was founded in July 2011 under the name Občané 2011 and its first chairman was Ludvík Adámek. The movement's first website listed Karel Janko, chairman of the [[czCSNS2005|Czech National Socialist Party]] (ČSNS 2005), Zbyněk Štěpán, chairman of the [[czNP|National Prosperity]] (NP), and Vladimíra Vítová, chairman of the [[czCMF|Czech Peace Forum]] (ČMF), as co-founders. The website also listed 13 advisors and consultants, including 3 former ministers for the [[czSOCDEM|Czech Social Democratic Party]] (Jaroslav Bašta, Ivan David, and Eduard Zeman).

On 2 June 2018, Vladimíra Vítová became chairman and on 2 July of the same year, the movement was renamed the Alliance of National Forces.

The movement dissolved itself at its national congress on 28 October 2024, effective from the same day.

parties.name: Alternative for the Czech Republic 2017
parties.description:
A Czech Eurosceptic, conservative and far-right political party registered on 16 June 2016. Richard Perman served as its chairman. 

The movement was formed by some former members of the [[bzBlokPI|Bloc Against Islam]], which dissolved in May 2016. At first, they got into a dispute over the name with the newly registered political party [[czAPC|Alternative for the Czechia]] (APČ).

Since its founding, the movement wanted to fight against Islamization and multiculturalism, wanted to transform the European Union back into the European Community and did not rule out supporting a "Czexit". It also wanted to simplify the tax system, reduce unnecessary regulations or laws, "cut off" political non-profit organizations from public budgets, abolish concession fees, and "reform" public media.

The leaders of the movement in its early days were Petr Hampl (elected chairman at the constituent assembly) and Martin Konvička, with musician and publicist Petr Štěpánek becoming vice-chairman. Support for the movement was also expressed by Ladislav Jakl and Ivo Strejček from the Václav Klaus Institute.

In the 2016 Senate elections, the movement's chairman Hampl (in Beroun) and vice-chairman Štěpánek (in Pardubice) ran for the movement, as did Martin Konvička (in Tábor), former director of Slovak Television Radim Hreha (in Český Krumlov), and chairwoman of the political non-profit organization Naštaváné matky Eva Hrindová (in Olomouc). After the split with [[czUsvit|Úsvit]], the movement did not run for office in the concurrent regional elections. Konvička won 8.07 percent of the vote in the Senate elections, Hampl finished in seventh place with 7.1 percent. After the failure in the elections, both Hampl and Konvička left the movement, and Petr Štěpánek was to remain in charge.

In April 2017, the Supreme Administrative Court of the Czech Republic suspended the Alternative's activities due to incomplete financial reports.

The movement participated in the 2019 European Parliament elections. Klára Samková was announced as the leading candidate, followed by Luděk Nezmar, Ivan Hrbek, Milan Vodička and Vojtěch Merunka. In these elections, it received 11,729 votes (0.49%) and did not win any mandate.

In January 2022, the government proposed suspending the movement's activities because it was not fulfilling its legal obligations, which happened on 16 March 2022. It was dissolved in December 2023.

description.text:
A Czech Eurosceptic, conservative and far-right political party registered on 16 June 2016. Richard Perman served as its chairman. 

The movement was formed by some former members of the [[bzBlokPI|Bloc Against Islam]], which dissolved in May 2016. At first, they got into a dispute over the name with the newly registered political party [[czAPC|Alternative for the Czechia]] (APČ).

Since its founding, the movement wanted to fight against Islamization and multiculturalism, wanted to transform the European Union back into the European Community and did not rule out supporting a "Czexit". It also wanted to simplify the tax system, reduce unnecessary regulations or laws, "cut off" political non-profit organizations from public budgets, abolish concession fees, and "reform" public media.

The leaders of the movement in its early days were Petr Hampl (elected chairman at the constituent assembly) and Martin Konvička, with musician and publicist Petr Štěpánek becoming vice-chairman. Support for the movement was also expressed by Ladislav Jakl and Ivo Strejček from the Václav Klaus Institute.

In the 2016 Senate elections, the movement's chairman Hampl (in Beroun) and vice-chairman Štěpánek (in Pardubice) ran for the movement, as did Martin Konvička (in Tábor), former director of Slovak Television Radim Hreha (in Český Krumlov), and chairwoman of the political non-profit organization Naštaváné matky Eva Hrindová (in Olomouc). After the split with [[czUsvit|Úsvit]], the movement did not run for office in the concurrent regional elections. Konvička won 8.07 percent of the vote in the Senate elections, Hampl finished in seventh place with 7.1 percent. After the failure in the elections, both Hampl and Konvička left the movement, and Petr Štěpánek was to remain in charge.

In April 2017, the Supreme Administrative Court of the Czech Republic suspended the Alternative's activities due to incomplete financial reports.

The movement participated in the 2019 European Parliament elections. Klára Samková was announced as the leading candidate, followed by Luděk Nezmar, Ivan Hrbek, Milan Vodička and Vojtěch Merunka. In these elections, it received 11,729 votes (0.49%) and did not win any mandate.

In January 2022, the government proposed suspending the movement's activities because it was not fulfilling its legal obligations, which happened on 16 March 2022. It was dissolved in December 2023.

parties.description:
A Czech political party founded in 2001 in Brno. From 2001 to 2007, its chairman was František Zoubek, and from 2007 until its dissolution in 2017, Karol Schneider.

The party ran in the 2013 Czech parliamentary election. Vladimír Stehlík, former general director of Poldi Kladno and BOHEMIA ART, ran for the party in the Central Bohemian Region, among others. Jiří Bezděk, who was prosecuted for threatening a bailiff with mutilation, was supposed to be the South Moravian leader, but the party ultimately did not run in this region.

The party intended to run in nine regions, but was excluded in five because it did not provide proof of payment of the mandatory election contribution. It therefore only ran in the Prague, Central Bohemian, Hradec Králové and Vysočina regions.

The party ran in the European Parliament elections held in May 2014. The election leader was Václav Prokůpek, the other candidates were Lukáš Kohout and Vladimír Stehlík.

parties.name: Budoucnost
parties.relations: Split from the [[czIdealistecz|Idealisté.cz]] association and the [[czZeleni|Green Party]].
parties.description:
The movement was registered in May 2020. Part of its preparatory committee consisted of former members of [[czIdealistecz|Idealisté.cz]] and the Zelená re:vize organization associated with the [[czZeleni|Green Party]]. In the 2020 Senate elections, the movement joined the Social Democrats (ČSSD) and the Greens in supporting the candidacies of Jiří Dienstbier Jr. and Michal Šmarda.

In the 2022 municipal elections, Budoucnost ran for the Prague City Assembly as part of the [[czSolidarita|Solidarity]] coalition with [[czSOCDEM|ČSSD]], the [[czZeleni|Green Party]], and the [[czIdealiste|Idealisté Movement]], but did not win any seats. The movement stood candidates in 16 other seats, with four members elected in Jilemnice, Slaný, Neratovice and Horní Domaslavice.

Budoucnost endorsed Josef Středula in the 2023 presidential election. He withdrew his candidacy on 8 January 2023.

In the 2024 European Parliament election, four members of Budoucnost ran on the candidate list of [[czSOCDEM|Social Democracy]].

The movement aligned with [[czLevice|The Left]] for the 2025 Czech parliamentary election.
parties.ideology: Budoucnost calls for a suspension of distraint by private entities and easing of debt relief by increasing pensions and reducing labor taxation. They would make housing more affordable in large cities by building public and cooperative housing, capping rent, fighting homelessness and limiting rental services such as Airbnb. The movement wants to address oligarchy by introducing wealth taxes, as well as tightening media ownership and campaign finance laws. Other priorities of the movement include ending privatisation, creating new state enterprises (particularly a public bank and phone operator) and transitioning to a carbon-free economy financed by those who have profited from the climate crisis.

parties.name: Civic Democratic Alliance
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[czHOS|Movement for Civil Liberties]] (HOS)
parties.description:
ODA was established as a conservative-liberal party in 1990, shortly after the Velvet revolution. The origins of the Civic Democratic Alliance date back to 1978, when Daniel Kroupa founded a seminar for young philosophers called Kampademia. The umbrella organization of this group became the [[czHOS|Movement for Civil Liberties]] (abbreviated as HOS), founded on 15 October 1988. 

In the 1992 legislative election, ODA received over 300,000 votes (5.93%) and won 14 seats in the Czech National Council. It became part of the first right-wing coalition led by Václav Klaus, together with the [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]] (ODS), [[czKDUCSL|Christian and Democratic Union]] (KDU–ČSL) and [[czKDS|Christian Democratic Party]] (KDS).

In the 1996 legislative election, ODA received 6.36% of the vote, and formed another coalition with ODS and KDU–ČSL. However, this government did not have a majority in the Chamber of Deputies, and was therefore reliant on the support of the centre-left [[czSOCDEM|Social Democrats]] (ČSSD). Following financial scandals within ODS, the coalition fell apart, and both ODS and KDU-ČSL participated in the caretaker government of Josef Tošovský.

ODA did not participate in the 1998 legislative election, in order to avoid splitting the right-wing vote. ODA formed the Four-Coalition with KDU–ČSL, [[czUSDEU|Freedom Union]] and [[czDEU|Democratic Union]], in opposition to the grand coalition of ODS and ČSSD. However, ODA became the coalition's weakest member, and partly as a result of financial difficulties, began to fade out of the Czech political scene, with only one senator remaining, Karel Schwarzenberg. The party ceased activity on 31 December 2007.

Czech billionaire Pavel Sehnal announced in December 2016 that he had established a new Civic Democratic Alliance, without the involvement of the original ODA leadership. New ODA was renamed to [[czAPB|Alliance for the Future]] in 2021.

parties.name: Civic Movement
parties.relations:
Preceded by the moderate wing of the [[czOF|Civic Forum]] (OF);

Merged into the [[czCSNS|Free Democrats – Liberal National Social Party]] (SD-LSNS)
parties.description:
A Czech social liberal political party between 1991 and 1996, with roots in the [[czOF|Civic Forum]]. Its chairman was Jiří Dienstbier throughout its existence. Its members also included Petr Pithart, Martin Bursík, Pavel Rychetský, Miloš Zeman and Jan Sokol.

The movement was established on 27 April 1991 after the separation of the [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]] from the [[czOF|Civic Forum]]. Most of its members sympathized with the idea of ​​"apolitical politics", which was promoted primarily by Václav Havel, which is why the Civic Movement was perceived as the main heir of the Civic Forum. Already by its name, the Civic Movement declared a reserved approach to party membership - for a certain period of the movement's operation, collective membership was also allowed. The differences in opinion among the movement's members did not allow it to profile itself as either right-wing or left-wing, and the movement was thus placed in the middle of the political spectrum. However, it openly declared its liberal orientation.

In the elections to the 1992 Czech National Council election, the Civic Movement won 4.6% of the vote, remaining just below the five-percent threshold. In response, the movement transformed itself into the Free Democrats (Svobodní demokraté) party in 1993. The party's liberal orientation and its demarcation towards the left (the [[czSOCDEM|Czech Social Democratic Party]]) and the right (the [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]]) were officially confirmed. At the turn of 1995 and 1996, the Free Democrats merged with the [[czCSNS|Liberal National Social Party]] into an entity called the [[czCSNS|Free Democrats – Liberal National Social Party]]. However, this union did not last long; in 1998, some of the original members of the Civic Movement founded the [[csSOS|Party for an Open Society]], which had one senator and participated in the government in the Liberec Region.

parties.name: Club of Committed Non-Party Members
parties.description:
In March 1968, 5 meetings of the preparatory committee were held, at which a decision was made on the name of KAN and the preparation of a program statement and statutes. On 5 April 1968, the inaugural meeting of KAN was held in the auditorium of the Institute of Computer Science and Engineering in Prague, in which 140 people signed an application for KAN registration. Two days later, the application for KAN registration was submitted to the National Committee of the Capital City of Prague, which accepted it the following day. On 16 May 1968, the Minister of the Interior, Josef Pavel (without consulting with the [[czKSC|Communist Party]] authorities) permitted KAN's preparatory activities, but without approving the statutes. At the same time, a new draft of the statutes was submitted to the Ministry of the Interior for approval, along with an application for nationwide registration. On 7 June 1968, MUDr. Jan Štěpánek was elected chairman of the preparatory committee of KAN in a secret ballot, replacing Ludvík Rybáček. In July 1968, Rudolf Battěk became the vice-chairman of the KAN Central Committee. It was at his place that, after the invasion of Czechoslovakia by the Warsaw Pact troops, it was decided at a secret meeting in Karlín that KAN would cease its activities. Subsequently, the lists of thousands of members were liquidated. On 29 August 1968, the PÚV NF (Presidency of the Central Committee of the National Front) declared that it considered the political system of the NF to be satisfactory and closed. On 5 September 1968, the Ministry of the Interior banned the activities of the Club of Committed Non-Party Members.

At the KAN meeting in the ÚKDŽ in Vinohrady in March 1990, a preparatory committee headed by Karel Soyček was formed. The Club of Committed Non-Party Members was registered by the Ministry of the Interior on 7 May 1990. The founding congress of KAN was held on 6 October 1990 and the first chairman was Bohdan Dvořák (1990–1993). In February 1993, he, like many municipal politicians of KAN, left the movement and joined the [[czODS|ODS]]. At the 5th congress of KAN in Prague in October 1993, Emil Dejmek was therefore elected chairman. However, in November 1995, at the 7th congress of KAN in Svitavy, Pavel Holba was elected.

In March 1999, in response to the opposition agreement, the club formed a loose political coalition under the name National Democratic Alliance together with the [[czCSNS|Czech National Social Party]], the Civic Coalition – Political Club, the [[czPB|Right Bloc]] and the [[czNEZ|Independents]] movement. However, in the 2002 parliamentary elections, KAN ultimately ran only with the Right Bloc.

On 29 November 2014, Jiří Domlátil was elected chairman at the 23rd KAN congress in Prague 6. On 19 October 2019, František Laudát, a former member of parliament for TOP 09, was elected chairman at the 26th KAN congress in Prague 6. On 16 November 2024, Miroslav Matějka, the current 1st vice-chairman, was elected chairman at the 30th KAN congress.

Split from the [[czSOCDEM|Czechoslovak Social Democratic Workers' Party]] (ČSDSD);

parties.description:
A communist and Marxist–Leninist political party in Czechoslovakia that existed between 1921 and 1992, member of the Comintern. Between 1929 and 1953, it was led by Klement Gottwald. The KSČ was the sole governing party in the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic though it was a leading party along with the Slovak branch and four other legally permitted non-communist parties. After its election victory in 1946, it seized power in the 1948 Czechoslovak coup d'état and established a one-party state allied with the Soviet Union. Nationalization of virtually all private enterprises followed, and a planned economy was implemented.

In 1968, party leader Alexander Dubček proposed reforms that included a democratic process and initiated the Prague Spring, leading to the invasion of Czechoslovakia by the Soviet Union. Under pressure from the Kremlin, all reforms were repealed, party leadership became taken over by its more authoritarian wing, and a massive non-bloody purge of party members was conducted. In 1989, however, the party leadership bowed to popular pressure during the Velvet Revolution and agreed to call the first contested election since 1946, leading to the victory of the centre-based Civic Forum in the 1990 election and the KSČ stepping down. That November, the party became a federation of the [[czKSCM|Communist Party of Bohemia and Moravia]] and the [[skKSS|Communist Party of Slovakia]]. It was then declared to be a criminal organisation in the Czech Republic by the 1993 Act on Illegality of the Communist Regime and on Resistance Against It.
parties.ideology: The KSČ was committed to the pursuit of communism, and after Joseph Stalin's rise to power Marxism–Leninism became formalized as the party's guiding ideology and would remain so throughout the rest of its existence.

The party organisation was based on Bolshevik-like democratic centralism; its highest body was the Party Congress, which convened every five years. When the Congress was not in session, the Central Committee was the highest body. Because the Central Committee met twice a year, most day-to-day duties and responsibilities were vested in the Politburo. The party leader was the head of government and held the office of either General Secretary, Premier or head of state, or some of the three offices concurrently, but never all three at the same time.

parties.name: Czech National Front
parties.description:
A Czech political party that was founded in 2016 and dissolved in 2018 by voluntary dissolution. The movement was not clearly defined on a right-left scale.

Theparty did not submit an annual financial report for 2016, and therefore the government submitted a proposal to suspend its activities.

The party participated in the 2017 elections to the Chamber of Deputies with the drawn number 18, but ran only in the Moravian-Silesian Region. In the student elections, the party received 29 votes, which corresponded to 0.07% of the valid votes cast. In the parliamentary elections, the movement received 117 votes, which is only 0.000023% of the total votes cast (in the Moravian-Silesian Region alone it was 0.02%), and thus took last place. The movement did not participate in other elections.

parties.name: Dawn – National Coalition
parties.relations:
Founded by independent senator sitting in the [[czKDUCSL|KDU-ČSL]] group;

De facto succeeded by the [[czSPD|Freedom and Direct Democracy]] (SPD).
parties.description:
The party was founded in May 2013 by Tomio Okamura, an independent senator attached to the [[czKDUCSL|KDU-ČSL]] parliamentary group. Tomio Okamura's Dawn of Direct Democracy supported the implementation of direct democracy at all levels "as a solution to the corruption, nepotism, clientelism and kleptocracy," the use of referendums, the direct election of deputies, senators, mayors and regional governors, a presidential system and, consequently, a stronger separation of powers.

Founding members of Dawn of Direct Democracy included members of [[czVV|Public Affairs]], a former member of the [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]], and a representative of Moravané.[17]

In the parliamentary election of 2013 the party obtained 342,339 votes (6.88%), winning 14 seats. These included two deputies elected in the Central Bohemian Region, and one each in all others except the Plzen Region and Karlovy Vary Region.

On 19 January 2015, Chief Whip Radim Fiala was removed and replaced by Marek Černoch.

In February 2015, most of the nine members of the party and the 14 members of the Dawn parliamentary group decided to establish a new party, without leader Tomio Okamura. On 26 February 2015, Okamura announced that the party was experiencing serious financial difficulties. Since their election to the parliament, the party had been receiving millions of Czech crowns from the state each year.

Several members of Dawn have created new parties, including [[czSPD|Freedom and Direct Democracy]], led by Okamura, and the [[czNZ|Party of National Interests]] led by Petr Adam.

On 7 July 2015, Dawn announced plans to merge with the Party of the [[czNZ|Party of National Interests]], which they did in August the same year. Retired veteran Miroslav Lidinský was elected as party chairman and the name was changed to Dawn – National Coalition. They also began working with the [[czIVCRN|We do not want Islam in the Czech Republic]] group led by Martin Konvička. However, this collaboration also failed soon after, and Dawn's popularity has continued to decline. According to opinion polling, Dawn was unlikely to exceed the threshold for entry into parliament at the 2017 legislative elections.

Dawn MP Martin Lank left the party in May 2017, which reduced the parliamentary group to six MPs, further reduced to five on 6 June 2017 with the departure of Jana Hnyková. On 7 June 2017, Marek Černoch also left Dawn.

Dawn did not participate in the 2017 legislative election. In July 2017, prominent party members stated their intention to participate in local elections in 2018. The party was dissolved in March 2018.

parties.description:
A Czech centre-right political party.

Its first chairperson was Alena Hromádková, followed by Ratibor Majzlík. The party won 1 Senate seat in 1996, 2.8% in the 1996 parliamentary elections, and only 1.44% in 1998. Since September 1998, it has been part of the Four Coalition, with which it ran in the Senate and regional elections in 1998 and 2000. On 1 December 2001, the DEU's assembly decided to dissolve the party on 31 December 2001 by merging with its four-coalition partner, the [[czUSDEU|Freedom Union]], the following day. The expanded party adopted the new name [[czUSDEU|Freedom Union – Democratic Union]] (US-DEU).

Some of the former DEU members broke away from the US-DEU at the beginning of 2004 and founded a new party, the [[czDEUCR|Democratic Union of the Czech Republic]] (DEUČR).

parties.description:
A Czech right-wing conservative political party that existed from 2004 to 2011. It was founded by a group of members of the former [[czDEU|Democratic Union]] after the original party merged with the [[czUSDEU|Union of Freedom]].

The party was founded in early 2004. It was initiated by a group around the Ústí nad Labem regional representative and businessman Jan Dorant, who was also elected its chairman in June 2004. The party profiled itself as right-wing, managerial in nature, and its statutes and program were based on similar documents of the original Democratic Union.

In the 2006 parliamentary elections, the party was a member of the Coalition for the Czech Republic, which received 0.15% of the vote and did not enter the Chamber of Deputies.

In February 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court, at the request of the government, decided to suspend the party's activities, due to the party's failure to submit to the Chamber of Deputies the annual financial reports for 2005 and 2006 in full, as required by law. The same court, at the request of the government, decided in August 2011 to dissolve the party due to the submission of an incomplete annual financial report for 2006 and the failure to submit annual financial reports for 2009 and 2010. From August 2011 to February 2012, the party was in liquidation and was removed from the register of political parties and political movements of the Ministry of the Interior on 6 February 2012.

description.text:
A Czech right-wing conservative political party that existed from 2004 to 2011. It was founded by a group of members of the former [[czDEU|Democratic Union]] after the original party merged with the [[czUSDEU|Union of Freedom]].

The party was founded in early 2004. It was initiated by a group around the Ústí nad Labem regional representative and businessman Jan Dorant, who was also elected its chairman in June 2004. The party profiled itself as right-wing, managerial in nature, and its statutes and program were based on similar documents of the original Democratic Union.

In the 2006 parliamentary elections, the party was a member of the Coalition for the Czech Republic, which received 0.15% of the vote and did not enter the Chamber of Deputies.

In February 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court, at the request of the government, decided to suspend the party's activities, due to the party's failure to submit to the Chamber of Deputies the annual financial reports for 2005 and 2006 in full, as required by law. The same court, at the request of the government, decided in August 2011 to dissolve the party due to the submission of an incomplete annual financial report for 2006 and the failure to submit annual financial reports for 2009 and 2010. From August 2011 to February 2012, the party was in liquidation and was removed from the register of political parties and political movements of the Ministry of the Interior on 6 February 2012.

parties.name: Idealisté
parties.relations: Founded by members of the [[czIdealistecz|Idealisté.cz]] political movement.
parties.description:
A Czech pro-European social democratic political party founded on 9 June 2020.

In the 2020 regional elections, Idealisté candidates appeared on the [[czHlasMoravy|Together for Moravia]] ([[czTOP09|TOP 09]], [[czZeleni|Green Party]], [[czLES|Liberal Ecological Party]] and [[czMZH|Moravian Land Movement]]) candidate list. No one was able to win a mandate. After the elections, Idealisté candidate Jan Schneider became a member of the Commission for Tourism, Interregional Relations and Marketing of the South Moravian Regional Council. Chairman Vojtěch Vašák was later elected by the South Moravian Regional Council as a member of the Control Committee. Idealists also ran in the coalition led by Josef Bernard ([[czSTAN|Mayors and Independents]], [[czPRO2014|PRO PLZEŇ]] and the Green Party) in the Pilsen Region. In the 2020 Senate elections, Anna Šabatová ran for Idealists, the Greens and the [[czSEN|Senator 21]] in district no. 60 – Brno-město.

In the 2021 parliamentary election, Idealisté candidate appeared on the joint candidate list of the [[czPirStan|Pirates and Mayors]] coalition in the South Moravian Region.

In the 2022 municipal elections, Idealisté ran for the Prague City Council as part of the [[czSolidarita|Solidarit]]y coalition, which consisted of the [[czSOCDEM|ČSSD]], the Greens, [[czBudoucnost|Budoucnost]] and Idealisté, with a result of 2.01%. For the Brno City Council, the Idealisté joined forces with the Greens and [[czZTB|Žít Brno]]. In fifth place on the Idealisté candidate list, Chairman Vojtěch Vašák ran, but he failed to win a seat, as the candidates before him won a seat with a result of 5.97%.

Individual members of Idealisté also ran in the city districts of Brno-Královo Pole (Vojtěch Vašák on the candidate list "[[czPirati|Pirates]] and Greens for Královo Pole", the result of the entire candidate list was 17.16%), Brno-Vinohrady (Lukáš Karnet on the candidate list "Jiří Čejka with citizens for Vinohrady", the result of the entire candidate list was 19.52%), Brno-Bystrc (Andrea Frajtová on the candidate list "Greens for Bystrc, Pirates and Bystrčáci", the result of the entire candidate list was 16.69%) and Prague 8 (František Novotný on the candidate list "ČSSD, [[czKDUCSL|KDU-ČSL]] and Greens with the support of the Eight Together", the result of the entire candidate list was 3.49%). Lukáš Karnet and Vojtěch Vašák won the mandate.

Jan Schneider, a member of Idealisté, ran in the city of Tišnov (on the "Open Tišnov" candidate list, with a total of 14.47%). The candidate managed to win two mandates. In the city of Tachov, non-party members Jiří Nenutil and Jan Michalec were elected on the "Idealisté for Tachov" candidate list (with a total of 10.18%). In Blansko, 3 non-party representatives were elected on the Idealists' candidate list called "Fórum Blansko" (with a total of 10.37%). And in Kyjov, 4 non-party representatives were elected on the Idealists' candidate list called "Pro Kyjov" (with a total of 17.52%).

In the 2023 presidential elections, Idealisté supported the candidacy of retired army general Petr Pavel in the second round.

In the 2024 European Parliament elections, Idealisté did not run.

In the second round of the 2024 Senate elections, Idealisté supported Břetislav Rychlík in district no. 59 – Brno-město.

In the regional elections, Idealisté ran on the [[czHlasMoravy|Hlas Moravy]] candidate list, which received 1.84% and no candidate from this list made it to the South Moravian Regional Assembly.

In the 2025 Czech parliamentary election, Idealisté supported the candidate list of the [[czPirati|Pirates]] and the [[czZeleni|Greens]], or the election of one of the smaller socially, ecologically and democratically oriented parties. The party itself and its members were not running.
parties.ideology: The Idealists Movement continues the tradition of the [[czIdealistecz|Idealisté.cz]] association and Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk in its efforts to promote the principles of freedom, solidarity and justice. One of the impulses for the establishment of the political movement is the dissatisfaction of the Idealists with the policies of the Andrej Babiš government and the state of Czech politics in general. According to the Idealists, values ​​and visions have disappeared from it. The movement wants to fight corruption, address the state of the environment, modernize education, raise the living standards of the lower and middle classes, or defend the democratic character and pro-European direction of the Czech Republic.
