parties.name: Idealisté.cz
parties.relations: In 2020, Idealisté.cz members founded a political party, [[czIdealiste|Idealists Movement]].
parties.description:
An independent association of social democratic orientation. The association was officially established on 2 January 2015, but the organization has a longer history. Originally, the Idealists were only part of the Young Social Democrats, youth wing of the [[czSOCDEM|Czech Social Democratic Party]] (ČSSD). Today, they are a completely independent organization, without formal ties to [[czSOCDEM|Social Democracy]] or any other party.

Idealisté.cz began its activities in 2010, just after the formation of the coalition of [[czODS|ODS]] and [[czSOCDEM|ČSSD]] (now SOCDEM) in the Prague City Hall, with the formation of which the association did not agree. At that time, however, it was only part of the youth organization of social democracy. At the same time, political reforms were underway by the right-wing government of Petr Nečas, which was another reason for the establishment of the platform. Idealisté.cz came to the attention of the general public when they initiated demonstrations in support of Bohuslav Sobotka after the so-called Lánský Putsch in the fall of 2013. In 2015, they advocated the introduction of more elements of direct democracy in the so-called social democratic primaries.

Although the organization is explicitly associated with social democratic ideology, it does not only associate members of the ČSSD. Many members are also non-partisans or people who sympathize with the [[czZeleni|Green Party]], or rather the left-wing faction of this party. Former minister Jiří Dienstbier Jr. is also a member of the association. Members of the organization's leadership are Vojtěch Vašák, Vendula Couvreur, Radim Hejduk, Karel Gargulák and Šárka Homfray.

In June 2020, some members, including the then chairman, founded the [[czIdealiste|Idealisté Movement]], which refers to the tradition of the association and is close to it, but it is a different organization and the Idealisté.cz association remains officially independent of political parties or movements.
parties.ideology:
The association adheres to the social democratic values ​​of freedom, solidarity and justice and defends the idea of ​​a welfare state. The Idealists emphasize public investment, especially in the development of infrastructure, job creation, a healthy environment and education. In economic terms, its views can therefore be classified as Keynesian or post-Keynesian. It is critical of globalization, e.g. in the form of TTIP.

On social issues, it identifies with progressivism and is close to cultural liberalism. On the issue of the functioning of public institutions, it supports measures increasing transparent financing and independence.

The Idealists belong to the liberal and pro-European camp within the broader social democratic movement.

parties.name: Jednotní
parties.relations: Split from the [[czSPD|Freedom and Direct Democracy]] (SPD); Partially merged into the [[czVB|Free Bloc]] (VB)
parties.description:
A Czech political movement founded by former member of the [[czSPD|Freedom and Direct Democracy]] (SPD) from the Moravian-Silesian Region (three of whom were members of the Chamber of Deputies), who left the movement due to ideological disagreements with the leadership.

The party was registered on 15 March 2019. A few weeks later, at the founding conference of the movement, Lubomír Volný was offered the position of chairman, which he accepted. According to Volný, the movement's ambition was to participate in the elections to the European Parliament as a unifier of patriotic movements in the Czech Republic. Volný also stated that he wanted the movement to be more consistent in promoting its goals and positions than the SPD.

In September 2020, Pynelopi Cimprichová was elected as the new chairman of the movement.

In February 2021, deputies Volný and Bojko transferred to the [[czCSSD|Volný Bloc]] party.

Since 28 February 2021, Martin Šatný has been the chairman. On 12 February 2022, a decision was made to voluntarily dissolve the party with liquidation, and on 30 March 2022, the movement was deleted from the register of parties and movements.

parties.relations:
Split from the [[czPirati|Czech Pirate Party]] (Piráti).

After party disolution, its leader participated inside [[czANS|Alliance of National Forces]] (ANS).
parties.description:
A Czech far-right pirate political party founded in 2018. The party operated mainly in the regions of Moravia and Silesia.

The Moravian and Silesian Pirate Party was founded as a reaction to the then policy of the [[czPirati|Czech Pirate Party]], allegedly also to "Prague-centrism". According to the statement of the Czech Pirate Party, the founder Karel Světnička was a registered supporter of the party and sought to run for the Senate in the Moravian-Silesian Region, but received 0 out of 20 votes. This failure allegedly led to the establishment of a Moravian branch of the Pirate Party. Other founders of the party were often from the Confederation of Political Prisoners of the Czech Republic.

The party was registered on August 16, 2018. It had already fielded candidates for the Senate elections in 2018. The deadline for submitting candidate lists was July 31 (17 days before the party was founded), but the party affiliation of the candidates was provided during the procedure where errors were corrected. The first candidate was Karel Světnička (party chairman), who ran in the Karviná district, where he received only 1,265 votes (4.28%) and finished in last place. Another candidate was Michal Drabík (1st Vice-Chairman of the party), who ran in the Rokycany district. Here he received only 524 votes (1.17%), finishing in last place. The party was also very active on the internet.

In 2019, the Moravian and Silesian Pirate Party wanted to participate in the European Parliament elections. However, the party leadership did not submit the nationality of the candidates to the Ministry of the Interior of the Czech Republic and did not pay the election fee of 15,000 Czech crowns, which led the Ministry to exclude MS Piráti from the elections. After this failure, the party turned to the Supreme Administrative Court, to which it filed a motion to annul the decision of the Ministry of the Interior and to cancel the candidacy of the [[czPirati|Czech Pirate Party]]. Both complaints filed with the Supreme Administrative Court were dismissed because the Ministry of the Interior acted in accordance with the regulations.

In 2020, the party participated in both regional and senate elections.

In the Olomouc Region, the party submitted its candidacy up to 16 seconds after the deadline. The submitted candidacy allegedly had other shortcomings (the name of the region was missing, no candidates were listed, etc.). This was the reason for candidacy not being accepted.

In the Moravian-Silesian Region, only the party chairman Karel Světnička ran for the regional council (he justified the absence of other members on the candidate list by fraud by Czech officials). The candidate received a total of 1,773 votes (0.56%), finishing 5th from the end. In the senate elections, only Světnička ran again in district no. 75 – Karviná. Světnička received 236 votes (1.05%), finishing in second-to-last place.
In the 2021 parliamentary elections, party chairman Karel Světnička ran in the Olomouc Region in 3rd place on the [[czCSSD|Free Bloc]] candidate list. In the 2022 municipal elections, he ran for the Havířov council on the candidate list of the Havířov náš [[czDOMOV|DOMOV]] bloc.

In January 2022, the government proposed to suspend the party's activities because it was not fulfilling its legal obligations. The suspension occurred on 16 March 2022. The party was dissolved by Supreme Administrative Court on 12 December 2023. Its former members later began to cooperate with various nationalist groups.

In 2024 European Parliament election, MS Pirati leader ran for the [[czANS|Alliance of National Forces]] (AND) in 23rd place on their candidate list.

parties.name: National Party
parties.description:
A Czech political party, mostly considered to be far-right, espousing a national-conservative orientation and Euroscepticism.

It was claimed to be a successor to the historical National Party ([[cz|OldCzechs|Old Czech Party]]), but was not legally considered as such. The National Party published the periodical Národní politika and operated a website] but was inactive in 2010. Its chairwoman from 2002 to 2009 was Petra Edelmannová, and the spokesperson for the National Party, editor-in-chief of Národní politika, and organizer of its events was Pavel Sedláček.

The National Party registered with the Ministry of the Interior of the Czech Republic in 2002. The Ministry of the Interior initially repeatedly refused to register it, but was subsequently forced to do so based on a ruling by the Supreme Court of the Czech Republic, which ruled that the ministry's reasons for refusing registration had no basis in law.

In 2004, the party ran for the European Parliament as the National Coalition together with the [[czCSNS|ČSNS]]; it received 0.12%. In January 2005, the NS became member of the so-called National Five coalition (together with [[czRMS|Republicans of Miroslav Sládek]], [[czKSH|National Unity]], [[czDS|Workers' Party]], and [[czKOAL|Czech Movement for National Unity]]). However, the coalition fell apart due to disputes with the Worker's Party. The National Party entered the elections alone, supported by Sládek's Republicans and a number of members of the [[czKOAL|Czech Movement for National Unity]]. It received a total of 9,341 (0.17%) votes.

In the 2006 parliamentary elections, the National Party ran in all 14 regions, but with 0.17% of the votes, it did not enter the Chamber of Deputies. The election leader in the Vysočina region at the time was Ladislav Bátora, later an advisor and personnel director at the Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports.

In the 2006 municipal elections, the National Party won seven seats, two in Frýdlant and five in Třemešná in the Osoblaž region, where National Party member Jindřich Galda became mayor. Jindřich Galda had already been mayor of Třemešná in the previous term, but as a member of the[[czCSNS|ČSNS]]. Shortly before the municipal elections, he switched to the National Party.

In the 2008 regional elections, the NS fielded its candidates in only two regions, Moravian-Silesian and Central Bohemian, and received a total of 2,711 votes.

Decline in party membership started showing in 2009. Resignation of the party's leader Petra Edelmannová on 1 December 2009 caused a disintegration of party's leadership and speeded up the process of downfall. On 17 August 2011, the Supreme Administrative Court suspended its activities at the request of the government and finally dissolved it on 15 May 2013.
parties.ideology:
They were strongly opposed to Czech membership of the European Union. Their main objectives were to restore a full national sovereignty by minimising influence of foreign institutions and to toughen the national immigration policies.

The Party proposed the so-called "A final solution to the Gypsy issue" to relocate the Roma population of the Czech Republic to India, based on perceived ethnic origins.

On 28 October 2007 the Czech National Party established a paramilitary National Guard.

Although the NS was classified as a far-right party, it rejected neo-Nazism.

parties.description:
A left-wing political party in the Czech Republic founded in October 2011 by Jiří Paroubek, former Prime Minister and former leader of the [[czSOCDEM|Czech Social Democratic Party]] (ČSSD).

Former Prime Minister Jiří Paroubek was elected chairman of his newly founded party at the constituent congress on 26 November. In the year 2012, the party had two representatives in the 200-seat Chamber of Deputies, Paroubek and Jiří Šlégr (ex-ČSSD).

The party name was a reference to the historical popular-socialist [[czCSNS|Czech National Social Party]], founded in 1897, and as such they did not advocate for German Nazism. National Socialists wanted to follow up the tradition of the left-wing Czechoslovak independence movement in the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Nevertheless, in the 2017 Czech legislative election, LEV 21 allied with the Czech Neo-Nazi party, [[czDSSS|Workers' Party of Social Justice]] (DSSS).

parties.name: New Social Democracy
parties.description:
The initiative to create a new party came from members of the [[czSOCDEM|Social Democracy]] after Jiří Nedvěd became party chairman at the December 2025 party congress, defeating critics of the party's previous direction, which had led to the party's unsuccessful attempt to run with the [[czStacilo|Stačilo!]] movement in the 2025 parliamentary election.

New Social Democracy held its founding congress on 1 May 2026. The application for party registration was submitted on 8 June 2026, and the party was registered on 19 June 2026. The committee collecting signatures to establish the new party included former ČSSD Prime Minister Vladimír Špidla, former Minister of Human Rights and Equal Opportunities Jiří Dienstbier Jr., and Nedvěd's opponent at 2025 leadership election, Petr Pavlík. The party was also supported by former [[czKSCM|Communist Party]] MP Jiří Dolejš.
parties.ideology:
The party declares itself to be the bearer of social democratic ideas. According to the founders of NSD, the original [[czSOCDEM|Social Democracy]] had ceased to represent these ideas, with no chance of reform. NSD founder Vladimir Špidla also sharply criticized Social Democracy's cooperation with the [[czKSCM|Communist Party]] and [[czStacilo|Stačilo!]].

NSD stated its intention to establish cooperation with other left-wing organizations, such as [[czBudoucnost|Budoucnost]], [[czLevice|The Left]], and [[czIdealiste|Idealisté]].

The party claims to be financed by small contributions to avoid dependence on oligarchs.

parties.name: Our Czechia
parties.relations: Split from the [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]] (ODS).
parties.description:
A centre-right political party in the Czech Republic, founded by South Bohemian Governor Martin Kuba.

Kuba left the [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]] (ODS) in November 2025 after 22 years as a member. He announced his intention to form a new party, declaring that ODS could not be "fixed" anymore. Senators Zbyněk Sýkora, and Tomáš Fiala, České Budějovice Mayor Dagmar Škodová Parmová, and former South Bohemian governor Jan Zahradník also suspended their ODS membership and followed Kuba to the new movement. 30 of the 34 South Bohemian representatives elected on the ODS candidate list in the regional elections in September 2024 also expressed their intention to join the new movement. There has also been speculation that Pardubice Governor Martin Netolický, former Moravian-Silesian governor Ivo Vondrák, and former Pilsen Governor Rudolf Špoták are also ready to cooperate with the movement.

Kuba registered 'Our Czechia' as a trademark, and formally announced his party on 2 February 2026. Journalists pointed out that the name 'Our Czechia' had been used by one of the funds of the J&T Group for several years.

On 13 April 2026, Kuba announced on Facebook that the party would cooperate with Netolický's party Us in the 2026 Czech municipal elections, and intended to cooperate in the next parliamentary election. Netolický announced that the parties would also cooperate in the 2026 Czech Senate election.

parties.name: Patriots of the Czech Republic
parties.description:
In the 2010 municipal elections, the association "Choice for Prague 8" ran for the Prague 8 municipal council, where it won two representative positions and in 2013 also the position of councilor for security in a coalition with [[czODS|ODS]] and [[czTOP09|TOP 09]]. 

The party was founded on 10 February 2014 by Jiří Vítek under the name Choice for Prague (VPP). Jiří Vítek is former professional firefighter, chairman of the Union of Security Forces of the Ministry of the Interior and holder of the Golden Rescue Cross for saving human life The party was formed from the membership base of the civic association Volba pro Prahu 8, which had been operating in Prague since 2004. 

In July 2014, the party changed its name to Patriots – Choice for Prague and its chairman was Jiří Vítek. The position of 1st Vice-Chairman was held by Petr Duchek, a representative and former councilor of Prague 21. Leoš Prokeš, a former [[czUsvit|Úsvit]] candidate for mayor of Brno, became the next Vice-Chairman of the party. In December 2014 the party changed the name Patriots of the Czech Republic. In August 2015, the party almost agreed with the [[czOKS|Civic Conservative Party]] (OKS) on a merger, but in the end it did not happen and the majority leadership of the OKS preferred to take advantage of Vít Bárta's offer to cooperate with [[czUsvit|Úsvit]].               

Vítek met several times with Heinz-Christian Strache, with whom he discussed the possibility of joining the European political faction [[euMENF|Movement for a Europe of Nations and Freedom]] (MENF), but the party did not have representation in the Czech Parliament and was rejected in favor of the [[czSPD|SPD]] party. At the end of 2016, Patriots closely cooperated with [[czAPACI2017|Alternative for the Czech Republic 2017]], which, however, was suspended due to discrepancies with the annual report. The party's chairman Jiří Vítek popularized the topic of lithium mining when he published articles about the non-transparency of its sale. Lithium mining became a major topic in the following 2017 parliamentary elections, in which Patriots supported the [[czREAL|Realists]].


In 2019, the party became closer to the newly founded [[cz|TrikoloraTrikolora]] movement, which was also joined by some members of the Patriots. In the 2021 parliamentary elections, Jiří Vítek ran from seventh place for the [[czTrikolora|Trikolora Svobodní Soukromníci]] coalition. However, after 2021, he left Trikolora due to its rapprochement with the SPD. Until the 2022 municipal elections, the party in Prague established cooperation with the [[czPrisaha|Přísaha]] party.

parties.description:
Following the 2020 regional elections, opposition parties began negotiations about potential electoral alliances. Speculation began about a liberal bloc composed of the [[czPirati|Pirate Party]] and [[czSTAN|Mayors and Independents]], with Ivan Bartoš as the leader.[

The leadership of Mayors and Independents agreed to start negotiations on 8 October 2020. The Pirates were required to ratify any alliance in a members' referendum. A poll on 20 October 2020 indicated that 51% of Pirate Party members were opposed to the alliance while 43% supported it. The referendum to start negotiations for an alliance was originally scheduled for 13 to 16 November 2020, but was rescheduled for 20 to 23 November 2020. Among Pirate Party members, 695 out of 858 voted in favor of negotiations, with a turnout of 80%. Ivan Bartoš was nominated as the Pirate Party's election leader on 25 November 2020, and was confirmed on 2 December 2020. The Pirates also offered the [[czZeleni|Green Party]] the possibility to join its electoral list. Ivan Bartoš was confirmed as the alliance's electoral leader on 14 December 2020. Pirate Party members voted to approve the alliance on 13 January 2021.

The alliance participated in the 2021 legislative election, finishing third with 15.6% of the votes and 37 seats, which was considered a disappointment. Due to preference voting, Mayors and Independents won 33 seats and the Czech Pirate Party won just 4 seats. Some media reports said that the atmosphere between STAN and Pirates had become more tense following the election, leading to speculation about the potential dissolution of the alliance, with the Pirates remaining in opposition. However, in early November, Pirates and Mayors signed a coalition agreement to form a government with [[czSPOLU|SPOLU]]. Following coalition negotiations with SPOLU, the alliance was assigned seven ministries of the government, out of which four are for Mayors and Independents and three for Pirates.

In November, Rakušan stated that STAN will not enter the next election on a joint list with the Pirates.

parties.name: Public Affairs
parties.description:
Founded in 2001, the party focused on local politics in Prague, particularly Prague 1, for most of its existence. 

In June 2009, Radek John was recruited as its chairman, and it emerged in late 2009 as a contender in the 2010 election, polling above the 5% threshold to win seats, and occasionally above [[czKDUCSL|KDU-ČSL]] and the [[czZeleni|Green Party]]. John competed with Karel Schwarzenberg for the title of the country's most popular politician.

In the election, VV received 10.9% of the vote, easily surpassing the 5% threshold, and won 24 seats. The party entered into a governing coalition with the country's two other centre-right parties: the [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]] (ODS) and [[czTOP09|TOP 09]].

In April 2011, Vít Bárta, Czech Minister of Transport, was accused of bribery by his party colleagues, deputies Jaroslav Škárka, Stanislav Huml, and Kristýna Kočí, who were subsequently expelled from the party. The incident caused serious problems in the Czech government coalition.

A lawsuit involving several members and deputies of the party began to be debated in court on 5 March 2012. Vít Bárta was accused by the State Prosecution of bribery and Jaroslav Škárka of receiving a bribe.

After Nečas's government collapsed, some members of Public Affairs split to form another party, [[czSKPRN|LIDEM]], hoping to continue their coalition with ODS and TOP 09, with Miroslava Němcová as Prime Minister. However, President Miloš Zeman refused and instead appointed Jiří Rusnok a caretaker Prime Minister. When this cabinet failed to win a confidence vote in the Chamber, the opposition called for dissolution of the Chamber and early elections. The remaining Public Affairs deputies voted in favour, and the motion of dissolution was passed with 143 out of 200 votes.

On 3 September 2013, Bárta announced that Public Affairs would not be standing in the October 2013 legislative election, leading to a split in the party's leadership. Some party members were later elected as candidates of [[czUsvit|Dawn of Direct Democracy]].

In August 2015, the party announced its dissolution, with chairman Jiří Kohout stating that the party no longer had enough money to operate.
parties.ideology: Besides opposing corruption, the party shares the fiscally conservative views of the other centre-right parties. It had a number of right-wing populist policies. The party lacked of a coherent ideology and gained voters across the political spectrum. The party was supportive of direct democracy – the members of the party could change the course of the party by Internet referendums – and was pro-European Union.

parties.description:
A Czech far-right political party. It was founded in 2016 as the successor to the previous party, the [[czSPRRSC|Rally for the Republic – Republican Party of Czechoslovakia]] (SPR-RSČ). During 2016, after its foundation, it was called the Rally for the Republic – Republican Party of Czechoslovakia 2016 (abbr. SPR–RSČ 2016) for several months. The party's chairman throughout its existence was Miroslav Sládek.

In January 2022, the government proposed to suspend the party's activities because it was not fulfilling its legal obligations. In April 2023, the Supreme Administrative Court, at the government's request, suspended the party's activities because it had repeatedly failed to submit annual financial reports on its finances. In January 2026, the Supreme Administrative Court decided to dissolve the party due to failure to comply with the legal obligation to submit annual financial reports.

Succeeded by the [[czSPRRSCMS2026|Rally for the Republic – Republican Party of Czechoslovakia 2016]] (SPR-RSČ 2016)
parties.description:
The party was founded on 30 December 1989 as one of the first political parties in post-communist Czechoslovakia. It peaked in the 1996 Czech parliamentary election with 8% of the vote (485,072 votes, 18 seats in the 200-seat Chamber of Deputies) but declined after that, and in 2001 disbanded due to financial irregularities – specifically the theft of party funds by the chairman, who used the money to fund his luxury lifestyle.

The party was reestablished in 2001 as [[czRMS|Republicans of Miroslav Sládek]] (RMS, Republikáni Miroslava Sládka). Sládek immediately set up a new party; to distinguish it from the other "republican" parties his name was added. The new party failed to attract a significant number of votes (0.9% during 2002 Czech parliamentary election was the highest). For the 2006 elections RMS joined with the [[czNS|National Party]], which obtained 0.1% of votes. The number of active members was estimated to be in the dozens at most.

On 17 May 2008 this new party merged with five other minor parties to form the SPR–RSČ. The renewed party chose Sládek as chairman, yet even after the merger the party failed to gain political traction. For non-compliance with statutory obligations, the Supreme Administrative Court of the Czech Republic (acting on a Czech government proposal) decided in December 2010 to temporarily suspend the Republican party's activities. Finally, on 15 May 2013, the Court ordered its complete dissolution.

The party was reestablished once again in February 2016 under the name [[czSPRRSCMS2026|Rally for the Republic – Republican Party of Czechoslovakia 2016]] (SPR-RSČ 2016). On 28 January 2026, the party was dissolved once again.

parties.name: Realists
parties.description:
The party was established on 24 November 2016, in response to Brexit and the victory of Donald Trump in the 2016 Presidential election in the United States. The Realists registered as an official party in December 2016 as the "Party of Regions", but changed its name to the Realists soon afterwards. Robejšek took the title of "mentor" before a new leader was to be elected in 2016. The party was ideologically close to the Civic Democratic Party and Dawn - National Coalition, but criticised ANO 2011, which they called a "left leaning" party. The party said that it would defend Czech national interests and govern according to the Pareto principle.

The Realists launched their campaign for the 2017 elections on 14 February 2017. Robejšek said that he hoped to win 20% of votes in the election.

Martin Lank, elected as a member of [[czUsvit|Dawn of Direct Democracy]], joined the Realists on 25 May 2017. Robejšek stated that the party was prepared to accept other MPs if their views were aligned with the party. Another MP from Dawn, Jana Hnyková, joined the Realists on 5 September 2017. On 21 August 2017, the Realists announced Jiří Hynek as their presidential candidate in the 2018 election.

The Realists received 0.7% of votes in the 2017 legislative election, failing to reach the 5% electoral threshold. The party leaders refused to describe the result as a defeat, and Jiří Hynek stated that the Realists should prepare for the next election.

The party announced on 16 July 2019 that it would vote on whether to dissolve itself due to electoral defeats and passive regional organisations. The party announced on 22 July 2019 that its members had voted to dissolve the party.

parties.description:
The Republicans of Miroslav Sládek (RMS) party was founded by Miroslav Sládek, the chairman and leader of the [[czSPRRSC|Rally for the Republic – Republican Party of Czechoslovakia]] (SPR–RSČ), on 12 July 2000, at a time when the SPR–RSČ was going through internal problems. 

The party's founding congress took place in December 2000, and Pavel Procházka was elected interim chairman. During 2000 and 2001, a large part of the members of the original SPR-RSČ transferred to the newly founded RMS. The original SPR–RSČ was also declared bankrupt in February 2001. Sládek considered the RMS to be the political successor of the SPR–RSČ, but he himself was not originally a member. The first party congress took place in September 2001, and Sládek, as chairman of the SPR–RSČ, was only a guest. Only after he had finished his term as chairman of the SPR–RSČ in February 2002, was he elected chairman of the RMS at the congress on 24 February 2002.

The RMS participated unsuccessfully in the 2002 parliamentary elections (less than 1% of the votes) and did not even set up an independent candidate list for the 2006 parliamentary elections. At that time, its members ran on the [[czNS|National Party]]'s candidate list.

On 27 February 2008, the Supreme Administrative Court, at the request of the government, decided to suspend the activities of the RMS, on the grounds that the party had failed to fulfil its legal obligation and had not submitted to the Chamber of Deputies the annual financial reports for the years 2004 to 2006.

The Congress of the Republicans of Miroslav Sládek held on 17 May 2008 decided that the party would be dissolved by merging with the [[czSPRRSC|SPR–RSČ]] (on the same day that the mass "Republican Congress" was held, other parties and entities were also merged with the SPR-RSČ). The party was removed from the Register of Political Parties and Political Movements of the Ministry of the Interior of the Czech Republic on 20 June 2008.
parties.ideology: In terms of program, the RMS was based on the program of the SPR-RSČ under Sládek's leadership (refusal to join the European Union, withdrawal from NATO, respect for the law, the creation of a professional army, preventing the influx of migrants).

parties.description:
A Prague electoral coalition formed for the 2022 City Council election. Its members are [[czSOCDEM|ČSSD]], [[czZeleni|Green Party]], [[czIdealiste|Idealisté]] and [[czBudoucnost|Budoucnost]], headed by former ombudswoman Anna Šabatová, who is running as an independent candidate.

The coalition officially launched its campaign on 6 June 2022 in front of the Municipal House in thecity centre Its slogan is "Solidarity against selfishness".

The coalition received 2.01% of the votes in the elections, and thus did not make it to the capital city council.
parties.ideology:
The coalition profiles itself as a "progressive project that emphasizes ecological and economic sustainability and social justice".

It advocates a solution to the housing crisis through the large-scale construction of affordable city-owned apartments so that they could be available to the middle class in addition to those most in need, support for cooperative construction, support for the Housing First project, strengthening of tenants' rights or granting developers the obligation to transfer part of new housing construction to the city fund. It also supports greater investments in public transport, schools and nurseries, social services, culture, urban greenery and other forms of adaptation to climate change or policies aimed at reducing the cost of living for youth, families, seniors and low-income residents of Prague.

parties.description:
SPOLU was an electoral coalition of Czech centre-right political parties: [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]] (ODS), [[czTOP09|TOP 09]] and [[czKDUCSL|KDU-ČSL]]. It was formed in December 2020. The leader was the then ODS chairman Petr Fiala. 

In 2021, the SPOLU coalition won the election to the Chamber of Deputies with 27.8% of the vote and 71 seats.[5] In 2025, it came in second (after ANO) and won 23.36% of the vote and 52 seats.

The coalition was initially called the Trojkoalice, but from 9 December 2020, after the announcement of cooperation and introduction, it was called SPOLU, under which name the parties ran in the Chamber of Deputies elections.

The coalition refused to cooperate with the [[czANO|ANO]] movement at the government level, as coalition leader Petr Fiala announced to journalists in December 2020. He was forced to repeat this statement due to constant speculation until the elections. Coalition representatives repeatedly identified the [[czPirStan|Pirates and Mayors]] coalition as their preferred partner, with whom they also began negotiating about the government after the elections.

The coalition parties created separate clubs in the Chamber of Deputies, with joint negotiations. However, they shared the post-election procedure. The SPOLU coalition formed Petr Fiala's government with the Pirates and Mayors coalition, which was appointed on 17 December 2021. The SPOLU coalition occupied 11 ministerial positions, while the Pirates and Mayors occupied 7 positions. In January 2026, the newly elected ODS leader Martin Kupka announced the end of the SPOLU coalition.

A Czech political party founded on 20 July 2017 by former [[czODS]] senator Vlastimil Sehnal. Initially founded as Sportsmen for Society (Sportovci pro společnost) party, in August 2017 it shortened its name to just Sportsmen (Sportovci).

The party ran in the 2017 Czech parliamentary election. On 11 August 2019, Miroslav Procházka became the new chairman. The party was voluntarily dissolved on 12 August 2019.

parties.description:
A Czech political party officially registered on 27 June 2022. The movement was active in Karlovy Vary and the Karlovy Vary Region.

Since July 2022, the main representatives of the movement have been Chairman Petr Ajšman, Vice Chairman Vladimír Valkoun and Board Member Daniel Stehlík.

The first elections in which the movement participated were the municipal council elections in 2022. However, SPRO… did not win any mandates.

In the 2022 elections to the Senate of the Czech Republic, the self-employed person and company executive Petr Ajšman ran for the movement in district no. 1 – Karlovy Vary. In the first round of the elections, he received 693 votes (i.e. 2.14%), finished in 9th place, and did not advance to the second round.

In the 2024 elections to the Senate of the Czech Republic, Dana Wittnerová is running for the movement in district no. 2 – Sokolov.

In the 2024 elections to regional councils, the SRDCEM PRO … movement unsuccessfully ran for the Karlovy Vary Regional Council. The leading candidate was Jitka Pokorná.

parties.description:
An electoral coalition of liberal and progressive Czech political parties and movements for elections to the South Moravian Regional Assembly.

The electoral coalition included the parties [[czTOP09|TOP 09]], the [[czZeleni|Green Party]], the [[czIdealiste|Idealisté]], the [[czMZH|Moravian Land Movement]] and the [[czLES|Liberal Ecological Party]], as well as two members of the [[czZTB|Žít Brno]] movement. The composition of the coalition changed before the regional elections in 2024. Since 2024, it included includes the Green Party, the [[czSEN|SEN 21]] movement, Idealisté and LES.

The leader of the electoral coalition was the deputy governor of the South Moravian Region and mayor of Židlochovice Jan Vitula ([[czTOP09|TOP 09]]). The second-place candidate was the regional representative and long-time mayor of the Brno-Nový Lískovec district Jana Drápalová ([[czZeleni|Green Party]]). The third place went to the mayor of Moravský Krumlov Tomáš Třetin (TOP 09), the fourth to the mayor of Tišnov Jan Schneider ([[czIdealiste|Idealisté]]). The fifth place was taken by the regional representative and deputy mayor of Brno Židenice Petr Kunc, the sixth by the historian and representative of Znojmo Jiří Kacetl ([[czMZH|MZH]]), and the seventh by the regional representative Michal Doležel (non-party member for TOP 09). The eighth place was taken by the religious scholar and chairman of the Green Party in the South Moravian Region, Matouš Vencálek (Greens), the ninth by the regional representative and mayor of Hustopečí, Hana Potměšilová (non-party member for TOP 09), and the tenth by the water manager and chairman of the Brno organization of the Liberal Ecological Party, David Veselý ([[czLES|LES]]).

In addition to politicians, the candidate list also included regional personalities, such as the dean of the Faculty of Regional Development and International Studies at MENDELU Jiří Schneider, the dean of the Faculty of Theatre at JAMU Petr Francán, the singer of the band Jablkoň Marie Puttnerová, and the director of the Meeting Brno festival Petr Kalousek.

In the regional elections in the South Moravian Region, the coalition won 6.62% of the vote and finished in sixth place behind ANO, KDU-ČSL, Piráty, ODS and Starosty.[7] The following representatives were elected: Michal Doležel (TOP 09), Jana Drápalová (Greens), Jan Vitula (TOP 09), Tomáš Třetina (TOP 09) and Barbora Antonová (TOP 09).[8] However, after the elections, only Drápalová, Vitula and Antonová formed a representative club. TOP 09 nominees Doležel and Třetina were outside the club.[9] The cause of the split was a dispute over who would fill the chair of the Commission for Education, Training and Sports.

At the end of January 2021, the number one and five candidates Jan Vitula and Petr Kunc were expelled from TOP 09. TOP 09 MP and chairman of the regional organization of the South Moravian Region Vlastimil Válek said that both of them repeatedly acted differently than the party bodies decided, according to Kunc and Vitula, this was an internal party struggle with the aim of consolidating power before the upcoming elections to the Chamber of Deputies in 2021.

In March 2023, Barbora Antonová resigned from the post of regional representative, and Petr Kunc replaced her at the April meeting of the Regional Assembly.

The Together for Moravia coalition ran in the elections to the South Moravian Regional Assembly in 2024, but under a new name (Voice of Moravia) and without the participation of TOP 09 and MZH. On the other hand, the [[czSEN|SEN 21]] movement became part of the coalition. The candidates were led by Jan Vitula, Jana Drápalová and Petr Kunc. The top five were completed by Jasna Flamiková and Matouš Vencálek.[14][15][16] The Voice of Moravia won 1.84% (i.e. 6,050 votes) and failed to win a seat in the South Moravian Regional Assembly.
parties.ideology: Among the main reasons for creating a joint candidate list, the coalition cited the effort to prevent the fragmentation of liberal forces, which was supposed to have occurred, for example, two years earlier in the municipal elections in Brno. The coalition's key themes were improving land, water and landscape management and mitigating the causes and impacts of climate change, developing public transport, especially rail transport, the quality of education and the availability of housing.

parties.name: Volt Czechia
parties.description:
Volt Czechia was founded in 2019. It operated from 11 April 2021 to 28 June 2022 as a registered association, Volt Czech Republic, chaired by Karolina Machová and Adam Hanka, with Jan Klátil as treasurer. On 29 June 2022 Volt Czechia was registered as a political party in the Czech Republic. Hanka was elected chair of the new party.

The party contested an election for the first time in the 2022 Prague municipal election, receiving 4,816 votes (0.14%).

In October 2022, Volt Czech Republic hosted the General Assembly of [[euVolt|Volt Europa]]. In October 2023, Volt and [[czSEN|Senator 21]] announced that they would be running a joint list of candidates in the 2024 European elections. In November, the party elected Adam Hanka and Barbora Hrubá as the party's lead candidates for the European elections. The [[czczSEN21V|SEN 21 and Volt]] joint list received 0.34%.

Volt Czechia will participate in the 2025 Czech parliamentary election. The party filed lawsuits against the so-called "non-coalitions" of [[czSPD|Freedom and Direct Democracy]] (SPD) and [[czStacilo|Stačilo!]], arguing that they were circumventing the higher threshold in place for coalitions, but all cases were rejected at the regional courts. Volt said they would appeal the case to the Constitutional Court, which will rule on the case after the election, during the result certification process.

parties.name: We do not want Islam in the Czech Republic
parties.description:
Aa Czech anti-Islam organisation led by Martin Konvička, founded in 2009. The Czech Ministry of the Interior has described the initiative as an Islamophobic populist entity which is attempting to take advantage of the rise of anti-Islamic and anti-immigrant sentiment. According to the ministry, it intentionally uses information that is taken out of context, misinterpreted or generalised.


IVČRN was created in July 2009 as a discussion community on Facebook, with a few hundred users. According to the Ministry of the Interior, the platform was created as a transformation of the pre-existing Czech Defence League (CzDL), based on the [[ukEDL|English Defence League]], which was assessed as extremist and subsequently disappeared. The group draws ideologically from the counter-jihad movement.

The group's Facebook page has been banned several times, first in 2014 when it had 162,000 followers, and then in 2016, when it had 73,000 followers.[5][6] The original page with 162,000 followers was restored in December 2016.

In May 2016, former DOMOV party rebranded to the [[czBPI|Bloc Against Islamization – Defence of the Homeland]] (BPI).

IVČRN was dissolved in 2025.

description.text:
Aa Czech anti-Islam organisation led by Martin Konvička, founded in 2009. The Czech Ministry of the Interior has described the initiative as an Islamophobic populist entity which is attempting to take advantage of the rise of anti-Islamic and anti-immigrant sentiment. According to the ministry, it intentionally uses information that is taken out of context, misinterpreted or generalised.


IVČRN was created in July 2009 as a discussion community on Facebook, with a few hundred users. According to the Ministry of the Interior, the platform was created as a transformation of the pre-existing Czech Defence League (CzDL), based on the [[ukEDL|English Defence League]], which was assessed as extremist and subsequently disappeared. parties.description:
An extremist, far-right, neo-Nazi and neo-Nazi political party that was founded on 20 December 2002 and dissolved on 17 February 2010 by a decision of the Supreme Administrative Court. The court concluded that it posed an immediate risk of endangering democracy because it was ideologically linked to national socialism and neo-Nazism and supported violence. On 15 March, it filed a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court of the Czech Republic against this judgment, but on 27 May 2010, the Constitutional Court rejected it and upheld the decision of the Supreme Administrative Court.[The legitimacy of the party's dissolution was then addressed by the European Court of Human Rights, which, however, stopped the proceedings on 26 March 2013 due to the procedural passivity of the complainants.

Its representatives, including Vandas, subsequently shifted their membership to the [[czDSSS|Workers' Party of Social Justice]] , founded in 2004.

parties.name: Workers' Party of Social Justice
parties.relations: In 2010, after the [[czDS|Workers' Party]] (DS) was banned, members of the Workers' Party took over SORČ and rebranded it as DSSS.
parties.description:
The party was founded in 2004 as the Party of Citizens of the Czech Republic (SORČ). SORČ had almost no members and practically no political activity. After a year of existence, its founder Jan Broj and 1st Vice-Chairman Tomáš Magnusek left the party, and SORČ was taken over by representatives of the [[csDS|Workers' Party]] (DS).

In 2006, Hana Pavlíčková, mother of Tomáš Vandas, became the party's chairwoman, who replaced her as chairwoman after the dissolution of the Workers' Party, which operated from 2002 to 2010, on 20 November 2010. Since the judicial dissolution of the [[csDS|Workers' Party]] in February 2010, the DSSS has acted as its successor.

On 19 October 2024, the party was dissolved and liquidated by a resolution of the congress.
parties.ideology:
The party's program called for the overthrow and subversion of the Czech political system, which the party described both as "liberal" and "totalitarian". Its official slogan for the 2009 European elections was: "Resist the totalitarian regime". Some high-ranking party officials, including a Prague party leader, were associated with neo-Nazi groups such as Národní odpor, the Czech subsidiary of an international militant neo-Nazi group.

The party's program included reducing national debt while increasing old age pensions and reducing the retirement age. Concrete proposals included restrictions on foreign investment, including a total ban on purchases of real estate by foreign nationals,[22] and nationalization of certain companies.

The party also wanted to restore the death penalty, criminalize "sexual deviation", including homosexuality, abolish registered partnership, reduce the rights of criminal defendants, and in some cases create new crimes with a retroactive effect. Some of the most controversial proposals included marking of ethnicity in ID cards, and giving the police discretion to treat arrestees inhumanely.[23]

In international affairs, the party opposed NATO and the European Union, and demanded that the Czech Republic leave those organizations. The party was strongly anti-American and pro-Russian, stating that the Czech Republic must "immediately and strongly restore its relations with Russia". The chairman of the party arbitration commission congratulated Mahmoud Ahmadinejad of Iran after his victory in the 2009 presidential election.

parties.name: Zlín Movement of Independents
parties.description:
A Czech political aprty that regularly participated in elections in the Zlín Region. The ZHN was registered by the Ministry of the Interior in May 1998.

In the 1998 municipal elections, the ZHN in Zlín came in fourth place, receiving 11.62% of the vote and winning 4 seats (Zdeněk Dostál, Svatava Nováčková, František Petr and Petr Kotík). The leader of the candidate, Zdeněk Dostál, was elected mayor of Zlín on 27 November 1998, after coalition negotiations (he held the position until 14 November 2002).

In the 2000 regional elections in 2000, ZHN finished in fifth place with a gain of 11.95%, which meant 6 mandates (Jaroslav Kubín, Jiří Deml, Jiří Severin, Pavel Horák, Zdeněk Pánek and Jaromír Čáp).

In the 2002 municipal elections, it came in third place with 14.52% of the vote and won 6 seats (Svatava Nováčková, František Petr, Zdeněk Dostál , Ludvík Pavlištík, Jaromír Šebek and Karel Jankovič). However, ZHN did not enter the city government and remained in opposition.

In the 2004 regional elections in 2004, ZHN ran with independent candidates under the name "ZHN and SNK together", but failed with a gain of 4.69%.

It remained outside the ruling coalition even after the municipal elections in 2006, when fifth place meant 7.23% of the votes and 3 mandates (Svatava Nováčková, Zdeněk Dostál and Karel Markytán).

In the 2008 regional elections, ZHN also ran with independent candidates, this time under the name "Mayors and Independents for the Zlín Region". This grouping came in fifth place with a share of the vote of 10.08% and five mandates (two were ZHN nominees, namely Jaroslav Kubín and Pavel Horák).

In the 2010 municipal elections, ZHN came in eighth place, winning 5.28  % of the vote and two seats (Karel Markytán, František Petr). After the 2010 elections (after an eight-year hiatus), ZHN became part of the ruling coalition, and Karel Markytán was elected as a non-vacant member of the Zlín City Council for social affairs, churches, culture, national minorities and heritage preservation. During the election period, František Petr resigned from his representative mandate and was replaced by Kateřina Francová.

For the 2012 regional elections, ZHN formed an electoral coalition with the movement Doctors for the Healing of Society. The joint candidate under the name "Doctors and Experts for the Healing of the Region" received 2.59% of the votes and its representatives did not make it to the regional council.

In the 2014 municipal elections, the movement did not run for the Zlín City Council on its own, but its members appeared on the candidate lists of other entities. Specifically, these were Kateřina Francová and Karel Bartoňek on the [[czSTAN|STAN]] candidate list and Karel Markytán, whom the Zlín 21 movement placed on the candidate list of the [[czKDUCSL|KDU-ČSL]] and "[[czZ21|Zlín 21]] - Together for Zlín" entities. Kateřina Francová and Karel Markytán succeeded and continue in their positions as city councilors.

Kateřina Francová became the deputy mayor for a non-vacant period, responsible for education, social affairs and care for the disabled. She also serves as a member of the Social and Disabled Committee and the Education and Training Committee. Karel Markytán is a member of the Cultural Committee.

The ZHN movement did not run in the 2016 regional elections. Accordingly, only one member participated in the elections in the Zlín Region, namely Vítězslav Vicherek on the [[czSTAN|STAN]] candidate list (however, he was not elected).

ZHN was legally dissolved on 17 June 2026.
parties.ideology: ZHN was founded on the belief that, in addition to political parties, a community of independent personalities should also be publicly active, with the ability to influence public affairs.
parties.leadership:
Chairperson:
František Petr


The highest body of the ZHN was the General Assembly. It was composed of all members of the movement. The General Assembly elected members of the ZHN bodies, i.e. the Supervisory Board, the Board of Directors and two spokesmen from among the members of the Board of Directors.

parties.name: Změna Political Movement
parties.relations: Split from the [[czZeleni|Green Party]] (SZ).
parties.description:
A Czech political movement founded in 2012 by Jan Korytář. 
The movement was active mainly in the Liberec Region and its strong theme was the fight against corruption. 

In 2013, Změna participated in the parliamentary election. In the municipal elections of 2014, 2018 and 2022, the movement ran independently, in electoral coalitions and in associations with independent candidates in a number of municipalities across the Czech Republic. By a resolution of its national assembly on 13 May 2023, the Změna movement voluntarily dissolved itself.
parties.ideology:
The ideology of political movement Změna was based on the principles of green politics, which it declared as its ideological foundation, especially the ideas of sustainable development, equal opportunities, civic participation and the promotion of the public interest.[9] It occupied an approximately central position in the right-left political spectrum.

In terms of program and personnel, Změna was close to the [[czZeleni|Green Party]], from which its founder Jan Korytář left in 2012. The two groups then cooperated, especially in Liberec municipal and regional politics, but did not agree on a common approach for the parliamentary elections in 2013.

parties.name: Alliance for Peace and Freedom
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[euENF|European National Front]]
parties.description:
A far-right European political alliance and former European political party founded on 4 February 2015. The main member parties were involved in the defunct [[euENF|European National Front]].

The alliance wishes to establish a network of nationalist movements across Europe that will cooperate to strengthen their shared ideals. It cooperates and supports other nationalist groups across Europe that are not members, these include former party members [[grXA|Golden Dawn]], [[itFT|Tricolour Flame]], [[seAfS|Alternative for Sweden]] and the [[cyELAM|ELAM]]. The alliance is described as neo-Nazi by several newspapers, and neo-fascist by others.

The group works for "a Europe of sovereign nations in which the independent states work together on a confederated basis", and for the perennity and the safeguarding of ancestral European traditions such as the Christian tradition.

parties.name: Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe Party
parties.description:
A liberal European political party composed of national parties from across Europe, mainly active in the European Union. The ALDE Party is affiliated with [[intLI|Liberal International]] and a recognised European political party, incorporated as a non-profit association under Belgian law.

It was founded on 26 March 1976 in Stuttgart as a confederation of national political parties under the name "Federation of Liberal and Democrat Parties in Europe" and renamed "European Liberals and Democrats" (ELD) in 1977 and "European Liberal Democrats and Reformists" (ELDR) in 1986. On 30 April 2004, the ELDR was reformed as an official European party, the "European Liberal Democrat and Reform Party" (ELDR Party).

On 10 November 2012, under the leadership of Sir Graham Watson MEP, the party chose its current name ALDE Party, taken from its then-European Parliament group, the Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe (ALDE), which had been formed on 20 July 2004 in conjunction with the [[euEDP|European Democratic Party]] (EDP). Prior to the 2004 European election, the European party had been represented through its own group, the European Liberal Democrat and Reform Party Group (ELDR) Group. In June 2019, the ALDE group was succeeded by Renew Europe.

As of 2024, ALDE Party is represented in European Union institutions, with 51 MEPs and five members of the European Commission. Of the 27 EU member states, there are two with ALDE-affiliated Prime Ministers: Kristen Michal ([[eeRE|Estonian Reform Party]]) in Estonia and Alexander De Croo ([[beOpenVld|Open VLD]]) in Belgium. ALDE Party members are also in governments in ten other EU member states: Cyprus, France, Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Ireland, Luxembourg, Lithuania, Germany and the Netherlands. Charles Michel, former Belgian prime minister, was the president of the European Council until December 2024.

ALDE's think tank is the European Liberal Forum, led by Jan-Christoph Oetjen MEP, and gathers 46 member organisations. The youth wing of ALDE is the European Liberal Youth (LYMEC), which is predominantly based upon youth and student liberal organisations but contains also a small number of individual members. LYMEC is led by Ines Holzegger.

In 2011, ALDE Party became the first European political party to create the status of individual membership. Since then, between 1000 and close to 3000 members (the numbers fluctuate annually) maintained direct membership in the ALDE Party from several EU countries. Over 40 coordinators mobilised liberal ideas, initiatives and expertise across the continent under the leadership of the steering committee, which was first chaired by Julie Cantalou. ALDE later took a step further when granting voting rights to individual members' delegates at the Party Congress. Individual membership was eventually discontinued in 2023.

In 2025, the Alliance was declared an undesirable organization in Russia.

A social democratic European political alliance gathering parties and labour councils in Nordic countries.

SAMAK consists of all social democratic parties and trade union organisations in the Nordic countries, including in Greenland, the Faroe Islands and Åland. The current president of the committee as of 2024 is Mette Frederiksen, the leader of the [[dkA|Social Democrats]] and Prime Minister of Denmark. The committee was formed during the first Scandinavian Workers' Congress in Gothenburg in 1886.

SAMAK holds a congress every four years, while the board meets four to six times per year.

A populist European political alliance founded in summer 2020 by non-attached MEPs Mislav Kolakušić and Dorien Rookmaker.

According to the EAFD, its policy is based on the following principles: the rule of law and the fight against corruption both at the level of the EU and at the level of its member states, freedom of thought and speech as well as equality between citizens and between the member states of the EU.

parties.name: European Communist Action
parties.description:
A Marxist–Leninist European political alliance. It was established on 18 November 2023 after its predecessor organization, the [[euINITIATIVE|Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties]], was dissolved.

The ECA was established with the aim of promoting scientific socialism, opposing the European Union (EU) and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and challenging capitalist exploitation and imperialism. The ECA regards the EU as an imperialist bloc and is dedicated to the principles of class struggle and the rights of workers, advocating for socialism as an alternative to the current capitalist system in Europe.

parties.name: European Democratic Party
parties.relations: Split from the [[euEPP|European People's Party]].
parties.description:
A centrist European political party in favour of European integration. Within the European Parliament, its MEPs form the Renew Europe group, together with those of the [[euALDE|Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe]] party and the French [[frRE|Renaissance]] party. The President is François Bayrou.

As of 2026, EDP members participate in the national government of two EU member states: [[be|LE|Les Engagés]] in Belgium, which participates in the government of Prime Minister Bart De Wever and, EDP individual member Marian Harkin, who participates in the government of Taoiseach Micheál Martin. Two European regions are also led by an EDP politician, with Spain's Basque Country being led by Imanol Pradales of the [[esEAJPNV|Basque Nationalist Party]] and with Spain's Canary Islands being led by Fernando Clavijo Batlle of the [[esCC|Canarian Coalition]]; EDP member [[deFV|Free Voters]] participates as a junior coalition partner in the state government of Bavaria in Germany, as does [[itIV|Italia Viva]] in Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany, Campania and Basilicata and Les Engagés in Wallonia and the Wallonia-Brussels Federation.

The European Democratic Party is also a member of the European Movement International and was a member of the World [[intAD|Alliance of Democrats]] until its dissolution in 2012.

parties.relations: Preceded by the [[euEFGP|European Federation of Green Parties]].
parties.description:
A European political party composed of national parties from across Europe who share Green values.

The European Greens works closely with the Greens–European Free Alliance (Greens/EFA) parliamentary group in the European Parliament which is formed by elected Green party members along with the European Free Alliance, European Pirate Party and Volt Europa. The European Greens' partners include its youth wing the Federation of Young European Greens (FYEG), the Green European Foundation (GEF) and the [[intGG|Global Greens]] family.

Green parties participate in the government of one country in Europe: Spain ([[esComuns|Catalunya en Comú]]/[[esSMR|Sumar]]). They also externally support the government in Poland ([[plZieloni|Zieloni]]/[[plKO|Civic Coalition]]).

parties.name: European People's Party
parties.description:
A European political party with Christian democratic, liberal-conservative, and conservative member parties. Founded by primarily Christian-democratic parties in 1976, it has since broadened its membership to include liberal-conservative parties and parties with other centre-right political perspectives. On 31 May 2022, the party elected as its President Manfred Weber, who was also EPP's Spitzenkandidat in 2019.

The EPP has been the largest party in the European Parliament since 1999 and in the European Council since 2002. It is also the largest party in the current European Commission. The President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen and the President of the European Parliament, Roberta Metsola are from the EPP. Many of the founding fathers of the European Union were also from parties that later formed the EPP.

The EPP includes major centre-right parties such as the [[deCDUCSU|CDU/CSU]] of Germany, the [[esPP|People's Party]] (PP) of Spain, [[itFI2013|Forza Italia]] of Italy, [[frLR|The Republicans]] of France, [[atOVP|ÖVP]] of Austria, [[hrHDZ|HDZ]] of Croatia, [[roPNL|PNL]] of Romania, [[ieFG|Fine Gael]] of Ireland, [[fiKok|National Coalition Party]] of Finland, [[grND|New Democracy]] of Greece, the [[seM|Moderates]] of Sweden, the [[plKO|Civic Coalition]] of Poland, the [[ptPSD|Social Democratic Party]] of Portugal, the [[huTISZA|Tisza Party]] of Hungary, and the [[bgGERB|GERB]] of Bulgaria.

parties.name: European Pirate Party
parties.description:
A pirate European political alliance. Despite its organisation and sometimes being referred to as a "European party" or "transnational party", the European Pirate Party does not meet the requirements to register as a European political party.

The European Pirates were founded on 21 March 2014 at the European Parliament in Brussels in the context of a conference on "European Internet Governance and Beyond", and consists of pirate parties of European countries. The parties cooperated to run a joint campaign for the 2014 European Parliament elections.

The founding meeting elected Amelia Andersdotter, Swedish Member of the European Parliament for Piratpartiet, as the first chairperson. The party's members elected to the European Parliament are in The Greens–European Free Alliance.

In November 2020, a new board was elected. Mikuláš Peksa was confirmed as a chairperson, Florie Marie (France) and Katla Hólm Vilbergs Þórhildardóttir (Iceland) were elected as chairperson. Alessandro Ciofini (Italy), Lukáš Doležal, Jan Mareš (both Czech Republic) and Mia Utz, Oliver Herzig (both Germany) were elected as ordinary members of the board.

In the 2024 European Parliament election, it lost three of its four seats.[6] The Pirate Party of Greece unanimously decided, in its 12th Congress held on 1 June 2025, to leave the PPEU and the Pirate Parties International, citing ideological issues, a lack of political added value, and a lack of room for "constructive and productive political discourse".

parties.name: Europeans United for Democracy
parties.description:
The party was set up under Danish law on 7 November 2005 and founded as a European Party in Brussels on 8 November 2005. Its first congress was held on 24 February 2006. Former Danish MEPs Jens-Peter Bonde and Hanne Dahl inspired the EUD's creation and first years. In January 2009, Swedish economist and former MEP Sören Wibe succeeded Bonde as President of the EUD. Following Wibe's sudden death in December 2010, former Irish Green MEP Patricia McKenna was named president of the EUD and Lave Knud Broch from [[dkN|People's Movement against the EU]] as vice president.

The founding parties of the party included the Danish [[dkJB|June Movement]] from Jens-Peter Bonde (who also became the first president of the party), the [[plSRP|Self-Defence of the Republic of Poland]], the [[seJL|June List]] from Sweden and the [[dkN|Danish People's Movement Against the EU]]. The party had to rely on the assistance of individual Members of Parliament in order to reach the representational threshold of seven member states — these members included Roger Helmer, UK [[ukConservative|Conservative]] Daniel Hannan, Igor Gräzin from the Estonian [[eeRE|Reform Party]], Nicolas Dupont-Aignan from [[frDLF|Debout la République]], Sandor Leszak and Andras Ptiski from [[huFidedz|FIDESZ]], Irish independent Kathy Sinnott, Klaus Buchner from the German [[deODP|Ecological Democratic Party]] and Iveta Grigule from the [[lvLZS|Latvian Farmers' Union]]. These parties and members came from all sides of the political spectrum and were united in their criticism of the EU, although in varying degrees.

In 2009, four of its affiliated MEPs were members of the [[euINDDEM|Independence/Democracy]] group in the European Parliament. Also, two affiliated MEPs - Roger Helmer and Daniel Hannan, both British [[ukConservative|Conservatives]] - sat as independents. Hannan left EUD in October 2009 to join the newly formed [[euAECR|Alliance of European Conservatives and Reformists]], while Helmer defected from the British Conservatives to British party [[ukUKIP|UKIP]]. From 2010 to 2014 EUD had one member in the European Parliament: Rina Ronja Kari (replaced Søren Søndergaard 5 February 2014), who sits as an associate member of the European United Left/Nordic Green Left Group. In the 2014 European Parliament elections two EUD members Rina Ronja Kari and Iveta Grigule were elected.

Ten members of national and regional parliaments from ten countries were also members of the EUD (as of 2014).
parties.ideology:
Eurosceptic and self-described Eurorealist European political party. It sought a radical decentralization or a complete abolition of the EU. It incorporated members from both the right and the left political spectrum; however, it was dominated by left-wing parties and represented ideologically left-wing faction of Euroscepticism.

Although the EUD's platform was not concerned with specific ideological matters, as it believed that such issues were best dealt with by national and regional parliaments under the democratic control of the people, the party itself was considered left-wing; David Hanley, head of the School of European Studies at Cardiff University, called it a "core statement of left-wing Euroscepticism". The EUD cooperated with other left-wing European parties. The party was committed to increasing transparency, subsidiarity, diversity and budgetary control in the European Union, wanting to limit the Union to a free-trade zone and a safeguard of social and environmentalist standards, with integration efforts being only optional and limited to the minimum. The EU was to be prohibited from dictating a common foreign, economic and security policy to all members, and elements of membership were to be elective, with member states able to choose to participate in the free-trade zone only, without partaking in other elements of the European Union.

parties.name: Federal Union of European Nationalities
parties.description:
An international non-governmental organization (NGO) established in 1949 in conjunction with the formation of the Council of Europe. FUEN is an umbrella organization, and as of 2023, it has more than 100 member organizations representing ethnic, linguistic and national minorities within Europe. FUEN has been instrumental in encouraging the Council of Europe to adopt the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages and the Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities. FUEN was organized to give expression to European cultures and languages that do not possess form as a nation-state. One in seven Europeans are members of such minorities and fifty-three languages are spoken in Europe by such minorities.

Its predecessor was the pre-war European Congress of Nations (German: Europäischer Nationalitätenkongress) founded by Ewald Ammende. The Congress published a journal "Nation und Staat" (1927–1944).[

FUEN organises the Europeada association football tournament.[3] In 2017-2018, FUEN collected 1,124,322 signatures from EU citizens for the Minority SafePack European Citizens' Initiative.

It is based in Flensburg, Germany, with offices in Berlin and Brussels. Its president is Olivia Schubert a German from Hungary, who succeeded in 2025 Lóránt Vincze, a Hungarian from Romania and MEP.

parties.name: Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties
parties.description:
A Marxist–Leninist European political alliance. Founded by the [[grKKE|Communist Party of Greece]] in 2013, the initiative had 30 member parties from all over Europe and the surrounding area.

Its goal was to "contribute to the research and study of issues concerning Europe, particularly concerning the EU, the political line which is drawn up in its framework and affects the lives of the workers, as well as to assist the elaboration of joint positions of the parties and the coordination of their solidarity and their other activities".

On 9 September 2023, the organisation was dissolved following ideological and political differences between the association's members over the topic of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The [[euECA|European Communist Action]] was established on 18 November 2023 as a continuation of the INITIATIVE association created by the [[grKKE|Communist Party of Greece]].

parties.name: Movement for a Europe of Liberties and Democracy
parties.nativeName: Mouvement pour l'Europe des libertés et de la démocratie
parties.description:
A national-conservative European political party founded in 2011, composed of parties belonging to the Europe of Freedom and Democracy (EFD) group in the European Parliament, with the notable absence of the [[ukUKIP|UK Independence Party]], which was a member of the EFD, but not of the MELD. In 2012, MELD received a grant from the European Parliament of €621,482. Its affiliated European political foundation was the Foundation for a Europe of Liberties and Democracy (FELD), which received a grant of €412,361. Both were headquartered at 18, rue Cler, in Paris, France. The president of the party was Jacek Wlosowicz.

MELD was dissolved in 2015 by the European Parliament due to misuse of EU funding.

parties.name: Volt Europa
parties.description:
A transnational pro-European and federalist European political movement. It operates as a pan-European umbrella for subsidiary parties sharing the same name and branding.

Volt aligns its political positions across Europe, presenting a common, pan-European manifesto. In the 2019 European Parliament elections, Volt ran in eight member states with a shared platform, emphasising solutions to supranational challenges, such as climate change, defense, energy policy, migration, economic inequality, terrorism, welfare, and the technological evolution of the labor market. The party advocates for a stronger, more integrated European Union, with the long-term goal of creating a federal Europe. Additionally, Volt endorses the formation of a European army, joint European debt and taxes, nuclear energy including the construction of new nuclear power plants, and stronger economic solidarity between the EU member states.

Initially using the slogan "Neither left nor right", Volt is now generally perceived as centrist or centre-left, with a core focus on evidence-based policy and best-practice sharing among EU countries and municipalities. It campaigns on these principles in both local and national elections.

Founded in March 2017, Volt's first national subsidiary party was established in Hamburg, Germany, a year later. Since then, Volt has developed local teams in all EU member states, as well as in non-EU countries like Albania, Switzerland, Kosovo, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom. Volt subsidiaries are now registered political parties in many of these countries, most recently expanding to Cyprus, Romania and Slovenia.

Despite its organisation and being referred to as a "European party" or "transnational party", Volt does not yet meet the requirements to register as a European political party.

parties.name: Christopistía
parties.description:
Χριστοπιστία is an compound formed from Χριστός (“Christ”) and πίστη (“faith”), it's not Greek name for "Christianity" (Χριστιανισμός).

The party was founded in 1993 by Efstathios Patsantzis, as a continuation of the parties he had formed in previous elections (the "Olympic Democracy" in the national elections of 1977, 1981, 1985 and 1989 and the "Vasilomachos" in those of 1990).

It took part in national elections in 1993, 1996, 2000 and 2004, while in European elections in 1994, 1999 with 4 candidate] and 2004. It participated in the Inter-Party Election Committee in 200]. Since then, it has stopped taking part in elections, since it did not submit a combination in the 2007 elections (although it had submitted a declaration of participation). In the 2014 European elections, Patsantzis participated in the ballot of the National Resistance Movement (KEAN) of Hippocrates Savvouras, but ultimately called for people to abstain, asking that he not be voted for either, when he discovered that Savvouras had not registered him on the ballot as "Patsantzis Efstathios tou Dimitris – Monogenes", as they had agreed, but had removed "Monogenis".

In 1993 Patsantzis received 66 votes, in the 1994 European elections 18 votes, in the 1996 parliamentary elections 71 votes, in the 1999 European elections 2,153 votes, in the 2000 elections 305 votes, in those of 7 March 2004 45 votes and in the 2004 European elections 95 votes.
parties.ideology:
The party’s defining ideas came from an idiosyncratic reading of Revelation. In 2004, Patsantzis told Kathimerini that voters should write the party's name on a blank ballot because a passage in Revelation referred to a white ballot; he explained the name as faith in the divine name of Jesus Christ. Its emblem was described as a circular double cross or "divine forehead seal of Revelation."

Patsantzis promised the resurrection of the dead after the election and claimed that supporters would receive a sacred apocalyptic seal protecting and separating them from the Antichrists.

It is reported that Patsantzis carried a Christopistia placard in Syntagma Square, which he had hanging from his neck and a "circular double cross" symbol on his forehead which is part of the party's emblem.

parties.nativeName:

parties.relations:
Founded by 1924 breakaway circles from [[grSEKE|Socialist Workers' Party of Greece (Communist)]] (SEKE(K));

Succeeded by [[grSAKE|Communist Archio-Marxist Party of Greece]] (KAKE) and [[grMLOE|Bolshevik-Leninist Organization of Greece]] (MLOE)
parties.description:
Trotskyist Archeio-Marxist organization that was active during the period 1929-1934.

In the autumn of 1921, a political movement was created within the [[grSEKE|SEKE]] under Frangiskos Tzulati, originating from the faction of the Communist Union. This movement, called the First Core, took on a specific structure and goals during the period 1922-1923. This process was completed on May Day 1923 with the publication of the journal "Arkeho Marxismo", from which they borrowed their name. The aim of the movement, which was later renamed Ergasia, was the educational intervention in the, class-wise immature at that time, Proletariat. The essence of its action was contained in the slogan "First education, then action". In February 1923, this movement was expelled from SEKE. In 1925, Tzoulati resigned from the leadership of the movement to give his place to Dimitris Giotopoulos, despite the fact that the latter did not participate in the formation of the First Core. In 1929, Giotopoulos played a leading role in the creation of the "Union of Communist Internationalists", an Archeio-Marxist organization that came into contact and collaborated with Trotsky and that intervened in the Labor Movement for the first time.

In 1930, the EKD, in its new framework, was transformed into KOMLEA. In the same year, the first split will occur, when a group under Michalis Raptis will leave to form the Communist United Group, also Trotskyist but not Archeio-Marxist, without however creating a problem for the newly formed KOMLEA. KOMLEA intervenes massively in the working class, winning over a series of labor unions of specific branches. A total of 27 unions come under its control. At the same time, KOMLEA leader Giotopoulos is elected a member, and later secretary, of the secretariat of the Trotskyist Left Opposition, using the pseudonym Witte. The official newspaper of the Organization will become the Class Struggle. At the same time, a series of archaic Marxist newspapers will be circulated in specific unions. KOMLEA would maintain several differences in its policy in relation to the KKE, especially on the issue of Macedonia, where the Archaeo-Marxist Organization would defend the Greek character of Macedonia, already from the Labor era, before the KKE adopted this stance. However, it would constitute the main opposition organization to the KKE, according to the Trotskyist standards of the time.

In 1934, the radical disagreements between Giotopoulos and Trotsky, combined with Witte's authoritarian deviations in the Left Opposition, will contribute to the split of KOMLEA into two warring groups: the Trotskyist group of Giorgis Vitsoris and the traditional archaeo-Marxist and no longer purely Trotskyist group of Witte, which will be transformed into the [[grSAKE|Communist Archaeo-Marxist Party of Greece]]. The new archaeo-Marxist formation will not acquire the mass character of KOMLEA, the most massive organization in the history of Greek Trotskyism.

parties.description: An anarchist urban guerrilla organization based in Greece. The SPF first surfaced in January 2008, with a wave of 11 firebombings against luxury car dealerships and banks in Athens and Thessaloniki. Monthly waves of arson have been followed by proclamations expressing solidarity with arrested anarchists in Greece and elsewhere. In September 2009, following an escalation to the use of crude time bombs, four suspected members of the group were arrested. In November 2010 two more suspects were arrested while attempting to mail parcel bombs to embassies and EU leaders and organizations.
