parties.name: Kach
parties.description:
A radical Orthodox Jewish, religious Zionist political party in Israel, existing from 1971 to 1994. Founded by Rabbi Meir Kahane in 1971 based on his Jewish-Orthodox-nationalist ideology (subsequently dubbed Kahanism), the party won a single seat in the Knesset in the 1984 elections, after several electoral failures. However, it was barred from participating in the next elections in 1988 under the revised Knesset Elections Law banning parties that incited racism. After Kahane's assassination in 1990 the party split, with [[ilKCh|Kahane Chai]] ("Kahane Lives") breaking away from the main Kach faction.

The party was ultimately also barred from standing in the 1992 elections and both organisations were banned outright in 1994 by the Israeli cabinet under 1948 anti-terrorism laws, following statements in support of Baruch Goldstein's massacre of 29 Palestinians at the Cave of the Patriarchs (Goldstein himself was a Kach supporter).

Both groups are designated as terrorist organisations by Israel, Canada, Japan, and formerly the European Union, as well as the United States. They are believed to have an overlapping core membership of fewer than 100 people, with links to the modern party [[ilOtzma|Otzma Yehudit]].

Following the outlawing of the Kach movement, some of the movement's activists chose to abandon the radical messages that led to the movement's disqualification and return to the legitimate political arena. The most prominent of these activists was Baruch Marzel, who, in the run-up to the 16th Knesset elections, joined Michael Kleiner in the [[ilHerutNM|Herut]] party. Applications to disqualify Marzel from running for the Knesset were rejected by the High Court of Justice, which accepted Marzel's claim that he had abandoned those parts of Kach's platform that were prohibited by law. Marzel ran again in the 17th Knesset elections as part of the [[ilHayil|Jewish National Front]] (later [[ilOtzma|Otzma Yehudit]]).

parties.name: Meimad
parties.description:
Founded as a political movement, transformed into a party in 1999.

The Meimad movement was founded on 1 June 1988 by Rabbi Yehuda Amital, and included former [[ilMafdal|National Religious Party]] Knesset member Yehuda Ben-Meir. It emerged from Oz ve Shalom (Strength and Peace), an Orthodox Jewish peace movement. It contested the 1988 Knesset elections, receiving 0.7% of the vote and failing to cross the 1% electoral threshold. Following the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995, his successor, Shimon Peres, invited Rabbi Amital to serve as a Minister without Portfolio. He held this position until 1996.

Eleven years later, a political party for the movement was established, and joined the [[ilOI|One Israel]] alliance that won the Knesset elections that year. Meimad received one seat, taken by Michael Melchior. It gained a second when Yehuda Gilad replaced Maxim Levy in 2002. Tova Ilan also represented Meimad in the Knesset for a brief spell in 2006, after several other Labor MKs resigned. It attracted moderates among immigrants from the English-speaking world, including Shimon Glick.

In November 2008, minister and former [[ilAvoda|Labor Party]] member Ami Ayalon joined Meimad. In the same month, the party ended its alliance with Labor after being told that 10th spot on the list would no longer be reserved for Meimad for the 2009 legislative elections.

Shortly afterwards, Ayalon announced his resignation from politics, and the party formed an umbrella alliance with the [[ilGM|Green Movement]]. The Green-Meimad list remained outside the Knesset, even though it received over twenty-eight thousand votes - the largest number of votes among the parties that did not pass the electoral threshold.

In 2012, Melchior announced that he would not stand for election. The party was revived in 2018. In 2019, ahead of the next Knesset elections, Rabbi Melchior explained why the party would not run for the Knesset, saying that raising the threshold would most likely result in a loss of votes, and that "Memad was the first religious party to come to the conclusion that we no longer need sectoral religious parties."

parties.description:
Telem was formed on 19 May 1981 during the ninth Knesset by Moshe Dayan and two ex-[[ilLikud|Likud]] MKs. Dayan had been elected to the Knesset as an MK for the [[ilAlignment|Alignment]], which had lost the election for the first time in its history. Menachem Begin formed a coalition including his Likud party, the [[ilMafdal|National Religious Party]], [[ilAgudat|Agudat Israel]], and [[ilDash|Dash]]. However, he also invited Dayan to serve as Minister of Foreign Affairs. Despite being a member of the Alignment, Begin's political rival, Dayan accepted the post, resulting in his expulsion from his own party.

After sitting as an independent MK for some time, Dayan formed Telem in 1981, together with Yigal Hurvitz and Zalman Shoval, who had previously broken away from Likud to form [[ilRafiNL|Rafi – National List]]. On 15 June 1981, they were joined by Shafik Assad, who had left [[ilAhva|Ahva]] (Assad had started the Knesset session as a member of Dash, then joined the [[ilDM|Democratic Movement]] before moving to Ahva).

The party won two seats in the 1981 elections, taken by Dayan and Mordechai Ben-Porat, and was invited to join the governing coalition, with Ben-Porat becoming Minister Without Portfolio. When Dayan died on 16 October 1981, he was replaced by Hurvitz. However, the party split up on 6 June 1983, when Ben-Porat created the [[ilMRSZ|Movement for the Renewal of Social Zionism]] and Hurvitz reformed Rafi – National List, which he later renamed [[ilOmetz|Ometz]].

Telem was formed on 19 May 1981 during the ninth Knesset by Moshe Dayan and two ex-[[ilLikud|Likud]] MKs. Dayan had been elected to the Knesset as an MK for the [[ilAlignment|Alignment]], which had lost the election for the first time in its history. Menachem Begin formed a coalition including his Likud party, the [[ilMafdal|National Religious Party]], [[ilAgudat|Agudat Israel]], and [[ilDash|Dash]]. However, he also invited Dayan to serve as Minister of Foreign Affairs. Despite being a member of the Alignment, Begin's political rival, Dayan accepted the post, resulting in his expulsion from his own party.

After sitting as an independent MK for some time, Dayan formed Telem in 1981, together with Yigal Hurvitz and Zalman Shoval, who had previously broken away from Likud to form [[ilRafiNL|Rafi – National List]]. On 15 June 1981, they were joined by Shafik Assad, who had left [[ilAhva|Ahva]] (Assad had started the Knesset session as a member of Dash, then joined the [[ilDM|Democratic Movement]] before moving to Ahva).

The party won two seats in the 1981 elections, taken by Dayan and Mordechai Ben-Porat, and was invited to join the governing coalition, with Ben-Porat becoming Minister Without Portfolio. When Dayan died on 16 October 1981, he was replaced by Hurvitz. However, the party split up on 6 June 1983, when Ben-Porat created the [[ilMRSZ|Movement for the Renewal of Social Zionism]] and Hurvitz reformed Rafi – National List, which he later renamed [[ilOmetz|Ometz]].

Ben-Porat subsequently joined [[ilTelem1981|Telem]] and was elected to the Knesset on its list in 1981. However, after becoming a Minister without Portfolio, he left Telem and established the Movement for the Renewal of Social Zionism as a Knesset faction on 6 June 1983 by Minister, following the break-up of (its other member, Yigael Hurvitz, refounded [[ilRafiNL|Rafi – National List]]).

The party failed to cross the electoral threshold in the 1984 elections and subsequently disappeared. Ben-Porat moved on, joining [[ilLikud|Likud]] in 1988.

parties.relations: Merged into the [[ilMaki1948|Maki]] in Israel and the [[joJCP|Jordanian Communist Party]] in the West Bank;
parties.description:
A political party in Mandatory Palestine, founded in early 1944 by Arab members of the [[ilPKP|Palestine Communist Party]] (which had experienced a split between Jewish and Arab members the previous year), Bulus Farah and his followers, and other trade unionists and left wing intellectuals.

The founders included Haidar Abdel-Shafi, Mukhlis Amer, Emil Habibi, Mufid Nashashibi and Emile Toma. It published the al-Ittihad newspaper in Haifa, a journal which still exists. It was the only Arab Palestinian party to support the 1947 UN Partition Plan, in line with the official position of the Soviet Union.

In October 1948, after the formation of the State of Israel, the NLL merged with [[ilMaki1948|Maki]]. Since both Arab and Jewish Communists still hoped to establish two states on the terms of the UN Partition Plan, it was decided that the Maki and NLL party organizations would merge in the areas that the UN had laid out for a Jewish state, while the NLL would continue to exist as an independent party in areas of Israel that were to have been part of an Arab state under the UN plan. NLL leaders were added to an expanded Maki Central Committee. In practice, the NLL quickly ceased to exist within Israel except in name, and in April 1949 al-Ittihad and its Hebrew sister paper, Kol HaAm, quietly dropped all references to the NLL. On July 20, 1949, Egypt destroyed the remnant of the NLL existing in Gaza, arresting 33 people. In 1951, its members in the West Bank joined the [[joJCP|Jordanian Communist Party]].

parties.relations:

parties.description:
A Zionist paramilitary organization that operated in Mandatory Palestine between 1931 and 1948. It was an offshoot of the older and larger Jewish paramilitary organization [[ilHaganah|Haganah]].

The Irgun policy was based on Revisionist Zionism, founded by Ze'ev Jabotinsky. Two of the most infamous operations for which the Irgun were known; the bombing of the British administrative headquarters for Mandatory Palestine in Jerusalem on 22 July 1946 and the Deir Yassin massacre, carried out with Lehi on 9 April 1948.

The organization committed acts of terrorism against Palestinian Arabs, as well as against the British authorities, who were regarded as illegal occupiers. In particular the Irgun was described as a terrorist organization by the United Nations, British, and United States governments; in media such as The New York Times newspaper; as well as by the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, the 1946 Zionist Congress and the Jewish Agency. Hannah Arendt and Albert Einstein, in a letter to The New York Times in 1948, compared Irgun and its successor [[ilHerut|Herut]] party to "Nazi and Fascist parties" and described it as a "terrorist, right wing, chauvinist organization".

Following the establishment of the State of Israel during the 1948 Palestine war, the Irgun began to be absorbed into the newly created Israel Defense Forces. Conflict between the Irgun and the IDF escalated into the 1948 Altalena Affair, and the Irgun formally disbanded on 12 January 1949. The Irgun was a political predecessor to Israel's right-wing [[ilHerut|Herut]] ("Freedom") party, which led to today's [[ilLikud|Likud]] party. Likud has led or been part of most Israeli governments since 1977.

Merged into [[ilJH|The Jewish Home]].
parties.description:
An Israeli political party representing the interests of the Israeli settlers and religious Zionist movement.

Formed in 1956, at the time of its dissolution in 2008, it was the second-oldest surviving party in the country after [[ilAgudat|Agudat Yisrael]], and was part of every government coalition until 1992. Originally a pragmatic centrist party in its first two decades of existence, it gradually leaned rightward in the following years, particularly becoming increasingly associated with Israeli settlers. Towards the end of its existence, it became part of a far-right political alliance centered around the [[ilNU|National Union]].

The 2006 elections saw the party slump to just three seats, the worst electoral performance in its history. In November 2008, party members voted to disband the party in order to join the new [[ilJH|The Jewish Home]] party created by a merger of the Mafdal and most of the National Union factions. However, most of the National Union left the merger shortly after its implementation.

parties.description:
A political party in Mandatory Palestine and Israel.

The party was established in 1942 by immigrants from Austria and Germany who had arrived in Palestine during the Fifth Aliyah. The party won 19 seats in the 1944 Assembly of Representatives elections, making it the third largest party after [[ilMapai|Mapai]] and the Left Bloc. The party's magazine was named Amudim (lit. Pages).

In May 1948 party leader Pinchas Rosen became a member of the provisional government. At the end of 1948 it merged with several other liberal parties, including the political arm of [[ilHaOtZ|HaOved HaTzioni]], to form the [[ilPP|Progressive Party]].

parties.relations: Historically preceded by the 1950s-1960s [[ilSA|Semitic Action]]
parties.description:
Semitic Action was revived in early 2011 as a grassroots peace movement by activists seeking what they call "a revolutionary alternative to foreign-backed organizations that only exacerbate local frictions and bring the peoples of our region further from genuine peace."

The new Semitic Action describes itself as "an Israel-based movement seeking to unite the indigenous peoples of the Middle East against the devastating influence of foreign powers in our region and the local conflicts created by the pursuit of their interests.[13] Since its resurrection, the movement has organized meetings between Palestinians and Israeli settlers in the West Bank,[14] initiated campaigns to raise support for an independent Kurdistan[15][16] and promoted a unified front of indigenous peoples against foreign political influences in the Middle East. The movement has also been vocal against westernization,[17] globalization,[18] pro-Israel support from the American Christian right,[19] Islamophobia in Israeli society,[20] capitalism[21] and the funding of local political organizations by foreign governments.[22][23]

parties.name: Tafnit
parties.relations: Merged into the [[ilLikud|Likud]].
parties.description:
An Israeli political party and a social movement established by the Aluf in reserve Uzi Dayan.

Tafnit was established as a social movement on 30 May 2005. On 25 December 2005 Dayan announced that the movement would run in the 2006 Knesset elections as an anti-corruption party. However, the party received just 0.6% of the vote, failing to cross the 2% electoral threshold.

In early February 2006 Tafnit unsuccessfully negotiated with the secular parliamentary faction formed by defectors from [[ilShinui|Shinui]], particularly figures around Tommy Lapid and Avraham Poraz (who later founded [[ilHetz|Hetz]] party).

Tafnit merged into [[ilLikud|Likud]] when Dayan joined the party in mid-2008.

parties.description:
On 29 December 2020, Ron Huldai, Mayor of Tel Aviv, announced the establishment of The Israelis party. He was joined by Justice Minister Avi Nissenkorn and MK Einav Kabla, both of whom had recently left the Blue and White party. The State Comptroller records that Huldai became a member of the separate Secular Zionist Party (המפלגה החילונית הציונית) on 11 January 2021, intending that that registered party submit a candidate list called "The Israelis."

However, Nissenkorn left the party on 31 January 2021, reportedly as a prerequisite by Israeli Labor Party leader Merav Michaeli for a merger between both parties, and on 4 February 2021 Huldai announced that the party would not contest the elections, having failed to reach an electoral agreement with other parties.

The Israelis list participated in the 2021 election, but it had no connection to Ron Huldai and was put forward by the previously inactive [[ilisraelis2008|The Israelis]] party, founded in 2008.

parties.name: The Israelis
parties.description:
The Israelis was created in 2008 around political scientist Prof. Gideon Doron. On 19 November 2008, the party had submitted its application to the Registrar of Political Parties. The Israelis was deliberately a "concept party" centred on governmental and electoral reform. Сhanging the electoral/government system was its raison d'être. It received only 865 votes in 2009.

After Doron's death, broadcaster David Kon took over the party and transformed it into a vehicle seeking support among Russian-speaking Israelis dissatisfied with Avigdor Liberman after the Likud–Yisrael Beytenu alliance. ynet explicitly described Kon as chairman and the party as appealing to the "Russian sector."

The party returned for a 2021 election under Yaron Shimon Regev, who had previously been no. 11 on Doron's 2009 list. The 2021 programme again focused on changing the electoral system, constitutional reform and installing professionally qualified ministers.  An unrelated list called [[ilIsraelis2020|The Israelis]], led by Mayor of Tel Aviv Ron Huldai, was scheduled to participate in the 2021 elections, but Huldai withdrew the list on 4 February 2021.

parties.relations:
Split from the [[ilAvoda|Israeli Labor Party]];

Legally succeeded by the [[ilIP|Independence]].
parties.description:
The party was formed on 7 March 1996 towards the end of the thirteenth Knesset's term when two MKs, Avigdor Kahalani and Emanuel Zisman, broke away from the [[ilAvoda|Labour Party]]. Kahalani and Zisman disagreed with the party's willingness to entertain the idea of withdrawing from the Golan Heights in return for peace with Syria. While the party objected to withdrawal from the Golan Heights and took a hawkish position as to Lebanon, it held more moderate views on the peace process.

The party ran in the 1996 elections and won 96,457 votes. This gave them four seats, with Yehuda Harel and Professor Alexander Lubotzky joining Kahalani and Zisman in the Knesset. They were invited to join Netanyahu's [[ilLikud|Likud]]-led government and Kahalani was appointed Minister of Internal Security. On 23 March 1999, Zisman left the party to sit as an independent.

The party ran in the 1999 elections, but faced with a massive loss of support, won only 26,290 votes (0.7%), well below the electoral threshold of 1.5%. After its failure, the party ceased to function, but remained registered. In 2011 its registration was taken over by [[ilIndependence|Independence]].

parties.description:
United Jewish Home was effectively an attempt to revive part of the April 2019 [[ilURWP|Union of Right-Wing Parties]] bloc of [[ilJH|Jewish Home]], [[ilTKuma|National Union–Tkuma]] and [[ilOtzma|Otzma Yehudit]]. In September 2019 election, Jewish Home and Tkuma ran as part of the [[ilYamina|Yamina|#CADB39]] coalition together with [[ilNR|New Right]]. Yamina was dissolved on 10 October 2019.

On the morning of 20 December 2019, [[ilJH|Jewish Home]] chairman Rafi Peretz and [[ilOtzma|Otzma Yehudit]] chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir concluded an agreement for their parties to contest the forthcoming March 2020 Knesset election together. Peretz justified it mainly as an attempt to prevent right-wing votes from being "wasted" below the electoral threshold.

The coalition's actual name came slightly later. On 31 December 2019, the two parties unveiled the joint branding and announced that the list would be called United Jewish Home led by Rabbi Rafi Peretz.

Jewish Home's Central Committee formally ratified Peretz's agreement with Otzma Yehudit on 13 January 2020, only two days before the alliance collapsed.

On 15 January 2020, the final day for submitting lists, Peretz abandoned his agreement with Ben-Gvir and agreed instead to bring Jewish Home into the reconstituted [[ilYamina|Yamina|#CADB39]] with the [[ilNR|New Right]] and [[ilTKuma|National Union–Tkuma]]. Otzma then filed an independent list shortly before the deadline.

parties.name: Unity
parties.relations: Split from the [[ilLikud|Likud]].
parties.description:
A right-wing political party in Israel which was founded in August 2026 by Yuli Edelstein and Gilad Erdan, ahead of the 2026 Israeli legislative election.

Yuli Edelstein, who served as the chair of the Knesset's Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, was removed from the position in July 2025 after he refused to support a bill which would have allowed many Ultra-Orthodox to be exempt from the draft.

Gilad Erdan, who served as a minister, confirmed in early May 2026 that he was considering forming a new party. Edelstein and Erdan were in talks in late May regarding the potential formation of a new party.

He and Erdan launched a new party on 6 August 2026 in Tel Aviv. Erdan stated that the party would form a "broad Zionist government" and would be in favor of a broad draft that included all people. Erdan will lead the party.

Former Beit Shemesh mayor Aliza Bloch joined the party on 10 August. The name of the party, Unity, was unveiled the following day. Oren Smadja joined the party on 12 August. On 13 August, it was reported that several Likud MKs were considering defecting to Unity after the former party decided to ban incumbent MKs from running on Likud regional district spots in the 2026 Likud primary leading up to the 2026 legislative election.

Erdan said in an interview in early September that Unity was considering allying with other parties to reach the electoral threshold.

Erdan held unsuccessful talks with Benny Gantz of [[ilBW|Blue and White]] over a possible alliance on 4 September; Erdan announced the same day that Unity withdrew from the election, citing poor polling that left the party below the electoral threshold, an unwillingness by the public to accept a unity government, and unfruitful alliance negotiations.

parties.description:
A short-lived one man political faction in Israel in the early 1990s.

The faction was formed on 25 December 1990 when Efraim Gur broke away from the [[ilAlignment|Alignment]] in 1990, during the term of the twelfth Knesset. Gur was invited to join Yitzhak Shamir's new government, which had been formed (minus the Alignment) on 11 June 1990, and accepted. He was initially appointed Deputy Minister of Communications, but became Deputy Minister of Transportation in November 1990.

Towards the end of the Knesset term, Gur merged his faction into [[ilLikud|Likud]] on 17 May 1992. Gur retained his seat in the 1992 elections on Likud's list, but broke away from his new party in March 1996 and saw out the remainder of his term as an independent. He formed a new party under the name Unity for New Immigrants (Hebrew: אחדות למען העלייה בראשות אפרים גור) which ran in the 1996 elections but failed to cross the electoral threshold and subsequently disappeared.

parties.name: Women's Party
parties.relations: Split from the [[ilISF|Independent Socialist Faction]]
parties.description:
A minor political party in Israel.

The party was established prior to the 1977 elections, with the founders including Israeli-American Marcia Freedman. Freedman had been an MK for [[ilRatz|Ratz]] in the eighth Knesset, but had broken away with Aryeh Eliav to form the [[ilISF|Independent Socialist Faction]]. Whilst the ISF chose to merge with several other small left-wing parties ([[ilMeri|Meri]], [[ilMoked|Moked]] and some [[ilBP|Black Panthers]]) to form the [[ilSheli|Left Camp of Israel]], Freedman decided to set up a new feminist party to fight the election.

However, the new party won only 5,674 votes and failed to cross the electoral threshold of 1%, subsequently disappearing. Freedman turned her attentions to charity, helping to found the women's centre Kol HaIsha (Voice of the Woman) in 1979, and returned to the United States in 1981.

parties.description:
The party was formed on 3 June 1975 during the eighth Knesset when the three MKs that made up [[ilRatz|Ratz]] (the full name of which was the Civil Rights Movement) joined with independent MK Aryeh Eliav to form a new party. Eliav had been elected to the Knesset on the [[ilAlignment|Alignment]]'s list, but had broken away to sit as an independent.

However, the party was dissolved on 27 January 1976 as Eliav and Marcia Freedman broke away to form the Social-Democratic Faction, which they soon renamed the [[ilISF|Independent Socialist Faction]]. The two remaining MKs, Shulamit Aloni and Boaz Moav, returned to [[ilRatz|Ratz]].

The Independent Socialist Faction also failed to make it to the next election, as it merged with [[ilMeri|Meri]], [[ilMoked|Moked]] and some members of the [[ilBP|Black Panthers]] to form the [[ilSheli|Left Camp of Israel]]. Freedman did not join the new party, but founded the Women's Party, which failed to cross the Electoral threshold. Ratz eventually merged into [[ilMeretz|Meretz]].

parties.description:
A minor right-wing political party in Israel.

The party was founded on 24 July 1995 when Shaul Gutman broke away from [[ilMoledet|Moledet]]. It ran in the 1996 elections, but failed to cross the electoral threshold of 1.5% and did not win a seat.

In the 2003 elections the party ran a joint list with [[ilHerutNM|Herut – The National Movement]]. Although together the parties won 36,202 votes (1.1%), they were 8,000 short of the threshold. For the 2006 elections the party ran alongside Baruch Marzel's [[ilHayil|Jewish National Front]], winning 28,824 votes (0.79%) and again failing to cross the threshold.

The party did not run in the 2009 elections.

parties.description:
An Israeli political alliance founded on 7 July 2026 by Hili Tropper, a former Minister of Culture and Sport, and Yoaz Hendel, a former Minister of Communications and leader of [[ilReserv|The Reservists]] party. The alliance was led jointly by the two founders, with Tropper heading the electoral list, and was set to contest the 2026 Israeli legislative election, scheduled for 27 October 2026, until it broke up in early September, when Tropper decided to join the [[ilYashar|Yashar]] list.

Polling near the electoral threshold, the alliance was viewed as a potential kingmaker if it had successfully entered the Knesset.
parties.ideology: The alliance had been described as center to center-right and presented itself as representing Israelis who serve in the military, particularly reservists. Its stated goal was the formation of a "broad Zionist government" that excluded both Haredi and Arab parties.

The party describes itself as "an advocate of progressive reforms, the creation of a Just Kazakhstan, strengthening the rule of law, and ensuring broad citizen participation in decision-making." On 14 June 2026, then-ruling political party in the country, the [[kzAmanat|Amanat]], merged into Ädilet.

parties.name: Amanat
parties.description:
The ruling [[kzNurOtan|Nur Otan]] party of Kazakstan was renamed to Amanat on 1 March 2022, following former President Nursultan Nazarbayev's retirement from active politics and the bloody January protests.

After Nazarbayev's withdrawal from active politics in 2022, Mäjilis chairman Erlan Qoşanov assumed the position of party leadership, becoming the first non-executive official to chair Amanat, following a brief tenure by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. 

Despite this leadership transition, Amanat remained a party of power, continuing to align towards Tokayev's administration. The party strongly supported Tokayev's constitutional reforms in the 2022 referendum that aimed at shifting to a more balanced president-parliamentary system, while also backing his successful independent campaign bid during the 2022 snap presidential election as part of the [[kzPC|People's Coalition]]. 

From 2023, Amanat had maintained its majority control of the Mäjilis, playing a central role in the nation's political and economic developments.[21] In June 2026, Amanat voted to dissolve its independent structure at an extraordinary congress, choosing to merge into the newly established Ädilet party ahead of the 2026 legislative election.[22]

During its existence, Amanat had been described as a big tent party, generally leaning conservative, with a focus on stability, national unity, and economic development. It promoted reforms in areas such as civil service, economic diversification, and the rule of law. The party's governance style had been described as authoritarian, with critics noting restrictions on political freedoms and limited opposition.

Amanat had a widespread presence across Kazakhstan's administrative divisions and held numerous local offices, maintaining legislative control through deputy groups in local assemblies (mäslihats) throughout the country.

On 14 June 2026 Amanat merged into newly-formed [[kzAdilet|Ädilet]] party.

Chairman:

parties.nativeName:

Qazaqstannyñ «Aq jol» demokratialyq partiasy
parties.description:
A liberal-conservative political party in Kazakhstan. 

Aq Jol was formed in early 2002, after its faction became being split from the [[kzQDT|Democratic Choice of Kazakhstan]]. From there, it was positioned as an opposition party though in a moderate tone. The party has experienced fragmentation over the years, leading to the formation of dissident factions. Despite its opposition stance, the Aq Jol had been repeatedly described as a pro-government party in Kazakhstan, with it joining the [[kzPC|People's Coalition]] in support of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in the 2022 election. The party has been led by Azat Peruaşev for many years.

The Aq Jol party advocates for political reform, economic liberalism, and secularism. It has participated in presidential and parliamentary elections, with varying levels of electoral success.

The party also advocates to lead the way for Kazakhstan to join the European Union in the future.[3]

parties.name: Auyl
parties.description:
It was originally founded by Gani Qaliev on 30 January 2000 before eventually merging with the [[kzQPP|Party of Patriots of Kazakhstan]] on 5 September 2015. Auyl has participated in every Kazakh parliamentary election since 2004 and nominated presidential candidate Toleutai Raqymbekov in the 2019 presidential election. 

It first entered the Mäjilis at the 2023 legislative election, winning eight seats and becoming the largest opposition party.

The Auyl declared its main values of spirituality, patriotism, loyalty, equality, cooperation. Basing its principles of social democracy, the party spoke out in favour of the rural population's interests by seeing its priorities as strengthening state regulation and supporting the agricultural economy, protecting the interests of rural workers, actively promoting the implementation of economic and political reforms aimed at further democratization of society, the implementation of justified forms of market relations in all sectors of the economy, improving the living standards of citizens, as well as the formation of patriotic education of the population.[2] It is supportive of incumbent President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev,[3] and has been accused of being controlled opposition and a front for agribusiness.

The party outlined its goal to promote the construction of an independent strong and prosperous Kazakhstan, with a high standard of living for all Kazakhstanis, in order to embark on the path of globalization, preserve the national spirit, cultural and spiritual potential and traditions, language and religion, as well as be open to new technologies.

parties.description:
According to the leader of the party, work on its registration has been carried out since 2015.

The founding congress of the party was held on 24 September 2022.

On 28 November 2022, the party was registered by the Ministry of Justice of Kazakhstan. The party has become the first registered party in Kazakhstan over the past 20 years, and the sixth after Amanat, Aq Jol, and People's Party, Auyl and JSDP.

In December 2022, the party announced that it would take part in the 2023 legislative election.

On 1 February 2023, the pre-election congress of the party was held, at which there was a scandal. Maral Koshenov, who came to the congress from Atyrau, said that he was on the list of nominated candidates when he was selected in the regions, but upon arrival in the capital he found out that he was "crossed out from the list." According to him, the son of the former deputy of the Mäjilis, Iraq Elekeev, was included in his place. At the congress, the head of the party said that it was necessary to prevent the party of oligarchs from entering the parliament, which he considers the Respublica and Aq Jol parties.

On 2 February 2023, the party was admitted to the regional elections of local assemblies (mäslihats) of the Abai, Akmola, Jetisu, North Kazakhstan and Ulytau regions.

The party is not considered an opposition party. At the pre-election congress on 1 February 2023, the party expressed its support for the course of President Tokayev.[6]

parties.name: Communist People's Party of Kazakhstan
parties.nativeName:
Қазақстан коммунистік халық партиясы
Qazaqstan kommunistık halyq partiasy
parties.description:
The party emerged due to a split in the [[kzQKP|Communist Party of Kazakhstan]] (QKP). The idea to create a new party belongs to the 12 members of the Central Committee of Communist Party of Kazakhstan, who withdrew its membership because of the disagreements with the First Secretary of the QKP's Central Committee Serikbolsyn Abdildin. The reason for the split with the QKP was the election of a Secretary and a member of Mazhilis Tolen Tokhtassynov. About 15,000 members left QKP for QKHP. The founding congress QKHP took place in April 2004, on 21 June 2004 the party was registered with the Ministry of Justice of Kazakhstan.

Following the elections to Mazhilis in 2004, the party received 1.98% of total voters (proportional system) and did not pass into Parliament.

In the 2005 presidential elections, QKHP nominated Erasyl Abilqasymov as its candidate who received 0.34% of the votes.

On 28 March 2007 the QKHP and the QPK held a joint press conference at which they announced an impending merger. QKHP subsequently abandoned the association with the QPK because of the sharp political differences.[4] At a press conference in June 2007, the First Secretary of QKHP Vladislav Kosarev named the fact that the Communist Party of Kazakhstan was considering associations with QKHP only at the highest level (Bureaus of Central Committee) as the main reason for refusing to merge, at the same time according to him consideration for such merger was not provided at local level. Kosarev said also that structures of QKP had been completely destroyed and the authority of the party among the people has been reduced to zero-level.

In elections to Mazhilis in 2007, the party won 1.29% of total votes and did not pass the electoral threshold to Parliament. In the 2012 election, the party won 7.19% of vote and 7 seats to become one of three parties to enter Parliament. Despite being officially in opposition, the party is considered as loyal to the regime and often votes with the government.

The 15th Communist People's Party of Kazakhstan Extraordinary Congress was held on 11 November 2020 in the capital Nur-Sultan. Delegates to the congress voted to rename the party the [[kzQHP|People's Party of Kazakhstan]] (QHP). Several changes were also made to the charters and programs of the party. The party also elected new leadership and began to declare itself social democratic.

parties.nativeName:
Қазақстан халық партиясы
Qazaqstannyñ halyq partiasy
Народная партия Казахстана
Narodnaya partiya Kazakhstana
parties.description:
At the 15th Extraordinary Congress of the [[kzQKHP|Communist People's Party of Kazakhstan]] held on 11 November 2020, a decision was made to rename the QKHP to the People's Party of Kazakhstan, with corresponding amendments to the party's charter and program. This decision was motivated by a desire to expand the party's electoral support ahead of the 2021 Kazakh legislative election. The Extraordinary Congress held a quorum of 33 delegates from the party. Every delegate voted in favour of the name change except Honorary Secretary Vladislav Kosarev. The party's parliamentary leader Aiqyn Qongyrov was unanimously chosen to be Chairman of the QHP, succeeding Kosarev who served as the QKHP's de facto leader since June 2013, while Jambyl Ahmetbekov, Turgyn Syzdyqov, Viktor Smirnov, and Gauhar Nugmanova were chosen to be Secretaries of the QHP.

Officially, the People's Party of Kazakhstan positions itself as a center-left political force, proclaiming the principles of social democracy and renewed socialism. Its program declares its commitment to the ideas of social justice, equality, social solidarity, and strengthening the role of the state in the economy and social spheres.

On 28 March 2022, at the XIX extraordinary congress of the party, Ermūhamet Ertısbaev was elected as the Chairman of the People's Party of Kazakhstan.

In October 2022, the QHP joined the [[kzPC|People's Coalition]], in support of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, ceasing to be even nominally part of the opposition.

On an Almaty press conference of 1 July 2024,[ some members of the party demanded the resignation of Ermukhamet Ertisbaev from party chairmanship. The party infighting is said to come from the apparently "emerging personality cult" of Ertisbaev. Former deputy chairman, Ashat Asylbekov also claimed, that on one of the interviews that neared the 2023 Kazakh local elections, Ertisbaev stated that he'd be forever loyal to Nursultan Nazarbayev. These acts of Ertisbaev are said to be damaging to the party's reputation and Asylbekov, Almaty branch chairman Töleujan Jündibaev and Mangystau Region representative Abdraşit Niyaz publicly criticised the chairman and his deputy Miras Aukenov and demanded an "extraordinary" congress. Ertisbaev's large spendings on his "Ertisbaev live" YouTube channel and his public support for Quandyq Bishimbaev during his trial had also greatly damaged the party's reputation, Asylbekov says.

On 7 June 2026, at an extraordinary congress of the People's Party of Kazakhstan, a new chairman, Nursultan Şoqanov, was elected, and the party's charter and new identity were approved. During the congress, former QHP chairman Ermukhamet Ertisbaev noted that the party's official digital platforms currently unite more than 1.1 million subscribers, the total reach of publications exceeds 600 million views, and the number of comments and requests has reached approximately 1 million, with these figures continuing to grow.

Nursultan Şoqanov (since 27 June 2026)

These acts of Ertisbaev are said to be damaging to the party's reputation and Asylbekov, Almaty branch chairman Töleujan Jündibaev and Mangystau Region representative Abdraşit Niyaz publicly criticised the chairman and his deputy Miras Aukenov and demanded an "extraordinary" congress. Ertisbaev's large spendings on his "Ertisbaev live" YouTube channel and his public support for Quandyq Bishimbaev during his trial had also greatly damaged the party's reputation, Asylbekov says.

On 7 June 2026, at an extraordinary congress of the People's Party of Kazakhstan, a new chairman, Nursultan Şoqanov, was elected, and the party's charter and new identity were approved. During the congress, former QHP chairman Ermukhamet Ertisbaev noted that the party's official digital platforms currently unite more than 1.1 million subscribers, the total reach of publications exceeds 600 million views, and the number of comments and requests has reached approximately 1 million, with these figures continuing to grow.

parties.name: Respublica
parties.description:
The creation of the party was announced in August 2022. The party's founding congress was held on 3 December 2022. An agricultural producer, the head of the Olzha Agro company, Aidarbek Qojanazarov, became the chairman of the party. The co-chairs are entrepreneurs Syrymbek Tau, Ruslan Berdenov, Maxim Baryshev, Dinara Shukizhanova, Kuanysh Shonbai, Beibit Alibekov and Nurlan Koyanbaev.

On 18 January 2023, the Respublica party received registration documents.

On 25 January, the first regional branch was opened in the Kostanay Region. On 27 January, all 20 regional divisions of the party received registration.

Kazakh political scientists Rakhim Oshakbaev and Gaziz Zhaparov positively assessed the party's chances of winning in the snap Kazakh parliamentary election, scheduled for 19 March 2023. It ultimately won around 11% of the vote, finishing in third place.

parties.name: Communist Party of Malta
parties.description:
After the 1917 October Revolution, secret communist cells were formed in Malta, however small in number. In 1933, an attempt by the colonial government and the Catholic Church to crack down on left-wing factions of the Malta Labour Party, dockyard workers and intellectuals were imprisoned for the "crime" of possessing socialist literature. Independent progressive movements faced large setbacks due to the sedition trials whilst Maltese communists militated either in the Italian Communist Party, the Communist Party of Great Britain or covertly within the [[mtPL|Malta Labour Party]]. Malta did not have its own explicitly communist party before the establishment of the PKM in a secret congress in the town of Gwardamangia in 1969 but nevertheless, state suppression of suspected communists continued until 1971.

After the right-wing administration of George Borg Olivier was defeated by the [[mtPL|Malta Labour Party]] in 1971 under Dom Mintoff, the PKM was able to establish itself and organise openly. The PKM organised protests and meetings as well as commemorations to Maltese working class figures in support of emancipation such as Manwel Dimech. According to the US intelligence department by 1970 PKM's membership was around 100 members. The PKM also took part in international seminars, and was key in helping the Maltese government establish positive relations with the Workers' Party of Korea and a subsequent Juche study group called The Juche Philosophy and Songun Policy Study Group. Despite having originally split off it, the party critically-supported the Malta Labour Party under Dom Mintoff and Karmenu Mifsud Bonnici and took part in several May Day demonstrations.

The party first contested the national general elections of 1987 when it obtained 0.1% of first preference votes and no parliamentary seats. Since then it has not stood for any other election whether at a European, national or local level.

In the 1990s, the party collaborated with the left-wing non-governmental organisation [[mtMG|Moviment Graffitti]], allowing it to hold meetings at the Communist Party headquarters in Valletta before it was able to lease its own office. In 2016, the two groups published a joint statement appealing for a reformation of the neutrality clause in the Constitution of Malta to ban warships from all countries from docking in Maltese ports.

Inactive after 29 December 2020.

parties.name: FRELIMO Party
parties.description:
A democratic socialist political party in Mozambique. It has governed the country since its independence from Portugal in 1975.

Founded in 1962, FRELIMO began as a nationalist movement fighting for the self-determination and independence of Mozambique from Portuguese colonial rule. During its anti-colonial struggle, FRELIMO managed to maintain friendly relations with both the Soviet Union and China, and received military and economic assistance from both. Independence was achieved in June 1975 after the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon the previous year. FRELIMO formally became a political party during its 3rd Party Congress in February 1977, and adopted Marxism–Leninism as its official ideology and FRELIMO Party as its official name.

FRELIMO has been the ruling party of Mozambique since then, initially as the sole legal party in a one-party system and later as the democratically elected government in a dominant-party system. FRELIMO fought a protracted civil war from 1976 to 1992 against the anti-communist Mozambican National Resistance or RENAMO. RENAMO received support from the white minority governments of Rhodesia and South Africa. FRELIMO approved a new national constitution in 1990, which ended one-party rule and established a multi-party system. FRELIMO has since become the dominant party in Mozambique and has won a majority of the seats in the Assembly of the Republic in every election since the country's first multi-party election in 1994.

parties.name: Mozambican National Resistance
parties.description:
A Mozambican political party and militant group. The party was founded with the active sponsorship of the Rhodesian Central Intelligence Organisation (CIO) in May 1977 from anti-communist dissidents opposed to Mozambique's ruling [[mzFRELIMO|FRELIMO Party]]. RENAMO was initially led by André Matsangaissa, a former senior official in FRELIMO's armed wing, and was composed of several anti-communist dissident groups which appeared immediately prior to, and shortly following, Mozambican independence.

Critics of RENAMO frequently described the movement as a proxy of Rhodesia, and subsequently, South Africa's apartheid government. It has been theorised that RENAMO was formed for the sole purpose of countering FRELIMO support for the Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army (ZANLA). On the other hand, RENAMO was also reflective of FRELIMO's own splintering support base and dwindling popularity in the immediate post-independence era. Its political programme centered around the abandonment of FRELIMO's socialist policies, the adoption of a free market economy, and more traditionalist concerns such as the reinstatement of traditional ethnic leaders to positions of authority. RENAMO's ranks included a number of Mozambican political exiles who genuinely opposed FRELIMO on principle, including FRELIMO defectors disillusioned with its Marxist–Leninist ideology, but also large numbers of recruits conscripted by force.

With Rhodesian support, RENAMO commenced an insurgency against the FRELIMO government in 1977, sparking the Mozambican Civil War. The war was characterised by severe human rights violations on both sides and crippled the already debilitated Mozambican economy. RENAMO and FRELIMO acceded to the Rome General Peace Accords in October 1992, which ended FRELIMO's one-party state and introduced multi-party democratic elections. In return, RENAMO pledged to abandon its armed struggle and conduct its future activities by political means within the framework of the new electoral system. Following the end of the war, RENAMO was responsible for promoting constitutional reforms as well as the promotion of a strong domestic private sector.

Renewed clashes broke out between RENAMO's militant forces and the FRELIMO government in 2013. RENAMO resumed its insurgency, citing state corruption and electoral fraud perpetrated by FRELIMO officials. A second peace agreement was reached between RENAMO and FRELIMO in August 2019, resulting in the virtual end of the insurgency. A RENAMO splinter group known as the RENAMO Military Junta (RMJ) was quickly formed from party dissidents opposed to the peace process; the RMJ continued to carry out minor guerrilla operations until December 2021, when the last of its members surrendered to Mozambican security forces.

RENAMO was initially led by André Matsangaissa, a former senior official in [[mzFRELIMO|FRELIMO]]'s armed wing. Matsangaissa, who died in 1979, was succeeded by Afonso Dhlakama, who led the organization until he died in 2018. He was succeeded by Ossufo Momade.

parties.name: National Democratic Union of Mozambique
parties.description: A nationalist organization founded in Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia (present-day Harare, Zimbabwe) in 1960. It was led by Adelino Gwambe and consisted mostly of migrant workers and disgruntled students who had fled central and southern regions of Mozambique. It was formed to oppose Portuguese colonial rule in Mozambique. In June 1962, UDENAMO merged with two other nationalist organizations, the [[mzUNAMI|National African Union of Independent Mozambique]] (UNAMI) and [[mzMANU|Mozambican African National Union]] (MANU) to form the [[mzFRELIMO|Mozambique Liberation Front]] (FRELIMO).

parties.name: Optimist Party for the Development of Mozambique
parties.nativeName: Partido Otimista pelo Desenvolvimento de Moçambique
parties.relations: Split from the [[mzFRELIMO|FRELIMO Party]].
parties.description:
A Mozambican political party of the democratic socialist ideology founded on 7 May 2019 by a sector of the ruling [[mzFRELIMO|FRELIMO Party]] dissident from the leadership headed by President Filipe Nyusi.

PODEMOS was founded in 2018 when the electoral court rejected the independent candidacy of Samora Machel Jr., son of Samora Machel, the first president of Mozambique, for mayor of Maputo in the 2018 municipal elections. Many members of the Youth Association for the Development of Mozambique (AJUDEM), an internal political group of FRELIMO that supported Machel, participated in the founding of PODEMOS in May of the following year. Despite this, both Machel and the party have denied any mutual relationship. The party finally obtained legal registration a week after the announcement of its foundation, on 14 May.

During the second half of May and the first half of June, the party began collecting signatures to be able to present candidates in the 2019 presidential and parliamentary elections. Less than a month after its founding, on 11 June 2019, PODEMOS announced Hélder Mendonça, a little-known musician, as its presidential candidate although he would be disqualified.

In the 2024 Mozambican general election, PODEMOS won 31 seats in the Assembly of the Republic, and supported Venâncio Mondlane candidacy for that year's presidential election. Mondlane would later move away from the party and found his own, which was registered as [[mzANAMOLA|ANAMOLA]].

parties.name: Agricultural People's Front of Peru
parties.nativeName: Frente Popular Agrícola FIA del Perú
parties.literalName: Agricultural People's Front FIA of Peru
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[peFIA|Agricultural Independent Front]] (FIA).
parties.description:
Ezequiel Ataucusi Gamonal created the Evangelical Association of the Israelite Mission of the New Universal Covenant (AEMINPU) in 1968, with The Guardian stating, "The messianic sect behind the party was founded in 1968 by Ezequiel Ataucusi, a self-styled spiritual leader who called himself the 'Christ of the west'". Followers of the movement regard Ezequiel Ataucusi Gamonal as a prophet and "the reincarnation of the Holy Spirit". The Agricultural People's Front of Peru party was officially founded by Ataucusi on 30 September 1989, succeeding [[peFIA|Agricultural Independent Front]] (founded 1984).

In 1995, the party received one seat in the Congress of the Republic of Peru, which was held by Javier Noriega Febres. Noriega was later accused of being the head of a hitmen group by the government of Alberto Fujimori.

The party was elected into two seats during the 2000 general election. The two seats, which were for Luis Cáceres Velásquez and his son Roger Cáceres Pérez, characters who joined the ranks of Fujimorism ([[peP2000|Peru 2000]]) after receiving money from Presidential Advisor and Intelligence Chief Vladimiro Montesinos. 

Ataucusi died in 2000 and was placed in a glass coffin, with followers expecting his resurrection. After which his son Jonás Ataucusi took over the party. Since the death of Ataucusi, the party experienced internal conflict. In the 2000s, the party won minor district and regional elections. The party lost its legal registration in 2010 and regained it in 2015.

In the 2020 Peruvian parliamentary election, the party received multiple seats in the Congress for the first time in nearly two decades.

On 21 January 2025, ethnocacerist leader Antauro Humala and Congressman Roberto Sánchez Palomino ([[peJP|JP]] leader) attended the 53rd anniversary event for Jonas Ataucusi Molina held in Cieneguilla. Media outlets speculated about a possible alliance between the Antauro Humala's political party [[peANTAURO|ANTAURO]], [[peJP|JP]], and FREPAP for the 2026 election. This speculation arose due to the threat of Humala's party being outlawed, which would exclude it from the electoral race. However, the FREPAP's general secretary, Filomeno Soto Leandro, asserted that the party would not form electoral alliances with any political party for the upcoming elections.
parties.ideology:
FREPAP calls for a strict adherence to the Ten Commandments and the decentralization of populated cities by forming agrarian communities. The party and its main religious organization AEMINPU have been described as having socialist traits in economic matters, while being heavily conservative on social matters.

They list their ideology as the following:
Theocratic – The recognition of divine law to confront corruption and to promote noble politicians
Nationalist – Defending of Peru's identity, culture and natural resources
Tahuantinsuyonism – Promoting the organization and moral ethics of the Inca Empire
Revolution – Moving those experiencing misery within Peru towards a path of liberty and self-reliance
Agrarianism – The promotion of agriculture as a way to improve the socioeconomic standards of Peru in every dimension
Integration – Unifying all Peruvians to benefit the nation.

The party calls for the elimination of extreme poverty through the promotion of agricultural industry and decentralization, which they believe will improve socioeconomic standards. For macroeconomic policies, FREPAP believes tourism should be secondary to agriculture and that science and technology should be promoted to develop human capital in order to replace Peru's commodity-driven economy, strengthening the competitiveness of the nation. Regarding the environment, FREPAP calls for the use of renewable energy and the protection of Peru's biodiversity. FREPAP believes that the Peruvian government needs to focus on transparency, accountability and preventing corruption, and has advocated in favor of repealing parliamentary immunity.

parties.name: Ahora Nación
parties.description:
Ahora Nación was founded on 13 May 2023, under the leadership of Alfonso López-Chau, former rector of the National University of Engineering (UNI), who became known for sheltering protesters at the university where he served as rector.

The party was formed during Peru's 2022-2023 social unrest. In June 2024, Alfonso López-Chau announced his intention to run for president in the 2026 elections.

In 2025, the National Elections Board (JNE), through the National Directorate of the Registry of Political Organizations, suspended the application for registration of the electoral alliance between Ahora Nación and [[peSalvP|Salvemos al Perú]] due to internal disagreements within the latter party regarding the continuation of the alliance.

Two Ahora Nación congresspeople of 2021-2026 Congress were part of the [[peBDP|People's Democratic Bloc]] parliamentary group.

AN managed to win four seats in the Senate and ten in the Chamber of Deputies during the 2026 election. In a presidential race, López-Chau finished seventh with 7.29% of voted.

parties.description:
In early 2005, [[peAvP2000|a party under the same name]] participated in the 2006 general election, launching Ulises Humala as its presidential nominee.  At the legislative elections, the party won 1.1% of the popular vote but no seats in the Congress of the Republic and its presidential ticket itself attained 0.2%, placing fourteenth nationally. 

After losing its formal registration as a political organization, the party began a re-founding stage on 10 May 2017, culminating in a new registration on the same year.

In the legislative election held on 26 January 2020, the party won 2.5% of the popular vote but no seats in the Congress of the Republic, as it failed to pass once again the 5% electoral threshold. In the legislative election held on 11 April 2021, the party won 7.5% of the popular vote and 7 seats in the Congress of the Republic.

In December 2021, Hernando de Soto left the party following a dispute for its control between Aldo Borrero Rojas, the leader of the party, and Edwin de la Cruz Ponce, the general secretary, who was previously removed but continued to denounce his removal. Following his departure, De Soto described the party as being far-right after members of Avanza País supported amnesty for authorities following massacres in Ayacucho and Juliaca during the widespread protests against President Dina Boluarte.
parties.ideology:
The party has been described as a supporter of far-right politics, though some media in Peru describe the party as center-right. Its members in the Congress of Peru have been described as being part of a "far-right" bloc allied with Popular Force and Popular Renewal.

Representatives of the party signed the Madrid Charter, an anti-leftist manifesto organized by the conservative Spanish party [[esVox|Vox]]. Economically, the party embraces classical liberalism and economic liberalism, generally supporting free markets.

The party does not have an official stance on social issues as it once did, as can be evidenced by the fact that the respective leading figures for de Soto's presidential campaign, Instituto Politico para la Libertad Peru (IPL) vice president, Beltrán Gomez Hijar, and IPL member and congressman Alejandro Cavero, have supported pro-LGBT and pro-choice causes, whereas congresswoman Adriana Tudela, daughter of former Vice President Francisco Tudela, is opposed to abortion.

Under de Soto's leadership, the party is described by analysts and pundits as right-leaning on the political spectrum. According to Georgetown University political scientist Eliana Carlín, de Soto was the one who chose the party for his election run, and the party welcomed him due to his international prominence in the economic academia. In Carlin's opinion, the party is an "electoral vehicle" that reached an agreement with de Soto and that "they are not interested in ideology".

parties.name: Bicentennial Peru
parties.relations:
Split from the [[pePL|Free Peru]].

Members of Congress from the following parties were part of the bloc:
- [[pePL|Free Peru]].
parties.description:
President and first spokesperson Jorge Marticorena, the congressman behind the group's creation, resigned from the [[pePL|Free Peru]] group on 26 May 2022, when the Congress of the Republic approved the censure of Minister Betssy Chávez.

Due to the government crisis of May 2022 and the wave of resignations from different factions within the Free Peru group (including the creation of the [[peBMCN|Magisterial Bloc]]), three congressmen Jorge Coayla, Elías Varas, and Víctor Cutipa also decided to leave Free Peru.

On 8 June 2022, congressman José María Balcázar also announced his resignation from the Free Peru parliamentary group.

On the same day, all five congressmen resigned due to the change in government and the internal divisions within Free Peru, and announced the creation of a new parliamentary group.

Two spokespeople for the group were appointed: the two parliamentarians Víctor Cutipa and Elías Varas.

The group was dissolved on 22 July 2024.
parties.ideology:
The group can be described as left-wing. All the members of parliament declared their disagreement and divergence with the attitude and relationships of Waldemar Cerrón and [[pePL|Free Peru]] in the Congress of the Republic and the evolution of their relationship with then-President Pedro Castillo.

However, they declared their support for the actions of former President Pedro Castillo and his government. The group announced the main measures it would implement, which were classified as left-wing and aligned with the ideas of Free Peru, such as constitutional reform, food sovereignty, the fight against corruption, increased taxes for the wealthiest citizens, and free access to education and healthcare. They were part of the opposition to the government of President Dina Boluarte.

parties.description:
A political party, which defines itself as a coalition of parties, political organizations, social movements, and citizen activists in Peru whose main objective is to consolidate the various left-wing, progressive, socialist, and environmentalist sectors.

It originated at the Meeting of Social and Political Organizations held in 2007, and its initial objective was to promote the defense of territories. It has been part of the Congress of the Republic since 2012 as part of the [[peAP|Popular Action]]-Broad Front parliamentary group, and since 2016 with its own parliamentary group. During the parliamentary interregnum following the dissolution of Congress in 2019, it had two members on the Standing Committee.

In the 2016 general elections, it participated by nominating Verónika Mendoza as its presidential candidate. In the elections, held on April 10, the party became the third largest political force in the country, obtaining the largest minority representation in the Congress of the Republic. During the 2016-2021 parliamentary period, before the dissolution of Congress, it obtained 20 congressmen; in July 2017 the caucus split and 10 of the 20 congressmen created the [[peNP|New Peru]] caucus.
parties.ideology:
The Broad Front is positioned in an environmentalist and reformist policy with a social democratic orientation. It seeks to implement a policy of transparency, allow citizens to participate in politics through participatory democracy, and decentralize political, fiscal, and administrative powers.

It advocates establishing an ecological commitment by generalizing renewable energy throughout the country and protecting the country's biodiversity from human activities, including a policy of reforestation, the fight against deforestation and illegal exploitation.

At the economic level, the party seeks to prohibit monopolies and oligopolies in the country's economy, giving priority to a pluralistic and social market economy, regulated by the State. It also wants to develop local production, improve support for small and medium-sized enterprises, give more protection to unions and improve working conditions in the country.

Faced with poverty, the party wants to increase minimum wages and pensions. He is in favor of a significant investment in education so that all children can go to school. The party proposes a social plan to eradicate inequalities, especially to improve women's rights, as well as an anti-racist policy to ensure that the country achieves the required human rights objectives.

The party wants to guarantee the protection of indigenous peoples and empower them in certain regions of the country, and it is also in favor of a revision of free trade agreements, as well as better cooperation among South American states.

parties.name: Christian People's Party
parties.relations: Split from the [[peDC|Christian Democratic Party]] (DC).
parties.description:
It was founded in 1966 by [[peDC|Christian Democratic Party]] (DC) dissidents, led by Luis Bedoya Reyes, at the time mayor of Lima.

Participating for the first time in elections in 1978, the PPC managed to solidify its presence in coastal urban areas throughout the 1980s, but it was not enough to win the Peruvian presidency, as Luis Bedoya Reyes placed third in both the 1980 and 1985 general elections. The 1990s saw the party experience an internal crisis while Fujimorism would dominate right-wing politics throughout the decade.

In 2000, the PPC's party registration was revoked by the National Jury of Elections under orders of the Fujimori administration. Recovering its registration in the aftermath of Fujimori's downfall, it became the dominant party of the [[peUN2000|National Unity]] coalition, placing third in both the 2001 and 2006 general elections under the candidacy of Lourdes Flores.

Following a series of political failures amid a more severe internal crisis throughout the 2010s, the PPC failed to overcome the electoral threshold at the 2021 general election, and lost its party registration for a second time at the National Jury of Elections.

The party attained its re-registration on 11 May 2024, and its projected to participate in the [[peUN2025|National Unity]] coalition for the 2026 general election with Roberto Chiabra as the coalition's presumptive presidential nominee.
parties.ideology: PPC is a centre-right and conservative political party based on the principles of Christian democracy.

parties.name: Civic Party OBRAS
parties.description:
Belmont was his OBRAS party's candidate in the 1995 presidential election, but received only 2% of the vote. In the Congress of the Republic, OBRAS won two seats out of 120.

In the 2006 general election, Belmont was an independent candidate on the [[peFC|Centre Front]] list of Valentín Paniagua, but failed to secure a seat. However, in 2009, he entered Congress as a replacement following the death of congressman Alberto Andrade, the former mayor of Lima.

In 2015, OBRAS formed an alliance with the [[peSU|Siempre Unidos]] party, and in 2016 with [[pePPS|Peru Secure Homeland]], with the aim of participating in the 2016 presidential election; however, this alliance ended with the withdrawal of candidate Renzo Reggiardo.

In the 2018 Lima municipal election, OBRAS ran within the [[pePL|Libertarian Peru]] party, with Belmont as the mayoral candidate, receiving 3.89% of the vote.

In 2020, Belmont and his movement joined the ethnocacerist [[peUPP|Union for Peru]], becoming the number one candidate on the Lima UPP list in the snap congressional election.

That same year, with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, Belmont began organizing COVID-19 denialist marches and promoting anti-vaccination slogans such as "Every vaccine you take [...] could make you infertile."

In 2021, Belmont again allied with [[pePL|Free Peru]], becoming an adviser to President Pedro Castillo. Despite the fact that a week before his appointment, Belmont described Castillo as "another one of those who ends up in jail or gets rich and flees the country."

In July 2024, the party was re-registered with the National Jury of Elections to participate in the next general election.

Belmont, the party leader, has become OBRAS's presidential candidate for the 2026 election. In his campaign, Belmont typically wears a Spartan warrior helmet, and his supporters refer to themselves as "Spartans".

During Belmont's OBRAS campaign, the party adopted some ideas from the government of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, former President of Mexico, such as the "Abrazos, no balazos" policy and the implementation of a government conference system similar to "Las Mañaneras del Pueblo" as its main proposals.

parties.name: Country for All
parties.description:
The party was founded by Vladimir Meza Villarreal, former mayor of the province of Huaraz. The party's registration application was submitted on 5 December 2023, to the National Directorate of the Registry of Political Organizations. On 2 August 2024, the National Elections Board (JNE) registered it as the 34th political party authorized to participate in the 2026 general elections.

In July 2024, comedian Carlos Álvarez announced his affiliation with the party and was promoted as a possible PPT presidential candidate in 2026. Carlos Álvarez himself faced rumors of a split with the party, which he later denied. In 2026, Álvarez was a PPT candidate, but the party confirmed that he was a "former candidate" after failing to reach the second round of the elections.

In March 2025, the Attorney General's Office initiated preliminary proceedings against the PPT to assess its possible disqualification, following a complaint alleging statements contrary to the constitutional order. The party president described the investigation as "a direct attack on democracy."
parties.ideology:
The party's main figurehead, Álvarez, presents himself as transcending the traditional left-right divide, with his phrase "I am left, right, and center." 

The party is associated with hardline rhetoric, order, and security, for example on issues of crime, the death penalty, and immigration control, according to journalistic reports.

On 19 May 2025, ID and [[pePUSL|United Peruvians: We Are Free!]], then associated with former supreme prosecutor Tomás Gálvez, announced an electoral alliance. Grozo said they intended to apply for its registration by the end of June. RPP announcement. However, the alliance was never registered with the JNE, and [[pePUSL|United Peruvians: We Are Free!]] subsequently chose to join other alliance - [[peUN2025|National Unity]].

In 2026 Peruvian general election, Wolfgang Grozo got 0.38% of the vote.

ID has submitted candidates for the October 2026 regional and municipal elections, but it did not register enough lists to satisfy the minimum territorial-participation requirement. El Comercio therefore includes ID among the parties whose registration will be cancelled, while clarifying that these cancellations take effect from 1 January 2027.

ideology.text: ID declares itself a centrist, humanist and republican party. Its programme advocates moderation, the rule of law, separation of powers, a secular state, cultural tolerance and a "social market economy."
La República
reported that Wolfgang Grozo was generally considered a centrist, while also recording his own more revealing description of himself as a "conservative" but not an extremist, a moderate conservative.

parties.relations:
Split from the [[pePL|Free Peru]].

Members of Congress from the following parties were part of the bloc:
- [[pePL|Free Peru]].

Partially merged into the [[peSP|We Are Peru]] (SP).
parties.description:
On 7 January 2022, five members of Congress from the [[peRP|Popular Renewal]], [[pePL|Free Peru]], [[peSP|We Are Peru]], and [[peAP|Popular Action]] parties requested the creation of a parliamentary group from the President of Congress, Maricarmen Alva. The first five members included Héctor Valer, Hamlet Echevarría, Carlos Zeballos, Luis Roberto Kamiche Morante, and Guillermo Bermejo, who was under investigation for terrorism.

On 10 January, just days after the parliamentary group's creation, then-Minister of Labor Betssy Chávez announced that she would join the group.

On 14 January, after a meeting with Pedro Castillo, President Héctor Valer declared that his parliamentary group was neither in opposition to nor in favor of the government, but solely in favor of a Constituent Assembly.

On 1 February 2022, Héctor Valer was appointed Prime Minister by President Pedro Castillo, replacing Mirtha Vásquez, who had resigned the previous day. Thus, the parliamentary group effectively became part of the government's composition and support, with the President of the Council and the Minister of Labor as members of the governing coalition.

In November 2022, Héctor Valer resigned from the group following the vote of confidence called by Prime Minister Aníbal Torres.

On 22 March 2023, the Congress of the Republic suspended Betssy Chávez due to her alleged participation in the attempted coup d'état orchestrated by Pedro Castillo in December 2022. As a result, the parliamentary group was dissolved.

The four members of Congress from PD (Guillermo Bermejo ([[peVP|VP]]), Hamlet Echevarría, Nieves Limachi and Luis Kamiche), who would have been left without a party after Betssy Chávez's suspension, joined the [[peBDP|Democratic Change – Together for Peru]] group.
parties.ideology:
The group can be described as leftist and a catch-all. Differences have existed since its inception, with Héctor Valer, during a meeting with Pedro Castillo, calling it a group that is neither in opposition nor in favor of the government. A few days later, Guillermo Bermejo, who had resigned from [[pePL|Free Peru]], referred to it as a parliamentary group supporting the government.

However, the group is characterized by shared ideological elements, encompassing those who remain in [[pePL|Free Peru]], those who have left the party, and dissidents from the [[peSP|We Are Peru]] and [[peAP|Popular Action]] parties. The parliamentarians particularly advocate for the convening of a Constituent Assembly, combating corruption, and restoring the image of legislators.

parties.name: Everything with the People
parties.relations: Split from the [[pePL|Free Peru]].
parties.description:
The TCP party was founded on 20 December 2023, in Lima, at an assembly presided over by Nicolás Bustamante, former Minister of Transport and Communications during the government of Pedro Castillo. The creation of the TCP was promoted by Pedro Castillo, imprisoned in Barbadillo prison after his arrest following the attempted self-coup of 2022, and its creation was announced on 8 February 2024, on Castillo's social media account, where he also requested that people join the organization. 

On 26 June 2024, Castillo announced his affiliation with the TCP. On 12 July, Castillo announced on his social media accounts the submission of the formal application for registration of his party to the National Elections Board (JNE). The party's name is a modification of the phrase "Always with the people," which was the official slogan of Castillo's presidency and was displayed on all public institutions and official executive communications during his administration.

On 17 August 2025, the TCP announced an alliance with Roberto Sánchez's [[peJP|Together for Peru]] (JP) party in Huaycán, forming the "Together for the People" alliance. On 19 August, the National Elections Board (JNE) registered the TCP in the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP), although it was ineligible to participate in the 2026 general elections due to its registration being outside the established deadline.

On 8 October, Castillo withdrew his confidence in Bustamante, stating in X that he "instructed Bustamante to convene the National Statutory Congress... his response was silence, arrogance, and disobedience." On 21 December 2025, Bustamante declared that there was "a movement in favor of expelling" Castillo within the party.

In the 2026 general elections, the TCP participated alongside Sánchez's party, an alliance forged by Castillo without consulting the party's grassroots members in exchange for a 20% quota to nominate his invited candidates, which drew criticism from Bustamante. Furthermore, the conflict between Bustamante and Castillo intensified, with Bustamante accusing the former president of deviating from the party line by joining forces with the group of Catherin Palomino Casavilca (a TCP member and elected deputy for JP as an invited candidate) and attempting to become party president without following proper procedures. For his part, Jaime Vásquez Castillo, the former president's nephew, criticized Bustamante, though he also criticized Palomino, Jorge Spelucín, and Íber Maraví. Although he was part of JP's campaign team at the beginning of the electoral contest, Vásquez was later removed due to his disputes with Palomino regarding campaign management, a removal endorsed by Castillo and instigated by Palomino.

For the regional and municipal elections of the same year, the TCP did not form an alliance to participate because internal disputes prevented the party from formalizing an alliance with [[peAEV|Venceremos]] (as proposed by Bustamante) or JP (as proposed by Castillo).

A federalist party founded by Virgilio Acuña, brother of César Acuña and former member of his [[peAPP|APP]] party.

During 2025, PDF attempted to negotiate an electoral alliance with [[pePUSL|United Peruvians: We Are Free!]]. parties.relations:
Partially split from the [[pePM|Purple Party]] (PM);
In 2024, [[peLoJusto|Lo Justo por el Perú]] merged into PLG.
parties.description:
In September 2022, Miguel del Castillo, Manuel Ato and Marco Zevalllos decided to found the political party First the People, a project that was later joined by congresswoman Susel Paredes, one of the three legislators elected by the [[pePM|Purple Party]] in 2021 and a member of the [[peFC|Fuerza Ciudadana]] party. Later, the Vamos Pueblo movement led by Marco Sipán was incorporated with bases in the northern mountains, Lima Provinces and the southern mountains, in 2024 the Convergencia collective led by the former director of the Naciones Unidas Luis Thais and the Innovadores Perú movement led by the evangelical leader Marcelino Salazar were incorporated with bases throughout Peru.

On 11 September 2022, the application for electoral registration is submitted to the National Elections Jury (JNE), which is granted on July 5 of the following year.

In February 2023, First the People joins the [[pePHP|Peruvian Humanist Party]], led by former Prime Minister Yehude Simon. The PHP was founded in 2001 and gave up its electoral registration in 2017 in favor of the left-wing coalition [[peJP|Together for Peru]], from which it withdrew in December 2021.

In August 2023, a faction of the [[pePHP|PHP]] decided to withdraw from First the People and obtain its own registration with the JNE. Athough many former militants of the [[pePHP|PHP]] maintained their membership in PLG.

In March 2024, Congresswoman Flor Pablo, [[pePM|PM]]-elected like Paredes, co-led the creation of the political party [[peLoJusto|Lo Justo por el Perú]] with Marisol Pérez Tello (former general secretary of the [[pePPC|PPC]]). Figures such as Daniel Olivares and Alberto de Belaúnde, former congressmen for the [[pePM|Purple Party]] (2020-2021), joined the ranks of Lo Justo. Finally, the group gave up seeking registration with the JNE and joined First the People in June 2024. 

The PLG party had parliamentary representation until 2026, wtih Congresswomen Susel Paredes and Flor Pablo serving into the [[peBDP|People's Democratic Bloc]].

In 2025, PLG announced an alliance with [[peAN|Ahora Nación]], [[peSaP|Salvemos al Perú]] and the [[pePTE|Workers and Entrepreneurs Party]] where Alfonso López-Chau would be the presidential candidate. However, after internal disagreements, said alliance was dissolved; In July, the party joins with the [[pePTE|Workers and Entrepreneurs Party]] to form the "Front of Workers and Entrepreneurs", however, after internal disagreements within the [[pePTE|Workers and Entrepreneurs Party]], the party ended said alliance, announcing that they would participate independently.

Finally, the party elected Marisol Pérez Tello as its presidential candidate, accompanied by Raúl Molina and Manuel Ato as first and second vice presidents. Marisol Pérez Tello finished 8th with 3.41% of votes.
parties.ideology: The party was described as progressive-liberal. While there are many currents within the party, the predominant ones are those that promote free markets, feminism, and gender identity.
