parties.name: Free Peru
parties.description:
The party was founded in August 2008 by former Junín governor Vladimir Cerrón. Cerrón had been elected in 2018 for a second non-consecutive term as governor, but his tenure was cut short due to the sentence. Still, he formally leads the party in his position of Secretary-General. 

Cerrón ran as a presidential candidate in the 2016 Peruvian general election, and registered his candidacy on 11 January 2016 but withdrew from the race two months later due to little support in his candidacy and also to prevent the party from losing its electoral registration.

In the 2018 regional and municipal elections, Cerrón took the businessman, journalist, and radio host Ricardo Belmont ([[peOBRAS|OBRAS]]) as a candidate for the Metropolitan Municipality of Lima, obtaining 3.89% of the votes validly cast in Lima.

In the 2020 Peruvian parliamentary election held on 26 January, the party won 3.4% of the popular vote but no seats in the Congress of the Republic of Peru, as the party failed to reach the electoral threshold. Months before the election, the party was in talks with the [[peJP|Together for Peru]] coalition and [[peNP|New Peru]] in order to run allied in the parliamentary election; however, due to Cerrón's criminal profile and many prominent [[peNP|New Peru]] members quitting their party as the union materialized, the alliance fell through and the parties ran separately in the election, in which neither achieved representation.  Their presidential nominee, Pedro Castillo, unexpectedly took the lead in the first round of the 2021 Peruvian general election, after seeing a surprise surge in support starting around one month before the election. After his victory in the first electoral round, Castillo asked to dialogue with other Peruvian political forces in order to achieve political agreement; however, he ruled out making a roadmap as Ollanta Humala did, maintaining ideological discourse. On 6 June, Castillo won the second-round run-off election for president.

In January 2022, vice president Dina Boluarte was expelled from Free Peru by Vladimir Cerrón after she stated during an interview with La República that she had never embraced the party's ideology. Cerrón said that Boluarte's comments threatened party unity. Her departure was followed by President Castillo's several months later, in June 2022, when he resigned from the party following a request by Cerrón. The latter accused Castillo of implementing policies out of step with Free Peru.
parties.ideology:
The party describes itself as "a left-wing socialist organization" that supports anti-imperialism, democracy, decentralization, federalism, humanism, internationalism, Latin American integration, and sovereignty. The party claims to uphold the works of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels, Vladimir Lenin, and José Carlos Mariátegui. Free Peru's political position has been variously described by observers as left-wing, to far-left, and the party's ideology has been described as Marxist, Marxist–Leninist, Left-wing populist, and socialist.

Both Pedro Castillo, Vladimir Cerrón, and the whole party have taken conservative stances on social issues, as did their right-wing opponents, including opposing same-sex marriage, but supports the decriminalization of abortion. Following his success in the first round of the 2021 presidential election, Castillo said that he opposes Chavismo and Nicolás Maduro, distanced himself from those on the far-left in the party, would not nationalize industry, and would honor the rule of law to placate market alarmism, adding that he would lead the party instead of Cerrón.

parties.name: Green Democratic Party
parties.description:
The Green Democratic Party  was founded on 21 February 2021, by Álex Gonzáles Castillo, then mayor of San Juan de Lurigancho, as a political alternative focused on environmentalism and social justice. Its official registration with the National Elections Board (JNE) Registry of Political Organizations was completed on 14 February 2023.

Prior to its legal registration, the PDV operated as a regional political movement. According to local reports, the membership collection kit was acquired on 15 January 2021, initiating a rapid process of organization and signature gathering, especially in San Juan de Lurigancho, which allowed it to register within the legal timeframe.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, a controversy arose: party leaders allegedly registered community kitchen leaders without their consent, using signatures collected under the pretext of registering for food aid networks. This practice triggered complaints of possible misuse of data and led to the National Registry of Identification and Civil Status (RENIEC) flagging more than 7,200 signatures on the party's membership list.

Following its formal registration, it gained national visibility. In February 2023, its leadership was received at the Government Palace by President Dina Boluarte, in an act of political openness toward newly created parties.

Among the subsequent milestones, the affiliation of former President Alejandro Toledo in July 2024 stands out, reinforcing the perception of an alliance between PDV and [[pePPosible|Perú Posible]] in the context of preparations for the 2026 elections.

Its participation in the 2026 general elections was officially announced, with Gonzáles as its presidential candidate.
parties.ideology:
The Green Democratic Party defines itself as an environmental organization that seeks the sustainable development of Peru through inclusive policies for all its inhabitants, promoting decentralization and transparency in public administration.

In this way, the party combines a green party profile with the tradition of Latin American social democracy, proposing a model of sustainable and equitable development.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, a controversy arose: party leaders allegedly registered community kitchen leaders without their consent, using signatures collected under the pretext of registering for food aid networks. This practice triggered complaints of possible misuse of data and led to the National Registry of Identification and Civil Status (RENIEC) flagging more than 7,200 signatures on the party's membership list.

Following its formal registration, it gained national visibility. In February 2023, its leadership was received at the Government Palace by President Dina Boluarte, in an act of political openness toward newly created parties.

Among the subsequent milestones, the affiliation of former President Alejandro Toledo in July 2024 stands out, reinforcing the perception of an alliance between PDV and [[pePPosible|Perú Posible]] in the context of preparations for the 2026 elections.

Its participation in the 2026 general elections was officially announced, with Gonzáles as its presidential candidate.

ideology.text:
The Green Democratic Party defines itself as an environmental organization that seeks the sustainable development of Peru through inclusive policies for all its inhabitants, promoting decentralization and transparency in public administration.

In this way, the party combines a green party profile with the tradition of Latin American social democracy, proposing a model of sustainable and equitable development.

parties.name: Lo Justo por el Perú
parties.relations:
Split from the [[pePM|Purple Party]] (PM);
Merged into the [[pePLG|First the People]] (PLG).
parties.description:
The Lo Justo party emerged in early 2024 as a faction of the [[pePM|Purple Party]] opposed to party president Luis Durán, who reorganized the party to the detriment of the party's communications wing that had supported Julio Guzmán's presidential campaign in the 2021 presidential election. Following the failure of Guillermo Flores' candidacy for mayor of Lima due to documentary errors, Flor Pablo proposed relaunching the party with another name and logo, because Guzmán had registered the trademark with INDECOPI and refused to give it up. 

By the end of 2023, Pablo, along with Marisol Pérez Tello, Eduardo Dargent and Daniel Olivares, began talks to form a new party if they failed to change the name and logo of the [[pePM|Purple Party]]. On 10 January 2024, Pablo sent a letter to Durán urging him to change the name and logo of the [[pePM|Purple Party]]. On 18 January, José Luis Márquez Molina, Pérez Tello's adviser, put forward Lo Justo's name before the National Jury of Elections (JNE). On 2 February, Pablo resigned from the Purple Party; on 14 February, Olivares would do the same; launching the Lo Justo party. Alberto de Belaúnde and Gino Costa also joined Lo Justo party.

Pablo and Pérez Tello mentioned that they sought to be a decentralized party, adding to its influx of members the likes of former governor of Cuzco, Jean Paul Benavente, among other regional officials.

By June 2024, Lo Justo’s leaders realized the party would not be able to register at the National Jury of Elections on time before the 12 July 2024 deadline, desisting of continuing the process and exploring possible parties to integrate. Following People's Liberty rejection, they reached an agreement with [[pePLG|First the People]] (PLG) party to fully integrate Lo Justo into their party in order to not lose the opportunity of participating of the 2026 election.

In 2026 election, Marisol Pérez Tello was PLG presidential candidate, finishing 8th with 3.41% of votes.

parties.name: Magisterial Bloc of National Concertation
parties.relations:
Split from the [[pePL|Free Peru]].
Partially merged into the [[peSP|We Are Peru]] (SP).
parties.description:
On 11 May 2022, ten members of Congress from the [[pePL|Free Peru]] (PL) parliamentary group announced their resignation due to a disagreement over the selection of new justices for the Constitutional Court, which was carried out without prior discussion. On 14 May, the ten resigning congressmen, from the "teachers' wing" of the Peru Libre party, announced the creation of the Magisterial Bloc of National Concertation.

With the creation of the "Teachers' Bloc" in May 2022, President Pedro Castillo (who resigned from [[pePL|Free Peru]] in June) secured a pro-government bloc. However, in the remaining six months of his administration, he aligned himself more closely with the legislators of [[pePeDe|Democratic Peru]] bloc, two of whom served as Prime Ministers.

The parliamentary group has not expressed any ideology. In the third impeachment process against Pedro Castillo, which was successful, the BMCN Bloc cast 3 votes in favor, 4 abstentions, and only 1 vote against.

The BMCN Bloc has demonstrated close ties with the subsequent government of Dina Boluarte.

The largest number of defections from BMCN occurred in July 2024. Legislators Francis Paredes and Edgar Tello migrated to [[pePP|Podemos Perú]]. Meanwhile, legislator Pasión Dávila, close to Pedro Castillo and promoter of his new political party [[peTCP|Everything with the People]] (TCP), also resigned from the BMCN in July 2024 and formed the [[peBS|Socialist Bench]] parliamentary group along with other dissidents from [[pePL|Free Peru]].

On 18 July 2025, Congressmen Álex Paredes, Elizabeth Medina, and Óscar Zea resigned from the caucus to join the [[peSP|We Are Peru]] caucus, leaving only four members: Segundo Quiroz, Germán Tacuri, Katy Ugarte, and Lucinda Vásquez. This fell short of the minimum of five members required to be considered a caucus, according to the Parliament's Rules of Procedure, leading to its dissolution.
parties.ideology:
The group can be designated as leftist, since the members are from a wing of Free Peru. The main difference in terms of which party supports Pedro Castillo is that teachers want to evolve within the committees and want to chair the Education Committee.

This presidency of the Education Commission is the main point of divergence between [[pePL|Free Peru]] and the teaching wing, since at the beginning of the legislature in July 2021, the presidency of the commission had been granted to the [[peRP|Popular Renewal]] party, positioned on the right, due to the bad negotiations of the leaders of the Free Peru, Waldemar Cerrón and Guido Bellido.

The group will not break the institutional balance since the group also supports Pedro Castillo, as indicated by Waldemar Cerrón, the leader of Free Peru in Congress. They do not want the presidential vacancy of the president, they are in favor of the Constituent assembly, and the magisterial wing has voted in the past in favor of the electoral and academic counter-reforms proposed by Free Peru.

However, this same group may try to interfere in the government and upset the balance created during the government. This teaching wing had been able to have a representative during the first government, with teacher Iber Maraví as Minister of Labor. In addition, Edgar Tello, one of the group's spokesmen, calls for President Pedro Castillo to "decide which party is really in power", since Pedro Castillo is in theory more linked to the teachers.

parties.name: Militarized Communist Party of Peru
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[peSenderoRojo|Sendero Rojo]]
parties.description: Following [[peSenderoLuminoso|Shining Path]] Abimael Guzmán's talks with the Peruvian government in 1992, his "pro-agreement" faction was opposed by Óscar Ramírez's Communist Party of Peru – Marxist-Leninist-Maoist (PCP-MLM), better known as [[peSenderoRojo|Sendero Rojo]], or as the Pro-Seguir faction (SL-Proseguir). This group operated until Ramírez's capture in 1999, after which the group was reorganised under the Quispe Palomino brothers. It formally renounced its links to the Shining Path and declared itself a separate entity in 2018.
parties.ideology:
The MPCP regards itself as a communist and Marxist–Leninist–Maoist party, though it explicitly denounces the Gonzalo Thought ideology of the original [[peSenderoLuminoso|Shining Path]]. Its actions are self-proclaimed as the "Prolonged Unitary Democratic People's War of Peru".

It has been compared to the [[coFARC|Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia]] due to its continued existence even after the collapse of its leadership. Unlike its predecessor, the MPCP claims to have abandoned its anti-religious sentiment and persecution, and seeks to reach an agreement through dialogue with the Peruvian government. In 2022, it proclaimed its allegiance to the [[cnCCP|Chinese Communist Party]] and its leader, Xi Jinping.

parties.name: Modern Peru
parties.description:
Founded and led by businessman Wilson Aragón Ponce, the party gained notoriety as its executive committee is entirely composed of the founder's family. According to PM itself, political organization named Modern Peru was founded in 2003.

In 2023, the party applied for registration with the National Elections Board, achieving its registration on 7 June of that year.

Upon confirming its party registration with the National Elections Board in 2024, the party announced the affiliation of Ajegroup businessman Carlos Añaños, indicating a possible presidential candidacy in the 2026 general elections. However, Añaños withdrew his presidential aspirations after disagreements with party leader Aragón regarding the nomination of candidates for Congress. Subsequently, Añaños left the party.

Among its members who competed for the party's presidential nomination for 2026 were former Minister of Energy and Mines Rómulo Mucho and architect Pedro Guevara

In 2025, the party held primary elections, where Carlos Jaico was chosen as the presidential candidate, with Miguel Almenara and Liz Quispe Santos as first and second vice-presidential candidates, respectively

In 2026, the party decided to run in the presidential elections that same year, but finished in last place with a mere 0.00248% of the vote, resulting in the party's failure.

parties.name: National Alliance of Workers, Farmers, University Students, Reservists and Laborers
parties.nativeName: Alianza Nacional de Trabajadores, Agricultores, Universitarios, Reservistas y Obreros
parties.relations: Split from the [[peUPP|Union for Peru]].
parties.description:
Following the 2021 general election, [[peUPP|Union for Peru[[ (UPP) lost its political registration, leaving the Ethnocacerism without a political vehicle. On 20 August 2022, the leader of the movement, Antauro Humala, was released from prison after 15 years imprisoned due to the Andahuaylazo. He recognized his plans to register two parties in order to compete in the upcoming presidential election: the United Revolutionary Ethnocacerist Party (PERU) and the ANTAURO itself. On 11 January 2023 he submitted the required signatures to register the party.

In September 2023, a private citizen filed a challenge against the imminent registration of the ANTAURO, contending that its leader, Humala, praises the Revolutionary Junta of Juan Velasco Alvarado and supports terrorism, thereby posing a threat to Peruvian democracy. However, on 7 December 2023, the National Jury of Elections (JNE) dismissed the complaint, asserting that Humala did not officially hold any leadership position within the party. Ultimately, the ANTAURO was registered on 12 December 2023 with Marco Antonio Vizcarra, another participant in the Andahuaylazo, as the president and former UPP congressman Rubén Ramos Zapata as the legal official.

Amid widespread concern regarding the party's registration, Prime Minister Alberto Otárola declared his intention to request authorities to investigate the party's ideology, aiming to determine its commitment to democratic principles. Additionally, Congressman Carlos Anderson proposed legislation to prohibit individuals convicted of homicide from assuming the presidency in Peru, a measure designed to preempt any potential presidential candidacy by Humala in the forthcoming 2026 Presidential election.
parties.ideology:
The party declares itself to be environmentalist, in favor of ethnic diversity, in favor of the liberal democratic system, and supportive of solidarity. It is also in favor of restoring mandatory military service, defending so-called "civic and moral values" related to social conservatism, nationalism, greater participation of the Peruvian Armed Forces in citizen security, food self-sufficiency, and the industrialization of the country through "prioritizing national production over all imports."

The party's acronym is named after its leader, which has led to the party be deemed as a surrogate, which has been rejected by Humala. The party's main ideology is ethnocacerism, which mixes racial superiority of the 'copper skinned' with anti-Chilean rhetoric and has been described as a form of Andean fascism. Nevertheless, in January 2023, Antauro Humala was denounced for praising the Peruvian communist guerrilla group  [[peSenderoLuminoso|Shining Path]].

The ANTAURO has strongly criticized the release of former President Alberto Fujimori, adopting an overtly Anti-Fujimorist rhetoric in its campaign. According to political analysts, Humala has recently sought to cast himself as the 'Peruvian Bukele', seemingly attempting to position himself as an authoritative leader. In its statute, the ANTAURO advocates for the restoration of the mandatory military service.

parties.name: National United Resurgence
parties.relations: Founded as political organisation in 1992.
parties.description:
According to its bylaws, the party began as an independent movement that later acquired the status of a political party upon its registration on 19 August 2002, and changed its name to RUNA on 15 June 2013.

In 1992, notary Ciro Gálvez founded the Andean Renaissance political party and later, in the 2001 general elections, ran for president of the Republic, finishing in sixth place. In those elections, the party also fielded candidates for Congress in all regions of the country; however, they only obtained one deputy: Eduardo Salhuana.

For the 2006 general elections, he again ran for president, but on 7 April 2006, two days before the election, he unofficially withdrew from the race, expressing his support for Lourdes Flores's candidacy. He did not submit a formal resignation, and this did not affect the vote. He received 0.186% of the vote, placing 15th in the election.

On 15 June 2013, Gálvez re-established his Andean Renaissance party, changing its name to National United Renaissance (RUNA) because, according to Gálvez, they wanted to "relaunch the movement with a more inclusive name." The party formed an alliance with the independent group Siempre Unidos, led by the mayor of Los Olivos, Felipe Castillo.

On 28 October 2020, Gálvez registered his pre-candidacy for the 2021 Peruvian general elections. He commented that they would "face the 2021 elections with their own members, without any electoral or political alliances, nor with well-known figures." As a result, the party obtained 0.50% of the vote, without parliamentary representation, thus losing its registration.

In July-October 2021, Ciro Gálvez served as Minister of Culture under Pedro Castillo ([[pePL|PL]]) presidency.

In 2024, the party changed its name to National United Resurgence, keeping its acronym RUNA, with the aim of re-registering to participate in the next elections. However, the party did not appeal its registration by the 12 April 2025 deadline. Gálvez rejected the challenge against his party, asserting that they had met all legal requirements and had no ties to the Perú Libre party.

In June of the same year, the party achieved its registration with the JNE, but would not participate in the 2026 general elections, instead participating in the regional and municipal elections of that year.

In 2026 elections, RUNA participated inside [[peAEV|Venceremos]] alliance.

The alliance was led by presidential candidate General Roberto Chiabra ([[pePUP|Unity and Peace]]), who received only 0.23% of votes.

parties.name: National Victory
parties.relations:
Preceded by the [[peRN|National Restoration]] (RN).
Merged into the [[peSP|We Are Peru]] (SP).
parties.description:
When Humberto Lay resigned from the [[peRN|National Restoration]] (RN) leadership in mid-2019, the party underwent a formal reorganization that involved a refounding with a name change. After multiple discussions with different political leaders, the party reached an agreement with former footballer George Forsyth to reorganize it.

In October 2020, the party announced its refounding under Forsyth's leadership, effectively dissolving National Restoration and establishing the name National Victory. The party subsequently nominated Forsyth as its presidential candidate for the 2021 Peruvian general election, but was disqualified on 10 February 2021. However, the disqualification was revoked by the National Jury of Elections on 5 March 2021, following to an appeal.[3] On Election Day, Forsyth placed 8th while in the Congressional election, the party failed to win any seats by a margin of 0.04%.

The party was deregistered on 7 September 2021.

Later, Forsyth rejoined [[peSP|We Are Peru]]. On 23 June 2026, the We Are Peru party distanced itself from Forsyth due to his support of Roberto Sánchez, saying that Forsyth "does not represent the feelings of the party."
parties.ideology:
In contrast to the evangelical roots of National Restoration, National Victory adheres to a liberal-conservative platform

On economic issues, Forsyth is seen as a pro-market candidate, although his positions on the Peruvian economy, according to American Quarterly, "are less clear."

parties.name: New Peru for Good Living
parties.nativeName: Nuevo Perú por el Buen Vivir
parties.relations:
Split from the [[peFA|Broad Front]].
Merger of the [[peSembrar|Sembrar Movement]], [[pePS2005|Socialist Party]] and [[peTyL|Land and Liberty]].
parties.description:
On 10 July 2017, 10 congressmen left the [[peFA|Broad Front]] caucus, and on July 26, New Peru appointed its coordinators and representatives to the Board of Spokespersons of Congress for the 2017-2018 period: Alberto Quintanilla, coordinator of the parliamentary bloc, and Tania Pariona, in charge of the alternate coordination.

The party was informally founded on 9 December 2017 in Metropolitan Lima. New Peru absorbed other groups, such as: [[peSembrar|Sembrar Movement]], [[pePS2005|Socialist Party]] and [[peTyL|Land and Liberty]].

The spokesperson for New Peru is Edgar Ochoa. New Peru had 10 seats in the Congress of the Republic of Peru who separated from the [[peFA|Broad Front]] coalition upon its formation. The group was legally recognized in September 2017. The movement is in the process of being registered as a political party to formally participate in the 2021 general election.

At the legislative elections held on 26 January 2020, the party ran allied with the [[peJP|Together for Peru]] coalition as its party registration was still pending. The exit polls gave the alliance 4.8% of the popular vote but no seats in the Congress of the Republic, as they failed to pass the electoral threshold. For the 2021 general election, Mendoza was unable to register New Peru, prompting her to reach an agreement with [[peJP|Together for Peru]] in order to run for the presidency for a second time. Confirmed as the coalition's presidential nominee, Mendoza failed to qualify for the run-off a second time, as she placed sixth in the election with 7.9% of the popular vote. Her loss in support throughout the campaign is widely credited to Pedro Castillo and Yonhy Lescano's voting share in the south of Peru, a traditional stronghold for the Peruvian left.

Following the removal of Pedro Castillo, New Peru joined the protests against Dina Boluarte. The movement participated in the various demonstrations organized by social organizations that took place in Lima and throughout the country. On 17 December 2022 of that year, their party headquarters, located in Plaza Bolognesi, was raided by the police in what the NP and various human rights groups described as an irregular operation. The headquarters provided lodging and food to delegations of protesters who had traveled from other regions.

New Peru members have been participating in the protests against Dina Boluarte since December 2022. They have joined the call for early elections and have reaffirmed their demand for a new Constitution. Together with other popular and social organizations, they form the CNUL, the National Unitary Coordinating Committee for Struggle, which has called for a national meeting at the end of September 2023.

On 5 July 2024, the party finally achieved its registration as a political party, naming itself New Peru for Good Living.

For the 2026 elections, New Pery formed the [[peAEV|Venceremos]] alliance with the [[peVP|Voices of the People]] party, led by Guillermo Bermejo.
parties.ideology: In New Peru's party documents, they describe the organization as "socialist, feminist, environmentalist, diverse and intercultural". According to party president Verónika Mendoza, New Peru is "part of a long socialist tradition that began with the Peruvian Marxist José Carlos Mariátegui in the 1920s", and that the party distanced itself from "ideologism and authoritarianism that has, where it appeared, isolated the Left". New Peru advocates for equal rights, the respect for diversity, protection of nature and sustainability that is achieved through a decentralized system which utilizes multiple viewpoints.

parties.name: Party of Good Government
parties.description:
The party was founded on 29 January 2020, by sociologist Jorge Nieto, former minister of Defense and of Culture under the presidency of Pedro Pablo Kuczynski. The party's name and Inti (Inca sun god) symbolism both alude to the 17th century illustrated chronicle El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno, authored by Quechua nobleman Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala. Nieto has described the chronicle as remarkably relevant to contemporary Peru, particularly for its denunciation of the enduring divide between the Indigenous and criollo worlds and its call for cultural equality and equal rights.

On 10 July 2024, Nieto announced the party's registration with the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP) of the National Elections Board (JNE) with the aim of participating in the 2026 general election. It achieved its registration on 2 August 2024, becoming the 33rd political party registered with the ROP.

In the 2026 general election, the PBG came in fourth place in its presidential candidacy and won seats in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies, securing the fourth and third largest blocs in each chamber, respectively. The party, under the leadership of Jorge Nieto, decided not to endorse either of the two candidates in the presidential runoff between the leftist Roberto Sánchez of [[peJP|Together for Peru]] and the rightist Keiko Fujimori of the [[peFP|Popular Force]], and, on the contrary, actively promoted spoiled ballots, urging its supporters to write "We want a Good Government" on the ballots. Nieto also questioned the "lesser evil" argument for choosing between the two candidates as problematic and maintained that "the left has to take responsibility for the consequences of permanently choosing the lesser evil."

parties.name: Patriotic Party of Peru
parties.description:
The Patriotic Party of Peru (PPP) was founded on 28 July 2017 by lawyer and former Former Navy officer Herbert Caller Gutiérrez.

The party's first formal registration attempt was in preparation for the 2020 parliamentary elections, but PPP was not admitted to participate. However, its president emphasized that they would participate in the 2021 elections, although the party was still in the registration process.

On 29 March 2022, the party achieved its registration with the National Elections Board's Registry of Political Organizations and participated unsuccessfully in the 2022 regional and municipal elections.

During this period, Caller, along with Secretary General Julio Lingán and Secretary Stephany Reyes, met with President Dina Boluarte after her swearing-in and assumption of office. There, Caller declared his support for holding early elections in 2023.

In 2024, Herbert Caller announced his presidential candidacy for the 2026 general elections.
parties.ideology:
The party defines itself as "a doctrinaire, democratic, and independent political party, a defender of liberty, justice, equal opportunities, and peace; respectful of the constitutional order and a defender of the interests of our nation, constituted in accordance with the Political Constitution of Peru." Its ideology emphasizes the concept of patriotism alongside measures aimed at improving public administration.

Its president has spoken out against Rafael López Aliaga and criticized the current Congress of the Republic, demanding snap elections. The party has categorized Parliament as the first power of the state.

parties.description:
In view of the 2018 regional and municipal elections, the various Peruvian left-wing groups formed the [[peJP|Together for Peru]] coalition (registered as a political party with the JNE). The alliance is maintained for the Peruvian general elections of 2021, whose presidential candidate was Verónika Mendoza of the [[peNP|New Peru]] movement. The alliance won 5 of 130 seats.

In April 2022, the congressmen of [[peJP|Together for Peru]] (a dissolved coalition that retains electoral registration as a political party) re-found the parliamentary group with the name Democratic Change - Together for Peru (CD-JP). It is made up of legislators Sigrid Bazán ([[peNP|New Peru]]), Ruth Luque (En Movimiento), Edgard Raymundo, Isabel Cortez, Roberto Sánchez (JP). They occupy an ordinary commission for the legislature August 2022 - July 2023.

The following year, March 2023, the four congressmen of the dissolved [[pePeDe|Democratic Peru]] bench (Guillermo Bermejo ([[peVP|Voices of the People]]), Hamlet Echevarría, Nieves Limachi and Luis Kamiche) join the parliamentary group CD-JP. In July 2023, the non-grouped congresswoman Susel Paredes ([[pePLG|First the People]]) joins. In total, they occupy 10 seats and chair 2 ordinary commissions for the legislature August 2023 - July 2024. In March 2024, legislator Víctor Cutipa joins.

In July 2024, Cambio Democrático is refounded as Democratic People's Bloc (initially as Frente Democrático) and brings together 5 congressmen of the 11 in the bench: Sigrid Bazán ([[peNP|New Peru]]), Susel Paredes ([[pePLG|First the People]]), Ruth Luque (En Movimiento), Edgard Reymundo and Isabel Cortez.

The bloc was dissolved with the dissolution of 2026 congress.

parties.name: People's Liberty
parties.description:
The party was founded on 31 December 2021 by Rafael Belaúnde Llosa, former Minister of Energy and Mines (2020).

The People's Liberty applied for registration as a political party with the National Elections Board (JNE) on November 14, 2022. Formal recognition by the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP) occurred in June 2023. Among its members was the famous writer Mario Vargas Llosa.

In 2026, several members of Popular Liberty resigned after it became known that Rafael Belaúnde Llosa supported Keiko Fujimori. Subsequently, Rafael Belaúnde became Minister of Defence in Keiko Fujimori's cabinet.
parties.ideology:
LP defines itself as a liberal party that promotes the social market economy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and democratic governance. Its public positioning places it on the center-right, although its own leaders refer to it as "decent center."

The party favors a strong emphasis on improving public infrastructure (roads, irrigation, hospitals) as an engine of economic growth. It also supports citizen security, crime control, and strengthening the prison system. Furthermore, the party rejects political extremism, both left and right.

parties.name: Peru Action
parties.description:
The Peru Nation party initially participated in the 2016 general elections, but withdrew its presidential candidacy and congressional lists ten days before the election, amid the risk of not reaching the electoral threshold.

In the 2018 Cusco regional elections, candidate César Zubiante was criticized after his campaign ad showed supporters with unusual names urging people to vote for the "PN," pronounced in a way that alludes to "penis", the male reproductive organ. This ad had been stolen from a sketch on the Mexican program ¡Que importa!. In the 2018 Lima municipal elections, former showgirl Monique Pardo participated in an advertisement for candidate Enrique Ocrospoma, where the expression "mark the penis [Pe Ene]" went viral. Social media users criticized the double entendres used in that ad.

In the legislative elections held on 25 January 2020, the party obtained 1.4% of the popular vote but no seats in the Congress of the Republic, ranking 21st out of 22 participating parliamentary lists.

It was confirmed that they would participate in the 2021 Peruvian general elections, with Francisco Diez Canseco as their presidential candidate, along with Nancy Cáceres and Manuel Salazar as vice-presidential candidates. The presidential ticket was not admitted because they did not meet the deadline for registering for the elections.

In late 2021, the party formed an alliance with the Popular Renewal and Peru Safe Homeland parties to participate in the 2022 regional and municipal elections.

In 2023, the party changed its name to Peru Action and in July of the same year, it obtained its registration with the National Elections Board (JNE) in the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP) with the aim of participating in the 2026 elections.

parties.name: Peru First
parties.description:
A Peruvian political party founded in 2021 by Martín Vizcarra, independent president of Peru from 2018 to 2020.

Since 2023, it has been registered with the National Elections Board (JNE) to participate in the 2026 general elections in. During the 2022-2023 Peruvian protests, the party supported the demonstrations against the government of Dina Boluarte and the Congress of Peru, which Vizcarra described as a "congressional dictatorship."
parties.ideology:
Peru First defines itself as a social-liberal party with a strong focus on decentralization. Its platform also includes positions against the policies of former president Alberto Fujimori and his political heirs. Its social-liberal approach promotes combining individual liberty with state intervention to guarantee social and economic justice. The P1 party also advocates for the redistribution of power in the country through policies that strengthen the regions and promote equitable development throughout the national territory.

Looking ahead to the 2026 elections, the party has identified four fundamental pillars in its political platform: citizen security, education, public health, and economic reactivation. The party maintains that these are the main challenges facing the country and that they require a strong response from the State. Furthermore, it promotes a humanist and democratic approach to addressing these problems, with policies aimed at strengthening public institutions and improving access to basic rights. Furthermore, their candidate, Mario Vizcarra, has supported the legalization of cocaine, the approval of abortion, LGBT marriage, same-sex adoption, and gender identity.

parties.name: Peru Secure Homeland
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[peC90|Cambio 90]].
parties.description:
A Peruvian political party created on 26 September 2013, by former members of the [[peC90|Cambio 90]] party, led by former members of Congress and the Constituent Assembly (1992) Luz Salgado, Andrés Reggiardo, and his son, also a former member of Congress, Renzo Reggiardo. This party emerged from the name change of the Cambio 90 political party, founded by Alberto Fujimori.

Debuting in national politics in the 2014 local and regional elections, Peru+ leader Salvador Heresi was invited to be the party's nominee for Mayor of Lima, finishing in fourth place with 5.9% of the popular vote, losing to Luis Castañeda of the [[pePSN|National Solidarity]].

In 2016, Renzo Reggiardo ran for president of Peru, but withdrew his candidacy after denouncing that there were candidates "riddled with irregularities."

In 2018, Perú Patria Segura nominated Renzo Reggiardo for mayor of Lima. He led in most polls throughout the campaign, but Reggiardo's absence from the mayoral debate proved decisive in the rise of candidates Jorge Muñoz and Daniel Urresti, ultimately finishing third in the election with 8.87% of the vote.

parties.name: Peruvian Nationalist Party
parties.description:
The Nationalist Party had as its antecedent the Peruvian Nationalist Movement (also known as Ethnocacerism). The party was originally conceived to be the main political expression of the ethnocacerist ideology, though the ideology was renounced by party founder Ollanta Humala in 2006.

Ollanta Humala was the Peruvian Nationalist Party's presidential nominee for the 2006 general election, running under a joint ticket with [[peUPP|Union for Peru]], as the party was not registered on time for the election. Humala lost the runoff against Alan García of the [[pePAP|Peruvian Aprista Party]]. However, the alliance with the Union for Peru would be dissolved, and the members of the Nationalist Party would form the Nationalist bench made up of 25 Congressmen. In 2010, PNP formed the alliance [[peGP|Peru Wins]] ("Gana Perú") to participate in 2011 general election. In the runoff vote on 5 June 2011, Humala was elected president against Keiko Fujimori of the Force 2011. He served in office on from 28 July 2011 to 28 July 2016.

Initially perceived as a full-fledged socialist government inspired by the Venezuelan Chavismo, Humala's presidency ultimately embraced free-market policies, although not at the same rhythm as previous administrations. Interpreting his sudden change as a betrayal to his voters, the Nationalist congressional caucus was reduced from 47 seats to 26, as most members rejected the government's inaction in fulfilling Humala's campaign initiatives. In addition, First Lady Nadine Heredia sought to be a controversial figure for the administration by indirectly taking a more active role in her husband's work, ultimately being seen as a dual presidency. Pundits agree on qualifying Humala's Nationalist presidency as mediocre, as no substantial changes were made in both economic and social aspects of Peru. Humala was also considered to have shifted towards neoliberalism and the political centre during his presidency.

The party opted to not take part in the 2016 general elections, in order to preserve its status as an official party; in Peru, a party that fails to obtain above 5% in a national election is automatically removed from the registry of political parties. With the party's prospective presidential candidate Daniel Urresti polling at around 1% in the run-up to the election, the PNP decided to refrain from electoral politics until local elections in 2018.

Following a dry spell by not participating in the 2018 regional and municipal elections and the 2020 snap parliamentary election, the party announced Humala as its presidential nominee for the 2021 general election. On election day, with only 1.6% of the valid votes in the presidential election and 1.51% in the parliamentary election, the party failed to overcome the electoral fence and the party lost its registration as a political party.

parties.name: Peruvians for Change
parties.relations:
Preceded by the coalition [[peAGC|Alliance for the Great Change]] (AGC).
Succeeded by the [[peContigo|Contigo]].
parties.description:
The incorrect spelling Kambio instead of Cambio ("change" in Spanish) was intended to make the party have the same initials as its founder. Founded and officially registered in October 2014. Its leader was Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, President of Peru from 2016 until his resignation in 2018.

In his short presidential tenure, Kuczynski held a government minority in the Peruvian Congress against [[peFP|Popular Force]]'s majority. Initially with 18 members, the party's parliamentary caucus ended splitting up into factions, as independent congressmen left following the pardon of Alberto Fujimori in December 2017. Amid scandal revolving on the president's past relationship with Odebrecht conglomerate, and facing two impeachment processes, Kuczynski tendered his resignation in March 2018.

The party in theory served as President Martín Vizcarra's government party even though he was not registered but ended up in a bitter conflict between the executive branch and the parliamentary caucus, as they held many disagreements on policy and government decisions. Following to the party's poor results at the 2018 regional and municipal elections, and Kuczynski's resignation to the party's presidency, the National Executive Committee agreed on re-founding the party under the name [[peContigo|Contigo]] in March 2019, thus effectively dissolving Peruvians for Change.
parties.ideology: The party was described as conservative and liberal.

parties.name: Political Party PRIN
parties.literalName: acronym for: Regionalist Party of National Integration
parties.description:
The party was founded on 29 December 2021 in Lima. Twenty-five founders headed by Walter Chirinos approved the party's name, symbol, ideology, statute and electoral regulations and elected him president.

The party was conceived as a national vehicle for regional and local leaders who considered the existing parties excessively concentrated in Lima. Its original leadership brought together relatively heterogeneous figures, including former parliamentary candidate Celina Palomino, former footballer Waldir Sáenz and local political organisers from several regions.

PRIN submitted its registration title on 15 February 2022. It documented committees in more than sixty provinces and revised its statute twice in response to DNROP observations. The JNE registered it through Resolution No. 000007-2023-DNROP/JNE, opening electronic record No. 30 on 19 January 2023.

parties.name: Popular Action
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[peFNJD|National Front of Democratic Youth]] (FNJD).
parties.description:
Fernando Belaúnde founded Popular Action (AP) in 1956 as a reformist alternative to the status quo conservative forces and the populist [[pePAP|American Popular Revolutionary Alliance]] party.

Although Belaúnde's message was not all that different from APRA's, his tactics were more inclusive and less confrontational. He was able to appeal to some of the same political base as APRA, primarily the middle class, but also to a wider base of professionals and white-collar workers. It also advocated scientific advancement and technocracy, a policy set that it took from the [[peMSP|Progressive Social Movement]], a splinter party which it eventually absorbed. The AP had significant electoral success, attaining the presidency in 1963 and 1980, but the party was more of an electoral machine for the persona of Belaúnde than an institutionalized organization. The AP was initially reckoned as a center-left party. However, by the 1980s, Peru's political spectrum had shifted sharply leftward, and the AP found itself on the center-right.

After AP's second administration, in 1985, the party was defeated by the APRA party, gaining only 6.4 percent of the vote. In 1990, AP participated in the elections as a part of the [[peFREDEMO|Democratic Front]], a center-right coalition headed by Mario Vargas Llosa.

In 2000, Víctor Andrés García Belaúnde was selected as the presidential nominee, being the worst general election for AP, gaining only 0.42% of the popular vote. Only three AP congressman were elected. As many assume the election was a fraud, Fujimori resigned after the corruption of his government was revealed by the opposition.

AP member Valentín Paniagua would become President of the Congress in November 2000 for a few days and, after the fall of the Fujimori administration, became the interim President of the Republic, holding office from November 2000 to July 2001.

In the 8 April 2001 election, the party won 4.2% of the popular vote and three out of 120 seats in Congress.

Likewise, in 2002, regional elections were held for the first time, which aimed to elect Regional Presidents for the 25 departments of Peru. In that sense, party participation was quite high (15 political groups). In these elections, AP ranked sixth by number of votes.

For the 2006 national election, the party joined forces with [[peSP|We Are Peru]] and [[peTPP|National Coordinator of Independents]] to form the [[peFC|Centre Front]] coalition. Paniagua was the presidential candidate, while the vice-presidential candidates belonged to AP's allies. The [[peFC|Centre Front]] ended in the fifth place in the national election, with 5.6% of the popular vote.

For the 2011 national election, the party joined forces with [[peSP|We Are Peru]] and [[pePPos|Possible Peru]] to form the [[peAEPP|Possible Peru Electoral Alliance]]. The presidential candidate was former Peru's president and leader of Possible Peru, Alejandro Toledo. The alliance ended in the fourth place in the national election, with 15.6% of the popular vote.

For the 2016 national election, the party ran alone for the first time since 2000, when Congressman Víctor Andrés García Belaúnde ran against the sitting president Alberto Fujimori, and it was the first time since 2006 that Popular Action participated with a party member as a presidential candidate when former President Valentín Paniagua ran for office. The presidential candidate was Alfredo Barnechea, journalist and political analyst, who won the party's primaries with 52% of the votes, defeating Mesías Guevara (40%), the party's president for the 2014–2018 term, the lawyer Beatríz Mejía (6%) and former Deputy Alejandro Montoya (2%). Popular Action ended in fourth place in the national election, with 6.97% of the popular vote. This was the best result for Popular Action since 1985. For the 2016–2021 term, AP had five congressmen out of 130 representing the party, until the snap election in 2020, when it increased its representation to 25 congressmen until the end of the 2016–2021 term. In the 2021 elections, Lescano placed 5th in a fractured race of 18 candidates while the party gained 16 seats for the 2021–2026 congressional term. On 26 July 2021, an alliance led by Popular Action member María del Carmen Alva successfully negotiated an agreement to gain control of Peru's Congress.
parties.ideology:
The party has its own official doctrine, "Acciopopulism", whose foundation, according to AP itself, is "situational humanism". This doctrine holds that the role of the State should be limited to regulating and incentivizing private enterprise and sustainable development. Within the main feature of its theory, situational humanism, it considers that in the Peruvian case it is specifically inspired by what has been called "Peru as Doctrine."

It affirms that its proclamation is "Democratic, nationalist, and revolutionary": Democratic, insofar as it respects, promotes, and defends the democratic system. Nationalist, insofar as it promotes local traditions and economic and cultural development. Revolutionary, insofar as it aspires to the continuous updating of the new modernity and to rapid change that improves social and cultural structures.

The idea of ​​"Peru as Doctrine" is based on the values ​​and principles that arose from the particular historical and cultural context in which Peru developed, but which have universal significance. Its most important values ​​are Truthfulness, Honesty, Diligence, and Solidarity. A significant part of its doctrine is developed in what they call Popular Cooperation.

In practice, Popular Action began as a center-left party close to democratic socialism with the first rise to power of Fernando Belaúnde (1963-1968). His second government (1980-1985) was characterized by a shift to the conservative right. Towards the end of the 1960s, a radicalized sector split from the party (the so-called "hotheads"), forming Socialist Popular Action (Manuel Seoane, Gustavo Mohme, among other intellectuals). Likewise, a good portion of the so-called "young Turks" (or "grasshoppers," party militants from the early 1980s), migrated to the right in the early 1990s (first to the [[peMoLib|Liberty Movement]] and then to Fujimorism). 

These are the two biggest losses in support suffered by this party. Consequently, from then on, Popular Action is identified as a catch-all party, with three factions: a conservative right-wing faction, close to neoliberalism and anti-communism; a centrist faction close to humanism and civic nationalism; and finally the progressive left-wing faction, linked to statism and democratic socialism.

parties.relations: Preceded by the [[peNM|New Majority]] (NM).
parties.description:
Force 2011 was formed in 2010 from the [[peNM|New Majority]], as the next incarnation of Fujimorist political party.

On 29 July 2012, Force 2011 was renamed to Popular Force.

Popular Force is the country’s most powerful and best-structured political force. The party governs Peru from Congress, where it holds a position of strength. It has managed to consolidate its political control by appointing individuals aligned with its interests to head several key institutions, such as the Constitutional Court and the Public Ministry. It has been responsible for the removal of three presidents in ten years. Keiko Fujimori has been its undisputed leader since her brother Kenji Fujimori’s withdrawal from political life and her father’s death in 2024.

parties.description:
Progresemos was founded on 22 November 2023, by Paul Jaimes Blanco, Former Secretary General of the Ministry of Agrarian Development and Irrigation of Peru during the presicency of Pedro Castillo.

On 3 July 2024, the party was officially registered with the National Elections Board (JNE) in the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP) with the aim of participating in the 2026 elections.

In March 2025, the party announced Hernando de Soto, right-wing economist and former [[peAvP2017|Avanza País]] presidential nominee, as its presidential pre-candidate for the 2026 elections, through an agreement with his party, [[peCaPo|Capital Popular]], to form an electoral alliance.

However, after refusing to compete in internal party elections, Hernando de Soto resigned from the party and withdrew his presidential candidacy.

Finally, after internal elections, the party designated Paul Jaimes as its leader and presidential candidate, and Luis Miguel Llanos, his opponent in the primaries, as its candidate for Congress representing Lima.

description.text:
Progresemos was founded on 22 November 2023, by Paul Jaimes Blanco, Former Secretary General of the Ministry of Agrarian Development and Irrigation of Peru during the presicency of Pedro Castillo.

On 3 July 2024, the party was officially registered with the National Elections Board (JNE) in the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP) with the aim of participating in the 2026 elections.

In March 2025, the party announced Hernando de Soto, right-wing economist and former [[peAvP2017|Avanza País]] presidential nominee, as its presidential pre-candidate for the 2026 elections, through an agreement with his party, [[peCaPo|Capital Popular]], to form an electoral alliance.

However, after refusing to compete in internal party elections, Hernando de Soto resigned from the party and withdrew his presidential candidacy.

Finally, after internal elections, the party designated Paul Jaimes as its leader and presidential candidate, and Luis Miguel Llanos, his opponent in the primaries, as its candidate for Congress representing Lima.

parties.name: Purple Party
parties.relations: Split from the [[peTPP|All for Peru]].
parties.description:
On 17 October 2016, Julio Guzmán led the First Purple Summit in Lima, Peru, announcing the organization's first steps towards making a party. At the Second Purple Summit (14–15 October 2017), held in Cusco, the presentation of their file for party registration with the corresponding Peruvian body was reported. On 18 November 2017, the party was officially founded. At the Third Purple Summit (13–14 October 2018), held in Ayacucho, the registration and consolidation work of the next party to be formalized was evaluated. After a long process of signature collection for registration, the party was legally recognized by the National Elections Jury on 4 March 2019.

At the Fourth Purple Summit (25–26 October 2019), held in Trujillo. Its objective was to prepare the organization of the party for the next extraordinary congressional elections in January of the following year.

At the 2020 snap parliamentary election on 26 January 2020, the party won 7.4% of the popular vote and 9 out of 130 seats in the Congress of the Republic. Congressmen Alberto de Belaunde and Gino Costa from the [[peBL|Liberal Bench]], who joined the Purple Party, were re-elected in a result of the election.

Following the removal of Martín Vizcarra and Manuel Merino's ascension to the presidency, the 2020 Peruvian protests kicked-off. The party's congressional caucus voted against Vizcarra's removal, being the only party which remained in full-opposition to the political move. Refusing to attend Merino's inauguration, congressman Daniel Olivares plead for the release of arbitrarily detained citizens at police stations, while Guzmán participated in the protests. The rest of the caucus remained vigilant against actions taken by Merino's government, which ended on 15 November 2020, only five days into his presidency.

In September 2020, the Purple Party formally signed a political accord with unregistered [[peFC|Citizen Force]], which lacked registration in order to participate independently, in order to prepare for the 2021 general election. Initially slated for the ticket as a possible running-mate for Julio Guzmán, FC leader and LGBT activist Susel Paredes was ultimately selected to lead the congressional list for the Lima constituency.

On 23 October 2020, former Miraflores mayoral candidate, Alejandro San Martín, officially registered an alternative ticket for the primary election. Two days later, congresswoman Carolina Lizárraga announced her candidacy for the PM's presidential nomination. Facing a competitive primary, Julio Guzmán filed his ticket on 28 October 2020. Choosing former Minister of Education, Flor Pablo, and congressman Francisco Sagasti, as his first and second running mate, his campaign was put on halt as the 2020 Peruvian protests started. Negotiations on which Purple congressman would assume the presidency were tumultuous, as Sagasti was viewed as the only consensus candidate for the role. Reports stated Guzmán ultimately accepted the proposal, thus making Sagasti quit the ticket as second running mate in order to assume the presidency until July 2021.

As Merino's resignation was accepted, Congress voted to elect a new Congress President between the 19 congress members who voted against Vizcarra's removal on 9 November. Talks to select a PM congressman for the position initiated. Congressman Gino Costa was the first proposal, but was unanimously rejected by the rest of caucuses. On the evening of 15 November 2020, Francisco Sagasti was proposed to run for the First Vice Presidency of Congress in a multiparty list led by leftist congresswoman Rocío Silva-Santisteban ([[peFA|FA]]). The single list was officially rejected by Congress, prompting to hold the election till the next day. In this second election, Francisco Sagasti led the multiparty list. As the second list led by María Teresa Cabrera ([[pePP|PP]]) was not approved to run for filing irregularities, the election was imminent. With 97 votes in favor, Sagasti was elected President of Congress, and was inaugurated on the next day as President of Peru to fulfill the end of 2016–2021 term.

On the primary election held on 29 November 2020, Guzmán was selected as the party's presidential nominee with 77% of the vote, while Lizárraga placed second with 19.2%, and ASan Martín attained 3.8%. Guzmán ultimately placed 10th in the election with 2.3% of the vote. The party only won 3 seats in the congressional election. The party was supposed to be dissolved after the 2021 elections on 9 September 2021, but on 2 October 2021, the public hearing was held before the plenary session of the National Elections Jury and, that same day, the resolution was issued which, according to Tello, revoked the ROP resolution and returned the party's registration.

At the 2022 regional and municipal elections, the Purple Party had their worst performance ever in their electoral history as the party failed to achieve office at this level.

The party’s initial three congressional representatives remained ambivalent in the impeachment processes against Pedro Castillo throughout his ill-fated presidency, taking varying stances that caused controversy. In August 2022, representative Edward Málaga refused to join the Integrity and Development caucus, leaving the party with only two representatives. Four months later, Susel Paredes announced she was quitting the party to join [[pePLG|First the People]], leaving Flor Pablo as the only purple representative in Congress until her resignation from the party in February 2024.

In the aftermath of Pablo’s exit from the party, a wave of members quit the party to join Marisol Pérez Tello and Pablo’s new political project, [[peLoJusto|Lo Justo por el Perú]], party which in turn failed to register on time at the National Jury of Elections in order to participate of the 2026 general election. Subsequently, [[peLoJusto|Lo Justo]] was annexed by [[pePLG|First the People]], which became the political harbor for former PM members.
parties.ideology:
The Purple Party defines itself as a radical republican center party. Its centrist stance is expressed in the color purple, positioned between red (alluding to political left) and blue (political right). It understands republicanism in a Peruvian sense: the "republican promise" alluded to by Jorge Basadre in what they call "the Republic of the 21st Century." Thus, they advocate for the creation of opportunities to promote social mobility, the defense of individual political and economic freedoms, the practice of a people-centered democracy, and the establishment of the rule of law. The merger with the [[peFC|Citizen Force]] (FC) party allowed social democratic ideas to enter the party, in addition to its embrace of other liberal positions, which is uncommon in Peruvian politics.

The Purple Party is considered an institutionalist organization, a defender of political and educational reforms, socially progressive, and a reformist advocate of the free market economy. It opposes the existence of a minimalist or stifling state, advocating instead a moderate welfare state to reduce social inequalities, better distribute income, and guarantee equal opportunities. Thus, it seeks to unite liberal and progressive voices in what it calls a "democratic center platform."

parties.name: Salvemos al Perú
parties.description:
The Salvemos al Perú party was founded on 30 August 2021 and registered on 29 May 2023 with the National Elections Board.

In 2025, the party attempted to form an alliance with the [[peAN|Ahora Nación]] party, but internally split over this issue. At the time, the party's president, Guillermo Suárez Flores, rejected the joint registration, while its secretary general, César Gamboa, confirmed the party's General Assembly's decision in support of the alliance. Ultimately, the National Elections Board suspended the alliance's registration. [[peAN|Ahora Nación]] responded by withdrawing its attempt to re-register the alliance, while Salvemos al Perú accused Chau's leadership of lacking initiative.
parties.ideology: According to the party, it defines itself as a centrist and progressive movement, although its discourse occupies an intermediate position with nuances of both the center-right and the center-left. The party emphasizes the family, individual liberty, dialogue and consensus, the independence of political powers, the defense of the social market economy and free enterprise, and the fight against social exclusion and corruption. Its platform focuses on equality, housing creation, healthy food, and technological development. The party's ideology advocates a moderate right-wing stance in economic and institutional-republican matters and a left-wing stance in the social sphere.

parties.description:
During the 2021-2026 parliamentary term, several congressmen elected under the [[pePL|Free Peru]] caucus resigned from the party or became politically disaffiliated, forming a dissident bloc that sought to articulate its own proposal. 

In July 2024, these congressmen formally constituted the Socialist Bench and presented a list for the Congressional Board of Directors, with Silvana Robles as their candidate to preside over that body.

The motions in Impeachment of Dina Boluarte were promoted by the Socialist Bench.

parties.description:
Political party and political coalition.

In May 2017, the organizations of the [[peUnete|Únete]] front ([[peFS|Social Force]], [[peCxC|Citizens for Change]], [[pePCPPR|Communist Party of Peru – Red Fatherland]], [[pePCP|Peruvian Communist Party – Unity]], and [[peMS|Movement for Socialism]])[4] and the [[pePHP|Peruvian Humanist Party]] (PHP) decided to form a political party under the latter's electoral registration. It would henceforth be known as Juntos por el Perú (Together for Peru). Roberto Sánchez ([[pePHP|PHP]]) was registered as president and Gonzalo García Núñez ([[peFS|Social Force]]) as general secretary.

Looking ahead to the 2018 regional and municipal elections, Together for Peru formed an alliance with the [[peNP|New Peru]] movement. It won 10 district mayoralties. This alliance remained in place for the 2020-2021 supplementary congressional elections, but failed to win any seats.

For the 2021 general elections, JP unsuccessfully nominated Verónika Mendoza, leader of [[peNP|New Peru]], for president. The alliance won five seats: four for [[peNP|New Peru]] and one for Together for Peru (Roberto Sánchez). Before, during, and after the election, JP faced internal divisions. [[peFC|Citizen Force]] (a union between [[peFS|Social Force]] and [[peCxC|CxC]]) decided to join the [[pePM|Purple Party]]. The [[pePHP|PHP]]) opted to support Pedro Castillo's candidacy ([[pePL|PL]]) in the first round and officially withdrew from JP in December 2021. [[pePCPPR|PCP – Red Fatherland]] followed suit around the same time. Members of [[peNP|New Peru]] resigned from JP starting in September 2021. [[pePCP|PCP – Unity]] withdrew from the coalition the following year.

In the Congress of the Republic, the parliamentary group Together for Peru has undergone several changes in its composition. Initially, it was known as [[peBDP|Democratic Change–Together for Peru]], which included Roberto Sánchez of JP and the four congressmen from [[peNP|New Peru]]. This group was later joined by dissidents from [[pePL|Free Peru]]: Guillermo Bermejo, Hamlet Echevarría, Roberto Kamiche, and Nieves Limachi. Congresswoman Susel Paredes also joined later. Following the withdrawal of the [[pePL|Free Peru]] congressmen, including Paredes, from the caucus, congressmen from the teachers' union, linked to Pedro Castillo, joined. With this, the parliamentary group became known as Together for Peru – [[peVP|Voices of the People]] – [[peBMCN|Magisterial Bloc]].

From 2022 onward, Together for Peru would be composed solely of a dissident faction of the [[pePHP|PHP]] under the leadership of Roberto Sánchez. In the subnational elections of that year, it won four provincial mayoralties for the first time (Santa in Áncash, Calca and La Convención in Cusco, and Chiclayo in Lambayeque) and 38 district mayoralties.

In 2024-2026, two JP Congressmen were members of the [[peBS|Socialist Bench]] parliamentary group.

For the 2026 general elections, Together for Peru registered the candidacy of its leader, Roberto Sánchez, for the presidency of Peru. They would do so in alliance with [[peTCP|Todo con el Pueblo]] (Everything with the People) of former president Pedro Castillo and the [[peANTAURO|National Alliance]] of ethnocacerist Antauro Humala. The coalition was named Together with the People (Juntos con el Pueblo, also abbreviated JP). [[peVP|Voices of the People]], JP's allies in Congress, ran in a coalition with [[peNP|New Peru]], JP's former allies, under the name [[peAEV|Venceremos]].

On the parliamentary lists, Together for Peru included Pedro Castillo's adopted daughter, Yenifer Paredes, and his siblings, José Mercedes Castillo and Inés Castillo. Former members of Castillo's government (Íber Maraví, Anahí Durand, Hernando Cevallos, and Walter Ayala) and congressmen who supported the former president (Víctor Cutipa, Pasión Dávila, Margot Palacios, Jaime Quito, Silvana Robles, and Elías Varas) also ran. Antauro Humala's father, Isaac Humala, and ethnocacerist allies such as "Pepe" Feria and Marlon Aguirre were also candidates for JP.

Due to irregularities in the receipt of contributions, the National Elections Board fined Juntos por el Perú S/ 175,000 and reduced its electoral airtime allocation.

Sanchez advanced to the second round, and Together for Peru placed second in seats in both houses of Congress. In June 2026, Sanchez was defeated by Keiko Fujimori of [[peFP|Popular Force]].

parties.name: Un Camino Diferente
parties.relations: Founded by former member of [[peSP|We Are Peru]].
parties.description:
A Peruvian political party mainly linked to the former mayor of Trujillo and Moche, César Arturo Fernández Bazán.

The party began its registration process in early 2025. On 11 April of that year, the National Elections Board (JNE) published the resolution authorizing its inclusion in the Registry of Political Organizations. Subsequently, on 16 August 2025, the JNE plenary issued Resolution No. 0308-2025-JNE, confirming its registration after declaring an appeal unfounded.

Various media outlets have reported questions surrounding the party's registration and operation: In June 2025, the Peruvian National Police initiated a preliminary investigation against Arturo Fernández and other leaders for alleged document forgery during the registration process. Citizens reported being registered as members without their consent, leading to requests for disaffiliation before the JNE. Yon Cruzado Tirado, one of the founders, accused Fernández of "betrayal" and attempted appropriation of the party, requesting the JNE to annul its bylaws.

In the La Libertad region, 12.5% ​​of miners in the formalization process (REINFO) were affiliated with Un Camino Diferente, making it the second largest group in this sector after [[peAPP|Alliance for Progress]].

In the La Libertad region, 12.5% ​​of miners in the formalization process (REINFO) were affiliated with Un Camino Diferente, making it the second largest group in this sector after [[peAPP|Alliance for Progress]].

parties.name: Union for Peru
parties.relations: Partially succeeded by the [[peANTAURO|ANTAURO]].
parties.description:
Union for Peru was founded in 1994 by the former Secretary General of the United Nations, the diplomat Javier Pérez de Cuéllar together with Daniel Estrada Pérez and José Vega Antonio, to participate in the elections generals of 1995, against the-then president Alberto Fujimori, who was running for reelection.

At the elections held on 9 April 2000, the party nominated former Fujimorist first vice president Máximo San Román as its presidential candidate, but he performed poorly in the elections placing last with 0.3% of the popular vote but in the legislative elections, the party won 2.6% of the popular vote and only 3 out of 120 seats in the Congress of the Republic, a decrease of 14. During this parliamentary period, UPP made an alliance with the [[peAP|Popular Action]] bench in the legislature and both showed their opposition to the dictatorship of Alberto Fujimori.

Shortly after Alberto Fujimori won the 2000 elections amid accusations of electoral fraud, he decided to resign after the "Vladivideos" scandal and call general elections for 2001.

At the legislative elections held on 8 April 2001, the party won 4.1% of the popular vote and 6 out of 120 seats in the Congress of the Republic. However, they did not present a presidential candidate for that year's elections.

In the 2006 elections, Union for Peru aligned itself with the [[pePNP|Peruvian Nationalist Party]] and endorsed Ollanta Humala, who faced Alan García in the presidential runoff election. In the congressional election, the alliance won with 21.2% of popular vote, and 45 out of 120 seats in the Congress. However, after the elections, the alliance split and the Nationalist sat on their own bench with Union for Peru sitting in their own bench too.

In the 2011 elections, the party joined forces with the [[pePSN|National Solidarity Party]] to form the [[peASN|National Solidarity Alliance]] to support the presidential candidacy of former Lima Mayor Luis Castañeda Lossio. The alliance placed fifth at both the presidential and parliamentary election, attaining 9 out of 130 seats, with Vicente Zeballos and Martin Belaunde Moreya as the only two elected congressman from Union for Peru. 

The party would retain its alliance with the National Solidarity Party for the 2016 elections as well, jointly nominating Hernando Guerra García but the ticket withdrew due to its low support at national polls and fears of losing its status as a political party. 

In the 2020 snap parliamentary elections, the party won 6.8% of the vote and 13 seats out of 130 seats in the Congress after almost four years of absence in Congress. 

In the 2021 elections, the party nominated the party Secretary-General José Vega for the presidency, but, he was disqualified on 29 December 2020, because of incomplete information regarding income on the nominees registration form, but he was reinstated on 6 February 2021. On the Election Day, Vega places 14th with 0.7% of the vote, while in the congressional election, the party lost all of its 13 seats and only won 2.1% of the vote and the party is expected to lose its party registration. Former mayor Ricardo Belmont ([[peOBRAS|OBRAS]]) was chosen as the lead candidate for the Congress of the Republic. However, the party was unsuccessful in the elections and lost its electoral registration.

The party is currently in the process of re-registration. Following the UPP de-registration, Ethnocacerist movement Antauro Humala formed a new party, named [[peANTAURO|ANTAURO]].
parties.ideology: Initially as a centrist and progressive party with left-wing factions, by former United Nations Secretary-General Javier Pérez de Cuéllar to participate in the 1995 general elections against then-President Alberto Fujimori. Over time, the party became the main political focus of the syncretic far-left/far-right ethnocacerist movement led by Antauro Humala from the mid-2010s onward.

parties.name: Voices of the People
parties.relations: Founded by former congressman elected on [[pePL|Free Peru]] list, also an [[peMPCP|MPCP]] liason militant.
parties.description:
On 9 July 2022, Guillermo Bermejo, Congressman who was elected on a [[pePL|Free Peru]] list in 2021, presented the organization Voices of the People. The launch was covered by state and national media. Ronald Atencio was named president and Jaime Laos general secretary. The registration process began on 9 June 2023, but was initially rejected by the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP) of the National Elections Board (JNE) for failing to meet requirements such as the minimum number of members and regional committees. The party appealed the decision, and the full JNE accepted the appeal, citing errors in the notification process, and ordered the process to continue. Finally, the JNE approved its official registration in the Registry of Political Organizations.

It is part of the [[peJP|Together for Peru]] – Voices of the People (JP-VP) bloc in the Congress of the Republic, which has approximately 12 members, making it the fourth largest congressional force.

In March 2024, the National Elections Board (JNE) rejected an initial registration application due to issues with the voter rolls and submitted documents. Subsequently, through Resolution No. 0153-2024-JNE, the Board upheld an appeal and ordered the procedure to continue.

On October 26, 2024, the JNE approved the registration of Voices of the People in the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP).

In October 2025, a trial began against Bermejo because, according to the arguments presented, Bermejo, as a member of the [[peMPCP|MPCP]], acted as a liaison and recruiter of political leaders between 2017 and 2018. In this way, Bermejo delivered ideological material on a USB drive to Vladimir Cerrón and Guido Bellido to "expand the base of the so-called [[peMPCP|Militarized Communist Party of Peru]] and promote the establishment of a new socialist state," fulfilling the aims of said terrorist organization.

In May 2025, Voices of the People joined the bloc that signed the political declaration "Unity to Win, People to Govern," along with [[peNP|New Peru]], the [[pePTE|Workers and Entrepreneurs Party]], and [[pePLG|First the People]], in support of a joint strategy for the 2026 general elections. Alliances were also launched, with [[peNP|New Peru]] and Voices of the People as central elements. Finally, it formed the [[peAEV|¡Venceremos!]] alliance together with [[peNP|New Peru]].
parties.ideology: Voices of the People presents itself as a socialist and popular group, committed to promoting a Constituent assembly, a Second Agrarian Reform, the industrialization of the country and structural reforms to the judicial system and the Public Ministry, with a plurinational vision and emphasis on the popular sectors.

parties.relations: Founded by members of the unregistered party [[pePCPPR|Communist Party of Peru – Red Fatherland]] (PCdelP-PR).
parties.description:
Founded in April 2023, the party was led by Napoleón Becerra, a left-wing perennial candidate. He co-founded it together with members of the [[pePCPPR|Communist Party of Peru – Red Fatherland]].

Among the party's most prominent members are historical former left-wing parliamentarians Rolando Breña Pantoja and César Barrera Bazán.

In November 2025, extraordinary congress of the [[pePCPPR|Communist Party of Peru – Red Fatherland]] approved the mass withdrawal of its militants from PTE. Its public break was announced on 26 November 2025.

The party was projected to participate in the 2026 general election. However, after Becerra's death on 15 March 2026 in a car accident in Huaytará, Huancavelica, the party's presidential list was ruled out according to the National Jury of Elections, given that Peruvian electoral law does not allow a replacement for a presidential nomination in the case of the candidate's death.

For the October 2026 regional and municipal elections, PTE formed the electoral alliance Partido de los Trabajadores y Emprendedores PTE Perú–Comunidad Política Inka Perú. It was legally registered on 25 March 2026 by JNE Resolution.

parties.relations: Split from the [[ptPSD|Social Democratic Party]] (PPD/PSD)
parties.description:
Founded by Pedro Santana Lopes, a long-time member of the [[ptPSD|Social Democratic Party]], the party was established in 2018, positioning itself as an alternative to the left in government and to the lack of opposition from the parliamentary right, being considered at that time center-right.

Its registration in the register of Portuguese political parties was accepted by the Constitutional Court on 23 October 2018.

It was announced that the head of the list for the European Parliament was Paulo de Almeida Sande, on 2 December 2018, but he fell short of achieving the objective of electing two MEPs.

Its founding congress was held on 9-10 February 2019, at the Arena de Évora, and concluded with the legitimization of Pedro Santana Lopes as president of the party.

In the 2019 legislative elections it did not elect any deputies, although it had set a goal of electing at least two.[

It was declared extinct by the Constitutional Court in 2025.

parties.description:
Two pre-electoral coalitions of Portuguese political parties, from left to center-right, that ran for the municipality of Funchal in the 2013 municipal elections and for the Legislative Assembly of Madeira in the 2015 regional legislative elections.

The 2013 alliance was made up of six parties: [[ptPS|Socialist Party]] (PS), [[ptBE|Left Bloc]] (BE), [[ptPND|New Democracy]] (PND), [[ptMPT|Earth Party]] (MPT), [[ptPTP|Portuguese Labor Party]] (PTP) and [[ptPAN|Party for Animals and Nature]] (PAN; in 2014 it changed its name to People-Animals-Nature). Coalition candidate for mayor was an independent nominated by the PS, Paulo Cafôfo, and he won the presidency of the City Council and the Municipal Assembly of Funchal, dethroning for the first time the [[ptPSD|PSD]], which had won all the local councils in the municipality since 1976.

In 2015, the new coalition included only the PS, PTP, PAN and MPT and was head of the regional legislative list by the leader of PS-Madeira, Victor Freitas. This coalition ended up coming in third place and losing deputies in relation to the total that the parties had obtained individually in the previous elections in 2011.
