parties.relations:
Preceded by the [[ptCMLP|Portuguese Marxist–Leninist Committee]] (CMLP);

In 1974, divided into the new PCP(m-l), the [[ptPT|Worker–Peasant Alliance]] (AOC) and the [[ptptPUP1974|Popular Unity Party]] (PUP).
parties.description:
A small far-left political group created in 1970, from the [[ptCMLP|Portuguese Marxist–Leninist Committee]] (CMLP), which had been founded in 1964 by Francisco Martins Rodrigues.

The party was gradually divided between a wing in exile, led by Heduíno Gomes, also known as Eduíno Vilar, and a wing in the interior of Portugal, led by Carlos Janeiro, known by the pseudonym Mendes.

From May 1974 onwards, the split between the two factions was consummated, with both calling themselves "PCP(m-l)". The Vilar faction ended up with the acronym, having created the [[ptPT|Worker–Peasant Alliance]] (AOC) as an "electoral front" to stand in the 1975 elections (AOC was banned from standing in these elections; in the following ones, both AOC and PCP(m-l) competed). The opposing faction gave rise to the [[ptPUP1974|Popular Unity Party]].

The main difference between the new party of Heduíno Gomes and the original of Martins Rodrigues had to do with the status of the main enemy of each of them: while the latter always maintained that the main enemies of the people were «monopolies and North American imperialism», Vilar's party chose the PCP, «Cunhal's Social-Fascism» and «Russian Social-Imperialism» as its primary targets. (Heduíno Gomes left the party in the 1980s, having dedicated himself to business activity in the area of ​​music, and is today a prominent [[ptPSD|PSD]] activist, associated with the most conservative faction of this party.)

Vilar's party had close relations to the [[cnCCP|Chinese Communist Party]]. It led the Democratic Portugal-China Friendship Association (ADAP-C).

In May 1974 the general secretary of the Communist Party of Portugal (Marxist–Leninist) (in Portuguese: Partido Comunista de Portugal (Marxista-Leninista)) was expelled, forming his own similarly-named party. Like the other PCP(M-L), Vilar's PCP(M-L) had a publication titled Unidade Popular.

At the VIII congress of the Party in March 1980 it was decided to dissolve the PCP(m-l).

parties.description:
A pre-election coalition between five Portuguese political parties, from left to center on the political spectrum, for the 2017 municipal elections in the municipality of Funchal. It was made up of the [[ptPS|Socialist Party]] (PS), the [[ptBE|Left Bloc]] (BE), [[ptJPP|Juntos Pelo Povo]] (JPP), the [[ptPDR|Democratic Republican Party]] (PDR) and [[ptNC|Nós, Cidadãos!]] (NC). It presented as a candidate for mayor the independent candidate nominated by PS member Paulo Cafôfo, already acting president at the time, elected by the Coalition for Change in 2013. Confidence Coalition was the list with the most votes, obtaining an absolute majority in the municipal council and Cafôfo being reappointed to the position. The ticket did not, however, win the presidency of the Municipal Assembly, which went to the [[ptPSD|PSD]].

The Confiança Coalition consisted, in essence, of a reissue of the [[ptCMudanca|Change Coalition]] that had run for Funchal in the previous municipal elections. It comprised the same two main parties, the PS and BE, and had many of the same candidates, notably Cafôfo. The big difference was the absence of the smaller parties that had supported the Change ([[ptPND|PND]], [[ptMPT|MPT]], [[ptPTP|PTP]] and [[ptPAN|PAN]]), now.

parties.description:
A left-wing political association formed in 1987, resulting from splits in the [[ptMDPCDE|Portuguese Democratic Movement]] (MDP/CDE).

In 1987 it elected two independent deputies for the [[ptCDU|Unitary Democratic Coalition]], João Corregedor da Fonseca (elected by the Lisbon Electoral District) and Raúl Castro (elected by the Porto Electoral District), forming a parliamentary group in the V Legislature, until July 1988.

It elected one deputy to the Assembly of the Republic in 1991, Raúl Castro (Porto Electoral District) and another deputy in 1995, João Corregedor da Fonseca (Lisbon Electoral District).

Since that date, its members have been participating as independents in the CDU coalition, together with the [[ptPCP|Portuguese Communist Party]] (PCP) and the [[ptPEV|Ecologist Party "The Greens"]] (PEV), during elections.

The association is the current owner and publisher of the magazine Seara Nova (www.searanova.publ.pt), an important publication in the resistance and intellectual struggle against the Estado Novo, the Portuguese dictatorship of 1933-74.

parties.name: Democratic Movement for the Liberation of Portugal
parties.nativeName: Movimento Democrático de Libertação de Portugal
parties.description:
A Portuguese nationalist organization active during the period following the revolution of 25 April 1974. Among the actions attributed to the MDLP are an attempted coup d'état on March 11, 1975, a wave of bomb attacks on the headquarters of left-wing parties, unions or culture in early 1976, including the bomb attack that killed candidate for deputy Padre Max and a student who accompanied him. The more than 500 attacks pointed to social destabilization and generalized a climate of terror, leading to the deaths of several people.

The MDLP was linked to the [[ptMMF|Maria da Fonte Movement]], the [[ptELP|Portuguese Liberation Army]] and [[ptCODECO|CODECO]], with which it shared sources, collaborators and sponsors. These groups, with links to the political power of the Estado Novo and large economic groups, the Church and right-wing parties sought to reverse the democratic changes introduced after the Carnation Revolution.

The MDLP was formally constituted on 5 May 1975, after the coup d'état attempt of 11 March 1975, and was led, from Brazil, by General António de Spínola, but its entire structure was based in Madrid. According to the newspaper Público, António de Spínola "dream[ed] of a return at the head of an invading army to expel the communists from power".

MDLP used illegal and violent methods of struggle. She actively participated in the political struggle during the "Hot Summer" of 1975. It dissolved itself after democratic elections and stabilization of the internal political situation.

Sponsored and led, although unofficially, by Otelo Saraiva de Carvalho, it had a gas station character, aimed at creating a popular front open to all revolutionary anti-fascists, in the fight for socialism, opposing any attempted fascist conspiracy that the PSD and CDS might want to impose.

He published the bulletin "A Luta Continua"[2] During his existence he only ran in the 1976 municipal elections where he failed to obtain more than 2.5% of the votes. Its disintegration resulted in the subsequent creation of the Unitary Workers Organization (OUT), the embryo of the Global Project that included the [[ptFP25|25th of April Popular Forces]] and the [[ptFUP|Popular Unity Force]].

A Portuguese social democratic party founded as parliamentary in 1979, officially registered with the Supreme Court of Justice on June 27, 1980. It was formed after the departure of some [[ptPSD|PPD/PSD]] deputies, including António de Sousa Franco, Joaquim Magalhães Mota, and Sérvulo Correia, among others. It advocated a political, economic, social, and cultural democracy that promoted freedom and equality, based on the principles of personalist and democratic socialism. Its members also included Olívio França, Artur da Cunha Leal, Guilherme de Oliveira Martins, Jorge Miranda, Manuel Tilman, and António José Marques Mendes.

The party participated in the 1980 legislative elections in coalition with the [[ptPS|Socialist Party]] (PS) and the [[ptUEDS|Left-wing Union for the Socialist Democracy]] (UEDS), under the name [[ptFRS|Republican and Socialist Front]] (FRS). It ran on PS lists in 1983 election.

Although not formally dissolved, its dissolution was decided at its II National Congress, on 12 January 1985. Most of its members joined to the Socialist Party.

parties.description:
A far-left, Maoist political party, created from a faction of the [[ptPCPml|Communist Party of Portugal (Marxist–Leninist)]], on the initiative of Heduíno Gomes, pseudonym Vilar.

Officially registered with the STJ in 1975, under the name of Aliança Operário-Camponesa, it changed its name and acronym to "Partido Trabalhista" (PT) in 1979, having run in the Portuguese legislative elections of 1980, the year in which its symbol became a closed hand holding a rose.

In 2000, its extinction was decreed by the STF for not carrying out any activity since 1983.

Just like the PCP(m-l) and the [[ptPPCTPMRPP|MRPP]], the AOC/PT distinguished itself from other far-left groups by electing the [[ptPCP|PCP]] and Álvaro Cunhal as its main enemies instead of the [[ptUDP|UDP]], for example, which coincided with the traditional left in designating capitalism and the United States of America as its main adversaries.

parties.description:
A Portuguese left-wing party founded in January 1978. The party has its origins in the Socialist Culture Association - Worker Brotherhood, a socialist organization and in groups of independent people linked to the Socialist Party.

The party participated in the legislative election of 1980 in coalition with the [[ptPS|Socialist Party]] and the [[ptASDI|Independent Social Democratic Action]] in the [[ptFRS|Republican and Socialist Front]]. In the subsequent elections, the party's members integrated the lists of the Socialist Party. In the Presidential election of 1986 the UEDS members split, one part supporting Mário Soares and the other supporting Maria de Lurdes Pintasilgo.

The party was disbanded in 1986 and most of its members joined the Socialist Party, while others participated on the foundation of the [[ptBE|Left Bloc]].

parties.name: Liberal Party
parties.relations:
Split from the [[ptCM|Monarchist Convergence]] (CM);

After PL being banned, some of party members joined the clandestine [[ptELP|Portuguese Liberation Army]] (ELP)
parties.description:
A Portuguese political party that was created on 28 May 1974, by dissidents from the [[ptCM|Monarchist Convergence]], who disagreed with the creation of the [[ptPPM|PPM]].

PL held its first rally on 15 August 1974 at the São Luís Theatre, its newspaper "Tempo Novo" served as its information organ, and it had links with African movements that opposed decolonization.

Among its most prominent members were Lieutenant Colonel António Luís Marques de Figueiredo and José Harry de Almeida Araújo, who would eventually become its secretary-general.

To participate in the first national elections, it formed an electoral coalition with the [[ptPPMFP|Progress Party]] (PP/MFP) and the [[ptPTDP|Portuguese Democratic Labour Party]] (PTDP), called the [[ptFDU|United Democratic Front]] (FDU). Following the so-called Palma Carlos Crisis, PL, along with the Portuguese Popular Movement (MPP), on 10 July, presented the President of the Republic with a joint resolution denouncing the isolation to which they were subjected, both in terms of expression through the media and in terms of representation in the provisional government.

In this sense, to show their displeasure, they were the main coordinators and the center of the preparation of the failed demonstration, called the "silent majority," planned for 28 September 1974 to support the far-right policies of President António de Spínola. An act that led to their ban and extinction. It was one of the first parties banned in Portugal after the Revolution of 25 April 1974.

On 6 January 1975, former PIDE deputy director Barbieri Cardoso founded the far-right paramilitary organization, the [[ptELP|Portuguese Liberation Army]] (ELP), in Madrid. This organization waged an underground armed struggle against the [[ptPCP|Communist Party]] and the government of Vasco Gonçalves. Prominent figures from the banned Liberal Party joined the ELP. Almeida Araújo and Bragança van Uden became Cardoso's closest associates, the former oversaw the ELP's political center, the latter its operational and combat structure. The ELP was one of the leading anti-communist organizations during the Hot Summer of 1975.

parties.name: National Front
parties.relations: Split from the [[ptE|National Renewal Party]] (PRN)
parties.description:
A Portuguese neo-Nazi group created in 2004, stemming from internal dissension within the [[ptE|National Renewal Party]] (PNR). Despite disagreements with the PNR, it re-established good relations with it in 2005, even going so far as to provide it with political guidance.

This group was named after the [[ptFN|National Front]] party that, in 1980, ran in coalition with the [[ptPDC|PDC]] and the [[ptMIRNPDP|MIRN/PDP]] and which, after obtaining only 0.4% of the vote, ended up ceasing its activity, with journalist and essayist Manuel Maria Múrias as its last president.

The leader of the group that would later adopt the name National Front was Mário Machado, sentenced in 1997 to four years and three months in prison for involvement in the death of Alcindo Monteiro, murdered in 1995 in Bairro Alto. The murder of Monteiro also led to the conviction of 15 Skinheads, some of whom would later join the "Hammerskins". Accused of several other crimes, illegal possession of various weapons and an electric shock machine, he claims to be a "political prisoner".

On 3 October 2008, Machado was sentenced to 4 years and 10 months in prison, 6 "skinheads" were sentenced to prison terms and 17 others had their sentences suspended.

On 17 August 2010, in another trial, Mário Machado was sentenced to 7 years and 2 months in prison. Three other people were sentenced to prison terms, and two had their sentences suspended.

In April 2008, Mário Machado said in court that the group was definitively dissolved and that this movement had to be separated from the Hammerskin Portugal (HP) skinhead faction, which he also leads, as the latter has no political connotation.

parties.name: New Order
parties.relations: Historically preceded by the [[ptMNS|National Syndicalist Movement|]] (MNS)
parties.description:
A Portuguese neo-fascist political movement that existed between 1978 and 1982. Its headquarters were located in Lisbon.[2]

The organisation was created by Gilberto Santos e Castro, a former commando leader in Portuguese Angola. The European Parliament report by the Committee of Inquiry into the Rise of Fascism and Racism in Europe defined its ideology as "revolutionary fascist" and "hyper-nationalist". The report also mentions close links to the [[esFN|Fuerza Nueva]] political party in Spain.[ Disbanded in 1982, it was said to continue its activities underground as of 1985, providing translations of [[esCEDADE|CEDADE]] publications for distribution in Brazil. The flag of the organization was inspired by the [[ptMNS|National Syndicalist Movement|]]. The organization mostly recruited young students and workers into its ranks. A youth wing of the organization led by Paulo Teixeira Pinto existed.

parties.description:
A Portuguese political organization opposed to the Estado Novo dictatorship. 

It was founded in Lisbon in December 1942 by a group of university students and later expanded to Coimbra. 

Among its members, some of whom were sons of leaders of the republican left during the First Republic, were José Magalhães Godinho, Vitorino Magalhães Godinho, Afonso Costa Filho, Mário de Castro, Gustavo Soromenho, António Macedo, Mário Cal Brandão, Artur Santos Silva, Paulo Quintela, José Joaquim Teixeira Ribeiro and Fernandes Martins. 

In 1944, the organization joined the Democratic Union to form the [[ptUS|Socialist Union]].

parties.name: Party of Progress / Portuguese Federalist Movement
parties.nativeName: Partido do Progresso / Movimento Federalista Português
parties.relations: After PP/MFP being banned, some of party members joined the clandestine [[ptMDLP|Democratic Movement for the Liberation of Portugal]] (MDLP)
parties.description:
A right-wing political party in Portugal, which was born on 6 May 1974, under the name Portuguese Federalist Movement (MFP) after the April 25 coup. It was outlawed following the Silent Majority demonstration on 28 September 1974.

This party initially attempted to mobilize support from those who wanted the continuation of Portugal's union with its overseas territories, its integration in a federalist manner, invoking the application of the theses of General António de Spínola's book, Portugal and the Future. It was after General Spínola's speech on June 27, recognizing the colonies' right to independence and altering the original [[ptMFA|MFA]] program of 25 April 1974, that the group began to call itself the Party of Progress.

It was chaired by Professor Fernando Pacheco de Amorim and its main adherents included "revolutionary nationalists" linked to the Cidadela Cooperative, active in Coimbra and Porto and led by José J. Sampaio Nora; the National Committee for Revolutionary Action (CNAR) of Porto, led by Fernando José Allegro; members of the Programa Association, such as José Vale de Figueiredo; monarchists from the Popular Monarchist League and former members of the [[ptANP|ANP]]. Among those listed as most active were José Miguel de Alarcão Júdice, Nuno Cardoso da Silva, Luís de Oliveira Dias, José da Costa Deitado, Diogo Miranda Barbosa, Francisco Caldeira Cabral and Luís Sá Cunha.

As a consultant they would have Clifton White, director of political campaigns such as Barry Goldwater's US presidential campaign in 1964, Ronald Reagan's Republican nomination in 1968 and Jesse Helms' Senate campaign in 1972.

To present itself in the first national elections it formed an electoral coalition with the [[ptPL|Liberal Party]] (PL) and the [[ptPTDP|Portuguese Democratic Labour Party]] (PTDP), called the [[ptFDU|United Democratic Front]] (FDU). And that, following the so-called Palma Carlos Crisis, they, along with the [[ptMPP|Portuguese Popular Movement]] (MPP), on July 10th, presented a joint resolution to the President of the Republic denouncing the isolation to which they were subjected, both in terms of expression through the media and in terms of representation in the provisional government.

Also in June, the MFP and the PL established the Foundation for the Dissemination of Political, Social and Economic Knowledge (DICOPSE). Among its objectives was the publication of the magazine Bandarra and the carrying out of activities to support right-wing organizations.

Its information organ was a newspaper, called Tribuna Popular, whose director was Joaquim Miguel Seabra Ferreira and which began on July 24th.

PP was soon banned and persecuted following the demonstration known to the silent majority, which was thwarted on September 28 of the same year, despite being one of its critics who called it an act of "adventurous opportunism or total unrealism".

At its headquarters, three floors in a building on Av. Infante Santo, COPCON soldiers found an arsenal on October 2, 1974, containing 200 submachine guns; 600,000 various rounds of ammunition; 5,500 grenades; dozens of other weapons; gas masks, chains, batons and iron bars; hundreds of bottles to be turned into Molotov cocktails.

The activists were persecuted. Pacheco de Amorim emigrated to Franco's Spain. Judice was arrested, escaped from prison, and also fled to Spain.

The escalating situation prompted leaders and activists of the banned PP/MFP to turn to illegal forms of political struggle. Many of them joined the right-wing underground [[ptMDLP|Democratic Movement for the Liberation of Portugal]] (MDLP). Fernando Pacheco de Amorim, José Miguel Judice, and José Valle Figueiredo served on the MDLP's political commission.

After the right-wing victory in the November crisis on 25 November 1975, former members of the MFP/PP oriented themselves toward the parties of the center-right [[ptAD1979|Democratic Alliance]]: the [[ptPSD|Social Democratic Party]], the [[ptCDS|Social and Democratic Center]], and the [[ptPPM|People's Monarchist Party]]. The radical tenets of integralism had to be abandoned in the new situation. Those figures who remained fully committed to their previous views, such as Pacheco de Amorin, withdrew from practical politics.
parties.ideology: The party united anti-communists of the Lusitanian-integralist and monarchist persuasions. It supported General Spinola and actively opposed the [[ptPCP|Communist Party]] and the left-wing forces of the Carnation Revolution. It advocated the preservation of Portugal's unity with the "overseas provinces." It was banned after the September Crisis. Party activists played a prominent role in the right-wing underground during the Hot Summer period and in Portugal's legal center-right forces.

parties.name: Party of the People
parties.description:
A Portuguese political party, created in 1995. They adopted as their symbol the letter "G" in white and a red broom, on a rectangle on a blue background.

The party belonged to the evangelical Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, owned by Bishop Edir Macedo, and was the second attempt by the followers of that Church to form a political organization, although the party president, Luís Farinha, always denied the connection between the Church and the party as an organization, but not between the Church and the party members. On 22 February 1995, the court had denied the registration of the Social-Christian Party, claiming that the Constitution does not allow religious parties. In January 1995, during the discussion of the party's statutes, the program project defended the improvement of health and pension systems and more funds for education.

PG only ran in the elections for the Assembly of the Republic in 1995, having obtained 8,279 votes, with a percentage of 0.14%, without electing any deputy.

In 1999, the party's dissolution was decided on the initiative of its members.

parties.relations:

Merged into the [[ptCMLP|Portuguese Marxist–Leninist Committee]] (CMLP)
parties.description:
A Portuguese Marxist-Leninist organization that was founded in January 1964 in Paris, following the rupture and expulsion of several members of the [[ptPCP|Portuguese Communist Party]] (PCP), the foundation of the FAP marked the beginning of Maoist and Marxist-Leninist organizations in Portugal.

Dissent from the PCP created in January 1964 by Francisco Martins Rodrigues, after differences at the central committee meeting in August 1963.

João Pulido Valente and Rui d’Espinay accompany him. They accused the PCP of mere electoralism. In April 1964, the [[ptCMLP|Portuguese Marxist–Leninist Committee]] (CMLP) emerged from this group, publishing the periodical Popular Revolution.

Upon returning to Portugal, elements of the FAP are denounced in Avante!.

In 1966, after the denunciation of an infiltrator, with the arrest of practically all elements, only one Foreign Committee remained and organized a 1st Conference in 1967.

But the fragmentation of these movements became inevitable, even due to the absence of Francisco Martins Rodrigues' theoretical guidance, the FAP is dissolved and the CMLP goes through a phase of “purification” from an ideological point of view.

It espoused an irreconcilable counterrevolution, actively fighting against the DVS, communists, socialists, leftists, Marxists, and anarchists. It was banned after the September Crisis. In 1975, its activists participated in the anti-communist movements of the Hot Summer.

parties.name: Portuguese Democratic Labour Party
parties.description:
PTDP was one of the first of the new political parties created after the Portuguese Revolution of 1974. The founding meeting was held in Lisbon on 3 May 1974. Fernando Correia Ribeiro was elected Secretary General of the PTDP, and Carlos da Silva Fernandes, Manuel Lopes Barbosa, José Gonçalves da Silva, José Gama, Francisco Sanches, and Luís Barroso were elected board members.

In early July 1974, the PTDP supported Prime Minister Palma Carlos's plan against the Communist Party and the left wing of the Armed Forces Movement. On 10 July 1974, the PTDP, the [[ptPPMFP|Portuguese Federalist Movement]] (PP/MFP), the [[ptMPP|Portuguese Popular Movement]] (MPP), and the [[ptPL|Liberal Party]] (PL) sent an appeal to President Spínola calling for active resistance to the political expansion of communists and left-wing radicals, primarily by breaking the information blockade in the media. The PTDP, MFP/PP, and PL were part of the right-wing coalition [[ptFDU|United Democratic Front]] (the openly Salazarist [[ptMAP|Portuguese Action Movement and the [[ptPNP|Portuguese Nationalist Party]] did not join this coalition).

The PTDP supported the "silent majority" movement in support of Spínola and the right-wing forces. Following the suppression of the protests on 28 September 1974, the PTDP was banned by the authorities.
parties.ideology:
The party's ideology is interpreted as right-wing anti-Marxist social democracy. The PTDP positioned itself as a workers' party and a democratic center. The party's slogans included "No to the exploitation of man by man!" "No to the exploitation of man by the state!" rejected all forms of totalitarian dictatorship (fascist, imperialist, communist, Marxist), and called for the unity of the working people and the integration of Portugal into democratic Europe. A set of socioeconomic demands was put forward to ensure the right to work, decent wages, universal access to education, and family support. (Similarities can be seen with the ideas of Bob Santamaría and the positions—even the name—of the Australian [[auDLP|Democratic Labor Party]].)

In relations with the colonies, they proposed a "true federation with equal rights and obligations", a "great community of the Lusophone world". The situation of Portuguese labor migrants in EEC countries, primarily in France, was also raised. The PTDP promised to revise existing interstate agreements in favor of Portuguese workers and improve the economic situation in Portugal itself—in order to create the opportunity for migrants to return to their homeland.

During the political conflicts of 1974, the PTDP took a sharply anti-communist stance. On 10 June 1974, the PTDP declared President António de Spínola, the leader of the country's right-wing forces, its honorary president and called for him to be promoted to the military rank of marshal.

parties.name: Portuguese Labour Party
parties.description:
A Portuguese labourist political party.

It was approved by the Constitutional Court of Portugal on 1 July 2009 following the application submitted on 16 June 2009.

There were previously at least three parties with similar names: the Labour Party (1947), a clandestine organization whose secretary-general was the lawyer Francisco Furtado Castanheira Lobo; the [[ptPTDP|Portuguese Democratic Labour Party]] (PTDP), announced on 3 May 1974, which never became legalized; and the [[ptPT|Labour Party]] (PT), founded in 1979, all of which have since been dissolved.

According to the court, after analyzing the statutes, manifesto and declaration of principles, "it does not appear that the party has a regional nature or scope" and there is no indication that its statutes do not respect the prohibition of "armed political parties, of a military, militarized or paramilitary type, racist parties or those that espouse fascist ideology".

In March 2011, José Manuel Coelho and João Paulo Gomes joined the PTP.

In 2015, the PTP ran in the legislative elections in coalition with the [[ptMAS|MAS]] under the banner of the [[ptAGIR|AGIR]] movement, bringing Joana Amaral Dias to the position of secretary-general of the party.

On 29 May 2025, Raquel Coelho, leader of the PTP Madeira and former deputy in the regional assembly, was elected President of the PTP at the national level. In July 2025 it was announced that the former president of the PTP, Amândio Madaleno, would be [[ptCH|Chega]]'s candidate for the Pampilhosa da Serra municipal council in the 2025 local elections.

parties.name: Portuguese Marxist–Leninist Committee
parties.relations:
Split from the [[ptPCP|Portuguese Communist Party]] (PCP);

Succeeded by the [[ptPCPml|Communist Party of Portugal (Marxist–Leninist)]] (PCP(m-l))
parties.description:
A Portuguese Marxist-Leninist organization that was founded in 1964 in Paris shortly after the founding of the [[ptFAP|Popular Action Front]] (FAP), following the rupture and expulsion of Francisco Martins Rodrigues from the [[ptPCP|PCP]] - these mark the beginning of Maoist and Marxist-Leninist organizations in Portugal.

Complementary to the unitary front constituted in the FAP, the CMLP intended to be the embryo of a future reconstructed communist party, publishing the organ “Popular Revolution”.

In 1965, the FAP/CMLP was affected by several arrests, including that of João Pulido Valente, resulting from an infiltration by PIDE secret police. PIDE undercover agent, Mário Mateus, will be executed in November of this year.

In 1966 Francisco Martins Rodrigues and Rui d’Espiney were arrested and the waves of repression weakened the FAP/CMLP, whose youth organization was the Union of Marxist-Leninist Communist Students [UEC (m-l)].

In 1968, what remained of the CMLP leadership gave rise to the newspaper O Comunista, with 14 issues published, closer to the Trotskyists, among which was Maria Albertina's group, led by the former communist and future PSD deputy, Silva Marques.

The FAP ended up being extinguished, with only the CMLP remaining in activity, which in 1970, at the V Congress (reconstitutive) of the communist party, transformed into the [[ptPCPml|Communist Party of Portugal (Marxist–Leninist)]] [PCP (m-l)], although it was only in 1971 that the fact was made public. The PCP (m-l) will develop an important role in emigration, particularly in France.

In 1975, PTP(m-l) splinter faction, the [[ptPUP1974|Popular Unity Party]] retook the name CM-LP months before forming the [[ptPCR|Portuguese Communist Party (Reconstructed)]] [PCP(R)].

parties.description:
An organization and later a Portuguese political party, now dissolved. It was created in 1973 from the merger of heirs of the Portuguese Marxist-Leninist Committee (CMLP), Núcleos O Comunista and the Porto group that published the newspaper O Grito do Povo.

In 1975, the group formed the "Electoral Front of the Communists (Marxists–Leninists)" - FEC(m-l), officially registering as a party at the Supreme Court of Justice. Its political line advocated the fight against North American imperialism and Soviet imperialism.

In 1976, it changed its name and acronym to the Portuguese Marxist–Leninist Communist Organization (OCMLP), and later that year, it joined the [[ptPUP1984|Portuguese Marxist-Leninist Committee (CM-LP) and the [[ptOPRCML|Organization for the Reconstruction of the Communist Party (Marxist–Leninist)]] (ORPC(ML) and founded the [[ptPCR|Portuguese Communist Party (Reconstructed)]] (PCP(R)). Shortly before the merger, the OCMLP had gone through a process of split the majority with a strong base in Porto, passed with the merger plans to the PC(R), a minority, which maintained a strong emphasis on the issue of fighting social fascism, refused the merger and continued a separate existence, continuing its action and running for elections until 1983.

In 1988, the STF noted the dissolution of the OCMLP, as had been resolved in its V National Congress.

It was banned during the September Crisis.

parties.name: Portuguese Party of Regions
parties.relations: Partially split from the [[ptCDSPP|Party of Democratic Social Centre]] (CDS).
parties.description:
A Portuguese political party, now extinct, created in 1995. 

The party was led by Arlindo Neves, former president of the Gondomar Chamber, with Avelino Ferreira Torres, a former [[ptCDSPP|CDS]] activist who presided over the Marco de Canaveses Chamber, as his "shadow man". Other important figures were Jorge Nuno Pinto da Costa, president of FC Porto, Manuel Vaz, former president of the Chamber of Póvoa de Varzim (for the CDS and later for the PSD) and sports director, who would head the PPR list in the Porto circle and José Gomes, former president of FC Paços de Ferreira. The sport's media figures also included football players Vítor Baía and João Pinto and Sicasal cyclist Paulo Ferreira.

PPR ran in the 1997 Portuguese local elections, presenting a single list for the Parish Assembly of Rossas (municipality of Arouca), having elected its head of the list as president of the Parish Council, with 37.31% of the votes.

The party was dissolved in 1998.
parties.ideology: PPR defended a democratic model based on regional, ethical and social values ​​of freedom, developed through national, regional and municipal bodies. A regionalist party force that only intended to compete in the Porto circle, advocated the defense and promotion, in general, of Porto's "regionalist values", with characteristics similar to Silvio Berlusconi's [[itFI1994|Forza Italia]] (FI). PPR adopted as their symbol a silver star over another blue star, surrounded by a blue circle.

parties.name: Portuguese People's Movement
parties.description:
From the first weeks of the Portuguese Revolution of 1974, revolutionary politics took a sharp leftward turn, with the strong influence of the [[ptPCP|Portuguese Communist Party]]. In response, right-wing and far-right forces began to consolidate. One of the new right-wing political organizations was the [[ptMPP|Portuguese Popular Movement]] (MPP). 

MPP organizational meetings began as early as early May. They were held in a private home in Lisbon and in the pine forest of Conimbriga, between Lisbon and Porto. The MPP was organized by members of the social-Catholic Vector Circle (Círculo de Estudos Sociais Vector), who grouped around the magazine Resistência (Resistance). The leaders included economist António da Cruz Rodrigues, the brother of Catholic priest Ángelo Galamba de Oliveira, and Catholic activists Adelino Barreto, José Luís Pesirra, José Rebelo Pinto, Paulo Moreira, and Manuel Braankamp Sobral. Fernando Pascheco de Amorim, founder of the [[ptPPMFP|Portuguese Federalist Movement]] (MFP/PP), participated in the first meetings.

There are discrepancies regarding the date of the MPP's establishment. The first public statement was published on 3 June 1974. Dates of 15 June 15 and 15 July 15 have also been cited.

In early July 1974, the MPP supported Prime Minister Carlos Palma's plan against the [[ptPCP|Communist Party]] and the left wing of the [[ptMFA|Armed Forces Movement]]. On 10 July 1974, the MPP, [[ptPL|PL]], [[ptPPMFP|PP/MFP]], and [[ptPTDP|PTDP]] sent an appeal to President Spinola calling for active resistance to the political expansion of communists and left-wing radicals, primarily by breaking the information blockade in the media. Prime Minister Carlos Palma received the MPP delegation.

The PPM developed plans to unite all radical anti-communist forces, from right-wing social democrats to far-right Salazarists, under the auspices of General Spínola, then president of Portugal. The closest allies were considered to be the [[ptPPMFP|PP/MFP]], the [[ptPL|Liberal Party]] (PL), and the [[ptPTDP|PTDP]]. The MPP's unifying project was called the National Democratic Front. In reality, a narrower [[ptFDU|United Democratic Front]] was created, comprising the MFP/PP, PL, and PTDP (the openly Salazarist [[ptMAP|Portuguese Action Movement]] and the [[ptPNP|Portuguese Nationalist Party]] did not join this coalition).

In August-September 1974, the party actively supported the "silent majority" movement in support of Spinola, against the communists and left-wing radicals. Several MPP activists were arrested for posting posters calling for participation in an anti-communist demonstration. The party went virtually underground, with activists hiding in Conimbriga. A rift developed between MPP representatives and other Spinolistas, with both accusing the other of adventurism. Following the suppression of the September protests, the MPP was banned and ceased its activities.

Some former MPP activists joined the small ultra-nationalist group Intervenção Nacionalista in the summer of 1980.

In 2000, António da Cruz Rodrigues became the founder and first chairman of the right-wing nationalist [[ptE|National Renewal Party]] (PRN).
parties.ideology:
Ideologically, the MPP adhered to positions of political Catholicism, ranging from fundamentalism to right-wing Christian democracy. In practical politics, the MPP's main founding principle was anti-communism. Communist ambitions for power were viewed as the main threat to the Portuguese nation and the Christian religion. Nationalism, Lusitanian integralism, and Lusotropicalism also played an important role. The initial idea was to unite all right-wing and center-right forces in a broad movement for a continuous and active struggle for two fundamental principles: anti-communism and the defense of the homeland from Minho to Timor.

The MPP's activities were primarily limited to active anti-communist propaganda. However, criticism of communism was conducted from a general democratic perspective. The [[ptPCP|PCP]] was accused primarily of intending to establish a dictatorship similar to Salazar's regime. Anti-fascist rhetoric was actively used, comparing communism to fascism.

Leaflets were distributed by groups of young MPP activists (such actions were quite risky in the political climate of the summer of 1974). The magazine "Resistência" remained the printed mouthpiece, subject to administrative persecution and fines. José Luís Peschirra published a pamphlet in Lisbon under a pseudonym, "PCP-um partido fascista"-tPCP-a fascist party. Activists resolutely resorted to violent confrontation, attempting to hold their rallies in Alentejo, a region considered a "communist stronghold".

Leaflets were distributed by groups of young MPP activists (such actions were quite risky in the political climate of the summer of 1974). The magazine "Resistência" remained the printed mouthpiece, subject to administrative persecution and fines. José Luís Peschirra published a pamphlet in Lisbon under a pseudonym, "PCP-um partido fascista"-tPCP-a fascist party. Activists resolutely resorted to violent confrontation, attempting to hold their rallies in Alentejo, a region considered a "communist stronghold".

parties.name: Regenerator Party
parties.description:
The Regenerator Party was one of the parties of the Portuguese constitutional monarchy's rotation system, alternating in power with the [[ptPP|Progressive Party]], and which emerged during the Regeneration period (1851–1868) as a conservative party opposed to the Historical Party.

With the death of Rodrigo da Fonseca Magalhães in 1858, it was led and promoted until 1887 by Fontes Pereira de Melo,[1] who was not chosen for the position through internal election.

The party's organ was the newspaper O Regenerador.

More than half of the presidents of the council in the second half of the 19th century belonged to this political formation. Its leaders were, in addition to the aforementioned Fontes Pereira de Melo (1856–1887), António de Serpa Pimentel (1887–1900), Ernesto Rodolfo Hintze Ribeiro (1900–1907), Júlio de Vilhena (1907–1909) and António Teixeira de Sousa (1909–1910).

In 1901, a dissent from a faction led by João Franco gave rise to the [[ptCRL|Liberal Regenerator Centre]].

In 1903 the same thing happened again, this time with the formation of the [[ptPN|Nationalist Party]], led by Jacinto Cândido.

These splits among leaders and supporters ultimately led to its dissolution.

The party disappeared after the Revolution of 1910.

parties.name: Revolutionary Party of the Proletariat
parties.relations: Succeeded by the [[ptOUT|Workers' Unitary Organization]] (OUT).
parties.description:
A Portuguese revolutionary socialist political organization, born underground in September 1973, still under the fascist regime.

It brought together former members of the [[ptMDPCDE|CDE|#FF7B43]], progressive Catholics, other anti-fascists and anti-capitalists with members of the Revolutionary Brigades. In the face of the then recurrent electoral fraud in Portugal and Pinochet's anti-democratic coup in Chile, the PRP defended the socialist revolution and the dictatorship of the proletariat (extracted from its constitutive manifesto of 1973).

Its newspapers Revolucion and Página Um conveyed anti-colonialist and anti-imperialist messages. Politically PRP was very active in 1975, during the "Ongoing Revolutionary Process". It promoted actions that directly involved citizens, getting involved in residents' committees, population awareness actions, urban occupations and initiatives to provide new housing (SAAL). They defended a "base democracy" in the party and society.

During this period, the PRP became confused with the Revolutionary Brigades, functioning in an articulated and organized way, receiving financial support and giving it political cover. It never ran in any legislative or municipal elections, however he supported Otelo Saraiva de Carvalho in the two presidential elections. After 25 November 1975, PRP and Revolutionary Brigades were formally separated. 

It ended its effective activity in 1978, with the arrest of most of its leaders, including Isabel do Carmo and Carlos Antunes, and there were civil society solidarity campaigns. Some of the militants would transfer to the [[ptOUT|Workers' Unitary Organization]], with the party declared extinct only on 5 June 1980.

A clandestine Portuguese political organization during the Estado Novo dictatorship. 

It was founded in 1944 by the merger of the [[ptNDAS|Nucleus of Socialist Doctrine and Action]] with the Democratic Union and initially called itself the "Democratic-Socialist Union". 

On 6 November 1949, the members signed a pact to form the "Socialist Union Party". 

During the 1950s, several international contacts were attempted for recognition of the organization, until in 1964 the [[ptASP|Portuguese Socialist Action]] was formed. Among the most active members were Manuel Sertório, Jacinto Simões, José Pessegueiro, António Lobo Vilela and Fernando Mayer Garção.

parties.relations: Citizen candidacy of the [[ptLIVRE|LIVRE]] party.
parties.description:
TA was a citizen candidacy that ran for the 2015 legislative elections in Portugal. It was founded at a convention that took place in Lisbon, on 31 January 2015.

This citizen candidacy was open to the free participation of all citizens in the preparation of its electoral program. Likewise, the method of selecting its candidates for elections followed the format of open primaries. Thus, all voting citizens could be candidates for this movement as long as they believed in its founding principles.

The movement presented itself for elections within the legal framework of the [[ptLIVRE|LIVRE]] party under the name LIVRE/Tempo de Avançar and its lists of deputies were voted on in open primary elections, having dissolved after the 2015 legislative elections.

In the elections, LIVRE/Tempo de Avançar obtained 39,340 votes, corresponding to 0.72% of the national total, failing to elect deputies to the Assembly of the Republic.[2]

The LIVRE/Tempo de Avançar candidacy presented itself in the Portuguese legislative elections, which took place on October 4, 2015.

Merged into the [[ptLIVRE]] on 10 May 2017.

parties.name: United Workers
parties.relations: Split from the [[ptMAS|Socialist Alternative Movement]] (MAS)
parties.description:
A Trotskyist political party in Portugal founded in 2024 by Renata Cambra, former spokeswoman for the [[ptMAS|Socialist Alternative Movement]] (MAS), who abandoned the latter following a leadership dispute. The party identifies itself as a socialist and revolutionary alternative to the other left-wing parties represented in the Legislative Assembly.

After the party was founded in September 2024, it was finally legalized in July 2026 by the Constitutional Court.

In September 2024, Renata Cambra, former leader of the MAS party, announced the creation of a new political party under the name of Trabalhadores Unidos (TU). The decision was taken following internal disagreements within MAS, including differences with founder Gil Garcia, which led to Cambra's departure accompanied by a group of activists. According to public statements, the TU intends to position itself as an independent force, critical of the actions of sectors of the left that it considers very close to the [[ptPS|PS]], defending a firmer opposition.

The official launch of the TU took place on 21 September 2024, in Lisbon. Final registration with the STF occurred after three attempts by the installation committee. Previous requests had been refused due to details in the statutes relating to internal discipline and rules for expulsion of militants. The process gathered more than 8,500 signatures from voting citizens to make its creation possible.
parties.ideology:
The party presents itself as a new political proposal focused on the issues of the working class and youth. Its criticisms cover the main centrist parties, such as PS and [[ptPSD|PSD]], as well as the advance of the extreme right. Among the measures it proposes are an increase in the minimum wage to R$1,000, a reduction in working hours to 35 hours a week without loss of pay and price controls on essential goods. The TU also values ​​involvement in social and union struggles as an integral part of its political practice

On an ideological level, the party takes a declared xenophile position in relation to immigration, proposing the "immediate regularization of all immigrants in an irregular situation, with documents for everyone and full access to social and political rights". In the field of foreign policy, the TU defends "Portugal's immediate exit from NATO", speaking out "against the militarization of the EU and the Fortaleza Europe project". Regarding the war in Ukraine, the party paradoxically claims that it defends "Ukraine's right to fight against Russian occupation and maintain its independence" while declaring itself "against the Zelensky regime."

parties.name: Workers' Revolutionary Party
parties.relations: Merged into the [[ptPSR|Revolutionary Socialist Party]] (PSR)
parties.description:
A far-left political party in Portugal. It was created on 31 January 1975 and formally registered with the Supreme Court of Justice on 25 March 1975. It followed the Argentine revolutionary Nahuel Moreno's form of Trotskyism, and was in sympathy with, but not formally affiliated to, the [[intUSFI|reunified Fourth International]]. The party's stated objective was to organise and lead the working class towards the seizure of power and a socialist revolution, with the ultimate aim of abolishing capitalism and progressively eliminating social classes. The party published the newspaper Combate Socialista (Socialist Combat).

The PRT emerged during the period of intense political radicalisation following the Carnation Revolution. Contemporary accounts identify it as one of several revolutionary left-wing organisations active during 1974–1975, alongside groups such as the [[ptPRPBR|Revolutionary Party of the Proletariat]] and [[ptLCI|Internationalist Communist League]], contributing to the broader shift towards revolutionary socialism in Portugal.

In 1979 the PRT merged with the [[ptLCI|Internationalist Communist League]] (LCI) to form the [[ptPSR|Revolutionary Socialist Party]] (PSR); the merger was approved by order of the Supreme Court of Justice dated 2 April 1979. The PSR eventually became part of the [[ptBE|Left Bloc]] (BE).

parties.description:
A left-wing, anti-fascist, anti-colonialist political organization that aimed for socialist revolution based on popular power and (theoretical) "armed revolutionary violence". It was founded in April 1978 in Marinha Grande, Portugal, in the presence of 1400 activists.

It is worth remembering that at the beginning of Portuguese democratization, all parliamentary parties had in their statutes the move towards Socialism, with the exception of the [[ptCDSPP|CDS]]. Despite the different understandings of Socialism and the way to get there, this was written in the preamble of the Portuguese Constitution.

The (relative) majority of its bodies were occupied by [[ptPRP|PRP]] militants, particularly after the extinction of the PRP in 1981. OUT integrated into the [[ptFUP|Popular Unity Force]] (FUP) with other parties with the aim of an expanded electoral front for the presidential and parliamentary elections in 1980.

parties.name: Civic Initiative
parties.description:
The founder and leader of the party, Andrey Nechayev, was the Minister of Economic Development from 1991 to 1994.

In 2018 presidential election, GRANI nominated Ksenia Sobchak. She finished 4th with 1.68% of vote.

On 13 March 2018, Vedomosti reported that Ksenia Sobchak and Dmitry Gudkov would announce the creation of a new right-wing party based on the Civil Initiative on March 15. Since then, the party has encountered legal problems with the Ministry of Justice, resulting in an informal rebranding.

On 23 June 2018, the Third (reorganizational) Congress took place, where a decision was made to create a new "Party of Changes" based on the Civil Initiative. Ksenia Sobchak and Dmitry Gudkov were appointed to the party's top positions.

On 1 March 2019, the youth movement "St. Petersburg – City of Changes!" was created in St. Petersburg with the aim of countering the Party of Changes's activities in the city during the municipal and gubernatorial elections. The Ministry of Justice refused to recognize the party's reorganization and deliberately obstructed its reorganization. In April 2019, it became known that Sobchak had ceased funding the Party of Changes. In March 2020, Dmitry Gudkov left the party, not wanting to interfere with the struggle to preserve the structure. Nechayev became the party's chairman again, and the name was restored to its previous form.

Boris Nadezhdin is a former member of the Russia State Duma and currently Moscow Oblast's local politician. On 6 October 2023, Nadezhdin's participation in the election was announced by Dmitry Kisiev, founder of the Candidates’ Headquarters, on his social media. On 31 October 2023, Nadezhdin publicly announced that he will run from the Civic Initiative party. He was not admitted to the election.

On 17 June 2025, the Supreme Court of Russia liquidated the party. Representatives of the Civil Initiative attempted to appeal this decision. Following the appeal, the Supreme Court upheld the decision on 30 September 2025.

On 19 October, the deregistered Civil Initiative announced the creation of its own youth organization.

In December 2025, Nechayev announced his intention to re-register the party. On 18 December, the Civil Initiative announced the registration of its organizing committee with the Russian Ministry of Justice.

parties.name: Civic Platform
parties.description:
Civic Platform was founded on 4 June 2012, by former members of the [[ruPD|Right Cause]] (PD) party who broke away from PD after it was seized by forces affiliated with the Presidential Administration. The party was initially led by businessman and oligarch Mikhail Prokhorov, who ran as an independent candidate in the 2011 presidential election, finishing third.

Initially, the party positioned itself as a pan-democratic, non-ideological umbrella party, or described as liberal. However, by 2015, it was "softly captured" by pro-government forces, leading to the departure of several members, including its founder, and the party itself becoming right-wing conservative and Putinist.

The party participated in the State Duma elections in 2016 and 2021. In both cases, the party's list garnered less than 1% of the vote, failing to cross the 5% electoral threshold. Rifat Shaikhutdinov was elected MP twice in a single-mandate constituency. Since October 2021, Shaikhutdinov has been a member of the [[ruLDPR|LDPR]] faction.

On 30 April 2026, the Supreme Court of Russia suspended the party's activities for three months after upholding a claim by the Russian Ministry of Justice. As a result, the party was barred from running in the 2026 State Duma election.

parties.name: Civilian Power
parties.description:
The party was founded by Alexander Ryavkin, president of the Russian medical corporation DENAS MS.

From 2002 to 2004, it was called the "Russian Network Party of Small and Medium Businesses."

From April 2004 to 2007, it was known as the "Free Russia" party.

In the elections of December 4, 2005, the party participated in the elections to the Moscow City Duma, gaining 2.22% (not gaining the required 10%). In its election campaign, it focused on anti-campaigning against the [[ruYabloko|Yabloko]] party with videos like “Don’t vote for Yabloko, it’s rotten!”

On October 8, 2006, the party overtook the 7% barrier on the legislative elections in Novgorod District. In November 2006, the 6th party conference was held. On February 27, 2007, Mikhail Barshchevsky, the chairman and plenipotentiary of the High Council of the Russian government, held a press conference. This was in aid of the party principles of Civilian Power. In the middle of April 2007, an organizational conference was held.

The chairman of the High Council is plenipotentiary of the Government of Russia in Constitutional, Supreme and Highest Arbitral Courts Mikhail Barshchevsky (a member since December 2006). The chairman of the Federal Political Council − The founder of the party, businessman Alexander Ryavkin from 2014 - 2015 year was the vice governor of Oryol Oblast.

The party won 1.05% of votes in the 2007 elections, not breaking the 7% barrier, and thus no seats in duma.

Civilian Power supported Dmitry Medvedev as their candidate in the presidential election in 2008.

It merged with [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]] and the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]] to form the [[ruPD|Right Cause]] on 16 November 2008.

Civilian Power was again registered as a political party on 7 June 2012. After its dissolution, it was transformed into the All-Russian public organization "Civilian Forces", which collaborated with one of the projects of the [[ruREPZ|Russian Ecological Party "The Greens"]], the organization "Green Patrol".

In the elections of 2014, the party won one seat in the regional parliament of Nenets Autonomous Okrug.

On 13 December 2015, Civilian Power Party Chairman Oleg Sidorov and [[ruRPSS|Communist Party of Social Justice]] Chairman Andrei Bogdanov announced at a joint meeting of the parties' Federal Political Councils their upcoming merger under the existing name "Communist Party of Social Justice," but using the organizational base of the Civil Power Party, which had been admitted to 2016 federal elections without collecting signatures. However, on 18 December 2015, Oleg Sidorov was removed from office.

In 2018, she did not nominate her own candidate in the presidential elections, supporting the current President Vladimir Putin.

In the 2019 Chelyabinsk Oblast gubernatorial elections, Alexey Sevastyanov became the party's candidate, which caused a scandal, some party representatives claimed that Civilian Power had not nominated him. However, he was still registered and received 3.23% of the vote in the elections.

At the end of November 2024, the Ministry of Justice of Russia appealed to the Supreme Court, demanding the liquidation of the Civilian Power political party. The Ministry of Justice argued that the party had not nominated candidates for federal elections for a long time and had hardly participated in local elections. On 15 January 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the appeal, dissolving the party.

On October 8, 2006, the party overtook the 7% barrier on the legislative elections in Novgorod District. In November 2006, the 6th party conference was held. On February 27, 2007, Mikhail Barshchevsky, the chairman and plenipotentiary of the High Council of the Russian government, held a press conference. This was in aid of the party principles of Civilian Power. In the middle of April 2007, an organizational conference was held.

The chairman of the High Council is plenipotentiary of the Government of Russia in Constitutional, Supreme and Highest Arbitral Courts Mikhail Barshchevsky (a member since December 2006). The chairman of the Federal Political Council − The founder of the party, businessman Alexander Ryavkin from 2014 - 2015 year was the vice governor of Oryol Oblast.

The party won 1.05% of votes in the 2007 elections, not breaking the 7% barrier, and thus no seats in duma.

Civilian Power supported Dmitry Medvedev as their candidate in the presidential election in 2008.

It merged with [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]] and the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]] to form the [[ruPD|Right Cause]] on 16 November 2008.

Civilian Power was again registered as a political party on 7 June 2012. After its dissolution, it was transformed into the All-Russian public organization "Civilian Forces", which collaborated with one of the projects of the [[ruREPZ|Russian Ecological Party "The Greens"]], the organization "Green Patrol".

In the elections of 2014, the party won one seat in the regional parliament of Nenets Autonomous Okrug.

On 13 December 2015, Civilian Power Party Chairman Oleg Sidorov and [[ruRPSS|Communist Party of Social Justice]] Chairman Andrei Bogdanov announced at a joint meeting of the parties' Federal Political Councils their upcoming merger under the existing name "Communist Party of Social Justice," but using the organizational base of the Civil Power Party, which had been admitted to 2016 federal elections without collecting signatures. However, on 18 December 2015, Oleg Sidorov was removed from office.

In 2018, she did not nominate her own candidate in the presidential elections, supporting the current President Vladimir Putin.

In the 2019 Chelyabinsk Oblast gubernatorial elections, Alexey Sevastyanov became the party's candidate, which caused a scandal, some party representatives claimed that Civilian Power had not nominated him. However, he was still registered and received 3.23% of the vote in the elections.

At the end of November 2024, the Ministry of Justice of Russia appealed to the Supreme Court, demanding the liquidation of the Civilian Power political party. The Ministry of Justice argued that the party had not nominated candidates for federal elections for a long time and had hardly participated in local elections. On 15 January 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the appeal, dissolving the party.

parties.name: Communist Party of the RSFSR
parties.nativeName:
Коммунистическая партия РСФСР
Kommunisticheskaya partiya RSRSR
parties.description:
Republican branch of the [[suCPSU|Communist Party of the Soviet Union]] in the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. Established on 19 June 1990 (before that, the RSFSR remained the only republic of the Soviet Union that did not have a republican communist party). The CP RSFSR was not an independent party and did not have its own charter or program.

Politically, CP RSFSR became a centre for communist opponents of Gorbachev's CPSU leadership.

The August putsch (19-21 August 1991) served as the basis for accusing the CPSU of unconstitutional activity. By decree of RSFSR President Boris Yeltsin on 6 November 1991, the activities of the CPSU and its republican organization, the CP RSFSR, were terminated, and their property was confiscated. However, the Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation issued a ruling on 30 November 1992, declaring the ban on the activities of the primary organizations of the CPSU/CP RSFSR unconstitutional.

Despite the ban, the party's activities continued until February 1993, when a restoration congress was held. Based on the primary organizations, the CPSU RSFSR was re-established as the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]].

parties.description:
Communists of Russia was founded on 23 May 2009, as a public association. Its founders were the Independent Union of Communist Youth of the Russian Federation (NSKM RF), the Communists of Saint Petersburg and the Leningrad Oblast (KPLO), and the Communists of the Far East (KDV).

On 22 May 2011, the Second Congress of the Communists of Russia organization was held. Representatives of the [[ruRKRPKPSS|RKRP–RPK]] attended the congress. A decision was made to begin transforming the organization into a political party. Maxim Suraikin was elected First Secretary of the Central Committee. Some party organs of the [[ruVKPB|All-Russian Communist Party of the Future]] were transferred to the party.

On 22 April 2012, the Third Congress of the organization was held, at which a decision was made to transform the organization into a political party. The party was registered by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation on 14 June 2012.

The party's main rival on the left is the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] (KPRF). KPKR considers itself an alternative to the KPRF, which it believes is no longer a Marxist party and will not be able to return to power as long as Gennady Zyuganov is First Secretary. However, the KPKR party has been widely described as a spoiler party, including by the KPRF.

In May 2016, the party held the founding congress of the public organization "Atheists of Russia." According to Suraykin, Russian atheists "are practically not represented in the public sphere".

Since the summer of 2018, the party has actively participated in protests against pension reform, both in the capital and in the regions.

Following the 9 September 2018, elections, the party overcame the 5% threshold in the elections for deputies to regional parliaments in five constituent entities of the Russian Federation: the Republic of Khakassia: 8.01% (2 out of 50 seats), the Nenets Autonomous Okrug: 5.29% (1 out of 19 seats), the Rostov Region: 5.06% (1 out of 60 seats), the Ulyanovsk Region: 5.83% (1 out of 36 seats), and the Yaroslavl Region: 6.63% (1 out of 50 seats). It also gained seats in many local government bodies, including the Abakan Council of Deputies, the Council of People's Deputies of the Maykop Urban District, and others.

On 8 September 2019, the Communists of Russia party received 5.67% of the vote in the Tula Regional Duma elections (1 seat out of 36).

On 13 September 2020, the Communists of Russia party received 7.47% of the vote in the Rostov-on-Don City Duma elections.

Following the September 19, 2021, elections, the party cleared the 5% threshold in the regional parliamentary elections in three constituent entities of the Russian Federation: Altai Krai with 12.1% (4 seats out of 68), Amur Oblast with 8.3% (1 seat out of 27), and Omsk Oblast with 11% (3 seats out of 44).

In the 2021 State Duma elections, the party placed 8th, receiving 1.27% of the vote.

On 18 March 2022, an extraordinary party congress was held, at which Sergei Malinkovich, the new chairman of the KPKR Central Committee, was elected. The change in party leadership was confirmed by the Ministry of Justice, although Suraykin did not recognize this congress. On 28 December 2023, Malinkovich was nominated by an overwhelming majority as the party candidate for president of Russia in the 2024 presidential election. Malinkovich promised a program like Stalin's ten blows, against United States capitalism and imperialism, and for victory in Russia's war against Ukraine.

parties.name: Cossack Party of the Russian Federation
parties.nativeName:
Казачья партия Российской Федерации
Kazach'ya partiya Rossiyskoy Federatsii
parties.description:
In October 2012, the head of the Council for Cossack Affairs, Alexander Beglov (future Mayor of Saint Petersburg), announced the creation of the Cossack Party of the Russian Federation. The idea of ​​a Cossack party provoked a negative reaction among politicians, the public, and the Cossacks themselves. The [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] (KPRF), for example, drew attention to the fact that its initials completely coincided with those of the new organization. This raised suspicions of creating a so-called "spoiler." The KPRF even attempted to rename KaPRF through the courts, but to no avail.

The first Supreme Ataman of the Union of Cossacks of Russia, Alexander Martynov, believes that the creation of the party is not a Cossack initiative, but a local one.

The founding congress of the Cossack Party of the Russian Federation was held on 24 November 2012. 96 delegates voted in favor of the party's creation, with only one voting against. Rostov Region Vice-Governor Sergei Bondarev, a former member of [[ruER|United Russia]], was elected chairman of the new party. The congress concluded with an Orthodox Christian prayer service.

In 2015, Bondarev was replaced as chairman of the KaPRF by Nikolai Konstantinov, a longtime friend of Alexander Beglov.

In 2015, the Leningrad Regional Branch of the KaPRF announced its intention to nominate a candidate for the gubernatorial election in the Leningrad Oblast. He turned out to be Vitaly Martynenko, then a member of the St. Petersburg Legislative Assembly and now deputy head of the Vasileostrovsky District Administration. However, the matter never progressed beyond talk. Martynenko was not a member of the CPRF and was a member of [[ruER|United Russia]].

In 2016, the Leningrad Oblast Electoral Commission certified the lists of candidates for the local Legislative Assembly of the 6th convocation. Among the candidates registered was the regional branch of the CPRF. This was a significant breakthrough for the party, and its representatives could appear in the regional parliament for the first time. The regional list was headed by Andrei Sorokvashin, then an independent deputy in the Semenovsky MO in the Admiralty District of St. Petersburg.

The KaPRF continues to periodically participate in elections across Russia, but cannot boast of any significant successes. The party can be used to promote people loyal to Beglov into parliamentary positions, facilitated by the fact that it is headed by the governor's personal friend, Nikolai Konstantinov. However, the party does not play a significant role in the political life of St. Petersburg, although it has attempted to promote city politicians to the leadership of the neighboring Leningrad Region.

Sergei Bondarev (2012 – 2015),
Nikolai Konstantinov (2015 – 2024),
Sergei Kolosok (2024 – )

parties.name: Democratic Party of Russia
parties.nativeName:
Демократическая партия России
Demokraticheskaya partiya Rossii
parties.description:
The Democratic Party of Russia was founded by Nikolay Travkin. Other early leaders included Stanislav Govorukhin and Sergey Glazyev. In the 1990s it was a prominent democratically oriented party holding seats in the first State Duma and was a member of the [[ruDR|Democratic Russia]] coalition. After the coup in 1991, the party evolved from liberal anticommunism to centrism (1992–1993) and later to moderate Russian nationalism (1994–1995).

In 1991, the Democratic Party differed from other liberal/democratic organizations with its 'demopatriotic' stance (similar to Aksyuchits' [[ruRKhDD|Christian Democratic Party]] and Astafyev's [[ruKDPPNS|Constitutional Democrats]]). The Democratic Party was opposed to the dissolution of the Soviet Union and criticised Latvia's and Estonia's policies towards their Russian-speaking minorities. After the signing of the Belovezhye treaty, the DP organized a number of demonstrations against the treaty.

In the 1993 parliamentary elections in Russia, the party received 5.52% of the Proportional Representation ballot vote (2,969,533 votes) as well as 2.1% (1,094,066 votes) of votes on individual district ballots. This translated into 14 and 7 seats, respectively, for a total of 21 seats in the 450-seat Duma.

The party's stance on Yegor Gaidar's economic reforms was confusing but developed more critical in the course of time. During the 1993 Russian constitutional crisis, the party did not have a unanimous position. The party called for balloting both for the re-election of the President as well as of the legislative bodies on the referendum in April 1993; however, some of the party's leaders took the pro-Yeltsin side. Similarly, during the October 1993 events in Moscow, Travkin initially supported the so-called zero variants (annulling both Yeltsin's decree nr 1400 and the Supreme Soviet's subsequent decisions). On 4 October, Travkin supported Yeltsin's actions in suppressing the armed rebellion. The party split, however, on the issue of support for the Chernomyrdin cabinet. Travkin who took a more conciliatory stand lost the power struggle to Govorukhin and Glazyev, who were determined opponents of the government course, and Travkin consequently left the party and joined the [[ruNDR|Our Home – Russia]] movement.

Glazyev was made the leader in 1994 but was disbanded before the following year's legislative election. The rump DRP split further between Govorukhin and Glazyev supporters. In the 1995 Russian legislative election, the Glazyev wing took part within the Congress of Russian Communities list, whilst Govorukhin formed his own list, called the Stanislav Govorukhin Bloc.

In the 1996 presidential election, the Democratic Party supported Alexander Lebed, though some of its regional leaders supported Yeltsin's campaign. In the 2000 presidential election, the party supported Vladimir Putin.

In 2001 the party was reformed by Mikhail Prusak. In 2005 Mikhail Kasyanov tried to be elected chairman of the party, but lost to Andrei Bogdanov. In June 2007, the party proposed a referendum on joining the European Union and in December it took part in the legislative election, but it did not win any seats. The DPR of that time was accused of being a virtual party used to draw away votes from the real opposition parties.

17 September 2007, with the support of the [[euEPP|European People's Party]] in the headquarters of the European Union in Brussels, hosted the XXI Congress of the Democratic Party of Russia, which adopted the decision on the accession of Russia to the European Union.

In the 2007 Russian legislative election the party won 0.13% of votes, not breaking the 7% barrier, and thus no seats in the Duma. As of 1 January 2007, according to the Federal Registration Service, the party had 82,183 members.

According to the results of the regional elections of 2012, 2013, and 2014, the party failed to win in regional and city parliaments.

In 2014 Andrei Bogdanov head created by the participation of the [[ruRPSS|Communist Party of Social Justice]], leader of the Democratic Party of Russia was elected his brother Timur Bogdanov.

In 2020, the party nominated two single-mandate candidates for the State Council of the Komi Republic, but only one, Igor Egorov, was registered. Alexey Utkin, a candidate for governor of the Kostroma Oblast, was also denied registration. Evgenia Pasternak, a sole proprietor and candidate for governor of the Jewish Autonomous Oblast, was also denied registration.

The party announced their support for incumbent president Vladimir Putin in the 2024 presidential election, after DPR candidate Irina Sviridova got her registration denied.

Za novyy sotsializm

A public movement [not a party] led by Russian opposition politician and former diplomat Nikolay Platoshkin. The movement's stated goal is the restoration of renewed socialism in Russia through peaceful, legal means, through elections and referendums.

parties.name: For Truth
parties.description:
Established as party in February 2020 and led by writer Zakhar Prilepin, former member of the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]]. Officially registered in April 2020.

The party participated in the 2020 regional elections in five regions. In Ryazan Oblast, the party received 7% of the vote, winning 2 seats in the regional Duma, and gaining free access to federal parliamentary elections. In other regions, the party received less than 5% of the votes.

In February 2021, ZP (together with [[ruPR|Patriots of Russia]]) merged into the [[ruSR|A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth]] party.

As a political movement, it was founded in October 2019 and continues to exist to this day.

parties.name: Front of National Revolutionary Action
parties.nativeName:
Фронт национал-революционного действия
Front natsional-revolyutsionnogo deystviya
parties.relations:
Split from the [[ruSKhV|Christian Revival Union]] (SKhV);

Succeeded by the Slavic Neopagan religious organization, Society of Nav', and the [[ruPNF|National Front Party]] (PNF).
parties.description:
The Union of Russian Youth (SRM) was founded on 11 November 1991, two days after the anniversary of the Beer Hall Putsch in Germany and on the birthday of the writer Dostoevsky. The SRV declared itself the legal successor to the [[ruVFP|All-Russian Fascist Party]] and the [[ruVFO|All-Russian Fascist Organization]], which had existed in exile in the 1930s and 1940s. For a time, the Union of Russian Youth was considered the youth branch of the [[ruSKhV|Christian Revival Union]] organization.

In 1992, the organization began publishing the newspaper "Our March," later renamed "People's System."

On 17 January 1993, SRM renamed itself to the Front of National Revolutionary Action (FNRD). In 1993, the FNRD participated in the creation of the National Bolshevik Front, but its integration into the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]] did not go beyond participation in a single rally on 9 May 1993.

Following the October 1993 White House shooting and the defeat of the opposition, sanctions against the FNRD were imposed by the executive branch: by order of the Minister of Press and Information of Russia, dated 14 October  1993, the newspaper "Our March" was banned.

However, taking advantage of the amnesty declared by the State Duma on 23 February 1994, the FNRD continued publishing the newspaper, but under the name "Narodny Stroy." This newspaper was subsequently closed, and its editor, Ilya Lazarenko, was charged with "inciting interethnic hatred." In connection with the amnesty announced to commemorate the 50th anniversary of victory in the Great Patriotic War of 1941-1945, Lazarenko was pardoned.

One of the FNRD's most high-profile actions was the rally on 22 March 1994, outside the South African embassy in defense of the white population of that country and against the dismantling of the apartheid system. Members of the [[ruPRP|Right Radical Party]] also participated in this action.

In 1994-1995, Lazarenko suddenly and radically shifted his Orthodox Christian orientation to a pagan one (a combined Germanic-Celtic-Slavic one), shocking most of his colleagues. He then disbanded the FNRD and formed, first, the National Front Party (PNF), and then a religious organization, the Society of Nav' ("Holy Church of the White Race"), using the Ku Klux Klan as its garb.

Some of his former comrades (Orthodox Christians) continued to call themselves the FNRD, while maintaining good relations with their former leader. This group published the magazines "Mrakobes," "Pod Nol," and "Runa," and the newspapers "Dver" and "Khuliganist"; there is evidence that they also became the first editorial board of the newspaper "Limonka." In 1998, on the eve of the National Front Party congress, Ilya Lazarenko officially transferred the right to use the FPRD name and symbols to Mikhail Moiseyev. The thus-revived FNRD participated in the congress as a collective member, representing the movement's Orthodox wing. The last known event organized by the FNRD (jointly with the PNF) was an evening in memory of Baron von Ungern-Sternberg at the Mayakovsky Museum on 18 September 1999.
parties.ideology:
Initially, the SRM's ideological platform represented the full national-patriotic ethos of the time: Orthodox fundamentalism, monarchism, and anti-Semitism. Pre-revolutionary Russia was seen as the ideal. A distinctive feature was the attempt to infuse this complex with Nazi ideas, leading the organization's members to call themselves "monarcho-fascists."

However, in 1992, a rapid and sharp shift to the right led to a break with traditional Orthodox-monarchist organizations. In the programmatic articles "Third Rus'" by Ilya Lazarenko and "National Revolution" by Alexei Shiropaev, the authors disassociated themselves from traditional Russian nationalists (the [[ruPamyat|NPF "Pamyat"]] and similar organizations) and proclaimed themselves "new rightists."

The leaders of the FNRD formulated and published the so-called "20 Points", a synopsis of contemporary Russian fascism. The declared goal of the FNRD was to establish a "Great National Socialist Russian Empire" through Russian national revolution. They recognize "total radicalism" and "national socialism of the Stalin-Strasser type" as their ideological basis.

From its inception, the FNRD proclaimed itself a right-wing radical organization, envisioning cooperation with similar organizations abroad. The first such organization was the [[intNSDAPAO|NSDAP/AO]] ("Foreign Organization of the [[deNSDAP|NSDAP]]").

parties.name: Green Alternative
parties.description:
The Green Alternative was created by Kremlin political strategist Vyacheslav Smirnov. 

Ruslan Khvostov, an environmental activist, member of the Moscow Region Civic Chamber, and former coordinator of the "Ecological Expedition" project of the youth environmental movement "[[ruMestnye|Mestnye]]" (2016-2018), was elected party chairman. From December 2019 to March 2020, the Green Alternative existed as a social movement. The congress was attended by representatives of the previously liquidated [[ruAZ|Green Alliance]] party.

Renowned artist Alexei Kudelin (known as Vasya Lozhkin) became the party's informal leader. His cat drawings served as the basis for the party's logo.

According to Khvostov, the party has nothing in common with the 2009-2012 movement of the same name, the [[ruGROZA|Civil United Green Alternative]] (GROZA), which was led by Oleg Mitvol.

According to party members, the Green Alternative is not exclusively associated with the environmental movement, but rather qualifies as a "moderate left-wing environmental party of the European type." In 2021, Green Alternative applied to join the [[euEGP|European Green Party]].

In June 2020, the party proposed erecting a monument to environmental activist Greta Thunberg in the center of Moscow's Hyde Park in Sokolniki.

The party contested the 2020 regional elections, receiving 10% of the vote in the Komi Republic and 5.4% in the Chelyabinsk Oblast, and winning a seat in both federal subjects' parliaments. Because the party won seats in regional parliaments, it gained the right to participate in federal parliamentary elections without collecting signatures.

In the 2021 legislative elections, Green Alternative came twelfth, winning 0.64% of the popular vote and no seats.

On 26 April 2026, in anticipation of the 2026 State Duma election, the party merged with the [[ruREPZ|Russian Ecological Party "The Greens"]] by decision of the general congress.
