parties.name: Liberal Democratic Party of Russia
parties.nativeName:
Либерально-демократическая партия России
Liberal'no-demokraticheskaya partiya Rossii
parties.description:
Successor of the [[suLDPSU|Liberal Democratic Party of the Soviet Union]] in Russia. The party was led by Vladimir Zhirinovsky since its inception until his death in April 2022. Opposing both communism and state capitalism of the 1990s, the party scored a major success in the 1993 Duma elections with almost 23% of the vote, giving it 64 seats of the 450 seats in the State Duma. In the 2021 elections, the party received 7.55% of the vote, giving it 21 seats.

Despite the party's name, it has been described as "neither liberal nor democratic nor a party". The LDPR was centered around Zhirinovsky, and is often described as populist, nationalist, or ultranationalist. It has been described as adhering to statism and authoritarianism, and has also been described as fascist, though this label has been disputed. The party, as part of the "systemic opposition", is considered to be traditionally loyal to the Kremlin. Besides the aforementioned accusations, it has also been described as right-liberal. The party has been a part of the federal government since 14 May 2024, with Mikhail Degtyarev serving as Minister of Sport.

parties.nativeName:
Движение в поддержку армии
Dvizheniye v podderzhku armii
parties.description:
Pro-military nationalist political movement [not a party] established in 1997 by the lieutenant general and State Duma member Lev Rokhlin from [[ruNDR|Our Home – Russia]]. Rokhlin, who had been radically opposed to Boris Yeltsin's government, was killed under unclear circumstances in July 1998 amid rumors that he was preparing a military coup against Yeltsin.

After Rokhlin's murder in July 1998, the movement took a more radical nationalist and antisemitic stance under the leadership of generals Viktor Ilyukhin and Albert Makashov, but after its defeat in the 1999 legislative election, DPA went into decline and by the end of the 2010s had become a full satellite of the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]].

parties.name: National Bolshevik Party
parties.relations:
Merger of [[ruNRP|National Radical Party]] (Limonov faction), [[ruFNRD|Front of National Revolutionary Action]], Movement in Support of Cuba, [[ruDNP|New Right Movement]].

After its ban, succeeded by the [[ruDRL|The Other Russia]].
parties.description:
The party's founding fathers are considered to be Eduard Limonov, Alexander Dugin, Yegor Letov (leader of the musical group "Civil Defense") and avant-garde composer Sergei Kuryokhin.

The party was founded by Eduard Limonov and Alexander Dugin following a split in the [[ruNRP|National Radical Party]] (NRP), established in 1992. It was originally called the National Bolshevik Front (NBF). The organization's formation was announced on 1 May 1993. The front included the [[ruNRP|NRP]]-Limonov faction, the [[ruFNRD|Front of National Revolutionary Action]] (FNRD), the Movement in Support of Cuba, and the [[ruDNP|New Right Movement]]. The declaration defined National Bolshevism as "the fusion of the most radical forms of social resistance with the most radical forms of national resistance." On 8 September 1993, NBF was registered by the Moscow Region Justice Department as the National Bolshevik Party (NBP). FNRD participated in the creation of the National Bolshevik Front, but its integration into the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]] did not go beyond participation in a single rally on 9 May 1993.

During the 1993 constitutional crisis, Eduard Limonov, on behalf of the NBP, became one of the signatories of the "Statement of Representatives of Public and Political Organizations of Russia from the Supreme Council of the Russian Federation," accusing Russian President Boris Yeltsin of violating the Russian Constitution by signing Decree No. 1400 which ordered the Congress of People's Deputies and the Supreme Council of Russia to cease their activities.

The first issue of the NBP newspaper "Limonka" was published on 28 November 1994.

Eduard Limonov and Alexander Dugin ran in single-mandate constituencies in the 1995 State Duma elections, but lost. Since 1996, the NBP has held annual "Days of the Russian Nation" rallies on April 5th.

During the 1996 Russian presidential election, the NBP initially called for a vote for Boris Yeltsin, based on the principle "the worse, the better," and opposed [[ruKPRF]]'s Gennady Zyuganov's candidacy. NBP ultimately supported independent Yuri Vlasov.

In May 1998, Alexander Dugin and his supporters broke away from the NBP, subsequently creating a number of political organizations with a "Eurasian" (more right-wing conservative) orientation: "Eurasian Invasion," the [[ruEurasia|Eurasia Party]], the [[ruMED|International Eurasian Movement]], and the [[ruESM|Eurasian Youth Union]].

In early 1997, the NBP was registered as an interregional organization, and on 9 February 1998, it was re-registered by the Justice Department of the Moscow Region Administration. On 1-2 October 1998, Nazbols held the First All-Russian Congress of the NBP. Members from 47 regions of the Russian Federation attended. In October 1998, the NBP submitted documents to the Ministry of Justice for registration as an All-Russian political party. The Ministry of Justice denied the NBP registration.

In 2000-2001, Nazbols attempted to organize a guerrilla detachment in Altai, on the border with Kazakhstan, to operate in Kazakhstan with the goal of annexing Northern Kazakhstan to Russia. On 7 April 2001, Nazbol members Aksyonov, Limonov, Pentelyuk, and others were arrested in Saratov and the Altai Krai. They were charged with attempting to seize East Kazakhstan territories from Kazakhstan, acquiring two shipments of weapons, machine guns, and explosives, and planning terrorist attacks against Western interests in Kazakhstan. The NBP members were sentenced to various prison terms.

On 26 June 2002, the Khamovnichesky Court of Moscow ruled to suspend publication of the Limonka newspaper for promoting war and calling for violent change of the constitutional order. On 15 April 2003, the Saratov Court sentenced Eduard Limonov to four years in prison for the illegal acquisition and possession of firearms. He was released on parole on 30 June 2003.

Since 2004, the NBP shifted its political line and emphasized demands for power turnover, democratic freedoms, and the release of political prisoners. Party members repeatedly held protests criticizing the Russian leadership. For example, on 2 August 2004, in protest against the monetization of benefits, a group of "Limonovites" occupied the office of the Russian Minister of Health and Social Development, Mikhail Zurabov. The activists were sentenced to various prison terms. On 14 December 2004, several dozen NBP activists, under corresponding slogans, nonviolently seized the reception office of the Presidential Administration in Moscow. Thirty-nine participants were later charged with organizing mass riots and sentenced to various prison terms. "From the fall of 2003 to July 2005, the National Bolsheviks carried out approximately 870 protests. This is at least 20 times more than any other political organization," wrote P. Danilin, a researcher of the Russian opposition.

The NBP program adopted at the 5th Congress was significantly less nationalistic and imperialist in its rhetoric. It included demands to "allow civil society to develop freely in Russia," "not to hinder the activities of independent media," "to ensure public oversight of law enforcement agencies," and so on.

In 2006, the NBP, together with other opposition organizations, including those with a liberal orientation ([[ruOGF|United Civil Front]], [[ruRNDS|Russian People's Democratic Union]], [[ruSolidarnost|Solidarity]]), and others, participated in the creation of [[ruDrugros|The Other Russia]] coalition, aimed to "restore the Constitution of the Russian Federation." As part of this coalition, party activists participated in "dissenters' marches" in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other cities in 2006–2007.

On 29 June 2005, the National Bolshevik Party was liquidated as a legal entity and subsequently banned by a decision of the Tagansky Court of Moscow.

On 29 August 2006, a congress of Nazbols who decided to leave the NBP was held in Moscow. This resulted in a split, after which the [[ruNBF|National Bolshevik Front]] was created. Its leaders were former prominent NBP activists and former prisoners Maxim Zhurkin and Alexei Golubovich. The reason for the split was the NBP leadership's new tactic of rapprochement with the liberal opposition, as well as the proclamation of a second political program, which, according to the "schismatics," signified a shift from the orthodox theoretical interpretation of National Bolshevism to more left-wing political positions.

On 25 September 2006, approximately 50 National Bolshevik members seized the Russian Ministry of Finance building.

On 19 April 2007, the Moscow City Court declared the Nazbol Party, "a public organization operating without a legal entity", extremist and banned its activities in the Russian Federation. On 7 August 2007, the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation upheld the Moscow City Court's decision to ban the NBP. After the NBP was banned, the Nazbols continued to operate within the "Other Russia" coalition. Since 2009, the party has participated in the regular "Strategy-31" protest in defense of Article 31 of the Russian Constitution (the right of the people to peacefully and unarmedly hold mass events).

In March 2009, party leader Eduard Limonov announced his intention to run in the 2012 Russian presidential elections.

On 4 July 2009, a third split occurred within the NBP, this time due to disagreements between the Moscow Nazbol leadership and members of Eduard Limonov's federal campaign headquarters. The breakaway National Bolsheviks formed the national democratic movement [[ruNS|Nation of Freedom]].

On 28 June 2010, Eduard Limonov announced in an interview that the founding congress of [[ruDRL|The Other Russia]] party, created on the basis of the coalition of the same name, would be held on July 10 "with the goal of participating in the upcoming parliamentary elections." The founding congress of The Other Russia party took place on 10 July 2010. By creating the new party, the Nazbols managed to circumvent the ban imposed by the National Bolshevik Party.
parties.ideology:
The party's central idea is National Bolshevism - a syncretic radical movement attempting to combine the ideas of Bolshevik socialism and radical nationalism. The NBP attempted to unite both left- and right-wing radicals within its ranks, but by the end of its existence, the NBP leaned somewhat toward left-wing populism.

The political objectives of the NBP (1993) were stated to be "the removal from power of the anti-national junta and the regime of social dictatorship of the overwhelming minority, and the establishment of a new order based on the national and social traditions of the Russian people."

The 1994 NBP program stated that the essence of National Bolshevism was a "withering hatred for the anti-human trinity system of liberalism/democracy/capitalism." External enemies were declared to be the United States, "European globalists," NATO, and the UN, while internal enemies were "boyar-bureaucrats, marauding New Russians, and the cosmopolitan intelligentsia." The NBP's global goal was declared to be the creation of an "Empire from Vladivostok to Gibraltar based on Russian civilization." The party intended to build a totalitarian state in which "human rights will give way to the rights of the nation." At the same time, it advocated for complete freedom in the cultural sphere. The program also noted the need to build a unitary system with the abolition of "national republics and territories" and to establish an "iron Russian order" within the country. By "Russians" they meant those "who consider the Russian language and Russian culture to be their own," regardless of origin or religion. As a model for economic development, the party proposed "Russian socialism," based on the "principle of progressive nationalization": the more workers a company has, the more nationalized it is.

In the mid-2000s, influenced by hatred of Putinism, the party gradually evolved from totalitarian ideas to those of "direct democracy." Toward the end of its existence, the NBP was part of [[ruDrugros|The Other Russia]] coalition with the liberals Kasparov and Kasyanov.

After its ban, succeeded by the [[ruDRL|The Other Russia]].

description.text:
The party's founding fathers are considered to be Eduard Limonov, Alexander Dugin, Yegor Letov (leader of the musical group "Civil Defense") and avant-garde composer Sergei Kuryokhin.

The party was founded by Eduard Limonov and Alexander Dugin following a split in the [[ruNRP|National Radical Party]] (NRP), established in 1992. It was originally called the National Bolshevik Front (NBF). The organization's formation was announced on 1 May 1993. The front included the [[ruNRP|NRP]]-Limonov faction, the [[ruFNRD|Front of National Revolutionary Action]] (FNRD), the Movement in Support of Cuba, and the [[ruDNP|New Right Movement]]. The declaration defined National Bolshevism as "the fusion of the most radical forms of social resistance with the most radical forms of national resistance." On 8 September 1993, NBF was registered by the Moscow Region Justice Department as the National Bolshevik Party (NBP). FNRD participated in the creation of the National Bolshevik Front, but its integration into the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]] did not go beyond participation in a single rally on 9 May 1993.

During the 1993 constitutional crisis, Eduard Limonov, on behalf of the NBP, became one of the signatories of the "Statement of Representatives of Public and Political Organizations of Russia from the Supreme Council of the Russian Federation," accusing Russian President Boris Yeltsin of violating the Russian Constitution by signing Decree No. 1400 which ordered the Congress of People's Deputies and the Supreme Council of Russia to cease their activities.

The first issue of the NBP newspaper "Limonka" was published on 28 November 1994.

Eduard Limonov and Alexander Dugin ran in single-mandate constituencies in the 1995 State Duma elections, but lost. Since 1996, the NBP has held annual "Days of the Russian Nation" rallies on April 5th.

During the 1996 Russian presidential election, the NBP initially called for a vote for Boris Yeltsin, based on the principle "the worse, the better," and opposed [[ruKPRF]]'s Gennady Zyuganov's candidacy. NBP ultimately supported independent Yuri Vlasov.

In May 1998, Alexander Dugin and his supporters broke away from the NBP, subsequently creating a number of political organizations with a "Eurasian" (more right-wing conservative) orientation: "Eurasian Invasion," the [[ruEurasia|Eurasia Party]], the [[ruMED|International Eurasian Movement]], and the [[ruESM|Eurasian Youth Union]].

In early 1997, the NBP was registered as an interregional organization, and on 9 February 1998, it was re-registered by the Justice Department of the Moscow Region Administration. On 1-2 October 1998, Nazbols held the First All-Russian Congress of the NBP. Members from 47 regions of the Russian Federation attended. In October 1998, the NBP submitted documents to the Ministry of Justice for registration as an All-Russian political party. The Ministry of Justice denied the NBP registration.

In 2000-2001, Nazbols attempted to organize a guerrilla detachment in Altai, on the border with Kazakhstan, to operate in Kazakhstan with the goal of annexing Northern Kazakhstan to Russia. On 7 April 2001, Nazbol members Aksyonov, Limonov, Pentelyuk, and others were arrested in Saratov and the Altai Krai. They were charged with attempting to seize East Kazakhstan territories from Kazakhstan, acquiring two shipments of weapons, machine guns, and explosives, and planning terrorist attacks against Western interests in Kazakhstan. The NBP members were sentenced to various prison terms.

On 26 June 2002, the Khamovnichesky Court of Moscow ruled to suspend publication of the Limonka newspaper for promoting war and calling for violent change of the constitutional order. On 15 April 2003, the Saratov Court sentenced Eduard Limonov to four years in prison for the illegal acquisition and possession of firearms. He was released on parole on 30 June 2003.

Since 2004, the NBP shifted its political line and emphasized demands for power turnover, democratic freedoms, and the release of political prisoners. Party members repeatedly held protests criticizing the Russian leadership. For example, on 2 August 2004, in protest against the monetization of benefits, a group of "Limonovites" occupied the office of the Russian Minister of Health and Social Development, Mikhail Zurabov. The activists were sentenced to various prison terms. On 14 December 2004, several dozen NBP activists, under corresponding slogans, nonviolently seized the reception office of the Presidential Administration in Moscow. Thirty-nine participants were later charged with organizing mass riots and sentenced to various prison terms. "From the fall of 2003 to July 2005, the National Bolsheviks carried out approximately 870 protests. This is at least 20 times more than any other political organization," wrote P. Danilin, a researcher of the Russian opposition.

The NBP program adopted at the 5th Congress was significantly less nationalistic and imperialist in its rhetoric. It included demands to "allow civil society to develop freely in Russia," "not to hinder the activities of independent media," "to ensure public oversight of law enforcement agencies," and so on.

In 2006, the NBP, together with other opposition organizations, including those with a liberal orientation ([[ruOGF|United Civil Front]], [[ruRNDS|Russian People's Democratic Union]], [[ruSolidarnost|Solidarity]]), and others, participated in the creation of [[ruDrugros|The Other Russia]] coalition, aimed to "restore the Constitution of the Russian Federation." As part of this coalition, party activists participated in "dissenters' marches" in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other cities in 2006–2007.

On 29 June 2005, the National Bolshevik Party was liquidated as a legal entity and subsequently banned by a decision of the Tagansky Court of Moscow.

On 29 August 2006, a congress of Nazbols who decided to leave the NBP was held in Moscow. This resulted in a split, after which the [[ruNBF|National Bolshevik Front]] was created. Its leaders were former prominent NBP activists and former prisoners Maxim Zhurkin and Alexei Golubovich. The reason for the split was the NBP leadership's new tactic of rapprochement with the liberal opposition, as well as the proclamation of a second political program, which, according to the "schismatics," signified a shift from the orthodox theoretical interpretation of National Bolshevism to more left-wing political positions.

On 25 September 2006, approximately 50 National Bolshevik members seized the Russian Ministry of Finance building.

On 19 April 2007, the Moscow City Court declared the Nazbol Party, "a public organization operating without a legal entity", extremist and banned its activities in the Russian Federation. On 7 August 2007, the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation upheld the Moscow City Court's decision to ban the NBP. After the NBP was banned, the Nazbols continued to operate within the "Other Russia" coalition. Since 2009, the party has participated in the regular "Strategy-31" protest in defense of Article 31 of the Russian Constitution (the right of the people to peacefully and unarmedly hold mass events).

In March 2009, party leader Eduard Limonov announced his intention to run in the 2012 Russian presidential elections.

On 4 July 2009, a third split occurred within the NBP, this time due to disagreements between the Moscow Nazbol leadership and members of Eduard Limonov's federal campaign headquarters. The breakaway National Bolsheviks formed the national democratic movement [[ruNS|Nation of Freedom]].

On 28 June 2010, Eduard Limonov announced in an interview that the founding congress of [[ruDRL|The Other Russia]] party, created on the basis of the coalition of the same name, would be held on July 10 "with the goal of participating in the upcoming parliamentary elections." The founding congress of The Other Russia party took place on 10 July 2010. By creating the new party, the Nazbols managed to circumvent the ban imposed by the National Bolshevik Party.

ideology.text:
The party's central idea is National Bolshevism - a syncretic radical movement attempting to combine the ideas of Bolshevik socialism and radical nationalism. The NBP attempted to unite both left- and right-wing radicals within its ranks, but by the end of its existence, the NBP leaned somewhat toward left-wing populism.

The political objectives of the NBP (1993) were stated to be "the removal from power of the anti-national junta and the regime of social dictatorship of the overwhelming minority, and the establishment of a new order based on the national and social traditions of the Russian people."

The 1994 NBP program stated that the essence of National Bolshevism was a "withering hatred for the anti-human trinity system of liberalism/democracy/capitalism." External enemies were declared to be the United States, "European globalists," NATO, and the UN, while internal enemies were "boyar-bureaucrats, marauding New Russians, and the cosmopolitan intelligentsia." The NBP's global goal was declared to be the creation of an "Empire from Vladivostok to Gibraltar based on Russian civilization." The party intended to build a totalitarian state in which "human rights will give way to the rights of the nation." At the same time, it advocated for complete freedom in the cultural sphere. The program also noted the need to build a unitary system with the abolition of "national republics and territories" and to establish an "iron Russian order" within the country. By "Russians" they meant those "who consider the Russian language and Russian culture to be their own," regardless of origin or religion. As a model for economic development, the party proposed "Russian socialism," based on the "principle of progressive nationalization": the more workers a company has, the more nationalized it is.

In the mid-2000s, influenced by hatred of Putinism, the party gradually evolved from totalitarian ideas to those of "direct democracy." Toward the end of its existence, the NBP was part of [[ruDrugros|The Other Russia]] coalition with the liberals Kasparov and Kasyanov.

parties.description:
A short-lived Russian political party with a nationalist-patriotic ideology. It was the predecessor of the National Bolshevik Party.

In November 1992, a group of members of the [[ruLDPR|LDPR]]'s "shadow cabinet", Limonov, Zharikov, Arkhipov, Buzov, Mitrofanov, Andrei Kursky, and several other radical figures, decided to leave the [[ruLDPR|LDPR]], dissatisfied with Zhirinovsky's leadership style.

The party was founded by Andrei Arkhipov, Sergei Zharikov, leader of the punk band DK, and writer Eduard Limonov on 22 November 1992, at the dacha of producer Alexei Mitrofanov. In addition to LDPR dissidents, members of the Nord hooligan group and dissidents from several other movements attended the founding congress. A total of about 30 people attended the congress. Eduard Limonov became the party's leader.

On 17 December 1992, the party was registered by the Russian Ministry of Justice.

Soon after its creation, some party members (including Mitrofanov) returned to the [[ruLDPR|LDPR]], and the NRP itself split into two factions: one led by Limonov and other led by Arkhipov and Zharikov. The first faction became the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]] in 1993, and the second became the [[ruPRP|Right Radical Party]] (PRP).

parties.name: New Force
parties.relations: Merged into the [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]] (SPS).
parties.description:
A Russian liberal-conservative political organization founded in 1998 by former Prime Minister Sergei Kiriyenko. One of the co-founders of the [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]].

The initiative group of the political organization of supporters of former Russian Prime Minister Sergei Kiriyenko was formed in November 1998. Initially, Kiriyenko simultaneously participated in the initiative group of the center-right coalition, and also considered joining Boris Nemtsov's [[ruRosMol|Young Russia]].

Like Young Russia, New Force began recruiting supporters and promoting its views primarily via the internet. The necessary number of regional groups to register Sergei Kiriyenko's movement was provided by regular internet users, as well as regional organizations of the [[ruRPR|Republican Party of the Russian Federation]] (RPRF) (which also assisted Nemtsov), and, in some regions, former activists of Sergei Shakhrai's [[ruPRES|Party of Russian Unity and Accord]] (PRES). Lukoil company provided financial support to New Force.

At a press conference on 9 December 1998, Kiriyenko described the main goal of the movement he was creating as "the preservation of a democratic regime of governance and a market economy in Russia" ("We are talking about uniting... not leaders, but people who will vote in elections,... those 30-40 percent who have not yet transformed their economic independence into political independence."

The movement was officially founded by Sergei Kiriyenko on 12 December 1998, and registered with the Ministry of Justice on 17 December 1998 (Reg. No. 3633).

On 24 December 1998, the New Force information server held an "Internet conference" with Sergei Kiriyenko, during which he answered 52 questions. In particular, Kiriyenko proposed that his supporters create an "Internet Parliament" to discuss "Russia's national strategy for the next millennium," the New Force economic program, constitutional reform, and "the development of a new political language." When asked by one of the "Internet conference" participants whether he would run in the next presidential election, Kiriyenko answered in the negative.

On 23-24 January 1999, an interregional conference of Sergei Kiriyenko's supporters was held in Nizhny Novgorod to discuss preparations for the founding congress of the New Force movement, scheduled for February 1999.

On 18-20 February 1999, a congress of New Force was held in Nizhny Novgorod. The event was held in one of the pavilions of the Nizhny Novgorod fair and was stylized as a carnival: masks of Zyuganov, Lebed, Luzhkov, and Yavlinsky served as doormen at the cloakroom; each delegate was given a sum in the party "currency" - "Kirienkos," which were accepted as money at the congress buffet; at the end, the delegates were given two effigies to burn, one of which represented "Cowardice" and the other "Lies" (journalists identified a vague resemblance between the first effigy and Yeltsin, and the second, to Zyuganov).

After the Nizhny Novgorod congress of New Force, Kiriyenko effectively distanced himself from the [[ruPDco|Right Cause]] coalition, advocating for the creation of a broader non-communist bloc with the participation of governors, and - ideally - also [[ruYabloko|Yabloko]].

On 28 May 1999, the press services of the New Forceand the gubernatorial bloc Konstantin Titov's [[ruGolosR|Voice of Russia]] movement issued a joint statement announcing the beginning of work on creating a broad center-right coalition.

At the congress of Right Force (the founding predecessor of the [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]]) on 29 May 1999, Kiriyenko attended only as a guest, although he reiterated his intentions as an ally to the coalition members.

In June 1999, Kiriyenko announced the possibility of running for Moscow mayor and harshly criticized Yuri Luzhkov as a model representative of nomenklatura capitalism and a leader who was building Moscow's prosperity by extracting resources from other regions. New Force launched a special website, "Moscow Alternative," on the internet, collecting ideas and proposals for Moscow's development. In fact, the website, which receives criticism and complaints rather than proposals, has become a hub for information on actual and alleged abuses by Moscow city administration officials.

On 23 July 1999, at a meeting between Chubais, Kiriyenko (New Force), and Konstantin Titov (Voice of Russia), an agreement was reached to create a bloc that would contest the elections as a single list. The "Declaration of Unification" and programmatic theses prepared by the joint program commission were approved.

On 29 August 1999, at a joint congress, the [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]] (SPS) was established, incorporating most of the Right Cause, New Force, and part of Voice of Russia.

In the 1999 State Duma elections, the SPS bloc received 8.52% of the party list vote (24 seats) and won five seats in single-mandate constituencies. Sergei Kiriyenko became the first head of the SPS faction in the State Duma.

During the 2000 presidential elections, some members of the SPS Coordinating Council (including Kiriyenko) supported Vladimir Putin.

On May 26, 2001, the SPS founding congress voted to transform the bloc into a party. All SPS member movements were required to dissolve, which Sergei Kiriyenko's New Force also did.
parties.ideology: Kiriyenko stated that New Force was ready to negotiate and unite "with anyone who holds the same views," including the center-right coalition of Gaidar and Chubais, Boris Nemtsov, Yabloko, Yuri Luzhkov's movement, etc.

parties.name: New People
parties.description:
In January 2020, businessmen, CEO of Faberlic cosmetic company, Alexey Nechayev announced the party's creation to the media.

On 1 March 2020, the constituent congress of New People was held. 55 party regional branches were created. Official party registration was received from the Russian Ministry of Justice at the end of March.

As of 1 July 2020, New People had 55 registered regional branches, which began preparing to take part in the regional elections of September 2020 in 12 regions of the country. Also, the party declared its readiness and intent to take part in the elections to the State Duma in 2021.

On 8 August 2020, the second congress of the party was held in Moscow at which its founder Alexey Nechayev was elected chairman of the party.

On 4 July 2021, a party congress was held at which the party's list and candidates for participation in the 2021 legislative election were nominated. Party leader Alexey Nechayev headed the federal list of the party. The second number in the federal list was the former Mayor of Yakutsk Sardana Avksentyeva.

According to the election results, the party gained 5.3% of the vote, winning 13 seats in the State Duma. New People became the first party not from the "big four" ([[ruER|United Russia]], [[ruKPRF|KPRF]], [[ruLDPR|LDPR]] and [[ruSR|SRZP]]) since 2007 to overcome the 5% barrier and form its own faction. In addition to the 13 deputies elected on the party list of the party, the New People faction also included two independent deputies elected in single-mandate constituencies: Dmitry Pevtsov and Oleg Leonov.

On 15 February 2022, New People's Duma faction voted against the recognition of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions as independent states. However, the party later withdrew its statement and proclaimed its support for the 2022 war.

On 16 August 2022, the party called for Instagram to be unblocked.

On 24 December 2023, it was reported that the [[ruROST|Party of Growth]] will be merged with New People, both parties are already part of the informal political alliance [[ruSPPS|Union of Progressive Political Forces]]. At a joint congress on 19 April 2024, the New People and the Growth Party announced a legal unification, and all delegates voted for the unification. The parties will operate under the general name “New People”. Growth Party leader Boris Titov will head the federal political council. The only State Duma deputy from the Growth Party, Oksana Dmitriyeva, announced that she would take the position of chairwoman of the regional branch of New People in Saint Petersburg. At the same time, she stated that she did not intend to join the New People faction in the Duma.

During the 2024 presidential campaign, some opposition forces considered Vladislav Davankov's New People's party as a target for protest voting after the Central Election Commission refused to register Boris Nadezhdin.

parties.description:
A long-lived proto-Eurasian political movement in Russia, led by philosopher Alexander Dugin and prominent writer Alexander Prokhanov.

The "New Right" movement emerged in the early 1990s as an intellectual current and political force in opposition to the Western aspirations of the Gorbachev-era Soviet Union.

In July 1992, Alexander Dugin, who worked at the Arktogeya publishing house, founded the New Right journal "Elements."

In February 1993, Alexander Dugin, with the support of a group of fans of the magazine "Elements" and the support of the [[ruFNRD|Front of National Revolutionary Action]], announced the creation of the "Movement of the New Right."

On 1 May 1993, together with the "new-left" leader of the small [[ruNRP|National Radical Party]], Eduard Limonov, Dugin signed an "order" to create the "National Bolshevik Front," which later became the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]].

On 1 May 1993, together with the "new-left" leader of the small [[ruNRP|National Radical Party]], Eduard Limonov, Dugin signed an "order" to create the "National Bolshevik Front," which later became the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]].

parties.description:
The party was founded on 21 May 2012, by Vladimir Ponomarenko, former chairman of the executive committee of the [[ruRPP|Russian Party of Pensioners]]. In 2007, Ponomarenko was elected to the Central Council of the [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] party. In 2011, he resigned from the Central Council and party membership due to disagreement with internal party policy.

The party has been accused of "spoiling" [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] and [[ruPARNAS|PARNAS]].

The party has participated in elections to regional legislative assemblies at various levels since 2012.

In 2013, the party participated in municipal representative elections in the Krasnodar Krai, Arkhangelsk, Vologda, Vladimir, Ivanovo, Moscow, and Chelyabinsk regions, and the cities of Volgograd, Veliky Novgorod, and Tyumen. In total, the party won five seats in these elections.

In the 2014 elections to the State Assembly of the Altai Republic, the party received 2.6% of the vote, beating [[ruYabloko|Yabloko]], [[ruPARNAS|PARNAS]], [[ruREPZ|the Greens]], and several others.

Since 2014, party leader Ponomarenko has served as the chairman of the All-Russian public organization "For National Interests, Sovereignty, and Territorial Integrity."

The party supports Russia's 2022's Special Military Operation in Ukraine, considering its proposals for the denazification of Ukraine to be correct.

parties.name: Party of Business
parties.literalName: Party of the Cause / Party of Action
parties.description:
The Party of Business was described as a spoiler for [[ruPD|Right Cause]] (also abbreviated PD), trying to draw business-affiliated votes away from it.

On 22 September 2010, a group of economists and entrepreneurs announced the imminent formation of a new party called the Party of Business. On 14 October 2010, the party's founding congress was held at the Izmailovo Hotel in Moscow, where 160 delegates from 51 regions of Russia approved the party's program and charter.

On 12 October 2010, a picket against the reduction of agricultural subsidies was held near the Russian Ministry of Agriculture building. Twenty people participated in the picket. On 3 November 2010, a picket against Russia's accession to the WTO was held at the same building. Party activists promised to hold rallies every Wednesday until Agriculture Minister Elena Skrynnik acknowledges the decision to reduce agricultural subsidies to WTO levels was a mistake. Since then, pickets on this issue have been held almost weekly. At one of them, even employees of the Ministry of Agriculture expressed support for the protesters.

On 10 November 2010, the first founding conference of the party's regional branch was held in the Republic of Bashkortostan. By 1 December, regional branches had been formed in 42 regions of Russia, which is sufficient to gain the status of an all-Russian political party.

On 27 December 2010, the party submitted documents for registration to the Ministry of Justice. In February 2011, the party was denied registration. The Ministry of Justice's decision was appealed in court.

On 4 April 2012, the registration process for the referendum on Russia's accession to the WTO was launched in the building of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Russia – the first meeting of the organizing committee and a meeting of the Moscow regional subgroup. More than 300 people attended the meeting of the regional subgroup, which was held in the building of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Moscow. The initiators were the public organization Russian People's Cathedral, the [[ruPGR|Trade Union of Citizens of Russia]], the Interregional Public Organization VECHE, and the Party of Business On 13 April, the Russian Central Election Commission deemed it impossible to hold a referendum in Russia on the country's accession to the World Trade Organization.

On 31 October 2012, delegates from Russia's regional branches held a new Founding Congress, at which they decided to establish the Party of Business along with its Charter and Program. On 14 December 2012, the party was registered by the Ministry of Justice.

On 5 March 2015, party members held their Second Congress to admit new members to the Federal Council, adopt a new version of the program, and discuss the development of the Non-Black Earth Region regions. The congress was held in Kostroma.

In 2016, members of the Party of Business won more seats in the Spassky Municipal District Duma elections in Primorsky Krai than representatives of [[ruER|United Russia]].

On 27 November 2017, the IV Congress of the Party of Business was held, where delegates supported the inclusion of new managers in the party's governing bodies.

The party’s activities were suspended by Russia’s Supreme Court in April 2024 after violations were found in the party’s charter. On 18 October 2024, Russia’s Ministry of Justice requested to dissolve the party. On 27 November 2024, the Party of Business was liquidated by the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation. After the dissolution of the party, Konstantin Babkin was accepted into the Supreme Council of the [[ruLDPR|Liberal Democratic Party of Russia]].

parties.name: Party of Direct Democracy
parties.nativeName:
Партия прямой демократии
Partiya pryamoy demokratii
parties.description:
The creation of the Direct Democracy Party was publicly announced on January 10, 2020. On March 5 of that year, a founding congress was held, at which its charter was adopted, a general secretary, and the first Supreme Coordination Council were elected. The party's founder, Vyacheslav Makarov, became its general secretary.

On April 1, 2020, the party was registered by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation.

In November 2020, Vyacheslav Makarov resigned as general secretary, citing a lack of long-term political plans and the need to immediately launch the party. Oleg Artamonov, head of the party's scientific and technical expertise, was elected as the new general secretary at an extraordinary congress.

In January 2021, the party's general secretary, Oleg Artamonov, announced that the party would not participate in the State Duma elections, focusing on elections to regional parliaments. In the 2021 elections to the Legislative Assembly of the Jewish Autonomous Region, the Direct Democracy Party received 5.93% of the vote, winning one seat.

In 2022 and 2023, the party barely participated in the elections, nominating only three candidates for local government, two of whom were denied registration.

In 2024, a by-election for a State Duma deputy in Khakassia's single-mandate constituency No. 35 was held. Anton Palyulin became the party's candidate. Palyulin received 1.79% of the vote (fifth place out of six candidates).

The Direct Democracy Party advocates the establishment of direct democracy through digitalization, expanding the capabilities of the application "Gosuslugi" to control the activities of deputies and elected officials, providing residents of municipalities with the opportunity to directly distribute part of the local budget. At the same time, the party refuses to approve any official ideology, since the policy of elected deputies should be determined directly on the ground by voters.

parties.name: Party of Growth
parties.description:
The party was founded in February-March 2016 by Boris Titov, the Presidential Commissioner for the Protection of Entrepreneurs' Rights, based on the [[ruPD|Right Cause]] party. Titov was a member of the pro-Putin [[ruONF|All-Russia People's Front]].

Since 2023, the Growth Party and the ideologically close [[ruNL|New People]] have been members of the [[ruSPPS|Union of Progressive Political Forces]] alliance.

On April 19, 2024, the party merged with [[ruNL|New People]]. Growth Party leader Boris Titov became the head of New People's federal political council. In 2025, the Russian Ministry of Justice filed a petition with the Supreme Court demanding the party's legal liquidation. On 20 November 2025, the party was officially liquidated.

parties.name: Party of Progress
parties.description:
The Party of Social Networks (PSS) was founded on 9 April 2012, and officially registered on May 29, 2012. It was created with the participation of Andrei Bogdanov, leader of the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]] and the Center for Political Technologies. The party did not publicly identify itself, had no website or official social media group, and nothing is known about its composition or official leadership, including its chairman, Dmitry Chirov. Similar parties created by Andrei Bogdanov are called party businesses, nominating candidates on a commercial basis and selling ready-made parties on a turnkey basis. The party's membership in 2012 was 500 (the minimum required number of members for political party registration following the May amendments to Federal Law No. 95-FZ).

The Party of Social Networks relied on a social-liberal ideology, advocating for an end to state funding of religious organizations, a reduction in military spending with a mass transition to a contract basis, the abolition of the Federation Council and a transition to a unicameral system of legislative power. In the regional elections, the PSS used the email symbol @ as its logo.

On 12 April 2013, at the Third Congress, the Party of Social Networks was reorganized into the Civic Position party, and Vladimir Albertovich Vekselman was elected Chairman of the Federal Council.

The Civic Position logo was almost identical to the [[ruGP|Civic Platform]] logo. On 22 May 2013, it was announced that Alexei Chesnakov, former Deputy Secretary of the General Council of the [[ruER|United Russia]] party and political scientist, intended to lead the Civil Position party. However, he never took over the party.

In 2012–2013, "Civic Position" participated in local elections in several regions of Russia; In particular, in the parliaments of Chechnya, Yakutia, and the Vladimir region. During the Vladimir elections, the party submitted a document to the local electoral commission containing information on the candidates' income and assets, according to which none of the 17 candidates owned any property or received any income for 2012. The electoral commission deemed this information inaccurate. The party's best result was 0.26%, which it received in the fall of 2012 in the elections to the Legislative Assembly of Krasnodar Krai. 

Following Vekselman, Andrei Poda, owner of the Madeleine Travel Salon, became chairman of the Civil Position political council in 2016. In 2015, Poda founded the public organization Investment Russia in Mordovia, also associated with Andrei Bogdanov.

In 2015, Andrei Bogdanov, speaking to Vedomosti, mentioned Civil Position among "his" parties. At the time, he offered to buy the party for at least $250,000.

On 22 February 2018, Vitaly Serukanov, former deputy head of Alexei Navalny's Moscow presidential campaign headquarters, announced on Facebook that he had submitted documents to the Ministry of Justice to register the Party of Progress based on the "Civil Position" party. This is also the name of the [[ruRB|unregistered party of Navalny and his supporters]], but Serukanov's organization has no connection to it. Navalny claimed that political strategist Andrei Bogdanov was trying to steal the party from him.

Serukanov stated that he did not know whether Bogdanov had any connection to Civil Position and that he was negotiating with "completely different people." He declined to name these people until the transformation process was complete. Serukanov noted that he had been a member of the Party of Progress since its founding, and now he and a group of like-minded individuals had "united to develop a new socio-political force without leaders or armchair theorists."

On 19 March 2018, the Unified State Register of Legal Entities (USRLE) recorded changes to the founding documents of the Civil Position party, according to which it was renamed the Party of Progress. Due to the registration of the Party of Progress, supporters of Alexei Navalny were forced to choose a new name for their party. Navalny's party was renamed [[ruRB|Russia of the Future]].

parties.description:
Founded by Speaker of the State Duma, Gennadiy Seleznyov, after he left the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]]; The party was founded on the basis of the Rossiya public movement, founded by Seleznyov in 2000.

Merged into the [[ruPR|Patriots of Russia]] on 9 September 2008. Re-established on 26 October 2012.

parties.name: Party of Russian Unity and Accord
parties.nativeName:
Партия российского единства и согласия
Partiya rossiyskogo yedinstva i soglasiya
parties.relations: Merged into the [[ruUnity|Unity]].
parties.description:
At the end of 1992, the Russian Minister for Nationalities and Regional Policy, Sergey Shakhray, announced preparations for the creation of his own party, which "will avoid any radicalism and the predominance of 'Moscow families'". Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Shokhin, former Chairman of the Council of Nationalities of the Supreme Soviet Ramazan Abdulatipov, Minister of Justice Yuri Kalmykov, Kremlin Chief of Staff Sergey Filatov, Presidential advisor Sergei Stankevich, Chairman of the "Entrepreneurs for a New Russia" association Konstantin Zatulin, and other government-affiliated personalities joined Shakhray's project.

On 17 June 1993, Shakhray, attending the congress of the "Entrepreneurs for a New Russia" association, announced that he was beginning to create the Party of Russian Unity and Harmony, which, according to him, "will rely on the political and economic forces of the regions and support the President of the Russian Federation".

On 17 August 1993, the founding conference of the party was held in Novgorod, where the program was adopted and the Federal Council was elected, which included Shakhray, Shokhin, Abdulatipov, Stankevich, Alexander Kotenkov, Governor of Novgorod Oblast Mikhail Prusak and others. The party was registered by Ministry of Justice on 21 October 1993.

On 26 October 1993, the PRES Federal Council nominated a federal candidates list for the 1993 State Duma elections. The list included four incumbent ministers: Shakhray, Shokhin, Kalmykov, and Gennady Melikyan. The association "Entrepreneurs for a New Russia," headed by Konstantin Zatulin, also informally joined the PRES.

In the 1993 Russian legislative election, PRES received 6.73% of the votes on party lists and 22 seats out of 450 in the 1st State Duma. Five members of the PRES were elected to the Federation Council. At the beginning of the State Duma's term, the PRES faction expanded to 30-33 deputies. During 1994-1995 the party fell into decline: In 1994, Konstantin Zatulin and Yuri Kalmykov  were expelled from the party, the latter for disagreeing with the party's endorsement of the First Chechen War. In May 1995, Alexander Shokhin also left the party, and by the fall of 1995, its faction had halved to only 15 deputies.

At the party's first congress (26–27 February 1994), Shakhray was elected chairman. The congress adopted the party's ideological program.

During the 1st State Duma, the PRES faction supported the government's budget proposals and blocked the opposition's attempts to pass a vote of no confidence in Chernomyrdin's cabinet. The party's most notable legislative initiative was the "Memorandum of Agreement," which, along with the resolution "On Declaring a Political and Economic Amnesty," was adopted by the State Duma on 23 February 1994. As a result, former GKChP members and participants in the 1993 constitutional crisis were amnestied and released, prompting sharp criticism of PRES from the liberal media press.

In April-May 1995, PRES took part in the creation of the Chernomydrin's [[ruNDR|Our Home – Russia]] (NDR) movement as a collective member, but left the NDR in early September 1995. According to estimates by the PRES leadership, in the summer of 1995 the party's membership was 31,000 people, and its regional organizations operated in 64 constituent entities of the Russian Federation. However, according to research, the actual number of party members did not exceed 3,000–5,000 people.

On 16 September 1995, the party's pre-election congress was held, where a federal list of candidates was nominated, again headed by Sergey Shakhray. In the 1995 Russian legislative election, PRES received only 0.36% of the vote. Party leader Sergey Shakhray was elected in a single-mandate constituency. PRES Executive Committee Chairman Alexander Arinin won in a single-mandate constituency running as an independent candidate, while PRES member Insaf Saifullin was elected on the NDR list. In the 2nd State Duma, Shakhray joined the Russian Regions parliamentary group, while Arinin joined the NDR faction.

At the 3rd PRES Congress on 25 May 1996, the party supported incumbent president Boris Yeltsin in the 1996 Russian presidential election.

On 27 June 1998, the 4th and final PRES Congress took place, at which Shakhray announced the party's likely participation in the next State Duma election and the possible support of Yury Luzhkov or Alexander Lebed in the next presidential election. After the 4th Congress, the party effectively ceased operations, unable to find the funds to continue its existence. In 1999, Shakhray joined the Unity movement, and on 27 May 2000, the Unity congress announced its transformation into a political party, with the NDR, All Russia, and the PRES joining it. Shakhray was elected as a member of the Presidium of the Political Council of the Unity party. PRES was legally liquidated on 13 October 2006, by court order.
parties.ideology:
PRES billed itself as a "conservative party of Russia's regions", aiming to improve and optimize the federal structure under a "strong center." The party also advocated an "economic federalism" and socially-oriented market economy without an emphasis on state power. The party was created under the slogans of federalism and respect for the economic rights of the regions, but was described as essentially a centrist "departmental party" of Shakhray-headed Ministry of Nationalities.

During the 1993 election campaign, the PRES party presented itself as a conservative alternative to the [[ruVyborR|Choice of Russia]], while supporting the policies of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

In its documents, the party supported Boris Yeltsin's actions during the September-October 1993 Russian constitutional crisis, although its ranks also included some pro-parliamentary supporters, such as Ramazan Abdulatipov.

The association "Entrepreneurs for a New Russia," headed by Konstantin Zatulin, also informally joined the PRES.

In the 1993 Russian legislative election, PRES received 6.73% of the votes on party lists and 22 seats out of 450 in the 1st State Duma. Five members of the PRES were elected to the Federation Council. At the beginning of the State Duma's term, the PRES faction expanded to 30-33 deputies. During 1994-1995 the party fell into decline: In 1994, Konstantin Zatulin and Yuri Kalmykov  were expelled from the party, the latter for disagreeing with the party's endorsement of the First Chechen War. In May 1995, Alexander Shokhin also left the party, and by the fall of 1995, its faction had halved to only 15 deputies.

At the party's first congress (26–27 February 1994), Shakhray was elected chairman. The congress adopted the party's ideological program.

During the 1st State Duma, the PRES faction supported the government's budget proposals and blocked the opposition's attempts to pass a vote of no confidence in Chernomyrdin's cabinet. The party's most notable legislative initiative was the "Memorandum of Agreement," which, along with the resolution "On Declaring a Political and Economic Amnesty," was adopted by the State Duma on 23 February 1994. As a result, former GKChP members and participants in the 1993 constitutional crisis were amnestied and released, prompting sharp criticism of PRES from the liberal media press.

In April-May 1995, PRES took part in the creation of the Chernomydrin's [[ruNDR|Our Home – Russia]] (NDR) movement as a collective member, but left the NDR in early September 1995. According to estimates by the PRES leadership, in the summer of 1995 the party's membership was 31,000 people, and its regional organizations operated in 64 constituent entities of the Russian Federation. However, according to research, the actual number of party members did not exceed 3,000–5,000 people.

On 16 September 1995, the party's pre-election congress was held, where a federal list of candidates was nominated, again headed by Sergey Shakhray. In the 1995 Russian legislative election, PRES received only 0.36% of the vote. Party leader Sergey Shakhray was elected in a single-mandate constituency. PRES Executive Committee Chairman Alexander Arinin won in a single-mandate constituency running as an independent candidate, while PRES member Insaf Saifullin was elected on the NDR list. In the 2nd State Duma, Shakhray joined the Russian Regions parliamentary group, while Arinin joined the NDR faction.

At the 3rd PRES Congress on 25 May 1996, the party supported incumbent president Boris Yeltsin in the 1996 Russian presidential election.

On 27 June 1998, the 4th and final PRES Congress took place, at which Shakhray announced the party's likely participation in the next State Duma election and the possible support of Yury Luzhkov or Alexander Lebed in the next presidential election. After the 4th Congress, the party effectively ceased operations, unable to find the funds to continue its existence. In 1999, Shakhray joined the Unity movement, and on 27 May 2000, the Unity congress announced its transformation into a political party, with the NDR, All Russia, and the PRES joining it. Shakhray was elected as a member of the Presidium of the Political Council of the Unity party. PRES was legally liquidated on 13 October 2006, by court order.

ideology.text:
PRES billed itself as a "conservative party of Russia's regions", aiming to improve and optimize the federal structure under a "strong center." The party also advocated an "economic federalism" and socially-oriented market economy without an emphasis on state power. The party was created under the slogans of federalism and respect for the economic rights of the regions, but was described as essentially a centrist "departmental party" of Shakhray-headed Ministry of Nationalities.

During the 1993 election campaign, the PRES party presented itself as a conservative alternative to the [[ruVyborR|Choice of Russia]], while supporting the policies of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

In its documents, the party supported Boris Yeltsin's actions during the September-October 1993 Russian constitutional crisis, although its ranks also included some pro-parliamentary supporters, such as Ramazan Abdulatipov.

parties.name: Party of Social Protection
parties.nativeName:
Партия социальной защиты
Partiya sotsial'noy zashchity
parties.description:
The party was established at its founding congress on 5 May 2012. Delegates from 53 regions attended the congress. The process of official registration of the party in the Unified State Register of Legal Entities by the Ministry of Justice was completed on 19 June 2012. Viktor Sviridov became the party's first leader.

PSZ candidate Viktor Perov ran for governor of Saint Petersburg in 2019. Previously, Viktor Perov was a member of the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] and the [[ruKPKR|Communists of Russia]]. He was also a deputy of the Slantsy Municipal Council. If he wins the gubernatorial election, Perov promises to build "developed socialism" in Saint Petersburg.

The Krasnodar branch of the party held a rally in July 2019 against the increase in public transport fares.

The party held two seats in the Kostroma Regional Duma (2020-2025).

In June 2022, a picket “No to nuclear war!” was held in Kostroma, approved by the authorities and initiated by Vladimir Mikhailov.

By the decision of the Supreme Court of Russia of 18 December 2025, which entered into force on 12 March 2026, the activities of the Political Party of Social Protection, its regional branches and other structural divisions were suspended for a period of two months. On 3 June 2026, the Supreme Court upheld the Ministry of Justice's request to liquidate the Party of Social Protection. According to the Ministry of Justice, the organization failed to correct violations identified during the previous year's inspection. In particular the party provided false information about its members: about two dozen people listed on the register turned out to be [[ruER|United Russia]] members.

parties.name: Patriots of Russia
parties.description:
Established in April 2005 by Gennady Semigin, who was expelled from the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] after he failed in a power struggle with Gennady Zyuganov. Legally, Patriots of Russia is a successor party of the [[ruRPT|Russian Party of Labour]].

In 2006 Gennadiy Semigin and his new Patriots of Russia party joined the [[ruRodina2005|Rodina]] faction in the Duma. Following Rodina's merger with the [[ruRPZh|Russian Party of Life]] and the [[ruRPP|Russian Party of Pensioners]] under the leadership of Sergey Mironov in October 2006 to form the [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] party, Patriots of Russia declared its intention to run as a separate party in the 2007 State Duma election. In the 2007 election, members of the unregistered [[ruVR2007|Great Russia]] party participated on the Patriots of Russia list.

In 2008, the VIII Congress approved the self-dissolution of the [[ruPME|Party of Peace and Unity]] (PME) and its entry into the Patriots of Russia party. However, in 2012, following legislative amendments to simplify the registration of political parties, the PME organizing committee decided to reinstate itself and leave the Patriots of Russia party.

The [[ruPVR|Party of Russia's Rebirth]] (PVR) merged into the Patriots of Russia on 9 September 2008. PVR was re-established on 26 October 2012.

In December 2017, the Patriots of Russia announced that they would not run in the 2018 Russian presidential election and that the party would support current president Vladimir Putin for the elections.

Since 2011, the party has been an ally of the [[ruONF|All-Russia People's Front]] (ONF), created at the initiative of Vladimir Putin.

Until 2021, PR maintained close ties with the [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] party, which it subsequently joined. In February 2021, PR (together with [[ruZP|For Truth]]) merged into the [[ruSR|A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth]] party.

As a political movement, it continues to exist to this day.
parties.ideology: The party was officially democratic socialist and collectivist. The party had many of the same policy positions as the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]].

parties.relations:
Preceded by the faction of the [[ruNRP|National Radical Party]] (NRP);
After party dissolution, some of its members joined the [[ruLDPR|Liberal Democratic Party of Russia]].
parties.description:
A small far-right political party founded in 1993 by LDPR dissidents Sergei Zharikov and Andrei Arkhipov from their wing of the short-lived [[ruNRP|National Radical Party]].

The party was founded in May 1993 from the Sergei Zharikov-Andrei Arkhipov wing of the [[ruNRP|National Radical Party]]. The other wing, led by Eduard Limonov, became the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]].

The PRP's most prominent activity is the magazine "Ataka" (Attack) edited by Zharikov (called "To the Axe" before it was banned in October 1993).

In 1994, together with the [[ruFNRD|Front of National Revolutionary Action]], the PRP held a rally in support of Afrikaners at the South African embassy.

In 1994, the party took part in the second [[ruKRO|Congress of Russian Communities]].

The party was dissolved in 1996. After several unsuccessful political projects, Andrei Arkhipov worked for the radical newspaper Stringer and served as an assistant to a State Duma deputy from the [[ruLDPR|Liberal Democratic Party of Russia]] (LDPR). The few members of the PRP worked in the staff of the State Duma Committee on Geopolitics and played a key role in hearings and seminars organized by the Committee on Geopolitics.

parties.name: Rodina
parties.description:
On 21 September 2011, the [[ruKRO|Congress of Russian Communities]], a public association, held a congress, at which the organization was reorganized into Rodina-Congress of Russian Communities. An organizing committee was created to restore the Rodina political party, which in 2006 co-founded [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] (SR). (In 2006, Rodina was led by Alexander Babakov, who attempted to give it a social democratic bent.) At the congress, Dmitry Rogozin accused SR leader Sergei Mironov of "hostile takeover" of the Rodina party.

In April 2012, the "Rodina-Congress of Russian Communities" organizing committee filed a notice with the Ministry of Justice to reinstate the political party.

On 29 September 2012, the founding congress of the "All-Russian Political Party «Rodina»" and the Special Purpose Volunteer Movement (DON) was held in Moscow. Delegates declared the full restoration of Rodina's organizational and political independence. Alexei Zhuravlev, a State Duma deputy from [[ruER|United Russia]], member of the Presidential Council for Interethnic Relations and chairman of the public organization [[ruKRO|Congress of Russian Communities]], was elected chairman of the party and the DON volunteer movement.

The party opposed the 2011–2013 Russian protests and members of the party's paramilitary have participated in attacks on migrants in Moscow.

The party's 2016 economic program was based on works by economist Sergei Glazyev. Its elements include the acquisition of "economic sovereignty," necessary under the current sanctions regime "and state capitalism with elements of a planned economy." In addition, sections were being prepared on the army and the defense industry, as well as the development of the Arctic region. In 2016 State Duma election Alexei Zhuravlev himself ran as a [[ru|ONF|ONF]]-supported candidate in the 89th Anninsky single-mandate constituency of the Voronezh Region, where he won. He was re-elected in 2021.

In July 2017, the Rodina party announced that it would not nominate a candidate in the 2018 Russian presidential elections, but would support the incumbent President Vladimir Putin. At the congress, the [[ruRSP|Russian Socialist Party]] merged into Rodina.

In December 2017, the former chairman of the [[ruRPPSS|Party of Pensioners]], Igor Zotov, was elected secretary of the political council of the Rodina party.

In December 2023, Rodina announced that the party will support current President Vladimir Putin for the 2024 presidential election.

parties.name: Russian All-People's Union
parties.nativeName:
Российский общенародный союз
Rossiyskiy obshchenarodnyy soyuz
parties.description:
A Russian political party formed in October 1991. Until 2011, it operated as a political movement.

The organization was founded by Russian nationalist-oriented members of the Russian Platform of the [[suCPSU|CPSU]], and was launched on 26 October 1991 by Russian Supreme Soviet deputies of the faction Rossiya. According to Nikolai Pavlov, one of the ROS leaders, the party was established as a "patriotic and democratic" force with the aim of uniting parties of socialist orientation. Pavlov also stated that they had similar positions with more centrist organizations like the [[ruKDPPNS|Kadet Party]] of Mikhail Astafyev, Viktor Aksiuchits' [[ruRKhDD|Christian Democratic Party of Russia]], and the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]]; one of the ROS member organizations in 1992 was the [[ruRPK|Russian Party of Communists]], which was led by Anatoly Kryuchkov. The ROS was part of the United Opposition and later [[ruFNS|National Salvation Front]], belonging to the FNS right-wing faction. Besides socialist tendencies, the ROS had connections with traditional Russian nationalists and monarchists, and promoted pan-Slavist policies, including support for Serbia's expansion.

The party published newspaper Vremya (Time). The ROS took part in the 1995 Russian legislative election within the bloc [[ruVlNa|Power to the People!]], which was led by Baburin and Nikolai Ryzhkov. It won 1.6% of votes, failing to pass the 5% barrier; the ROS got nine seats, all from majoritarian districts. The party co-operated with other formations of nationalist-communist orientation, such as the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of Russian Federation]], whose candidate Gennady Zyuganov (supported by the ROS) was defeated in the 1996 Russian presidential election by incumbent Boris Yeltsin. In 2001, the ROS joined with three other nationalist parties to form the [[ruNarS|Narodnaya Volya/People's Union]]. In 2008, the ROS was reorganized when People's Union dissolved itself.

On 22 December 2017, the ROS nominated Sergey Baburin as its candidate for the 2018 Russian presidential election. On 24 December, Baburin filed registration documents with the Central Election Commission (CEC). The CEC rejected Baburin's bid on 25 December because it identified violations in the information provided regarding 18 of his party's 48 representatives.[8] Baburin resubmitted the documents, and they were approved by the CEC.

Baburin was nominated by his party again in December 2023 during the party's congress. He submitted documents to participate in the election on 26 December, which were registered on 29 December. Baburin collected the required number of signatures, but decided to withdraw on the day before the deadline to submit signatures 30 January 2024 and endorsed Putin for the 2024 election.

In June 2025, the Russian Ministry of Justice filed a lawsuit in the Supreme Court to liquidate ROS, citing the party's failure to participate in elections over the past seven years. On 21 July 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the claim, liquidating the party. The party's leader, Sergey Baburin, expressed his disagreement with its dissolution, calling it a "political action."

parties.nativeName:

Rossiyskaya ekologicheskaya partija «Zelyonyye»
parties.description:
A green centrist political party in Russia, founded on June 19, 2002. It was founded by the non-political organization [[ruKedr|Kedr]], and until 2002 was known as the Ecological Party of Russia "Kedr".

From 2008 to 2012, it merged with the [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] party and operated as the Russian Ecological Movement (RED) "The Greens."

The party endorsed Vladimir Putin in the 2018 Russian presidential election.

On 26 April 2026, the party announced the unification of the Green Party and [[ruZA|Green Alternative]] with the retention of the Green Party's name and imagery. As a symbolic gesture, Green Alternative leader Ruslan Khvostov gave Alexandra Kudzagova a red cat, the symbol of Green Alternative.

parties.name: Russian Party of Freedom and Justice
parties.nativeName:
Российская партия свободы и справедливости
Rossiyskaya partiya svobody i spravedlivosti
parties.description:
Communist Party of Social Justice (KPSS, same abbreviation as [[suCPSU|CPSU]]) was founded on 9 April 2012 with the participation of Andrei Bogdanov, leader of the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]] and the Center for Political Technologies. This was announced on 18 July 2012, at a joint press conference of the "Coordinating Council - Inter-Party Conference" - an association that was also created on the initiative of Andrei Bogdanov.

In the 2013 regional elections in Volgograd, it received 5.04% (9,055 votes), overcoming the 5% threshold and winning one seat in the Volgograd City Duma.

In 2014, Andrei Bogdanov himself became the party's leader, replacing Yuri Morozov. Andrei Brezhnev, the grandson of Leonid Brezhnev, General Secretary of the [[suCPSU|CPSU]] Central Committee, was elected First Secretary of the party's KPSS Central Committee. Brezhnev headed the party lists in the elections, which resulted in the party receiving 2.21% (5,085 votes) in the State Assembly of the Republic of Mari El. In the Republic of Crimea, it received 0.84% ​​(6,199 votes). In the Legislative Assembly of the city of Sevastopol, it received 0.53% (886 votes). 

On 13 December 2015, [[ruGS|Civilian Power]] Party Chairman Oleg Sidorov and KPSS Chairman Andrei Bogdanov announced at a joint meeting of the parties' Federal Political Councils their upcoming merger under the existing name "Communist Party of Social Justice," but using the organizational base of the Civil Power Party, which had been admitted to 2016 federal elections without collecting signatures. However, on 18 December 2015, Oleg Sidorov was removed from office.

KPSS did not participate in the 2016 State Duma elections. The Central Electoral Commission did not include the party in the list of parties exempt from collecting voter signatures for the State Duma elections. The party did not independently collect signatures.

On 12 January 2018, the secretary of the party's Central Committee and Volgograd City Duma deputy Oleg Bulaev submitted documents to the Russian Central Electoral Commission for the 2018 Russian presidential election, but withdrew his candidacy before registration.

On 28 March 2021, at the KPSS congress, former State Duma deputy of the 5th convocation (from the [[ruER|United Russia]] faction) and political strategist Konstantin Rykov was elected as the new chairman of the party's Central Committee. Iit was decided to change the party's name to the "Russian Party of Freedom and Justice" (RPSS).

On 29 March 2021, news sources reported that public figure and journalist Maxim Shevchenko may run for the State Duma from the RPSS. Shevchenko himself confirmed that this issue was being considered. On March 31, the first party conference was held, during which an agreement was reached on Shevchenko's nomination for the 208th (Central) electoral district of Moscow. The politician will also head the party's federal list and become its leader.

On 15 April 2021, Maxim Shevchenko's YouTube channel announced the first candidates from the RPSS party list for the upcoming State Duma elections. They were entrepreneur and economist Dmitry Potapenko and expert on the North Caucasus and Islam, Ruslan Kurbanov.

On 27 April 2021, Moscow City Duma deputy Elena Shuvalova, previously expelled from the [[ruKPRF|KPRF]] for voting against the Moscow budget and organizing a roundtable with Navalny supporters, was presented as the party's candidate. She topped the party's Moscow list. On 8 May, Maxim Kukushkin, a deputy of the Khabarovsk Krai Legislative Duma who had previously been expelled from the [[ruKPRF|KPRF]] for participating in a pro-Navalny rally on 23 January 2021, was presented as the party's candidate.

Like its predecessor KPSS, RPSS party was described as a spoiler for the Communist Party of the Russian Federation in the 2021 State Duma elections, in which it received only 0.77 votes.

On 9 September 2022, Maxim Shevchenko announced on his official Telegram channel that he no longer considers himself the leader of the RPSS and is no longer involved in the party's activities.

In 2022, the party's official website (https://rpss.ru/) was shut down for non-payment.

In December 2023, Andrei Bogdanov ran for the RPSS in the 2024 presidential election, but withdrew from the race in January 2024.

name.text: Russian Party of Freedom and Justice

description.text:
Communist Party of Social Justice (KPSS, same abbreviation as [[suCPSU|CPSU]]) was founded on 9 April 2012 with the participation of Andrei Bogdanov, leader of the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]] and the Center for Political Technologies. This was announced on 18 July 2012, at a joint press conference of the "Coordinating Council - Inter-Party Conference" - an association that was also created on the initiative of Andrei Bogdanov.

In the 2013 regional elections in Volgograd, it received 5.04% (9,055 votes), overcoming the 5% threshold and winning one seat in the Volgograd City Duma.

In 2014, Andrei Bogdanov himself became the party's leader, replacing Yuri Morozov. Andrei Brezhnev, the grandson of Leonid Brezhnev, General Secretary of the [[suCPSU|CPSU]] Central Committee, was elected First Secretary of the party's KPSS Central Committee. Brezhnev headed the party lists in the elections, which resulted in the party receiving 2.21% (5,085 votes) in the State Assembly of the Republic of Mari El. In the Republic of Crimea, it received 0.84% ​​(6,199 votes). In the Legislative Assembly of the city of Sevastopol, it received 0.53% (886 votes). 

On 13 December 2015, [[ruGS|Civilian Power]] Party Chairman Oleg Sidorov and KPSS Chairman Andrei Bogdanov announced at a joint meeting of the parties' Federal Political Councils their upcoming merger under the existing name "Communist Party of Social Justice," but using the organizational base of the Civil Power Party, which had been admitted to 2016 federal elections without collecting signatures. However, on 18 December 2015, Oleg Sidorov was removed from office.

KPSS did not participate in the 2016 State Duma elections. The Central Electoral Commission did not include the party in the list of parties exempt from collecting voter signatures for the State Duma elections. The party did not independently collect signatures.

On 12 January 2018, the secretary of the party's Central Committee and Volgograd City Duma deputy Oleg Bulaev submitted documents to the Russian Central Electoral Commission for the 2018 Russian presidential election, but withdrew his candidacy before registration.

On 28 March 2021, at the KPSS congress, former State Duma deputy of the 5th convocation (from the [[ruER|United Russia]] faction) and political strategist Konstantin Rykov was elected as the new chairman of the party's Central Committee. Iit was decided to change the party's name to the "Russian Party of Freedom and Justice" (RPSS).

On 29 March 2021, news sources reported that public figure and journalist Maxim Shevchenko may run for the State Duma from the RPSS. Shevchenko himself confirmed that this issue was being considered. On March 31, the first party conference was held, during which an agreement was reached on Shevchenko's nomination for the 208th (Central) electoral district of Moscow. The politician will also head the party's federal list and become its leader.

On 15 April 2021, Maxim Shevchenko's YouTube channel announced the first candidates from the RPSS party list for the upcoming State Duma elections. They were entrepreneur and economist Dmitry Potapenko and expert on the North Caucasus and Islam, Ruslan Kurbanov.

On 27 April 2021, Moscow City Duma deputy Elena Shuvalova, previously expelled from the [[ruKPRF|KPRF]] for voting against the Moscow budget and organizing a roundtable with Navalny supporters, was presented as the party's candidate. She topped the party's Moscow list. On 8 May, Maxim Kukushkin, a deputy of the Khabarovsk Krai Legislative Duma who had previously been expelled from the [[ruKPRF|KPRF]] for participating in a pro-Navalny rally on 23 January 2021, was presented as the party's candidate.

Like its predecessor KPSS, RPSS party was described as a spoiler for the Communist Party of the Russian Federation in the 2021 State Duma elections, in which it received only 0.77 votes.

On 9 September 2022, Maxim Shevchenko announced on his official Telegram channel that he no longer considers himself the leader of the RPSS and is no longer involved in the party's activities.

In 2022, the party's official website (https://rpss.ru/) was shut down for non-payment.

In December 2023, Andrei Bogdanov ran for the RPSS in the 2024 presidential election, but withdrew from the race in January 2024.
