parties.name: Russian Party of Pensioners for Social Justice
parties.nativeName:
Российская партия пенсионеров за социальную справедливость
Rossiyskaya partiya pensionerov za sotsialnuyu spravedlivost
parties.description:
Direct successor to the [[ruRPP|Russian Party of Pensioners]] (RPP), which was dissolved in 2006 as a result of a merger with [[ruRodina2006|Rodina]] and the [[ruRPZh|Russian Party of Life]] to form [[ruSR|A Just Russia]].

Following the RPP's dissolution, on 4 September 2007, the public organization "Russian Pensioners" was created on its basis, chaired by former party leader Igor Zotov.

In February 2012, the Pensioners' Party announced its withdrawal from [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] and its support for Vladimir Putin, as well as the holding of a party congress.

On 7 April 2012, a congress of the public organization "Russian Pensioners for Justice" was held, at which a decision was made to establish a political party with a new name, "Russian Party of Pensioners for Justice," while retaining its previous symbols. Igor Zotov, a deputy of the 6th State Duma, who had led the Pensioners' Party since December 2005, was elected party chairman.

On 13 June 2012, the Pensioners' Party was officially registered by the Ministry of Justice.

On 27 November 2015, Igor Zotov resigned as party chairman. On 26 December 2015, at the party congress, Yevgeny Artyukh, a deputy of the Legislative Assembly of the Sverdlovsk Oblast and Vladimir Putin's confidant in the 2012 presidential election, was elected RPPS chairman.

In July 2016, the Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation removed 42 candidates from the party's federal list, citing errors and missing information in the submitted documents. Artyukh later stated that pressure was exerted on the party to remove candidates "not cleared" with the Presidential Administration. On 29 July Yevgeny Artyukh was removed from his leadership position and later withdrew from the Sverdlovsk Oblast elections. Vladimir Burakov became chairman. 

On 11 March 2017, the party changed its name to the "Russian Party of Pensioners for Social Justice," changed its emblem, and abolished the position of chairman.

In 2018 the party announced that they would support incumbent president Vladimir Putin in the 2018 presidential election. Putin ultimately won with approximately 77% of the vote.

In the 2021 State Duma elections, the party received 2.45% of the vote, becoming the largest among those that failed to pass the 5% threshold.

In 2023 the party again announced that they support incumbent president Vladimir Putin in the 2024 presidential election.

Vladimir Burakov died at the age of 70 on December 23, 2024, as a result of a long illness. In May 2025, Eric Prazdnikov was elected as the new RPPSS chairman.

parties.name: Scarlet Swan
parties.relations: Some founders were previously affiliated with the [[ruNL|New People]] and the [[ruLDPR|LDPR]] Youth Organization.
parties.description:
A short-lived grassroots socio-political movement advocating for internet freedom.

It was founded on 14 March 2026, as part of a decentralized grassroots initiative of teenagers and young adults aged 14 to 20 with the goal of organizing rallies against internet blocking and restrictions.

In mid-March 2026, political strategist Dmitry Kisiev announced large-scale protests against internet blocking and restrictions across Russia. Kisiev proposed gathering for the protest on March 29, symbolically invoking Article 29 of the Constitution on freedom of speech and the prohibition of censorship. 

Kisiev's proposal resonated with activists and opposition representatives, who began submitting applications to hold protests in at least 28 cities and 17 regions of Russia. That same day, March 14, neural network-generated calls for participation in protests began appearing en masse on the social network TikTok. These videos typically featured a link to the Telegram chat channel "Scarlet Swan Rally 29.03." The channel also adopted its recognizable symbol: a red swan against the backdrop of the Russian flag. 

The Scarlet Swan announced the organization of rallies for internet freedom and a search for volunteer organizers. By March 18, the recruitment process had closed, with the number of moderators and organizers exceeding 30. At the same time, the organizers began building a decentralized association into a movement, stating their future intention to transform the movement into a youth organization. Kisiev denied any ties to the movement, but stated his willingness to cooperate with it and that, in his opinion, it was not connected to the FSB. The unregistered [[ruRassvet|Rassvet]] party reported attempts by the movement's organizing committee to contact the party and establish cooperation, but the party declined, stating that it considered the movement a provocation.

The movement's organizing committee was de-anonymized on March 18, when police officers searched the home of one of the organizers. Following this, members of the organizing committee began receiving threats. Subsequently, one of the organizers, under threat of criminal prosecution, sold his Telegram account with administrator rights, leading to reports of a hack and the organization's split.

On March 19, the organization published a demand to the authorities, demanding "complete freedom" to obtain and exchange information, as well as the lifting of blocks on Discord, Telegram, and YouTube, a "revision of Roskomnadzor's area of ​​responsibility," and an "end to the excessive promotion of the Max messenger." At the same time, improvisational statements about the intention to use force at the protests began appearing in the movement's chat, forcing the organizers to establish moderation. The movement itself repeatedly emphasized its intention to act strictly in accordance with Russian law. On March 20, the channel was hacked, and later, reports emerged of the organization splitting into two independent entities. According to independent media, the dissident faction had previously been detained by police and may have been coerced into their actions.

On March 19, one of the movement's organizers was detained and later released with a "warning against violating the law." That same day, police also attempted to detain another organizer. On 27 March, police arrested some of the organizers for 15 days on charges of "participating in and disobeying police officers at an unauthorized event against internet blocking on Bolotnaya Square."
parties.ideology: The movement claimed not to be an opposition project and to speak out solely on issues of internet blocking and restrictions. The movement itself had ties to the [[ruLDPR|LDPR]] Youth Organization and the [[ruNL|New People]] party and, according to some opinions from journalists, political scientists, and activists, is a provocation by the security services to initiate criminal cases against its participants or to drain protest sentiment among young people.
parties.leadership:
Decentralized leadership

Prominent members: Stepan Razin, Sofiya Chepik, Evgeny Ladygin, Alexandra Meshcheryakova, Artyom Neverov, Maxim Kheifets, Nikita Ulanov.

According to independent media, the movement consisted of an organizing committee, which at its peak consisted of 31 organizers, as well as channels and chats on Telegram with the same name, which at their peak attracted up to 6,000 members. The organizing committee is primarily made up of young people and teenagers aged 14 to 20; it has also been subject to splits and scandals. Media outlets have discovered that one of the organizers was a member of the pro-government LDPR Youth Organization, while others left the movement amid controversy, declaring their support for Vladimir Putin.

parties.name: The Other Russia of E. V. Limonov
parties.nativeName:
Другая Россия Э. В. Лимонова
Drugaya Rossiya E. V. Limonova
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]] and coalition [[ruDrugros|The Other Russia]].
parties.description:
The party's founding congress took place on 10 July 2010, in Moscow, attended primarily by former activists of the banned [[ruNBP|National Bolshevik Party]] (NBP). The party was named after Eduard Limonov's book "The Other Russia: Outlines of the Future," which he wrote while in prison. The party's name is also associated with the socio-political coalition [[ruDrugros|The Other Russia]], which united a wide range of opposition organizations, from left-wing radicals and National Bolsheviks to liberals. Eduard Limonov was elected chairman of the party's executive committee unopposed.

On 20 December 2010, party leaders Alexander Averin and Eduard Limonov submitted documents to the Ministry of Justice. More than a month later, they were denied registration due to the party's charter not complying with the federal law "On Political Parties." The party considers the registration denial to be purely political.

Since 2010, the party has been repeatedly denied official registration (most recently in 2024). Criminal cases have been brought against party members for their political activities.

Activists from The Other Russia party participated in numerous Russian opposition protests, such as Strategy-31, the Bolotnaya Square protests of 2011-12, and others.

In 2014, The Other Russia supported the reunification of the Republic of Crimea and Sevastopol with the Russian Federation and opponents of the Maidan protests in the conflict in southeastern Ukraine. In particular, it founded the "Interbrigades" movement, whose ranks included approximately 2,000 volunteers from Russia and other countries who participated in military operations in Donbas.

On 26 March 2016, Eduard Limonov handed over leadership of the party to members of the DR Executive Committee (Alexei Volynets, Alexander Averin, and Andrei Dmitriev), while nominally remaining chairman of this body. At the 6th DR Congress on 24 September 2016, a triumvirate (Volynets, Averin, and Dmitriev) was elected, governing the party while Limonov retained political leadership.

In 2016, the party held a series of protests against the installation of a memorial plaque to Marshal of Finland Carl Gustaf Mannerheim in Saint Petersburg. In 2017, the DR launched the "Seize and Divide" campaign under the slogans of revising the results of voucher privatization and loans-for-shares auctions; nationalizing the gas, oil, and other extractive industries; and "returning to the people stolen capital held in Cypriot and other offshore zones."

At the 7th DR Congress on 22 September 2018, party leadership transitioned from the triumvirate to the executive committee, while Eduard Limonov retained his political leadership. Declarations were adopted on foreign policy, proposing the division of part of Ukraine's territory between neighboring states (Russia, Poland, and Hungary), and on domestic policy, proposing to lower the age of citizenship in the Russian Federation to 14.

The leader of the Russian Nazbols, Eduard Limonov died on 17 March 2020 in Moscow. Following the decision of the DR congress held on 26 September 2020, the party dissolved itself, and on the same congress, participants created a new party called "The Other Russia of E. V. Limonov" (DRL).

The party supported Russia's war in Ukraine, but criticized the Russian government for half-measures and concessions during the operation. DRL members participated in raising aid for the Donbas population and military personnel, and also directly participated in the conflict on Russia's side. Authorities conducted searches of Russian Nazbols since 2023. DRL have participated in conferences of the [[ruKRP|Club of Angry Patriots]].
parties.ideology:
The Other Russia program adopted at the founding congress contained demands of both general democratic nature (democratization of the country, debureaucratization of the state, repeal of the Law on Political Parties and the "police procedures" for party registration, restoration of "genuine independence of the judiciary," "genuine adherence to the principles of federalism," abolition of conscription and media censorship, and disbandment of anti-extremism units) and leftist nature (nationalization of the raw materials industry, prioritization of domestic producers, introduction of a progressive tax scale and a luxury tax).

The party program adopted in 2016 saw a shift toward a leftist and pro-imperialist agenda. Russia's strategic interest was declared to be "the return of territories lost in 1991": "Donbass and all of Novorossiya from Kharkov to Odessa, Transnistria, and Northern Kazakhstan must inevitably become part of Russia. In the long term, the unification of friendly peoples formerly part of the USSR." According to DR ideologists, Russia's goal as an "independent civilization, not an appendage of Europe or Asia," is to "form a geopolitical pole capable of resisting American hegemony in the world." In the socio-economic sphere, the party's priorities were "People's Socialism instead of liberal capitalism," "reviewing the results of the privatization of state property carried out in the 1990s and returning what was stolen," "Russia's economic self-sufficiency," which implied renunciation of WTO membership, and others. The DR program declared it a National Bolshevik organization. The document also called for moving the Russian capital to southern Siberia.

parties.name: Workers' Power
parties.description:
The organization was formed in September 2024. Its founders had previously been members of the [[ruOKI|Organization of Communists-Internationalists]] (OKI), a section of the international organization called the [[intRCI|Revolutionary Communist International]], but left the OCI due to a split. The OKI was created in May 2023 through the merger of the [[ruNK|New Reds]] and [[ruMT|Marxist Tendency]].

At Workers' Power meetings, they held film screenings and exhibitions, discussed industry's contribution to climate change, discussed workers' rights, supported political prisoners with leftist views (such as Boris Kagarlitsky), addressed the problems of teachers, and economic inequality. The organization's manifesto, published in March 2025, offered a left-wing analysis of the current situation in capitalist countries, including Russia, and called for the unification of communist forces and the working masses to combat socioeconomic problems and, ultimately, the creation of a communist party to mobilize the masses to destroy capitalism.

In April 2025, Russian law enforcement agencies turned their attention to Workers' Power after an anonymous group of St. Petersburg State University students, the Office for Work with the Administration (URA), claimed responsibility for an action in which unknown individuals hung a doll depicting the goddess Minerva on a monument to Count Uvarov, with the note "Science is dead." The state-run Russian media outlet RIA Novosti, citing a source in the security forces, reported the "discovery" of a cell at St. Petersburg State University consisting of "unemployed students from wealthy families" that was part of an "international network with a command center in the UK." Workers' Power and URA denied any connection between the organizations.

A few weeks after the action, two students were arrested for organizing it and sentenced to a fine of 20,000 rubles and three days in jail, respectively. The URA denied the students' affiliation with their organization, and the students themselves claimed to be unaware of the existence of either the URA or Workers' Power. On 13 May 2025, the Primorsky District Court fined the lead singer of the musical group Silver Machine 20,000 rubles for the satirical song "Za Nashikh." The song's lyrics contained ironic calls to go to war "for the masters, their comfort" and "for Gazprom and Tinkoff" at the call of the "genetic code." The court found the song's content aimed at inciting "hatred or hostility" and "humiliating human dignity based on gender, race, nationality, language, origin, religious affiliation, or social group."

On 15 May 2025, searches were conducted at students' homes at St. Petersburg universities; The published photographs show dozens of printed copies of the Workers' Power manifesto. Six people were detained and one of them was reportedly beaten. A criminal case was opened against Garry Azaryan, a student at St. Petersburg State University from Kazakhstan, for "calls to terrorism." According to investigators, from January to February 2025, Azaryan publicly expressed slogans "justifying terrorist activity, allegedly verbally called for mass murder, and planned to use students to carry out direct action." The case was opened based on an audio recording from an informal meeting, where Azaryan discussed revolution, class hatred, and the "power of the street." Azaryan denied the charges: "Our goal is not to incite hatred; we are not extremists. Our goal is to explain to people that capitalism is to blame." In September 2025, it was reported that Azaryan had been sent for a forensic psychiatric examination at the request of the investigation.

On 22 May 2025, Workers' Power announced its dissolution due to "mounting police pressure" and the risk of mass arrests and persecution. On 11 February 2026, Azaryan was sentenced to two years in prison.

parties.name: Yabloko
parties.nativeName:
Российская объединённая демократическая партия «Яблоко»
Rossiyskaya obyedinyonnaya demokraticheskaya partiya "Yabloko"
parties.description:
A social liberal political party in Russia, founded as a Yavlinsky–Boldyrev–Lukin (YaBL) bloc in October 1993. Yabloko positions itself as "Russia's only democratic party". A number of political scientists and researchers characterize Yabloko as the only legally registered party in the country that stands in actual opposition to the current government. Party representatives and independent observers state that the Yabloko's members face systemic government pressure and repression.

The party consequently participated in the elections of deputies of the State Duma of all eight convocations. Until 2003, Yabloko was represented by a faction in the State Duma and later until 2007 by individual deputies. In March 2002, the party became a full member of the Liberal International, having previously held observer status since November 1998. The founder of the party Grigory Yavlinsky is an honorary vice-president of the Liberal International and winner of its Prize for Freedom. Yabloko was a member of the [[euALDE|Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe]] from 2006 to 2025. As of 2021, the party was represented by factions in 4 regional parliaments of the Russian Federation. In addition, members of the party were deputies of 13 administrative centers of the subjects of the Russian Federation, 183 representatives of the party were municipal deputies in Moscow and 84 in Saint Petersburg.

Yabloko is the sole officially registered party to openly oppose the Russo-Ukrainian war, openly calling "for peace and freedom". The party plans to partake in the 2026 Russian legislative election under their anti-war slogan.

parties.name: Young Russia
parties.relations: Merged into the [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]] (SPS).
parties.description:
A Russian political social movement that existed from 1998 to 2001. Its leader was Boris Nemtsov. The movement was one of the co-founders of the [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]] bloc and party.

On 29 October, Kommersant newspaper published an article stating that Boris Nemtsov had launched a political initiative on his website. Nemtsov reportedly believed that Sergei Kiriyenko, Irina Khakamada, Grigory Yavlinsky, and indeed all "decent people with a head on their shoulders" could join his bloc. However, Kiriyenko had no intention of joining Nemtsov's bloc and intended to run for the Duma elections separately. In a poll conducted by VTsIOM from November 20-25, 1998, Young Russia received 1%.

On November 27, 1998, the Young Russia movement's declaration was published on the website nemtsov.ru. It was also suggested that people join the movement online by filling out a special form. Its charter was approved on 14 December 1998.

The All-Russian political public movement "Young Russia" was registered by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation on December 17, 1998. On 18 December 1998, its leader, Boris Nemtsov, received a registration certificate from Justice Minister Pavel Krasheninnikov. According to Boris Nemtsov, no other political movement in the world has ever been born like Young Russia: "My interlocutors on the Internet forced me to officially register the movement." "Our branches have already been established in 49 regions," Boris Nemtsov stated. "A total of just over 1,000 people have signed up for the movement. But literally a hundred more are joining every day."

At the first congress, held in February 1999, the decision was made to join the [[ruPDco|Right Cause]] coalition. In April 1999, the Young Russia movement announced its participation in the Right Cause bloc's initiative to collect signatures to end the war in the Balkans. At the Right Cause coalition congress on 29 May 1999, Nemtsov was approved as number one on the coalition's list of candidates for the State Duma.

Between 28 and 29 April 1999, it was announced that the official website of the Young Russia movement had been launched at www.rosmol.ru. The movement's first congress was held on 15-16 May 1999, in St. Petersburg.

After the formation of the [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]] (SPS) in August 1999 to replace Right Cause, Nemtsov received second place on the bloc's list (after Sergei Kiriyenko, leader of [[ruNovayaSila|NS]]). On 28 August 1999, the 2nd Congress of the Young Russia was held.

In the 1999 State Duma elections, the SPS bloc received 8.52% of the party list votes (24 seats) and won five deputies in single-mandate constituencies.

On 16 January 2000, a meeting of the Young Russia activists was held in Moscow, at which they resolved: to participate in the creation of a unified political association based on the SPS electoral bloc and the preparation of a unification conference; to preserve the Young Russia in the near future to ensure participation in regional elections at various levels; and to consider it advisable to participate in the new association as a collective member.

On 18 September 2000, a meeting of the movement's Political Council was held in Moscow under the leadership of Boris Nemtsov, Chairman of the Young Russia and leader of the Union of Right Forces faction in the State Duma of the Russian Federation.

On 28 April 2001, the Young Russia movement announced its self-dissolution in order to subsequently join the Union of Right Forces party. This decision was made at the 4th Congress of this socio-political movement, held in Moscow. At the congress, 28 delegates from Young Russia were elected to the SPS Congress, and the draft charter and program of the new right-wing party and the draft code of political responsibility for SPS members were adopted as a basis.

parties.name: Yuri Boldyrev Movement
parties.nativeName:
Движение Юрия Болдырева
Dvizheniye Yuriya Boldyreva
parties.description:
The movement was founded in the summer of 1998 as the "Yuri Boldyrev Bloc" to participate in elections to the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly. It was registered on 23 November 1998, by the Saint Petersburg Department of Justice.

On 3 January 1999, a split was announced within the Yuri Boldyrev Bloc faction in the Legislative Assembly. Three deputies from the Yuri Boldyrev Bloc who left the faction, together with a member of the bloc who never joined Boldyrev's faction, and a member of the "Petersburg Districts" faction who joined them, formed a faction called "Industrial." Speaking at a press conference in the Mariinsky Palace, members of the new faction accused the leadership of the Yuri Boldyrev Bloc of "systematically violating" its own statutory and programmatic principles, in particular the provision regarding the right of movement members to convene an extraordinary meetings.

Yuri Boldyrev ran in the 2000 St. Petersburg gubernatorial elections as part of the bloc. He placed third with 3.79% of the vote.

On 6 June 1999, the founding congress of the Yuri Boldyrev Movement was held in Perm. The congress approved the charter and elected a seven-member Political Council (Yuri Boldyrev, Sergei Levitan, Dmitry Varvarin, Alexander Yelshin, Anatoly Krivenchenko, Boris Lapshov, and Vladimir Yudin). Some Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly deputies from the Yuri Boldyrev Bloc faction did not participate in the Yuri Boldyrev Movement.

Since the Yuri Boldyrev Movement, registered too late, did not have the right to independently participate in the State Duma elections or be the official founder of the bloc, Boldyrev had to negotiate with organizations that did. The [[ruMK|Inter-Ethnic Congress]] (MK) movement of Abdallah Mikitayev was used as a front organization. MK had participated in the 1995 election as the [[ruMnS|Inter-Ethnic Union]] and finished last

On 29 September 1999, Dmitry Rogozin's [[ruKRO|Congress of Russian Communities]] (KRO), Yuri Boldyrev Movement, and the [[ruMK|Inter-Ethnic Congress]] created the "Congress of Russian Communities and Yuri Boldyrev Movement" electoral bloc, with KRO and MS becoming its official founders. The top three candidates on the federal list included Yuri Boldyrev, Dmitry Rogozin, and Viktor Glukhikh, Chairman of the International Congress of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs. Mikitayev received ninth place in the central part of the federal list. Alexander Krasnov's [[ruPNTI|Party of Scientific and Technical Intelligentsia]] (PNTI), which does not have the status of a "political public association," also informally joined the bloc.

On 11 October 1999, the Central Election Commission registered the bloc and certified both candidate lists.

In the election, the bloc received 0.61% of the vote and elected only one single-mandate deputy - KRO leader Dmitry Rogozin.

After the elections, Yuri Boldyrev's Movement declined and remained inactive since late 2000 and early 2001.

parties.name: Democratic Convergence Party – Reflection Group
parties.nativeName: Partido de Convergência Democrática – Grupo de Reflexão
parties.description:
A political party in São Tomé and Príncipe. It was founded on 4 November 1990 by [[stMLSTPPSD|Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe]] (MLSTP) dissidents, independents, and young professionals. Leonel Mário d'Alva is the party leader.

The one-party period of São Tomé and Príncipe lasted from the country's independence in 1975 to 1991, when the dominant party, Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe – Social Democratic Party, lost in the first multiparty elections to the PCD-GR. The party won the 1991 parliamentary election and was the ruling party from 1991 to 1994. Since 1994 its power has declined, and it has maintained coalitions with other parties, first the MLSTP and then the Forces for Change Coalition of President Fradique de Menezes. It was led for several years by Alda Bandeira.

At the legislative elections, March 3, 2002, the party won together with the Force for Change Democratic Movement-Liberal Party (MDFM-PL) 39.4% of the popular vote and 23 out of 55 seats. The same alliance won at the legislative election, held on 26 March 2006, 36.79% and 23 out of 55 seats. The party supported incumbent Fradique de Menezes in the 30 July 2006 presidential election. He was re-elected with 60.58% of the vote.

In the 2011 São Toméan presidential election, Delfim Neves represented both the PCD and the Force for Change Democratic Movement – Liberal Party (MDFM-PL), the part of the previous president, Fradique de Menezes. He won 13.9% of the vote.

In 2022 election, its candidates joined the [[stBasta|Basta Movement]].

parties.name: Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe – Social Democratic Party
parties.nativeName: Movimento de Libertação de São Tomé e Príncipe – Partido Social Democrata
parties.description:
The Committee for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, was founded in 1960 as a nationalist group opposed to Portuguese colonial rule. In 1961 it joined the CONCP with other communist and socialist groups fighting against the Portuguese Empire in Africa. The CLSTP was set up by exiles who eventually established their base in nearby Gabon. Manuel Pinto da Costa, who would eventually become President of an independent São Tomé and Príncipe, was the leader of the party. In 1972, the CLSTP became the MLSTP.

After the April 1974 Carnation Revolution in Portugal, the new government agreed to hand over power to the MLSTP. Later that year, the MLSTP was recognized as the sole legitimate representative of the Santomean people.

Following a brief period of transitional government, elections were held for a constituent assembly and the MLSTP won all 16 of its seats.

Independence was achieved on 12 July 1975, with Manuel Pinto da Costa as president and Miguel Trovoada as prime minister. The constitution promulgated on 12 December 1975, effectively vested absolute power in the President and the MLSTP became the nation's sole legal political party.

During the late 1970s and 1980s, the party's socialist orientation and in turn the nation's orientation led to strong ties with Cuba, East Germany and the Soviet Union.

In late 1989, a progressive faction within the party embarked on a transition to full multi-party system, after a debate at the national party conference.

A democratic constitution introduced by the MLSTP Central Committee was approved overwhelmingly in an August 1990 referendum.

At the MLSTP Party Congress in October 1990, Carlos Graça was appointed as the new Secretary-General, in succession to Manuel Pinto da Costa. In addition, the party's name was amended to the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe – Social Democratic Party (MLSTP/PSD).

In an extraordinary Congress of the MLSTP/PSD held in May 1998, Manuel Pinto da Costa was elected unopposed as President of the party, a post that he held until 2005.

At the party's Fourth Congress, Guilherme Posser da Costa, a former prime minister, was elected as president of the MLSTP/PSD on 27 February 2005, succeeding Pinto da Costa. There were 708 votes in favor of Posser da Costa, who was the only candidate, and three votes against him. As of June 2008, the President of the MLSTP/PSD is Joaquim Rafael Branco.

In June 2008, after Prime Minister Patrice Trovoada of the [[stADI|Independent Democratic Action]] (ADI) party was defeated in a vote of no confidence, President Fradique de Menezes asked the MLSTP/PSD to form a government, and it chose Branco to become the next prime minister. The ADI denounced Menezes' designation of the MLSTP/PSD to form a government as unconstitutional, arguing that it was too late in the parliamentary term to do so, and it took the matter to the Supreme Tribunal of Justice.

The current president of the MLSTP/PSD, Américo Barros, was elected on 7 September 2024.

Today the MLSTP/PSD has friendly relations with political parties in other Lusophone countries, including the [[ptPS|Socialist Party]] (PS) in Portugal and the [[aoMPLA|People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola]] (MPLA).

name.text: Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe – Social Democratic Party

nativeName.text: Movimento de Libertação de São Tomé e Príncipe – Partido Social Democrata

description.text:
The Committee for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, was founded in 1960 as a nationalist group opposed to Portuguese colonial rule. In 1961 it joined the CONCP with other communist and socialist groups fighting against the Portuguese Empire in Africa. The CLSTP was set up by exiles who eventually established their base in nearby Gabon. Manuel Pinto da Costa, who would eventually become President of an independent São Tomé and Príncipe, was the leader of the party. In 1972, the CLSTP became the MLSTP.

After the April 1974 Carnation Revolution in Portugal, the new government agreed to hand over power to the MLSTP. Later that year, the MLSTP was recognized as the sole legitimate representative of the Santomean people.

Following a brief period of transitional government, elections were held for a constituent assembly and the MLSTP won all 16 of its seats.

Independence was achieved on 12 July 1975, with Manuel Pinto da Costa as president and Miguel Trovoada as prime minister. The constitution promulgated on 12 December 1975, effectively vested absolute power in the President and the MLSTP became the nation's sole legal political party.

During the late 1970s and 1980s, the party's socialist orientation and in turn the nation's orientation led to strong ties with Cuba, East Germany and the Soviet Union.

In late 1989, a progressive faction within the party embarked on a transition to full multi-party system, after a debate at the national party conference.

A democratic constitution introduced by the MLSTP Central Committee was approved overwhelmingly in an August 1990 referendum.

At the MLSTP Party Congress in October 1990, Carlos Graça was appointed as the new Secretary-General, in succession to Manuel Pinto da Costa. In addition, the party's name was amended to the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe – Social Democratic Party (MLSTP/PSD).

In an extraordinary Congress of the MLSTP/PSD held in May 1998, Manuel Pinto da Costa was elected unopposed as President of the party, a post that he held until 2005.

At the party's Fourth Congress, Guilherme Posser da Costa, a former prime minister, was elected as president of the MLSTP/PSD on 27 February 2005, succeeding Pinto da Costa. There were 708 votes in favor of Posser da Costa, who was the only candidate, and three votes against him. As of June 2008, the President of the MLSTP/PSD is Joaquim Rafael Branco.

In June 2008, after Prime Minister Patrice Trovoada of the [[stADI|Independent Democratic Action]] (ADI) party was defeated in a vote of no confidence, President Fradique de Menezes asked the MLSTP/PSD to form a government, and it chose Branco to become the next prime minister. The ADI denounced Menezes' designation of the MLSTP/PSD to form a government as unconstitutional, arguing that it was too late in the parliamentary term to do so, and it took the matter to the Supreme Tribunal of Justice.

The current president of the MLSTP/PSD, Américo Barros, was elected on 7 September 2024.

Today the MLSTP/PSD has friendly relations with political parties in other Lusophone countries, including the [[ptPS|Socialist Party]] (PS) in Portugal and the [[aoMPLA|People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola]] (MPLA).

parties.nativeName: Movimento de Cidadãos Independentes de São Tomé e Príncipe – Partido Socialista
parties.description:
A political party on São Tomé and Príncipe founded in 2018 by António and Domingos Monteiro, who represented the [[stMLSTPPSD|Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe]] (MLSTP/PSD) in the National Assembly until May 2018. Its main base is the southernmost municipality on São Tomé, Caué. 

Until 2020 it was known as simply the Movement of Independent Citizens of São Tomé (MCISTP).

At the 2018 parliamentary elections it got 1,659 votes and won two seats in the Caué constituency. The party only received 608 votes outside of Caué.

In 2022, allied with the new [[stPUN|National Unity Party]] (PUN), the MCI/PS confirmed its presence by becoming the third largest force in the National Assembly. It campaigned among disadvantaged populations, Serviça immigrants, Angolans, and the peasant class descended from the roças (plantations).[6] It won four seats: three in Caué (with a 42% majority) and one in Lembá, while the PUN won one in Príncipe, allowing the coalition to form a parliamentary group. In the municipal elections held simultaneously, the MCI-PUN coalition won all nine seats in the Caué district, as well as one in Cantagalo.

parties.name: National Unity Party
parties.description:
A political party in Principe, the second largest island of São Tomé and Príncipe, founded in 2021.

Óscar Baía announced the founding of the National Unity Party in June 2021. He stated, among other things, his desire to expand the multi-party system.

He formed a coalition for the 2022 legislative elections with the [[ststMCIPS|Movement of Independent Citizens of São Tomé and Príncipe – Socialist Party]] (MCI/PS), a splinter group of the [[stMLSTPPSD|MLSTP/PSD]]. The coalition campaigned among disadvantaged populations, Servicean immigrants, Angolans, and the peasant class descended from the roças. The PUN managed to win one of the five parliamentary seats in the province of Príncipe, with 20% of the votes cast.[ João Batista sat with the MCI/PS-PUN group.

Since 2022, it has representation in the National Assembly as part of a joint group with the [[ststMCIPS|Movement of Independent Citizens of São Tomé and Príncipe – Socialist Party]] (MCI/PS).

parties.description:
A parliamentary group in the National Assembly of Serbia and electoral coalition, led by the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS).

SNS gained its parliamentary status following the formation of the "Forward, Serbia" parliamentary group in 2008, and was later renamed "Serbian Progressive Party", following the registration of the party. It had cooperated with the [[rsDSS|Democratic Party of Serbia]] (DSS) and [[rsNS1998|New Serbia]] (NS) from its formation until 2010, when SNS formed a coalition with NS, and two other parties, the [[rsPS|Movement of Socialists]] (PS) and [[rsPSS|Strength of Serbia Movement]] (PSS). The coalition was formalised for the 2012 parliamentary election under the "Let's Get Serbia Moving" banner, in which it won 73 seats, and formed a government with the [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] (SPS) and [[rsURS|United Regions of Serbia]] (URS).

Tomislav Nikolić, then president of Serbia, called snap parliamentary elections to be held in March 2014. SNS formed the "Future We Believe In" list, in which the [[rsSPO|Serbian Renewal Movement]] (SPO) and [[rsDHSS|Christian Democratic Party of Serbia]] (DHSS) also participated, and the list won 158 seats in total. After the election, Aleksandar Vučić, president of SNS, was appointed prime minister, succeeding Ivica Dačić. Vučić called snap elections in early 2016, and after which, the [[rsPUPS|Party of United Pensioners of Serbia]] (PUPS) and [[rsSNP|Serbian People's Party]] (SNP) joined. It participated under the "Serbia is Winning" banner, which won 131 seats in the National Assembly. The "For Our Children" coalition, participated in the 2020 parliamentary election, in which it won a supermajority of seats, and the convocation lasted until February 2022. The SNS-led coalition participated in the 2022 general election under the "Together We Can Do Everything" banner.

The coalition has also ruled Belgrade since 2014, and Vojvodina since 2016, while the presidency is currently held by Aleksandar Vučić.

parties.relations: Split from the [[rsSSP|Party of Freedom and Justice]] (SSP)
parties.description:
Dejan Bulatović left [[rsSSP|SSP]] in December 2022, shortly after which he claimed that Marinika Tepić allegedly lobbied for the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS). However, Bulatović then met with SNS ministers such as Aleksandar Martinović and Irena Vujović. He agreed to cooperate with Vujović and her ministry of environmental protection. On 28 January 2023, he formed the Alliance of Social Democrats political association. Bulatović then became supportive of Aleksandar Vučić and the incumbent government and a critic of the opposition. He was a candidate of the SNS-led [[rsSNSDS|Serbia Must Not Stop]] coalition in the 2023 Serbian parliamentary election. He was successfully re-elected.

The SSD planned to establish itself as a political party in May 2023, however, this did not happen.

In November 2024, SSP accused Bulatović of coordinating SSP MP's who are leaving its parliamentary group.

parties.description:
A liberal political party in Serbia. It was founded in 2019 by former members of the [[rsPSG|Movement of Free Citizens]] (PSG). It has positioned itself as a party that opposes the rule of Aleksandar Vučić, although it has also criticised other opposition parties.

When Saša Janković resigned as president of Movement of Free Citizens, candidates for his successor were actor Sergej Trifunović and Aleksandar Olenik. The interim president was Rade Veljanovski. When Trifunović won with 60% of the vote, Veljanovski, Olenik, and several other members left the movement. On 2 March 2019, they formed Civic Democratic Forum.

In April 2019, they signed an cooperation agreement with [[rsSMS2018|Party of Modern Serbia]]. Together they issued a statement in which they present a solution for Kosovo. Their stance is that Serbia should exchange territories with Kosovo and recognise its independence.

In February 2020, the party formed a "European bloc" with the Party of Modern Serbia and [[rsLSV|League of Social Democrats of Vojvodina]]. It was also consisted of the newly-formed [[rsS21|Serbia 21]], and they announced their participation in the 2020 Serbian parliamentary election under the [[rsUDS|United Democratic Serbia]] banner. It failed to pass the electoral threshold after winning less than 1% of the vote.

It kept close ties to the [[rsSzS|Together for Serbia]] political party and its leader Nebojša Zelenović until early 2021. It did not participate in the 2022 general election, and instead, it stated its support for the [[rsM|We Must]] coalition.

A political party in Serbia, representing the Croat ethnic minority.

Over time, some party members were unsatisfied with party's policy, so they separated and formed new Croat parties: [[rsHNS|Croatian National Alliance]] (HNS), [[rsHBSS|Croatian Bunjevac-Šokac Party]] (HBŠS), [[rsDZH|Democratic Union of Croats]] (DZH).

It has occasionally condemned attacks by Serbian nationalists, and it has issued protests over ethnic assimilation. It is also supportive of further autonomism.

parties.name: Democratic Party
parties.relations: Claims itself as successor of the historical Yugoslav [[yuDS|Democratic Party]] (DS) (1919–1946/48).
parties.description:
A social democratic political party in Serbia. The party is colloquially known as the žuti (yellows) because of one of its main colours.

DS was founded in 1990 by a group of intellectuals who sought to revive the [[yuDS|Democratic Party]], which was active in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Dragoljub Mićunović was the first president of DS until 1994 and under his leadership DS gained representation in the National Assembly of Serbia and took part in anti-government protests against Slobodan Milošević. After Zoran Đinđić's election as president of DS in 1994, DS was reorganised. Đinđić led the party into the [[rsZajedno|Together]] coalition, and DS took part in the 1996–1997 protests that occurred after the Electoral Commission invalidated local election results in cities in which the Together coalition had won. DS later led the [[rsSzP|Alliance for Change]], which became part of the [[rsDOS|Democratic Opposition of Serbia]] (DOS) in January 2000. DOS won the 2000 Yugoslav general election, but Milošević, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and president of the [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] (SPS), declined to accept the results of the presidential election, in which the DOS candidate was shown to be placed first, culminating in his overthrow.

DS assumed power in Serbia after winning parliamentary elections in December 2000 and Đinđić then became prime minister. Đinđić was assassinated in March 2003 and succeeded by Boris Tadić as president of DS. Tadić also became president of Serbia while DS was in opposition from 2004 to 2007, when it became part of a coalition government led by [[rsDSS|DSS]]. Tadić led DS to victory in 2008 when a coalition government with SPS was formalised. DS was defeated by the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] in 2012 and went into opposition. Dragan Đilas became the president of DS in December 2012; he was ousted as mayor of Belgrade in 2013 but survived an internal motion of no confidence in January 2014. He was succeeded by Bojan Pajtić in May 2014. Dragan Šutanovac became the president of DS after Pajtić's resignation in 2016. Šutanovac was then succeeded by Zoran Lutovac in 2018. Lutovac led DS into several opposition coalitions and boycotted the 2020 parliamentary election, causing a schism in the party. He successfully led DS back into the National Assembly in the 2022 election. Milivojević succeeded him as leader in late 2024.

DS was a catch-all party in its early years, occupying the centrist and centre-right positions. It supported the establishment of a market economy, denationalisation, and union rights. DS shifted to a centrist and socially liberal profile under Tadić and became the leading party of the pro-European bloc of Serbian politics. It shifted towards social democracy in 2013, and is now positioned on the centre-left on the political spectrum. Its supporters tend to be female, high school or university educated, tolerant towards diversity, socially progressive, and opposed to authoritarianism and nationalism. DS is an associate member of the [[euPES|Party of European Socialists]] and a member of the [[intPA|Progressive Alliance]] and [[intSI|Socialist International]].

parties.name: Enough is Enough
parties.nativeName:
Доста је било
Dosta je bilo
parties.description:
A right-wing populist political party in Serbia. Until 2022 - political association.

It was established on 27 January 2014 around the former minister of economy Saša Radulović and his associates from the ministry. Initially, the party had strong liberal, reformist, and progressive views, and in the 2016 parliamentary election they entered the parliament with 16 seats in total. Between early 2017 and 2018, its pro-European and liberal factions split off due to the internal conflict in the party. Since then, the party has shifted to the far-right and it began advocating souverainist and eurosceptic policies alongside numerous right-wing populist stances such as opposition to immigration. Its leader, Saša Radulović also promoted misinformation and several conspiracy theories during the COVID-19 pandemic.

description.text:
A right-wing populist political party in Serbia. Until 2022 - political association.

It was established on 27 January 2014 around the former minister of economy Saša Radulović and his associates from the ministry. Initially, the party had strong liberal, reformist, and progressive views, and in the 2016 parliamentary election they entered the parliament with 16 seats in total. Between early 2017 and 2018, its pro-European and liberal factions split off due to the internal conflict in the party. Since then, the party has shifted to the far-right and it began advocating souverainist and eurosceptic policies alongside numerous right-wing populist stances such as opposition to immigration. Its leader, Saša Radulović also promoted misinformation and several conspiracy theories during the COVID-19 pandemic.

parties.relations: Preceded by the [[rsNDB|Don't Let Belgrade Drown]] (NDB)
parties.description:
A political party in Serbia that advocates for green politics. It is the successor of [[rsNDB|Don't Let Belgrade Drown]] association and four local citizens' groups.

Formed in July 2023, and registered as a political party a month later, ZLF was one of the organisers of the 2023 Serbian protests. It later became part of the [[rsSPN|Serbia Against Violence]] coalition, which contested the parliamentary, Vojvodina provincial, and Belgrade City Assembly elections in December 2023. They won 10 seats in the National Assembly of Serbia and 14 seats in the City Assembly of Belgrade. Regarding the latter, their number of seats was reduced to five after the 2024 Belgrade City Assembly election.

ZLF is a left-wing and progressive party that declares itself to be supportive of solidarity, social justice, and environmental protection. It supports extending LGBTQ rights, proposes anti-gambling policies, and opposes the Rio Tinto project near Loznica and the privatisation of public transport in Belgrade. On foreign policy, they support the accession of Serbia to the European Union, while condemning the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the Gaza genocide. They have also supported the student-led anti-corruption protests that began in 2024. ZLF is a member of the [[intPI|Progressive International]] and the [[euEGP|European Greens]]; while on national level, it cooperates with the [[rsPSG|Movement of Free Citizens]].

parties.name: Greens of Serbia
parties.description:
A green political party in Serbia. Established on 14 September 2007, the Greens of Serbia advocates for environmental and ecological wisdom, social justice and solidarity, direct democracy, green economics, sustainability, respect for diversity and human rights, and prevention of all forms of violence. Zeleni had observer status in the [[intGG|Global Greens]] and was an applicant for the [[euEGP|European Green Party]].

In early 2014 the Zeleni had signed political cooperation with the [[rsNDS|New Democratic Party]], a political fraction of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] led by its former leader and the nation's president Boris Tadić. Originally agreeing to form a political cooperation and jointly go at the forthcoming 2014 elections, by mid-February 2014 the NDS had collectively joined the Greens, who chose a new Statute, programme and Tadić as their party leader, officially preregistering under the name New Democratic Party–Greens. On 14 June 2014, the New Democratic Party seceded and became independent political party, so the name of the party was changed again to "Greens of Serbia". Since 2016, it has allied itself with the [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] and [[rsJS|United Serbia]].

parties.name: Healthy Serbia
parties.relations: Split from the [[rsSNP|Serbian People's Party]] (SNP)
parties.description:
A right-wing political party in Serbia. It was founded in 2017 by Milan Stamatović, the long-time mayor of Čajetina.

After leaving the [[rsDSS|Democratic Party of Serbia]] and further disagreements with the President of the [[rsSNP|Serbian People's Party]] Nenad Popović over Popović's support for the ruling party's leader Aleksandar Vučić's candidacy at the 2017 Serbian Presidential election, Milan Stamatović decided to run for President himself. Together with his supporters, he founded the "For a Healthy Serbia" Citizens' Group, which nominated him. Stamatović received 1.15% of the overall votes in Serbia, but the fact that he won 61.23% of votes in his hometown of Čajetina encouraged him to found his own political party.

Healthy Serbia was officially founded on 5 June 2017 in the western Serbian village of Ljubiš, where Stamatović received 99% of the votes. Among the founders were famous Serbian poet Ljubivoje Ršumović and Serbian writer Milan Paroški. At that occasion, Stamatović said that "Healthy Serbia would be an authentic regional party, but also a party devoted to making entire Serbia healthier by working from the interior, and not from Belgrade."

On 21 August 2017, Healthy Serbia and Dveri signed an agreement on joint political action. Stamatović said that neither of these two political parties have ever flirted with the ruling [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS), which he considers to be a huge advantage. He also mentioned that these two political organisations do not wish to topple the Government on the streets, but through elections.

In the 2020 parliamentary elections, Healthy Serbia participated in a coalition with [[rsBS2017|Better Serbia]].

In April 2023, anti-vax and far-right [[rsZZS2018|I live for Serbia]] merged into ZS. Stamatović was present at the 15th anniversary since the founding assembly of the Serbian Progressive Party in October 2023. Healthy Serbia participated in the 2023 parliamentary election as part of the SNS-led [[rsSNSDS|Serbia Must Not Stop]] coalition and won 3 seats in the National Assembly.
parties.ideology: ZS is opposed to sanctioning Russia due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine. It advocates for the establishment of closer relations with Russia and China, claiming that "they are strongest guarantors of the territorial integrity of Serbia".

A political party in Serbia, representing the Bosniak ethnic minority concentrated in the Sandžak region of Serbia.

parties.name: Liberal Democratic Party
parties.relations: Split from the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] (DS)
parties.description:
A liberal political party in Serbia. It is led by Čedomir Jovanović.

The Liberal Democratic Party was founded on 5 November 2005 by former members of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]], led by Čedomir Jovanović, who were expelled in a party purge in 2004. Jovanović had become critical of the new direction of the Democratic Party and its newly elected president, Boris Tadić. The LDP gained its first seat in parliament after Đorđe Đukić defected from the Democratic Party. Members of the foundation board were: Nenad Prokić, Nikola Samardžić, Branislav Lečić and Đorđe Đukić. in 2007 the [[rsGSS|Civic Alliance of Serbia]] merged into the LDP. The LDP had a long-standing relationship with the [[rsSDU|Social Democratic Union]] and [[rsLSV|League of Social Democrats of Vojvodina]].

LDP's activity decreased following the 2018 Belgrade City Assembly election, mainly due to the size of the party's debt. As of November 2023, LDP is in debt of din. 201,323,626, approximately around 2 million euros.
parties.ideology:
LDP is a liberal party, and it is supportive of secularism and multiculturalism. It has been also described as progressive and social liberal. The LDP is one of the few political parties in Serbia to actively support Serbia's membership into NATO and the independence of Kosovo. The LDP is also highly supportive of LGBT rights in Serbia. Regarding the economy, it is classical-liberal, market-orientated, and supports privatisation, although it is also in favour of social welfare. Additionally, it economic beliefs been described as neoliberal, libertarian, and conservative-liberal.

relations.text: Split from the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] (DS)

description.text:
A liberal political party in Serbia. It is led by Čedomir Jovanović.

The Liberal Democratic Party was founded on 5 November 2005 by former members of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]], led by Čedomir Jovanović, who were expelled in a party purge in 2004. Jovanović had become critical of the new direction of the Democratic Party and its newly elected president, Boris Tadić. The LDP gained its first seat in parliament after Đorđe Đukić defected from the Democratic Party. Members of the foundation board were: Nenad Prokić, Nikola Samardžić, Branislav Lečić and Đorđe Đukić. in 2007 the [[rsGSS|Civic Alliance of Serbia]] merged into the LDP. The LDP had a long-standing relationship with the [[rsSDU|Social Democratic Union]] and [[rsLSV|League of Social Democrats of Vojvodina]].

LDP's activity decreased following the 2018 Belgrade City Assembly election, mainly due to the size of the party's debt. As of November 2023, LDP is in debt of din. 201,323,626, approximately around 2 million euros.

ideology.text:
LDP is a liberal party, and it is supportive of secularism and multiculturalism. It has been also described as progressive and social liberal. The LDP is one of the few political parties in Serbia to actively support Serbia's membership into NATO and the independence of Kosovo. The LDP is also highly supportive of LGBT rights in Serbia. Regarding the economy, it is classical-liberal, market-orientated, and supports privatisation, although it is also in favour of social welfare. Additionally, it economic beliefs been described as neoliberal, libertarian, and conservative-liberal.

Its political positions have been described as centrist, although its social policies are positioned on the left-wing, while it is economically oriented towards the right.

In the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, LDP was associated with the [[euALDE|Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe]].

parties.relations: Split from the [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] (SPS)
parties.description:
A left-wing nationalist political party in Serbia. It was founded in 2008 by Aleksandar Vulin, who served as the party's president until 2022 when he was succeeded by Bojan Torbica.

It was founded on 8 August 2008 by Aleksandar Vulin, a former high-ranking member of [[rsJUL|Yugoslav Left]] who left it in 1998 after perceiving the party to have "betrayed its programme and became a political mask for the wealthy sitting in the party". It is a part of the governing coalition with the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS). It was formed by former members of the [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] because they disagreed with the pro-European policy of the party; however, it was a member of the pro-European SNS-led coalitions in the 2012 (as part of Let's Get Serbia Moving alliance) and in the 2014 Serbian parliamentary elections. In December 2022, Vulin resigned as the leader of PS after being appointed as the director of the Security Intelligence Agency.
parties.ideology:
It is a self-described radical left or leftist political party. Observers have described it as a centre-left, social-democratic, and left-wing nationalist party. Its foreign policy views are Eurosceptic and anti-Western. PS is supportive of further cooperation with China and Russia.

It was created as a party vehicle for Vulin, who has been described as a nationalist, and has expressed irredentist views. In 2022, PS proclaimed the "Serbian world" idea as its primary political idea and goal. It has been also described as a satellite party of the ruling [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]].

In an opinion article, Miloš Baković Jadžić, now-leader of the Political Platform Solidarity and member of the party [[rsZ|Together]], criticised PS by describing it as a conservative and neoliberal party "with nothing in common with progressive left-wing politics but its name, symbolism, occasional rhetoric and a somewhat radical programme," having engaged in active anti-worker and anti-progressive politics. Sociologist Jovo Bakić has also disputed the leftism of PS due to "their support for the nationalistic and neoliberal policies". Political theorist Srećko Horvat noted PS' participation in the governing coalition's "harsh neoliberal measures, including pension cuts, public sector wage cuts, deregulation and labour market flexibilization" and minister Vulin's direct responsibility for "one of the worst new labour laws" that had been passed in Serbia in 2014. He further discredited the party as having nothing to do with socialism or left-wing politics.

In 2015, Vulin said that he was opposed to same-sex marriage and that, as minister for social policy, he would never sign a law making it possible.

parties.relations: Split from the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] (DS)
parties.description:
A national-conservative political party in Serbia. Miloš Jovanović serves as the current president of NDSS.

DSS was formed as a conservative split from the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] (DS) and has played a key role in the opposition during the 1990s. It was a part of the [[rsZajedno|Together]] coalition and was later a founding member of the [[rsDOS|Democratic Opposition of Serbia]] (DOS). Its first leader, Vojislav Koštunica, was elected president of Yugoslavia in 2000, a role which he served until 2003. DSS left the DOS government in 2001 and served in the opposition until the 2003 parliamentary election, after which it managed to form a government with other right-wing parties. Koštunica was appointed prime minister, and after 2008, it went to the opposition again after being unable to form a government. It saw its decline in the 2010s and failed to pass the threshold in the 2014 parliamentary election, leading to Koštunica resigning from the position as party leader. He was replaced by Sanda Rašković Ivić, and in 2016, DSS managed to enter the National Assembly again, this time in a coalition with [[rsDveri|Dveri]]. Rašković Ivić was ousted after the parliamentary election and was replaced by Miloš Jovanović as president of the party.

A former member of the [[euEPP|European People's Party]], it maintained a centre-right and moderate conservative image until the early 2010s, when the party shifted to a more right-wing and eurosceptic position. It leads the [[rsNADA|National Democratic Alternative]] (NADA) coalition, which took part in the 2022 and 2023 general elections.

parties.description:
A liberal political party in Serbia. It was founded in 2013 as the New Party by Zoran Živković, the former Prime Minister of Serbia and former member of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]]. Following the merger in 2022, Vladimir Kovačević became the party president.

Established in early 2013, the party advocates close ties to the western powers and European integration. The party contested the 2014 parliamentary election as part of a wider coalition of moderate parties led by the Democratic Party. It formed a coalition with the [[rsSDS2014|Social Democratic Party]] led by former President of Serbia Boris Tadić for the 2022 general election. In late April 2022, Movsesijan stepped down as party leader. A month later, the party left the [[euLIBSEEN|Liberal South East European Network]].

In July 2022, New Party merged with the "Experts Should Have a Say" movement and the party was renamed to New Party–Experts Should Have A Say. Vladimir Kovačević, a former high-ranking member of the [[rsNarodna|People's Party]] was elected president of the party. In November 2024, Slavica Radovanović, an MP from the [[rsNPS|People's Movement of Serbia]] (NPS), defected from NPS and was appointed deputy president of Nova-D2SP, thus making Nova-D2SP a parliamentary party. The party joined the parliamentary group led by Željko Veselinović and his [[rsUSSSloga|United Trade Unions of Serbia "Sloga"]].

Established in early 2013, the party advocates close ties to the western powers and European integration. The party contested the 2014 parliamentary election as part of a wider coalition of moderate parties led by the Democratic Party. It formed a coalition with the [[rsSDS2014|Social Democratic Party]] led by former President of Serbia Boris Tadić for the 2022 general election. In late April 2022, Movsesijan stepped down as party leader. A month later, the party left the [[euLIBSEEN|Liberal South East European Network]].

In July 2022, New Party merged with the "Experts Should Have a Say" movement and the party was renamed to New Party–Experts Should Have A Say. Vladimir Kovačević, a former high-ranking member of the [[rsNarodna|People's Party]] was elected president of the party. In November 2024, Slavica Radovanović, an MP from the [[rsNPS|People's Movement of Serbia]] (NPS), defected from NPS and was appointed deputy president of Nova-D2SP, thus making Nova-D2SP a parliamentary party. The party joined the parliamentary group led by Željko Veselinović and his [[rsUSSSloga|United Trade Unions of Serbia "Sloga"]].

A political party in Serbia, representing the Albanian ethnic minority.

The Party for Democratic Action (PVD) was established on the 19th of August 1990 in the Preševo Valley, its founders include figures like Riza Halimi, Selajdin Abdiu, Behlul Nasufi, Ramadan Ahmeti and Rexhep Hasani.

At the latest legislative election in 2016, the party received one seat in parliament, a drop from its peak of two seats in 2014 election. It raised to 3 seats in 2020, following a campaign by Albania's foreign service to increase the political participation of Albanian ethnic minority from the Presevo Valley in Serbia's political elections.

parties.description:
A social democratic political party in Serbia. It is led by Dragan Đilas, the former mayor of Belgrade.

Founded in 2019 as the merger of the [[rsZEPZeleni|Green Ecological Party – The Greens]] and [[rsLS2015|Serbian Left]], SSP was a member of the [[rsSZS|Alliance for Serbia]] (SZS), a coalition of opposition political parties that was initiated by Đilas in 2018. Together with SZS, SSP boycotted the 2020 parliamentary election, claiming that the election would not be free and fair. After the election, SSP became part of the [[rsUOPS|United Opposition of Serbia]] (UOPS), the successor of SZS. UOPS would be eventually dissolved in January 2021, due to disputes between SSP and the [[rsNarodna|People's Party]] (Narodna). In late 2021, SSP and Narodna returned together with the [[rsPSG|Movement of Free Citizens]] and [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] to form the [[rsUZPS|United for the Victory of Serbia]] (UZPS) alliance, which was officially formalised in February 2022, to take part in the 2022 general election. The elections resulted in the SSP gaining 10 seats in the National Assembly and 6 seats in the City Assembly of Belgrade. UZPS was also dissolved after the elections. In the 2023 elections, it was part of the [[rsSPN|Serbia Against Violence]] alliance.
parties.ideology: SSP is a centre-left political party and it serves in opposition to [[rsSNS|SNS]]. A self-described anti-corruption party, the party is also opposed to party employment, while regarding economy, SSP has called for tax reforms that would bring in progressive taxation. SSP supports financing free textbooks and school meals for school children, and has called for the introduction of a new labour law. The party supports the accession of Serbia to the European Union, wants Serbia to harmonise its foreign policy with the European Union, and initiate sanctions on Russia regarding the Russian invasion of Ukraine. SSP has criticised Chinese investments into infrastructure and it had adopted a platform in which they pledged "reconciliation, cooperation, and the acceptance of diversity" between countries in the Balkans. Supporters of SSP are pro-European while they also see themselves as socially progressive. SSP is an associate member of the [[euPES|Party of European Socialists]].

parties.relations: Split from the [[rsDSS|Democratic Party of Serbia]] (DSS)
parties.description:
A political organisation in Serbia and Kosovo that represents the Serbian minority in Kosovo. It is led by the former Mayor of Zubin Potok, and a prominent figure in the Kosovo Serb community, Slaviša Ristić.

The organisation has heavily criticised the [[xkSL|Serb List]], and it claims that Kosovo is an integral part of Serbia.

"Fatherland" was founded on 19 January 2017 in North Mitrovica by the former Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija board members of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]], [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]], and the [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]]. The first president of the organisation was Aleksandar Vasić. In 2018, Slaviša Ristic was selected as the president.

The organisation was a member of the [[rsSzS|Alliance for Serbia]], a major opposition alliance in Serbia, during its existence. The organisation has criticised the Serb List for participating in the Kosovan elections, and for joining the Government of Kosovo. The organisation boycotted the 2019 Kosovan parliamentary elections as it claims that participating in the Kosovan elections violates the constitution of Serbia, and it called for the boycott of the 2020 Serbian parliamentary elections.

"Fatherland" endorsed presidential candidate Zdravko Ponoš and the [[rsUZPS|United for the Victory of Serbia]] coalition in the 2022 Serbian general election.

parties.name: People's Party
parties.relations: Preceded by the [[rsNPS|People's Movement of Serbia]] (NPS)
parties.description:
A conservative political party in Serbia. It has been led by Vladimir Gajić since 2024.

Narodna was formed in October 2017 after Vuk Jeremić re-organised the [[rsNPS|People's Movement of Serbia]] (NPS), a political party led by Miroslav Aleksić. It cooperated with Dragan Đilas and the [[rsPSG|Movement of Free Citizens]] and [[rsLS2015|Serbian Left]], with whom Narodna took part in the 2018 Belgrade City Assembly election and won 19% of the popular vote. Narodna then joined the [[rsSzS|Alliance for Serbia]] (SZS), a coalition formed by Đilas, which organised mass anti-government protests after the physical attack on Borko Stefanović in November 2018. Together with SZS, Narodna boycotted the 2020 parliamentary election, claiming that its conditions would not be free and fair. Narodna was later a member of the United Opposition of Serbia, which existed between August 2020 and January 2021, and then the [[rsUZPS|United for the Victory of Serbia]] (UZPS) coalition.

With UZPS, Narodna took part in the 2022 general elections and nominated Zdravko Ponoš, a then-member of Narodna, as their presidential candidate. Ponoš lost the presidential election while Narodna won 12 seats in the National Assembly, although due to conflicts between Narodna and the [[rsSSP|Party of Freedom and Justice]] (SSP), UZPS was dissolved after the elections. Narodna had its own parliamentary groups in the National Assembly and City Assembly of Belgrade, while serving in opposition to the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]]. A schism within the party occurred in 2023, which resulted in Aleksić and other members leaving Narodna and refounding NPS. Narodna failed to retain its representation in the 2023 elections. Initially a centre-right party, Narodna has throughout time shifted to very right-wing and nationalistic positions. Previously supportive of the accession of Serbia to the European Union, it has shifted towards Eurosceptic positions and it declares itself to be in favour of military neutrality.

Narodna seljačka stranka
parties.description:
An agrarian political party in Serbia.

It was founded in 1990, its first president being Dragan Veselinov. At this point, its policies were Vojvodina autonomist and social democratic.

In the 1990 election it won one seat. In the 1992 election it entered into a coalition with the [[rsLSV|League of Social Democrats of Vojvodina]] (LSV), as well as Serbian successors to [[yuSRSJ|Union of Reform Forces of Yugoslavia and Association]] for the [[yuUJDI|Yugoslav Democratic Initiative]], respectively renamed the [[rsRSS|Reform Party]] and the Republican Club. The coalition was called the [[rsGSS|Civic Alliance of Serbia]] (GSS) and won no seats. The LSV and NSS left the GSS coalition before the 1993 election. In the 1997 election it was part of the regionalist Vojvodina Coalition and won one seat.

Since 2002, the party has been led by Marijan Rističević. In 2003 it was expelled from the Vojvodina Coalition.

In the 2003 election, it was part of the far-right [[rsSSJ|SSJ]]-led "For National Unity" coalition which won no seats. In the 2007 election the party ran on [[rsSPO|Serbian Renewal Movement]]'s list, which won no seats. In the 2012 election it was part of a centre-right coalition around the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] and won one seat. In the 2014 election it was not formally in coalition with the Serbian Progressive Party, however it won one seat as Marijan Rističević was listed on the [[rsSNSDS|Progressives' electoral list]].

In the 2012 election it was part of a centre-right coalition around the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] and won one seat. In the 2014 election it was not formally in coalition with the Serbian Progressive Party, however it won one seat as Marijan Rističević was listed on the [[rsSNSDS|Progressives' electoral list]].

parties.relations: Split from the [[rsNSS|People's Peasant Party]] (NSS)
parties.description: A political party in Serbia that claims to represent the Russian ethnic minority. The party gathers a number of pro-Russian citizens, mostly Serbs. The party's president is Slobodan Nikolić, a former vice-president of the [[rsNSS|People's Peasant Party]]. The party competed in the 2023 parliamentary election in alliance with the [[rsNKPJ|New Communist Party of Yugoslavia]].
parties.ideology:
According to its programme, the Russian Party advocates Serbia's entry into the Eurasian Economic Union, and the full membership of Serbia in the Collective Security Treaty Organization. The party also advocates increasing cooperation with the Russian Federation in the field of economy, culture and education.

The party has faced accusations of being a satellite organisation of the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS) that exploits minority party electoral advantages. Legal expert Sofija Mandić described the party's participation as a "satellite" of the ruling party, suggesting that "these are votes from Serbian Progressive Party, which in this way tries to create another 'reserve player' for itself." Mandić characterised the party as "a political group that does not exist in real political life, appearing only when elections come." Minority parties in Serbia benefit from lower electoral thresholds, needing only to pass the "natural threshold" rather than the standard 3% census required for majority parties.

In the June 2024 Niš local elections, the party won a single mandate with 1,224 votes in a city where only 121 residents identified as ethnically Russian in the 2022 census. This mandate proved decisive, as both the SNS and the opposition lists had won exactly 30 seats, which is one short of a majority. The party's representative, Tihomir Perić, subsequently formed a coalition with SNS, stating "I'm not Russian, I'm a Russophile." Of the eight candidates on the Niš list, only one had a Russian name.

parties.name: Serbia Centre
parties.relations: Split from the [[rsNS1990|People's Party]] (NS)
parties.description:
A centrist political party in Serbia. It is led by Zdravko Ponoš, the former chief of the General Staff of the Serbian Armed Forces from 2006 to 2008.

Ponoš was the presidential candidate of the [[rsUZPS|United for the Victory of Serbia]] alliance in the 2022 presidential election. Shortly after the election, SRCE was formed as a split from the [[rsNarodna|People's Party]]. It became a registered political party in July 2023, after which it became a member of the [[rsSPN|Serbia Against Violence]] coalition that contested the parliamentary, Vojvodina provincial, and Belgrade City Assembly elections in December 2023. In those elections, SRCE gained representation in all bodies. However, they lost representation in the City Assembly of Belgrade because they boycotted the 2024 Belgrade City Assembly election.

SRCE is opposed to the ruling [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] and supports the accession of Serbia to the European Union. It supports fighting climate change, increasing child allowance, and the reform of the pension system. Since the beginning of the student-led anti-corruption protests in 2024, SRCE has voiced its support for the students and called for early parliamentary elections and the formation of a transitional government as an end to the crisis started by the protests. It is a member of the [[rsPES|Platform for a European Serbia]] coalition.

A political party in Serbia. It was established in January 2022, as a direct successor of the [[rsKP2009|Communist Party]], an unofficial descendant of the former [[rsSKS|League of Communists of Serbia]];

The Serbian Left (SL) was formed in January 2022 as a successor to the Communist Party.

It planned to contest the 2022 Serbian parliamentary election, but it ultimately did not. According to Milojičić, the party is in opposition to the Aleksandar Vučić and [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS)-led government, although Broz still served in the [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] parliamentary group after SL was formed. For the 2023 Serbian parliamentary election, SL participated on the [[rsSNSDS|SNS electoral list]] and gained one seat in the National Assembly.

In June 2024, Milojičić resigned as the party president and joined SNS. Broz passed away next year.

parties.nativeName:

Srpski pokret Dveri
parties.relations: Operated as student movement until 2015
parties.description:
A nationalist and right-wing populist political party in Serbia. Its current president since 2024 is Ivan Kostić, who succeeded Boško Obradović, one of the co-founders of the party.

Formed as a youth-orientated political organisation in 1999, it published an eponymous student magazine that promoted clerical and nationalist content. Through the 2000s, it operated as a non-governmental organisation that campaigned in favour of Christian right views, that included opposition to abortion and opposition to gay rights. Dveri took part in the 2012 elections where it failed to obtain any seats in the National Assembly, although in the 2016 elections it entered the National Assembly in a joint list with the [[rsDSS|Democratic Party of Serbia]], obtaining 13 seats in total, 7 of which belonged to Dveri. Two years later, it took part in the 2018 Belgrade City Assembly election in a coalition with the [[rsDJB|Enough is Enough]] but failed to win seats.

It joined the opposition [[rsSzS|Alliance for Serbia]] later that year, and became a prominent voice in the alliance, with whom it boycotted the 2020 parliamentary election. It did not take part in its successor alliance, the [[rsUOPS|United Opposition of Serbia]], but remained independent during 2021, after which it formed an [[rsPB|electoral coalition]] with Žika Gojković's faction of the [[rsPOKS|Movement for the Restoration of the Kingdom of Serbia]] for the 2022 general election. It returned to the National Assembly after the 2022 election, winning 6 seats in total. Together with [[rsSSZ|Serbian Party Oathkeepers]], Dveri became a founding member of the [[rsNO|National Gathering]], which failed to cross the threshold in the 2023 elections.
