parties.name: Serbian Party Oathkeepers
parties.nativeName:
Српска странка Заветници
Srpska stranka Zavetnici
parties.relations: Split from the [[rsSRS|Serbian Radical Party]] (SRS)
parties.description:
A far-right political party in Serbia. Milica Đurđević Stamenkovski has been the party's president since 2021.

Initially known as Serbian Council Oathkeepers, SSZ was formed in 2012 with Stefan Stamenkovski as its first president. SSZ began its actions by organising protests against the recognition of Kosovo, the Brussels Agreement, and Belgrade Pride parades. SSZ entered electoral politics in 2013 and it participated in the 2014 parliamentary election in which it did not win any seats. They later organised protests opposed to the commemoration of Srebrenica massacre and NATO; they also organised a rally in support of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić. SSZ unsuccessfully sought to win seats in the National Assembly of Serbia and City Assembly of Belgrade up to 2022, when SSZ for the first time gained parliamentary representation. It was in the parliamentary opposition to the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS). SSZ lost all of its representation in the 2023 elections, in which it contested as part of the [[rsNO|National Gathering]]. After the elections, it aligned itself with SNS, with Đurđević Stamenkovski becoming a government minister in May 2024.

SSZ is an ultranationalist party that pursues sovereignist views towards Kosovo and supports the unification of Serbia and Republika Srpska, an entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is also socially conservative and supports restricting Serbia's immigration system. SSZ supports labelling non-governmental organisations funded from abroad as "foreign agents". An Eurosceptic and anti-NATO party, it is in favour of forging closer relations with Russia and China. It is also opposed to sanctioning Russia in regards to the Russian invasion of Ukraine. SSZ has closely cooperated with [[ruER|United Russia]], the ruling party of Russia, and has also received support from the far-right [[deAfD|Alternative for Germany]].

parties.relations: Split from the [[rsDSS|Democratic Party of Serbia]] (DSS)
parties.description:
A right-wing populist and national-conservative political party in Serbia. It was formed in 2014 by former members of the [[rsDSS|Democratic Party of Serbia]] and is currently led by Nenad Popović.

The SNP was founded in September 2014 in the village of Kriva Reka in the Zlatibor region. Its founding members included Popović, Jovan Palalić, Milan Stamatović (who left the party two years later), and the political philosopher Bogdana Koljević.

The party's first member of the assembly was Milan Petrić, who had been elected on the list of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] in the 2014 election and joined the SNP in March 2015. The SNP subsequently contested the 2016 election on the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]]'s [[rsSNSDS|Aleksandar Vučić – Serbia Is Winning]] electoral list and elected three members to the assembly: Jovan Palalić, Ognjen Pantović, and Snežana Petrović.

Popović, who has been the SNP's leader since its founding, was appointed to a ministerial position in the first cabinet of Ana Brnabić on 29 June 2017 and served until 2022. In 2024, he was once again appointed as a minister in the cabinet of Miloš Vučević.
parties.ideology:
The SNP advocates for national conservatism, as well as right-wing populism. It is located on the right of the political spectrum. Popović has advocated for the construction of a border fence on the Serbian border with North Macedonia to reduce illegal immigration. He has also opposed allowing LGBT+ content in children's books in Serbia. In terms of foreign policy, the SNP advocates for improving relations between Serbia and Russia, and has supported Russia in the war in Ukraine. She opposes Serbia's accession to the European Union.

SNP has collaborated with members of the [[euID|Identity and Democracy Party]], such as the [[frRN|National Rally]], the [[atFPO|Freedom Party of Austria]], and the [[deAfD|Alternative for Germany]].

parties.name: Serbian Progressive Party
parties.nativeName:
Српска напредна странка
Srpska napredna stranka
parties.relations: Split from the [[rsSRS|Serbian Radical Party]] (SRS)
parties.description:
A major political party in Serbia, described as populist and catch-all. It has been the country's ruling party since 2012.

Founded by Tomislav Nikolić and Aleksandar Vučić in 2008 as a split from the [[rsSRS|Serbian Radical Party]], SNS served in opposition to the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] until 2012. SNS gained prominence and became the largest opposition party due to their anti-corruption platform and the protests in 2011 at which they demanded early elections. In 2012, Nikolić was elected president of Serbia and succeeded by Vučić as president of SNS. A coalition government led by SNS and [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] (SPS) was also formed. Vučić became prime minister in 2014 while SNS became the largest party in Belgrade and Vojvodina in 2014 and 2016, respectively.

SNS chose Vučić as their presidential candidate for the 2017 election, which he ultimately won. Mass protests were organised following his election, while Ana Brnabić, an independent who later joined SNS, succeeded him as prime minister. SNS was later faced with protests from 2018 to 2020 and gained a supermajority of seats in the National Assembly of Serbia after the 2020 election, which was boycotted by most opposition parties. The Serbian Patriotic Alliance merged into SNS in 2021 while environmental protests were also organised in 2021 and 2022. Vučić was re-elected as president in 2022, while SNS has since continued to lead the government with SPS. A year later, Vučić was succeeded by Vučević as president of SNS, who led the party in the 2023 parliamentary election. Since 2024, SNS has faced student-led anti-corruption protests.

As of 2024, SNS has at least 700,000 members, making it one of the largest political parties by membership in Europe.
parties.ideology: Political scientists have described SNS as a populist and catch-all party that either has a weak ideological profile or that is non-ideological. SNS supports Serbia's accession to the European Union but its support is rather pragmatic than ideological. An economically neoliberal party, SNS has pushed for austerity, market economy reforms, privatisation, economic liberalisation, and has reformed wages, pensions, the labour law, introduced a lex specialis for Belgrade Waterfront, and reformed the Constitution in the part related to judiciary. SNS is an associated member of the [[euEPP|European People's Party]] and a member of the [[intIDU|International Democracy Union]]. Critics have assessed that after it came to power, Serbia has suffered from democratic backsliding into authoritarianism, as well as a decline in media freedom and civil liberties. As of 2024, SNS has at least 700,000 members, making it one of the largest political parties by membership in Europe.

Miloš Vučević (since 27 May 2023)

parties.name: Serbian Radical Party
parties.nativeName:
Српска радикална странка
Srpska radikalna stranka
parties.relations: Merger of the [[rsSCP|Serbian Chetnik Movement]] (SČP) and faction of the [[rsNRS|People's Radical Party]] (NRS)
parties.description:
A far-right ultranationalist political party in Serbia. Founded in 1991, its co-founder, first and only leader is Vojislav Šešelj. During the Yugoslav Wars, it became prominent, enjoying the status of the second largest party in the Serbian parliament under the regime of Slobodan Milošević. In this period and in the following decade, it had been described as neo-fascist.

The SRS was founded in 1991 as a merger of the [[rsSCP|Serbian Chetnik Movement]], led by Šešelj, and the [[rsNRS|People's Radical Party]]'s faction, led by Tomislav Nikolić. Upon formation, they became the president and deputy president of SRS respectively. During the first half of the 1990s the SRS supported the ruling [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] regime led by Milošević, which had contributed greatly to the rise of SRS through the use of media. The SRS was endorsed by Milošević and collaborated with him as a part of his coalition; later it experienced persecution for competing with him and then a reconciliation, with Milošević making Šešelj his Deputy Prime Minister. The party had strong support until the 2000 election, when SRS suffered a major defeat, but through populist rhetoric it became the most voted party in the early-to-mid 2000s. Šešelj voluntarily surrendered to the ICTY to defend himself against charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity that he was alleged to have committed during the Croatian War of Independence and the Bosnian War. Nikolić assumed de facto party leadership until he left the party in 2008.

During the years of Nikolić's leadership, SRS blended ultranationalism with brash, populist, and anti-corruption rhetoric. Due to disagreements with Šešelj over European Union integration, Nikolić took many of the high-ranking members of the party to form the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS), which became the ruling party of Serbia in 2012. After the split, Dragan Todorović assumed de facto leadership, and the party went into a major decline, only pulling 4% of the vote in 2012 and 2% in 2014, the first time that SRS was not represented in the parliament. Shortly after Šešelj's return to Serbia in 2014, the party gained back some of its popularity and it placed third with 8% of the vote in the 2016 election. In late 2019, the party went into decline again, and in the 2020 election it ended up only with 2% of the vote and gaining no seats in the parliament again.
parties.ideology: A right-wing populist party, SRS supports the creation of a Greater Serbia. It is Eurosceptic, anti-Western orientated, opposed to the accession of Serbia to the European Union and supports establishing closer ties with Russia instead. Some journalists described SRS as neo-fascist in the 1990s; this definition of the party is met in scholarly and academic materials written in the 1990s and the 2000s or describing the party in that period. Regarding social issues, SRS is traditionalist. It also holds local branches in some of the neighbouring states.

parties.name: Serbian Renewal Movement
parties.nativeName:
Српски покрет обнове
Srpski pokret obnove
parties.relations: Split from the [[rsSNO|Serbian National Renewal]] (SNO)
parties.description: A monarchist and liberal political party in Serbia. From its founding in 1990 to 2024, its president was Vuk Drašković. Since 12 July 2024, it has been led by Aleksandar Cvetković.
parties.ideology:
During the 1990s, the Serbian Renewal Movement was orientated towards ultranationalism and irredentism, and it supported revisionism and anti-communism. During that period, it was positioned on the right-wing on the political spectrum. It was also characterised as a right-wing populist party, and it was backed by the Serbian Orthodox Church. It also held conservative views.

Although after the 2000s, the party rejected its radical nationalist past and statism, and embraced liberal-democratic elements. It also shifted to liberalism, and economic liberalism, and it adopted a more moderate right, and centre-right position. It was also described as moderate nationalist during that period.

Since its inception, it has been described as monarchist, and it advocates for the restoration of parliamentary monarchy. Since the late 2000s, it has been supportive of accession of Serbia to the European Union and NATO, and in the early 2010s, it shifted its support towards the recognition of Kosovo.

President:

Aleksandar Cvetković (since 12 July 2024)

parties.nativeName:
Slováci vpred
Словаци напред
Slovaci napred
parties.description:
A political party in Serbia, representing the Slovak ethnic minority in Vojvodina. Its leader is Pavel Surovi. The party is aligned with Aleksandar Vučić and the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]].

Slovaks Forward won nine out of twenty-nine seats in Serbia's 2014 Slovak National Council election and eight seats in the 2018 election. Surovi was chosen as council vice-president after the 2018 election, although he was removed from this role in February 2021.

Slovaks Forward was registered as a political party in late 2015. It joined the Serbian Progressive Party's [[rsSNSDS|electoral alliance]] for the 2016 Vojvodina provincial election; Surovi was included on the Progressive Party's electoral list in the thirty-third position and was elected when the list won a majority victory with sixty-three out of 120 mandates. He was promoted to the fifteenth position on the Progressive list in the 2020 provincial election and was re-elected when the list won an increased majority with seventy-six mandates. As of 2021, Surovi is the sole representative of his party in the assembly. He sits in caucus with the Progressive Party's Aleksandar Vučić – For Our Children parliamentary group.

Surovi was confirmed for a new term as party leader in December 2019.

parties.name: Social Democratic Party
parties.relations:
Split from the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] (DS)
Originally founded in February 2014 as [[rsZeleni|New Democratic Party – The Greens]] (NDS-Z) based on [[rsZeleni|Greens of Serbia]] (Zeleni) registration, but in June 2014 NDS-Z split into NDS and Zeleni
parties.description:
A centre-left political party in Serbia.

The party was founded and is headed by Boris Tadić, who was previously president of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] and the former President of Serbia. Between June and October 2014, the name of the party was the New Democratic Party. In May 2019, the party formed a union with Democratic Party and [[rsZZS2013|Together for Serbia]].

Tadić revealed in February 2014 his intention to secede from the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] and to form a new party to take part in the 2014 parliamentary election. But, after realising that they don't have enough time to register a new party before the election, Tadić and his supporters made a deal with the [[rsZeleni|Greens of Serbia]]. As part of this deal, Tadić and his supporters joined the Greens of Serbia, and then on 10 February 2014 the name of the party was changed to the "New Democratic Party – Greens". Although Ivan Karić was still officially president of this party, Tadić became its de facto leader. Party then participated in the 2014 parliamentary election under that name in coalition with [[rsZZS2013|Together for Serbia]], [[rsLSV|League of Social Democrats of Vojvodina]] and some other minor parties. This coalition won 5.7% of the electoral vote and 18 seats in the National Assembly of Serbia. Of these, 11 seats were allocated to the "New Democratic Party – Greens", but only one to the original Greens (Ivan Karić) and 10 to the group around Boris Tadić.

After the 2014 parliamentary election, a divergence emerged in the "New Democratic Party – Greens" between the original Greens and group of members that joined the party with Tadić. On 14 June, Tadić and his supporters decided to secede from the Greens and form "New Democratic Party" as a separate party, while the name of the "New Democratic Party—Greens" was changed back to the "Greens of Serbia". In the National Assembly, 10 deputies of the New Democratic Party are part of the parliamentary group of 12 deputies together with Ivan Karić of the Greens and Blagoje Bradić of Together for Serbia, and they are in the opposition to the current Government of Serbia. First internal party elections were held on 4 October 2014. Boris Tadić was elected president of the party. On the same day, the official name of the party was changed to the "Social Democratic Party".

As of January 2017, the Social Democratic Party holds four seats in the National Assembly of Serbia. It exists in a parliamentary alliance with the [[rsNPS|People's Movement of Serbia]], which holds one seat. On 10 January 2022, it was announced that the Democrats of Serbia, a break-away faction from the Democratic Party, will merge with SDS. In the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, SDS was associated with the Socialist Group. In the 2023 Serbian parliamentary election, SDS contested as part of the [[rsDJS|Good Morning Serbia]] alliance.
parties.ideology: It supports accession of Serbia to the European Union and it is a member of the [[intPA|Progressive Alliance]].

parties.description:
A centre-left political party in Serbia, orientated towards the principles of social democracy.

The Social Democratic Party of Serbia (SDPS) was formed on 5 October 2009 by Rasim Ljajić, the long-time leader of [[rsSDP1996|Sandžak Democratic Party]]. Ljajić has been the president of SDPS since its formation. In late 2013 SDPS had joined in coalition with the Sandžak Democratic Party, forming a political union. Rasim Ljajić was elected as the SDPS-SDP's first head. Despite taking part with the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]]-led [[rsIZBZ|Choice for a Better Life]] alliance in the 2012 Serbian parliamentary election, SDPS has aligned itself with the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS) after the election. Since then, it has contested every election on the SNS electoral list.

SDPS is a centre-left political party, orientated towards the principles of social democracy. Ljajić has described SDPS as an anti-fascist, anti-populist, and solidarist party in 2023.

Its headquarters is at Dečanska 1/III in Belgrade. In 2015, it was reported that SDPS had 44,658 members. In 2020, SDPS had 48,623 members.

In June 2018 the party was admitted in the [[intSI|Socialist International]] as observer member, and promoted to full member in 2024.

parties.description:
A social democratic and populist political party in Serbia.

SPS was founded in 1990 as a merger of the [[rsSKS|League of Communists of Serbia]] and [[rsSSRNSSocialist Alliance of Working People of Yugoslavia]] with Slobodan Milošević as its first president. In the 1990 general elections, SPS became the ruling party of Serbia while Milošević was elected president of Serbia. During Milošević's rule, SPS relied on the [[rsSRS|Serbian Radical Party]] (SRS) from 1992 to 1993 while it later led several coalition governments with SRS, [[rsLS1990|New Democracy]], and [[rsJUL|Yugoslav Left]]. Mass protests against SPS were held in 1991, and after being accused of falsifying votes in major urban cities, such as Belgrade and Niš, 1996–1997 protests were also organised. The [[rsDOS|Democratic Opposition of Serbia]] coalition defeated SPS in the 2000 general elections but Milošević declined to accept the results. This resulted in Milošević's overthrow.

SPS was in opposition until 2003 after which it served as confidence and supply to the government led by Vojislav Koštunica until 2007. Dačić led SPS into a coalition government with the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] after the 2008 parliamentary election, while four years later he became the prime minister of Serbia after the formation of a coalition government with the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS). He remained prime minister until 2014, while SPS has since then remained a junior member of SNS-led governments. Although it described itself as a democratic socialist party, SPS promoted mixed economy and populist nationalism under Milošević's leadership and was accused of authoritarianism. SPS has remained populist under Dačić but it shifted towards social democracy and a centre-left and more pragmatic, pro-European image. SPS shares a parliamentary group with the [[rsZeleni|Greens of Serbia]] in the National Assembly of Serbia, while it has also participated with [[rsJS|United Serbia]] in electoral lists.

parties.description:
Anational-conservative political party in Serbia. It split from the [[rsSSJ|Party of Serbian Unity]] in 2004. 

The party has supported every government formed since its creation, and was briefly in government in 2022–23.

It was founded on 15 February 2004, as a split from the far-right [[rsSSJ|Party of Serbian Unity]] with Dragan Marković Palma elected as the leader on the first party assembly. During its early years, the party had close relations with other right-wing parties such as [[rsNS1998|New Serbia]] and [[rsDSS|Democratic Party of Serbia]], even participating with them in the 2007 parliamentary election.

During the 2008 parliamentary election, they participated in a coalition around the [[rsSPS|Socialist Party of Serbia]] and supported the accession of Serbia into the European Union. After the election, United Serbia was the first to announce the beginning of talks with the coalition [[rsZES|For a European Serbia]], led by the President Boris Tadić, on forming the new government.

The United Serbia, including its leader Palma, supported the "Serbs for Trump" campaign and Donald Trump in the 2020 United States presidential election.

parties.relations: Politically succeeded by the [[rsRP2026|Workers' Party]] (RP)
parties.description:
Atrade union and a left-wing political organisation in Serbia. It was founded in 2008 and has been headed by Željko Veselinović since its foundation.

United Trade Unions of Serbia "Sloga" was formed in 2008 by Željko Veselinović. It had regularly organised International Workers' Day walks. USS Sloga later organised media campaigns regarding workers' conditions, and had also criticised the economic model that has been pursued by Aleksandar Vučić. It participated as a political organisation in the 2014 parliamentary election as part of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] (DS) coalition list. Veselinović became a member of the National Assembly afterwards

According to USS Sloga, they had 100,000 members in 2017. Its members were threatened by the president of the Municipality of Ub Darko Glišić in 2018. USS Sloga regained its seat in the National Assembly following the 2022 general election.
parties.ideology:
It has been described as a left-wing trade union. USS Sloga defines itself as "an independent democratic trade union organisation of employees that they join for the purpose of representation and protection of their professional, labor, economic, social, cultural and other individual and collective interests". Veselinović is a member of Trade Union Network of the [[euPEL|Party of the European Left]] and [[euESF|European Social Forum]]. USS Sloga is a member of the [[intWFTU|World Federation of Trade Unions]]. USS Sloga opposes neoliberalism. It supports changing the Labor Law.

USS Sloga had also criticised the approach of other trade unions in Serbia. In 2017, they had argued that increasing the minimal wage for 15% would not be enough to cover the costs of a minimum consumer basket. In August 2022, they had proposed an increase in the minimum wage, wages, and pensions.

United Trade Unions of Serbia "Sloga" was formed in 2008 by Željko Veselinović. It had regularly organised International Workers' Day walks. USS Sloga later organised media campaigns regarding workers' conditions, and had also criticised the economic model that has been pursued by Aleksandar Vučić. It participated as a political organisation in the 2014 parliamentary election as part of the [[rsDS|Democratic Party]] (DS) coalition list. ideology.text:
It has been described as a left-wing trade union. USS Sloga defines itself as "an independent democratic trade union organisation of employees that they join for the purpose of representation and protection of their professional, labor, economic, social, cultural and other individual and collective interests". Veselinović is a member of Trade Union Network of the [[euPEL|Party of the European Left]] and [[euESF|European Social Forum]]. USS Sloga is a member of the [[intWFTU|World Federation of Trade Unions]]. USS Sloga opposes neoliberalism. It supports changing the Labor Law.

USS Sloga had also criticised the approach of other trade unions in Serbia. In 2017, they had argued that increasing the minimal wage for 15% would not be enough to cover the costs of a minimum consumer basket. In August 2022, they had proposed an increase in the minimum wage, wages, and pensions.

The trade union was a part of several opposition coalitions, including the [[rsSZS|Alliance for Serbia]], [[rsUOPS|United Opposition of Serbia]], [[rsUZPS|United for the Victory of Serbia]], and [[rsSPN|Serbia Against Violence]].

parties.description:
A political party in Serbia. It is led by Željko Veselinović, a member of the National Assembly of Serbia formerly affiliated with the [[rsSSP|Party of Freedom and Justice]], founded in 2026. The RP is represented in the National Assembly and Assembly of Vojvodina. It is affiliated with the [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]].

Željko Veselinović is the president of the [[rsUSSSloga|United Trade Unions of Serbia "Sloga"]] who was elected to the National Assembly of Serbia on the quota of the Party of Freedom and Justice (SSP) in the 2023 Serbian parliamentary election. Together with Đorđo Đorđić, he left the SSP parliamentary group in October 2024. Veselinović and Đorđić announced the formation of the new Workers' Party (RP), with Veselinović stating that he believes that no political party in Serbia truly concentrates on workers' rights. They were followed by MPs Sonja Pernat and Irena Živković on 19 November. Together they formed a parliamentary group in the National Assembly.[4] The RP began collecting signatures in December 2024. The opposition [[rsSRCE|Serbia Centre]] political party alleged that the ruling [[rsSNS|Serbian Progressive Party]] (SNS) helped the RP collect signatures needed for the registration of the party in Leskovac. Veselinović denied this.

The RP was officially formed on 6 February 2026. Members of the Sloga parliamentary group took part in the negotations related to early parliamentary elections, led by president of Serbia Aleksandar Vučić in April. In response to this, Pernat and Slavica Radovanović left their parliamentary group. Veselinović went on to form a parliamentary group with the pro-government parties [[rsRS2013|Russian Party]] and [[rsUSS|United Peasant Party]] soon after. Veselinović claims that their cooperation is on technical and practical level. On 27 April, the RP was registered as a political party. Veselinović said that their path to registering the party was obstructed by both the government and the opposition.

The RP announced their participation in the parliamentary elections, as well as the creation of local boards and a broad coalition for the elections. It has denied participating in the coalition electoral list led by the SNS.[14] Despite this, Branislava Pandurov, who serves in the City Assembly of Novi Sad, is part of the SNS-led parliamentary group, but claims the cooperation is only on technical terms. The RP initially negotiated with [[rsMISN|We – Power of the People]] of Branimir Nestorović on participating together in the parliamentary elections, but abandoned it after the party allegedly wanted to recruit RP members into its own party. In September, RP announced that it would participate on the SNS electoral list [[rsUS|United Serbia]] for the 2026 parliamentary elections.
parties.ideology:
The RP declares itself to be in favour of expanding the rights of workers, pensioners, farmers, and students. They drafted a new Labour Law, which would bring a 35-hour workweek in Serbia. The RP declares itself to be Eurosceptic while still supporting the accession of Serbia to the European Union, partly due to its perceived respect for human and workers' rights. It opposes the recognition of Kosovo, while supporting retaining ties with Russia and especially China. Veselinović criticised neoliberalism and endorsed left-wing policies. While still in formation, the RP denied that it would cooperate with the [[rsSNS|SNS]]. Their MPs also announced that they would vote against the formation of the cabinet of Đuro Macut.

Vladimir Pejić of Faktor Plus and Đorđe Vukadinović of Nova srpska politička misao argued that there was a political space for a workers' rights party, though the newspaper Danas noted that the relatively minor [[rsPRL|Party of the Radical Left]] exists. The political scientist Zoran Stojiljković stated that the founders have to be cautious due to the failed experiment of the [[rsLPS|Labour Party of Serbia]] (LPS), reminding that it received less votes in the 2003 Serbian parliamentary election than it collected for it to be registered as a political party. In an interview with Danas, Veselinović, however, said that the RP will not follow the failures of the LPS, which was the political arm of the [[rsASNS|Association of Free and Independent Trade Unions]].

The RP has said that they would support the SNS, or any other government, if it were to introduce a new Labour Law.

parties.name: Liberal Democratic Party of the Soviet Union
parties.nativeName:
Либерально-демократическая партия Советского Союза
Liberal'no-demokraticheskaya partiya Sovetskogo Soyuza
parties.description:
In the summer of 1989, Vladimir Bogachyov left Lev Ubozhko's [[ruKPR|Democratic Party]], which in turn had split from the [[ruDS|Democratic Union]] in 1988 due to disagreement with its policies. Both Ubozhko and Bogachyov represented right-wing liberalism and conservatism. Toward the fall of 1989, Bogachev convened an initiative group to create a "liberal democratic party."

In late autumn, Vladimir Zhirinovsky, who had previously attempted to organize a "social democratic party of Russia" and even managed to develop a program for it, joined Bogachyov. This program was ultimately adopted as the basis, and the word "social" was replaced throughout with "liberal." According to the recollections of high-ranking KGB and [[suCPSU|CPSU]] Central Committee officials, with Zhirinovsky's arrival, the project became completely under the control of government officials and was formed at their instigation.

The formal first (founding) congress took place on 13 March 1990, at the Rusakov Palace of Culture, where the founding group received its official name, the "Liberal Democratic Party of the Soviet Union." According to recollections, this name was coined by representatives of the KGB's 5th Department shortly before the formal congress. Delegate cards, along with LDPSU membership cards, were distributed at the congress to anyone who wanted one. By the time of the first congress, the party had united 3,000 members across 31 regions of the Soviet Union. The party quickly received registration and the right to establish its own publication, the newspaper "Rech."

On 8 June 1990, Zhirinovsky and Vladimir Voronin (the future President of Moldova, [[mdPCRM|PCRM]]) founded the "Centrist Bloc of Political Parties and Movements." During autumn 1990, the bloc held a series of consultations with Nikolai Ryzhkov on the possible formation of a so-called "government of national unity" with the CPSU.

On 6 October 1990, at Bogachyov's initiative, the Second (Emergency) LDPSU Congress was held in Moscow. Zhirinovsky was expelled from the party for collaborating with the KGB, and the party was renamed the "Liberal Democratic Party." In response, an all-Union LDPSU conference with congressional powers was convened on 20 October, chaired by Zhirinovsky. Zhirinovsky amended the party charter and expelled Bogachyov and his supporters.

Between late 1990 and early 1991, the party advocated for a state of emergency in the country and a temporary ban on all political parties. On 27 February 1991, the LDPSU participated in the "For a Great, United Russia!" conference organized by the [[ruKPRSFSR|Communist Party of the RSFSR]].

On 12 April 1991, the party was formally registered by the USSR Ministry of Justice. That same year, Zhirinovsky nominated the party for the first direct presidential election in the RSFSR, finishing third with 7.81% of the vote.

During the August 1991 coup, Zhirinovsky and the LDPSU officially supported the putschists (GKChP) and welcomed their actions. After the coup's failure, the party's activities were suspended in Moscow, and the Ministry of Justice issued a warning to the party. The investigative group for the GKChP subsequently prepared charges against Zhirinovsky and the party for violating six articles of the Criminal Code, but these were never brought.

Several months after the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Third Congress of the Liberal Democratic Party was held in Moscow on 18-19 April 1992, attended by 627 delegates from 43 regions. The LDP was reorganized into the [[ruLDPR|Liberal Democratic Party of Russia]]. Zhirinovsky was again elected party chairman.

In subsequent years, in addition to the LDPR, several similar liberal democratic parties were created in the post-Soviet space:
- [[byLDPB|Liberal Democratic Party of Belarus]], a splinter of Zhirinovsky's party, reorganized in 1994;
- [[uaLDPU|Liberal Democratic Party of Ukraine]], independent of the LDPR, a group that had contacts with Bogachev's group in 1990, condemned the pro-Zhirinovsky coup of 1990, and retained a liberal and pro-Western orientation;
- [[pmrLDPP|Liberal Democratic Party of Transnistria]], previously the Transnistrian branch of the LDPR, reorganized into a separate party in 2006.

parties.description:
A centre-right liberal-conservative political alliance in Sweden. The Alliance consisted of the four centre-right political parties in the Riksdag. The Alliance was formed while in opposition, and later achieved a majority government in the 2006 general election and a minority government in the 2010 general election, governing Sweden from 2006 to 2014 with Fredrik Reinfeldt of the Moderate Party serving as Prime Minister of Sweden until 2014. The Alliance was co-chaired by every component party's individual leaders.

After defeat in the 2014 Swedish general election, the Moderate Party's parliamentary group leader Anna Kinberg Batra announced to the Riksdag that the political alliance "would operate in opposition". On 11 January 2019, during the 2018–2019 Swedish government formation, the Centre Party and Liberals agreed to tolerate the re-election as Prime Minister of Social Democratic incumbent Stefan Löfven. Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson and Christian Democrat leader Ebba Busch denounced the agreement, with Busch calling the Alliance "a closed chapter".

On 11 January 2019, during the 2018–2019 Swedish government formation, the Centre Party and Liberals agreed to tolerate the re-election as Prime Minister of Social Democratic incumbent Stefan Löfven. Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson and Christian Democrat leader Ebba Busch denounced the agreement, with Busch calling the Alliance "a closed chapter".

parties.name: Alternative for Sweden
parties.relations:
Split from the [[seSD|Sweden Democrats]] (SD);
Preceded by the [[seSDU|Sweden Democratic Youth]] (SDU)
parties.description:
A far-right political party in Sweden. It was founded in March 2018 by Gustav Kasselstrand and William Hahne, along with other members of the Sweden Democratic Youth, who were collectively expelled from the Sweden Democrats in 2015. The party's most prominent issue is return migration, advocating for the forced remigration of immigrants to their countries of origin, alongside Sweden's withdrawal from the European Union.

AfS ran in the general elections of 2018 and 2022, but failed to enter the Riksdag. With 0.26% of the vote, AfS is the second largest party without representation in the Riksdag. In the 2019 European Parliament election in Sweden, the party ran on an anti-EU platform, receiving 0.46% of the vote. In November 2020, AfS announced its intention to run in the 2021 election to the Church of Sweden council. It won 1.26% of the votes, giving it three seats in the Church council. In 2025, AfS lost its three seats despite winning 1.64% of the vote this time, due to a newly introduced 2% threshold.

parties.name: Ambition Sweden
parties.relations: Split from the [[seSD|Sweden Democrats]] (SD).
parties.description:
Elsa Widding was elected to the Riksdag as a member of the [[seSD|Sweden Democrats]] (SD) in the 2022 Swedish general election, but left the SD in May 2023 following a controversy over her participation in a conference in Norway that was accused of spreading conspiracy theories, including about the climate, vaccines and the Holocaust. Widding believed that the SD did not clearly enough defend her against criticism from, among others, the then Minister for Education, Mats Persson. Since then, Widding served as independent MP, despite SD's urges to resign her seat. For 11 days in January 2024, Widding was a member of [[seMoD|Human Rights and Democracy]] party (MoD), saying she made a mistake joining the party when revelations were made that the party is vaccine-skeptical.

In May 2025, Widding announced the formation of a new party, with a founding conference scheduled for 12 June 2025 and with the ambition to participate in the 2026 Swedish general election.[6] The party was originally called Sweden First (Sverige först), but in September 2025 the name was changed to Ambition Sweden due to a name conflict and because "it has been too easy to confuse the party with other things that have nothing to do with the party."

The Ambition Sweden party name was registered by the Swedish Election Authority on 10 March 2026, allowing the party to participate in the 2026 general election.

In April 2026, Katja Nyberg, another independent MP who left SD in January due to accusations of drug-impaired driving and driving without a license, announced that she was joining Ambition Sweden and would be on the AS parliamentary list. Elsa Widding said regarding the criminal suspicions against Nybert that "there has been a terrible push against her." Among other former SD members of the Riksdag on the AS lists were Unni Björnerfors, known for anti-vaccination statements, and Olle Larsson, who left the party because the SD had not prioritized rural issues.

On 10 July 2026, it was announced that Katja Nyberg dropped from the Ambition Sweden list for the 2026 general election. Nyberg explained her decision with personal reasons.
parties.ideology:
Ambition Sweden advocates Sweden's exit from the European Union, emphasizing national sovereignty, direct democracy and skepticism towards supranational organizations. The party sets the release deadline for 2030-2034. At the same time, party Sweden wants to cooperate internationally through trade agreements. In addition, the party criticizes Sweden's membership in NATO, believing that "it increases the risk of Sweden being drawn into conflicts."

Ambition Sweden wants to abolish state income tax. The party is critical of wind power, preferring invest in nuclear power instead.

Since leaving SD in 2023, Elsa Widding has established herself as a climate change sceptic. Among other things, Widding has claimed that the media is spreading an excessively alarmist picture of climate change and has published texts on the climate change denialist blog Klimatrealisterna.

The party is described as competing for votes with other anti-immigration and Eurosceptic parties such as [[seSD|Sweden Democrats]] and [[seAfS|Alternative for Sweden]].

parties.name: Bevara Sverige Svenskt
parties.relations: Merged into the [[seSveP|Sweden Party]], and, later, into the [[seSD|Sweden Democrats]]
parties.description:
A racist, right-wing extremist and national revolutionary campaign organisation formed in the summer of 1979, modelled on the British National Front.

The organisation's aim was to campaign for limited immigration and for the repatriation of immigrants living in Sweden. Sven Davidson was elected chairman at the association's first annual meeting in 1983, a position he held until the organisation's dissolution on 16 November 1986. 

In 1988, the [[seSD|Sweden Democrats]] were formed by former BSS members. The Sweden Democrats have been described as a transformation of BSS into a political party, and the party used "Bevara Sverige Svenskt" as its slogan until the late 1990s.

parties.name: Centre Democrats
parties.relations: Split from the [[seC|Centre Party]] (C)
parties.description:
A minor political party in Sweden, founded in 1974. While the party has described itself as a "centre alternative", it has been described externally as a right-wing populist party. It agitated against immigration from the 1980s, but toned down the issue in the 2000s, focusing more on local, social and economic issues. The party had some local representation from the 1970s, until 2006, when it lost its final local seat.

The party was founded in June 1974 by the lead of John Görnebrand of Simrishamn as an alliance of multiple local parties in Scania. It was mainly modeled after the Danish [[dkCD|Centre Democrats]], including influences from Mogens Glistrup and his [[dkFrP|Progress Party]]. The party won several local municipal seats in elections during the 1970s and 1980s, and was even represented in the municipal government in Båstad in a cooperation with the [[dkM|Moderate Party]] after the 1979 election. Before the 1982 election, Harry Franzén was elected as new party chairman, and the party started to focus considerably more on immigration issues. The party began speaking against immigrant native language education and called the refugee policy a "travel agency mafia" for refugees. During the refugee controversy in Sjöbo, the party supported the side of Sven-Olle Olsson.

Right after the 1988 election, the Centre Democrats split in two factions, led by Harry Franzén and John Nielsen. Nielsen broke away in early 1989 with the local Svedala chapter, and turned it into a local chapter of the [[seFsP|Progress Party]]. By the 1991 election, he had however gone back to the Centre Democrats. In turn, many leading members of the Centre Democrats went over to [[seNyD|New Democracy]] by the same election. By 1997, the party had just around 300 members. For the 2006 election the party lost its final local representation, a seat it had held in Svalöv.

parties.name: Centre Party
parties.description:
A liberal political party in Sweden, founded in 1913. It is represented in all of the Riksdag's parliamentary committees, currently holding 24 seats. 

The party focuses on the national economy, the environment, political decentralisation and social integration. From 2019 to 2021, it provided confidence and supply to the Löfven II cabinet.

Traditionally part of the Nordic agrarian family of political parties, the Centre Party has increasingly switched focus towards economic liberalism, environmental protection, equality of the sexes and decentralisation of governmental authority. The party describes itself as liberal feminist, campaigning for policies which enhance gender equality on an individualist basis. Its environmental policies stress the importance of consent and voluntary action, including working with foresters and private landowners to promote biodiversity within a mutually agreeable framework.

The Centre Party has produced two prime ministers of Sweden, who served a total of three terms; Thorbjörn Fälldin was the last Centre Party prime minister, and held the post for a total of five years, from 1976 to 1978 and then again from 1979 to 1982. It is a member of the [[euALDE|Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe]], the [[intLI|Liberal International]] and Renew Europe. It was originally named the Farmers' League (Bondeförbundet).

parties.name: Centre Party
parties.relations: Legally succeeded by the [[seC|Centre Party]] (C)
parties.description:
A political party in Örebro. The party was founded by Nils August Nilsson in 1924. Nilsson was strongly committed to peace issues, abortion rights and the world language (Ido).

Nilsson and the party repeated the motto "First-class people in first-class societies" as a mantra. The party's manifesto demanded universal suffrage, but with the addition "for every enlightened adult citizen".

The Civilisation Party ran in the 1924 parliamentary election and in the 1926 municipal election. The ballot papers had the words Arbetarepartiet/Socialdemokratiska listan written on them with the subtitle Civilisation Party. The ballot papers had N.A. Nilsson as the first name and then a number of prominent [[seSAP|Social Democrats]]. The Social Democrats protested against Nilsson's move, as he had included the names on the ballot papers without the people's knowledge or permission. The Civilisation Party received 447 votes in the 1926 Örebro municipal election. The party managed to get a seat on the municipal council.

In the 1932 second chamber election, the party stood under its new name, the Centre Party, and received 2,501 votes (0.1%). Four years later, the distribution was a modest 96 votes.

The party's 1933 program had some similarities to National Socialism, but when Nilsson was asked, he replied that "it does not fully express what we want, because we are not only Swedish-minded, but we are also world citizens at the same time". The party also did not want to describe itself as socialist, as they advocated both private, state and municipal ownership.

The party published Centerbladet between 1933 and 1940 with N.A. Nilsson as editor. After Nilsson's death in 1940, only two issues were published.

In the summer of 1957, when the Farmers' Union decided to change the name of the party to the [[seC|Centre Party]], it was discovered that the name was already registered. A delegation from the Farmers' Union, including Gustaf Jonnergård, traveled to Örebro to try to get permission to take over the name. They met with the registered representative of the dormant party, and received permission to take over the name.

parties.name: Christian Democrats
parties.relations: Preceded by the lobby organization [[seCSR|Christian Social Responsibility]] (CSR)
parties.description:
A Christian democratic political party in Sweden founded in March 1964. It first entered parliament in 1985, through electoral cooperation with the [[seC|Centre Party]]; in 1991, the party won seats on its own. The party leader since 25 April 2015 has been Ebba Busch.

The party name was initially abbreviated to KDS (Christian Democratic Unity), from its foundation in 1964 to 1996, when the party changed its name to the current Christian Democrats and its abbreviation to KD.

The party was a minor party in centre-right coalition governments led by Moderate Party Prime Ministers Carl Bildt from 1991 to 1994 and Fredrik Reinfeldt from 2006 to 2014, with the latter under a formalised cooperation within the [[seAlliansen|Alliance for Sweden]]. The party has been a minor party in the coalition government led by [[seM|Moderate Party]] Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson since 2022, this time with Moderate Party and the [[seL|Liberals]] with support from the [[seSD|Sweden Democrats]].

parties.name: Christian Values ​​Party
parties.description:
A Swedish political party. The party has a Christian and conservative foundation and has the abortion issue as its main profile issue, where they stand for an abortion-critical line. The party was formed on 4 January 2014. Mats Selander is the chairman of the party.

The Christian Values ​​Party stated in 2017 in its principles and party program that they are based on Christian values.

The Christian Values ​​Party has its roots in abortion opposition and its organizations in Sweden.

In 2004, the organization Human Rights for the Unborn (MRO) was founded to work against abortions in Sweden. According to Swedish Association for Sexuality Education (RFSU), they are the extremists of abortion opponents, as they base their methods on blaming and shaming women instead of working against unwanted pregnancies.

When the [[seKD|Christian Democrats]]' party leader Göran Hägglund in 2007 supported allowing foreign women to come to Sweden to perform abortions, Joseph Christenson and Per Kronlid started the "Network for Christian Value Conservatism in Swedish Politics". At the same time, the idea of ​​starting a new value-conservative party was born.

The Christian Values ​​Party was formed by eight people in a Stockholm church on 4 January 2014 with the intention of representing a clear value-conservative alternative in the Swedish political landscape. Among the founders were MRO chairman Mats Selander and its vice-chairman Annette Westöö. Per Kronlid was elected as the party's first chairman. The new party wanted to reach those who wanted to avoid having to "choose between an increasingly liberal KD and a nationalist [[seSD|SD]]".

On 14 February 2014, they had collected the 1,500 signatures required for registration of the party name with the Swedish Election Authority. They have since participated in all parliamentary elections, all EU elections and some regional and municipal elections.

Ahead of the 2014 EU elections, the newly formed party had not ordered any ballot papers, but the party was registered and received 481 handwritten votes with correct spelling and 160 votes with incorrect spelling.

In its first parliamentary election in 2014, the party received 3,553 votes (0.06%).

In the 2018 parliamentary election, the party received 3,202 votes (0.05%). 

The party's ballot paper for the 2019 EU elections was topped by artist Patrick Tikkanen in Stockholm and teacher Annette Westöö in Gothenburg. The party received 1,586 votes (0.04%).

In the 2022 parliamentary election, they received 5,983 votes (0.09%), making them the fourteenth largest party and the sixth largest outside the Riksdag.

In the 2024 European elections, the party received 3,896 votes (0.09%). The party's ballot was topped by the party leader.[

Human Rights for the Unborn

(MRO) was founded to work against abortions in Sweden. According to Swedish Association for Sexuality Education (RFSU), they are the extremists of abortion opponents, as they base their methods on blaming and shaming women instead of working against unwanted pregnancies.

When the [[seKD|Christian Democrats]]' party leader Göran Hägglund in 2007 supported allowing foreign women to come to Sweden to perform abortions, Joseph Christenson and Per Kronlid started the "Network for Christian Value Conservatism in Swedish Politics". At the same time, the idea of ​​starting a new value-conservative party was born.

The Christian Values ​​Party was formed by eight people in a Stockholm church on 4 January 2014 with the intention of representing a clear value-conservative alternative in the Swedish political landscape. Among the founders were MRO chairman Mats Selander and its vice-chairman Annette Westöö. Per Kronlid was elected as the party's first chairman. The new party wanted to reach those who wanted to avoid having to "choose between an increasingly liberal KD and a nationalist [[seSD|SD]]".

On 14 February 2014, they had collected the 1,500 signatures required for registration of the party name with the Swedish Election Authority. They have since participated in all parliamentary elections, all EU elections and some regional and municipal elections.

Ahead of the 2014 EU elections, the newly formed party had not ordered any ballot papers, but the party was registered and received 481 handwritten votes with correct spelling and 160 votes with incorrect spelling.

In its first parliamentary election in 2014, the party received 3,553 votes (0.06%).

In the 2018 parliamentary election, the party received 3,202 votes (0.05%). 

The party's ballot paper for the 2019 EU elections was topped by artist Patrick Tikkanen in Stockholm and teacher Annette Westöö in Gothenburg. The party received 1,586 votes (0.04%).

In the 2022 parliamentary election, they received 5,983 votes (0.09%), making them the fourteenth largest party and the sixth largest outside the Riksdag.

In the 2024 European elections, the party received 3,896 votes (0.09%). The party's ballot was topped by the party leader.[

parties.name: Citizens' Coalition
parties.description:
A right-wing political party in Sweden that was founded in 2014. The party considers itself liberal-conservative and green conservative, while observers described it as a right-wing party critical of immigration and conservative.

Citizens' Coalition received 0,18 % of the vote in the 2022 Swedish general election, making it the third largest party with no seats in the Riksdag, behind the Nuance Party and Alternative for Sweden. The party received 0.15% of the votes in the EU parliament election 2019. As of the 2022 Swedish municipal elections, the party holds eleven seats total in five municipal assemblies: Höör, Laholm, Karlshamn, Järfälla and Österåker.

parties.name: Citizens' Coalition
parties.description:
A Swedish right-wing party, which was formed in 1964 and was dissolved after the 1968 election. It aimed to increase cooperation between the right-wing parliamentary parties, which at that time consisted of the [[seC|Centre Party]], the [[seL|People's Party]] and the [[seM|Right Party]]. After the last election of the 1950s, the bourgeois parties had been in opposition despite having greater support in the electorate than the [[seSAP|Social Democrats]]. This was because the Social Democrats had passive parliamentary support from the Communist Party of Sweden. But it was also believed to be due to the fact that the bourgeois votes were distributed between different parties and the idea was that cooperation or merger between them would increase the chances of defeating the Social Democrats.

In the aftermath of the 1968 election, MbS was dissolved and the majority of those active returned to their respective party organizations.

The Citizens' Coalition started as a pressure movement against the bourgeois parties, primarily in the Fyrstadskretsen constituency, pressure that was supported by the then leadership of Sydsvenska Dagbladet newspaper. However, there was no interest in such cooperation among the respective bourgeois party leaderships, and for this reason, MbS was constituted in April 1964 as an independent bourgeois electoral organization at a meeting in Lund by people who were already active in one of the existing bourgeois parties. In the 1964 election, the MBS list received strong support in the Fyrstadskretsen (27.8 percent of the votes in that constituency, corresponding to approximately 65,000 votes), which gave it three parliamentary seats, which were won by Bertil Rubin, Sten Sjöholm and Carl Göran Regnéll. By way of comparison, the [[seM|Right Party]] and the [[seL|People's Party]] each received one mandate in that constituency.

In 1965, [[seSfF|Assembly for Progress]] was formed, which can be said to have been a national organization for the idea of ​​a bourgeois coalition. Within this group, the idea of ​​a completely new general bourgeois party began to gain more and more traction, and ahead of the 1966 municipal elections, bourgeois lists under a collective name were put up in several places in both the Fyrstadskretsen and outside Skåne (for example, "Assembly 66" in Gothenburg). In parallel with this, the bourgeois parties managed to negotiate electoral reforms with the Social Democrats that meant that the bourgeois vote split no longer had as much effect. With this, some of the incentives for the coalition movement disappeared.

Before this election, MbS failed to unite the three party leaderships in the Fyrstadskretsen and came to field several lists under the name Coalition 68. Due to personal and private conflicts in different rounds, the result was that voters in the constituency were given five electoral lists with different combinations of bourgeois members to decide on. After the 1968 election, the bourgeois retained the majority of its mandates, but the enthusiasm for cooperation under the name MbS had waned. In the aftermath of the election, MbS was dissolved and the majority of those active returned to their respective party organizations. However, a minority under the former MP Bertil Rubin started a new party, the [[seFsP|Progress Party]].

parties.name: Clerical People's Party
parties.relations: Split from the [[seAVF|General Electoral League]] (AVF)
parties.description: A minor pro-fascist party in Sweden founded in 1930. The party was formed and led by Ivar Rhedin, a priest in the Church of Sweden. Rhedin was the editor of Göteborgs Stiftstidning (Magazine of the Diocese of Gothenburg), in which he wrote many pro-German articles. The party was an ally of the main Nazi party in Sweden, [[seNSAP|National Socialist Workers Party]]. But the cooperation between the two parties did not last. Although both groups were staunch antisemites, their approaches toward the Jews were somewhat different. Rhedin, as a conservative Christian, was against the Jews as a religious community. NSAP were against the Jews as a race. Rhedin had no problem in accepting Jews who converted to Christianity, whereas NSAP and other Nazi groups considered that converted Jews continued to be Jews in racial aspects. The party was closed down in 1936 and officially dissolved in 1938.

parties.name: Climate Alliance
parties.description:
A Swedish political party with a focus on climate issues that describes itself as a non-ideological, party- and bloc-crossing influence organization, neither of the right nor left. The party's electoral platform has been described by classical liberal business think tank Timbro and newspaper Norran editorial board as left-wing.

The Climate Alliance was started in autumn 2021 by people who have long been active in the social debate within various parties or outside party politics, such as Gudrun Schyman, Anders Wijkman, Kristina Persson and K. G. Hammar. The party decided in February 2022 to stand in the parliamentary election, further, on 17 March 2022, the Climate Alliance registered as a party with the electoral authority. The party's parliamentary list is topped by Gudrun Schyman and K. G. Hammar.

In connection with the party announcing that they are standing in the parliamentary elections, Wijkman announced that he will not participate in party work. The party received 0.03% of the vote in the 2022 parliamentary elections.

In June 2022, the party announced that they would also stand in the municipal elections in 2022, including in the city of Stockholm. The list was topped there by former [[seMP|Green Party]] regional politician Petra Schagerholm. Party leader Gudrun Schyman was elected as a member of the municipal council of Simrishamn in the 2022 elections, though this was on the list of the formally separate Climate Initiative (Swedish: Klimatinitiativ) Simrishamn.

parties.name: Communist Labour League of Sweden
parties.relations:
Split from the [[seV|Communist Party of Sweden]] (SKP);

Partially succeeded by the [[seKFML|Communist League Marxists–Leninists]] (KFML)
parties.description:
A far-left party was formed in 1956 by the former left-wing opposition within the [[seV|Swedish Communist Party]], with Set Persson as its central figure.

The league considered that the SKP had deviated from the Marxist-Leninist line, in favor of opportunist and reformist policies. The union published the magazine Revolt, in which the SKA's attitude towards developments within the international communist movement, the [[suCPSU|CPSU]] and the SKP, was presented.

When the SKP and the Soviet leadership began to distance themselves from Joseph Stalin and his policies, the SKA continued to defend the same. It was believed that only the path of Joseph Stalin and Marxism-Leninism could lead to the abolition of capitalism and war. In November 1961, the association sent a telegram to Nikita Khrushchev on the occasion of the latter having (at night) had Stalin's remains removed from his mausoleum, in which it wrote, among other things: "In the name of thousands and thousands of Swedish Marxist-Leninists, we hereby express our disgust and protest against the desecration of Stalin's dust and ideas that has been carried out on your orders."

In the 1958 municipal elections, SKA stood in Köping, where it received two mandates, Bollnäs, where it received one mandate, and Södermalm and Gamla stan in Stockholm, where it received 1,387 votes or 1.9%.

Gunnar Gustavsson and John Eriksson represented the union in the Köping council and the workshop worker Karl Roberg in Bollnäs.

After Set Persson died in 1960, SKA led a waning existence, ending completely in 1967. The organizational experiences of the people who were active in SKA became important for the later generation of leftists, such as the [[seKFML|KFML]].
parties.ideology: The SKA harshly criticized the direction led by Nikita Khrushchev in the Soviet Union, which it saw as reformist and revisionist. It also criticized what it perceived as a lack of human rights in the Soviet Union and the so-called people's democracies and called for the abolition of the death penalty in the world's socialist countries.

parties.name: Communist Party
parties.relations: Split from the [[seKFML|Communist League Marxists–Leninists]] (KFML)
parties.description:
A Marxist–Leninist political party in Sweden started in 1970. From 1970 to 1977, it was known as the Communist League Marxist–Leninists (Revolutionaries) (KFML(r)) and from 1977 to 2004 as the Communist Party Marxist–Leninists (Revolutionaries) (KPML(r)). At the 14th Party Congress held in Gothenburg in January 2005, it was decided to change the name to the current one.

KFML(r) was unofficially founded in 1970 by a splinter group from the pro-Chinese [[seKFML|Communist League Marxists–Leninists]], which in turn had split from the Eurocommunist [[seV|Left Party]] in 1967. "The (r)s" ("(r)-arna") considered that KFML had approached reformism and was not a genuine workers' movement. In 1970, it began publishing the weekly Proletären (The Proletarian), and the group was officially registered as a political party in 1977. During the 1980s, KPML(r) achieved representation in some municipalities, including Gothenburg, Sweden's second-largest city. The Gothenburg region has always been the strongest area for the party, partly because the party was started there. During the period of 1970 to 1999, the party chairman was Frank Baude. Baude was succeeded by Anders Carlsson, who held the post as chairman between 1999 and 2014. Between 2014 and 2019, Robert Mathiasson was the chairman of the party, he was succeeded by Ulf Nilsson, who only led the party for a short time. Ulf Nilsson resigned as party chairman in January 2020. On the Communist Party's 19th congress in September 2020, Povel Johansson was elected new chairman.

Its members and sympathisers includes, or included, several Swedish celebrities such as actors Sven Wollter, Lasse Brandeby and Kent Andersson and musicians Ken, Totta Näslund and Fred Åkerström, all of whom have participated in events and gatherings arranged by the party.

parties.name: Communist Party in Sweden
parties.relations:
Merger of the breakaway group from [[seKFML|SKP]]: Norrköpings Kommunistiska Förening, and the [[seKEG|Stockholm Communist Unity Group]] (SKEG);

Succeeded by the informal newspaper network, Nya Arbetartidningen (together with [[seSKA1982|SKA]]).
parties.description:
A pro-Albanian communist party in Sweden. KPS was formed in 1982. It was dissolved in 1993.

In 1978, a pro-Albanian group had broken away from the [[seKFML|Communist Party of Sweden]] due to disagreements arising from the Sino-Albanian split. This group formed Norrköpings Kommunistiska Förening (Communist Association of Norrköping). In 1979 NKF merged with [[seKEG|Stockholms Kommunistiska Enhetsgrupp]] to form Sveriges Kommunistiska Förbund - ml (Communist League of Sweden - ml). The magazine Kommunisten started publication in 1979. SKF-ml founded Organisationen för skapandet av Kommunistiska Partiet i Sverige (Organization for the creation of the Communist Party in Sweden) in October 1981. This organization later gave birth to KPS.

The leader of KPS was Anders Persson.

The youth league of KPS was called Ungkommunisterna i Sverige (Young Communists in Sweden). KPS maintained a publishing house called Kommunistiska Arbetarförlaget (Communist Workers Publishing House).

A series of expulsions 1983-1984 led to the refoundation of the NKF.

KPS considered parties like [[seVPK|VPK]], [[seKPS1995|APK]] and [[seK|KPML(r)]] as revisionist. The latter was described as the "left-wing alibi of Moscow in Sweden". KPS urged communists to struggle against both the United States and the USSR.

Gradually KPS started to distance itself from the Albanian line, somewhat similar to the development of the Nicaraguan [[niMAPML|MAP-ML]].

In 1989, KPS suffered a major split, with a large section leaving the party. The splinters started a magazine called Vänstertidningen (Left Magazine), which was supposed to be a broader non-party marxist, socialist and ecologist forum. It disappeared rapidly.

At its height the party only reached in the low hundreds of members and sympathisers, and eventually dissolved in 1993.

The publication Kommunisten was later fused with Kommunistiska Arbetartidningen of [[seSKA1982|Sveriges Kommunistiska Parti (Marxist-Leninisterna)]] to form Nya Arbetartidningen.

The SKP is a founding member of the [[euECA|European Communist Action]] (ECA), as well as a former member of the [[euINITIATIVE|European Communist Initiative]], from its founding in 2013 until it was dissolved in 2023. The party has also been participating in the [[intIMCWP|International Meetings of Communist and Workers' Parties]] (IMCWP).

parties.name: Communist Party of Sweden
parties.relations: Split from the [[seVPK|Left Party – the Communists]] (VPK)
parties.description:
A Swedish political party that was formed in 1967 under the name Communist League Marxist-Leninists (KFML). It was a pro-Chinese and anti-Soviet breakaway from the [[seVPK|Left Party Communists]] (VPK, now the Left Party). In 1973, the party changed its name to SKP, a name that has been used by several related communist movements in Sweden over the years.

KFML/SKP was the largest organization within the Maoist movement in the Swedish left, and formed a central part of the so-called 68 left. During the Vietnam War, the party played an important role in Sweden by organizing solidarity work via the United FNL Groups (DFFG), but KFML/SKP suffered many splits during its existence and its star declined from the early eighties. The party eventually renounced communism and changed its name to the Solidarity Party (1986), but the national organization was dissolved in 1989-1990. Remaining groups operated locally, but the last one died out in 1994.

The party received over 10,000 votes in the 1979 parliamentary election, but in 1982 the result was only a handful of votes. It won occasional municipal mandates during the 1970s and 1980s, with the 1985 municipal election as its main success.

parties.description:
The Communist Party of Sweden is a historical political party that existed from 1924 to 1926 and was led by Zeth Höglund. The unusual spelling of "Sveriges" in the party name followed a then-proposed spelling reform that many on the political left appreciated.

Höglund, who had been expelled from the [[seVPK|SKP]] in 1924 over the dispute of increasing [[intComintern|Comintern]] influece on it. He then formed his own independent communist party with about 5,000 members. In 1926, after the death of Hjalmar Branting, the party merged with the [[seSAP|SAP]].

parties.name: Communist Workers' Party of Sweden
parties.relations:
Split from the [[KFML|Communist Party of Sweden]];
Succeeded by the informal newspaper network, Nya Arbetartidningen (together with [[seKPS|KPS]]).
parties.description:
A Swedish communist political party that existed between 1980 and 1993.

The party had its roots in the Maoist section of the Swedish 1968-left. It was founded on 1–2 November 1980 as the Communist Party of Sweden (Marxist-Leninists) by people who were expelled from the pro-[[cnCCP|CCP]] [[seKFML|SKP]], previously known as KFML, that same year. The expelled came from the SKP branches in Sundsvall and Södra Järva. The conflict concerned, among other things, the excluded group's criticism of how China had turned right after the death of Mao Tse-tung, and the expelled people came from factions in SKP that had previously had great influence.

The name Communist Workers' Party of Sweden was adopted at the congress in 1982. The Kommunistiska Arbetartidningen was started as a press organ in 1981. The formation of the new party was in many ways a return to the position that SKP had held around 1976.

SKA's collaboration with another small left-wing organization, the pro-Albanian [[seKPS|Communist Party in Sweden]] (KPS), ended with the editorial boards of each organization's newspaper merging on 16 May 1993 to publish Nya arbetatidningen. Both SKA and KPS ceased to exist around this time.

SKA was a very small group throughout its existence and never participated in any elections in Sweden. The party had some collaboration with Maoist movements in other countries, including [[deMLPD|MLPD]] (Germany), [[noAKPml|AKP(m-l)]] (Norway) and [[dkKFML|KFML]] (Denmark). The party's representatives used to participate in Maoist international conferences organized by the German MLPD.

parties.name: Demoex
parties.relations: Succeeded by the [[seDD|Direct Democrats]] (DD)
parties.description:
A local political party in Vallentuna municipality that was founded in 2002 and was a co-founder of the [[seDD|Direct Democrats]] in 2014. The party name Demoex was an abbreviation for "Democracy Experiment in Vallentuna" ("Demokratiexperimentet i Vallentuna"). Demoex made decisions through direct democracy and used the internet to organize debates and votes on political issues at the municipal level.

All residents of Vallentuna municipality who were 16 years old or older could participate in the votes on the Demoex website. The results of the online votes determined how Demoex representatives voted when the Vallentuna municipal council made decisions. The party's representatives had signed contracts. According to the contracts, the representatives had to follow the results of the votes. No membership fee was charged - participation was free.

On October 3, 2000, Vallentuna Gymnasium arranged a study day on the theme of "IT and Democracy". An electronic debate system was tested there, which several participants experienced as an exciting setting for political discussion. Per Norbäck, a teacher at the gymnasium, took the initiative to form a political association.

In 2002, Demoex was founded in the spring. The party gained access to an internet-based conference system through Mikael Nordfors, then known as a pioneer in direct democracy. Demoex ran in elections for the municipal council that same year. The party made no election promises, apart from an opportunity for increased popular influence in local politics through direct democracy. Newspapers, radio and TV paid attention to Demoex. In the election, Demoex won a mandate. The party has been represented in the municipal council by Parisa Molagholi since 4 November 2002.

Demoex demonstrated on 1 May 2004 under the slogan "Universal voting rights on substantive issues". Demoex participated in the Stockholm Social Forum. At the annual meeting in March, the goal was stated that 100 participants should take part in Demoex's votes. The goal was gradually reached. Dagens Nyheter's editorial writer Henrik Berggren wrote about Demoex in the newspaper.

In 2005, Demoex's initiator, Per Norbäck, was awarded second prize in the Utopi-VM at an awards ceremony at Färgfabriken in Liljeholmen. In the fifty matters that the council raised during the year, Demoex voted with the bourgeois coalition in 35 matters and against in 13. In two matters, the votes ended in a tie, after which Demoex abstained from voting on these matters.
The first two motions were rejected. In 2005, the council voted on the proposal to install lighting over a popular walking path.

On March 20, 2006, 144 users had been registered. Of these, 112 had full voting rights. The average Demoex user was a middle-aged man, 30–45 years old.

The party ran for the municipal council again in 2006. Demoex's ballot was topped by Parisa Molagholi. The party received 2.9% of the votes and retained its mandate in the council.

The party ran for the municipal council again in 2010. Demoex's ballot was topped by Per Norbäck. The party received 1.76% of the votes and retained its mandate in the council.

In 2014, they merged with two other direct democratic parties, [[seAkD|True Democracy]] and [[seAD|Active Democracy]], and formed the party [[seDD|Direct Democrats]].

parties.name: Donald Duck Party
parties.description:
An originally fictional Swedish political party. It was probably originally intended as a joke, but was established as a party designation on blank ballot papers during the 1980s. The first time the results of votes for the party were reported was in the 1979 election. It received a maximum of 1,535 votes in the 1991 election.

Since blank votes without a party name were invalid and were subtracted from the total, while those with a party name were counted and reported, the name was used to show that one had taken a position against the established parties. The votes were then lumped together under the item other parties.

After the 1994 election, an investigation was conducted into the free right to nominate for general elections. It was believed that the freedom was being abused and, among other things, looked into requiring registration of parties for general elections in order to avoid high voter turnouts for parties that did not exist. The introduction of a registration requirement was then discussed before several elections and was introduced in 2018, and the Kalle Anka party was not registered that year.

Malmö profile Bosse Persson (1941–2014) printed 1,000 ballot papers for the party before the 2002 election. The party name has been registered with the Election Authority for the 2022 election in all parliamentary constituencies under the spelling "Kalle ankapartiet". Before the 2026 election, the KAP was registered with a logo.

parties.name: European Workers' Party
parties.relations: Founded by swedish branch of the LaRouchist [[intLaRouche|European Labour Committees]], which was established in 1974.
parties.description:
A political party in Sweden that describes itself as part of the American [[intLaRouche|LaRouche movement]], founded by the American self-taught economist and politician Lyndon LaRouche.

The party's name comes from the fact that the party initially saw the labor movement as its main target group. After being described by the Swedish Security Service since the 1970s as left-wing extremist with roots in communist ideology and expressed sympathies for the Soviet Union, it later developed beyond the right-left scale, and approached fascism and right-wing extremism, the latter also according to the Swedish Armed Forces.

The party is characterized by a cult of personality of its founder Lyndon LaRouche, a conspiratorial worldview, a cult-like organization, utopianism, elements of anti-Semitism and opposition to the environmental movement. The party's activities and campaigns have often taken place through sister and subsidiary organizations.

Merged into [[seM|The Parliamentary Right]] (H)
parties.description:
A Swedish moderate conservative party in the Second Chamber from 1912 to 1934.

The party was formed in 1912 through a merger of the [[seNFP|National Progress Party]] and the [[seLmp|Lantmanna Party]]. Its first party chairman was the farmer Carl Persson in Stallerhult. From 1913, Arvid Lindman was the party chairman, with the exception of 1917 when the sugar mill director Hans Andersson in Skivarp was the party chairman.

The party merged in 1934-1935 with the [[seFKNP|National Party of the First Chamber]] under the name of the [[seM|Right's parliamentary group]], which from 1969 was called the Moderate Coalition Party's parliamentary group.

parties.name: Feminists
parties.description:
A feminist political party in Sweden. The party was formed in 2005 from a pressure group of the same name, and has since taken part in every election to the Riksdag (Parliament) and the European Parliament. The party won its first elected representative in 2014, with Soraya Post taking one seat in the European Parliament.

Fi received 3.1% of the vote in the 2014 general election, the best result in its history, and won seats in thirteen municipalities in the 2014 municipal elections – including in Sweden's largest cities of Gothenburg and Stockholm, where it became part of governing "red-green-pink" coalitions.

Support for Feminist Initiative dwindled, however, and the party only managed to obtain 0.4% of the vote in the 2018 general election, making it the largest political party without representation in the Riksdag. The party lost four seats in the municipal elections, and did not gain any county council seats.

In October 2018, party co-founder Gudrun Schyman announced that she would step down as leader of the party at the next party congress.

In 2023, Agnes Lundgren and Luis Lineo became co-leaders of the party, succeeding Teysir Subhi.

parties.name: First Chamber Moderate Party
parties.relations: Merged into [[seFKNP|First Chamber National Party]]
parties.description:
A parliamentary group formed in 1905. The chairman was Gustaf Tamm from 1905 to 1908, Ivar Afzelius from 1909 to 1910 and Axel Asker from 1911. The party merged with the [[seFHP|United Right Party]] in 1912 to form the [[seFKMP|National Party of the First Chamber]]. It is one of the historical predecessors of the [[seM|Moderate Coalition Party]].

The group was formed at the end of the 1905 Riksdag by those members of the Chamber who took a more moderate position on political issues than its majority. Without marking any distinct position on the tariff issue, the party nevertheless came to include the majority of the Chamber's free traders, but also some protectionists. The first council of trustees included Gustaf Tamm (chairman), Olof Melin and Olof Björklund from the free traders side, and Filip Boström and Edvard Montgomery from the protectionists.

Among the party's trusted men or more prominent members in the following years are Olof Jonsson i Hof, Carl Swartz, Gustaf Lagerbring and August Wijkander. After the proportional electoral system was applied in 1910 in committee elections, the party's influence was strengthened. In 1910, 46 to 50 members of the 150 members of the chamber gathered around its lists, and it could now also fill a third of the committee seats from its own circle. After the Staaff government in the autumn of 1911 succeeded in obtaining the king's permission to dissolve the first chamber and the left-wing groups returned after it with a strength of 63 men (51 liberals and 12 socialists), a definite desire emerged within the country for a merger of the right-wing groups in the chamber, which led to the dissolution of the Moderate Party and the formation of the First Chamber's National Party at the beginning of the 1912 Riksdag.
